# To the Reader.

Having had the honor to be constantly with my Lord <note>Francis Bacon</note> during the compilation of this work, and having been employed in it myself, I thought it appropriate (with his Lordship’s permission and approval) to make known some of his Lordship’s intentions regarding the organization and publishing of this book, for the benefit of those who will read it. 

I have often heard his Lordship say that if he had been serving the glory of his own name, he would have been better off not publishing this *Natural History*. This is because it may seem to be an unorganized collection <note>original: "indigested heap"</note> of specific details, and it cannot have the polish <note>original: "lustre"</note> that books structured into formal methods possess. However, he was determined to prioritize the welfare of mankind—and whatever might best ensure it—above anything that might relate to his own reputation. And he knew well that 

<summary>William Rawley, Francis Bacon's secretary and editor, explains that Bacon prioritized the practical benefit of humanity over his own literary reputation by publishing this collection of scientific observations, despite its lack of a formal, polished structure.</summary>
<keywords>William Rawley, Francis Bacon, Natural History, Sylva Sylvarum, scientific method, public good, reputation</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface "To the Reader" by William Rawley. It explains Francis Bacon's philosophical rationale for focusing on raw data and "natural history" rather than polished theories, framing this work as a foundational part of his "Great Instauration."</meta>

...there was no other way to free people's minds—which were bound and, in a sense, bewitched <note>original: "Maleficiate"</note> by the spells of deceptive notions and theories, making them unable to produce practical works—except to never stray from sensory observation and clear experience. Instead, he had to stay close to these, especially at the start. Besides, this *Natural History* was a debt he owed, as it was designed and recorded as the third part of his *Great Instauration* <note>The *Instauratio Magna*, Bacon's ambitious, multi-part plan to reorganize and restore all human knowledge through scientific inquiry</note>.

I have also heard his Lordship discuss how people will undoubtedly think many of the *experiments* contained in this collection are *common* and *trivial*; *lowly* and *vile*; or *overly specific* and *useless*. Therefore, he wishes that they would constantly keep in mind the work currently being performed and the difference between this *Natural History* and others. Those *natural histories* currently in existence were gathered for pleasure and utility; they are full of pleasant descriptions and pictures, seeking to provoke wonder by focusing on rarities and secrets.

On the contrary, the goal his Lordship intends is to write a *Natural History* that may serve as the foundation for erecting and building a true *philosophy* <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to natural science or the study of the physical world</note>: for the illumination of the *understanding*, the extraction of *axioms* <note>general principles or laws of nature derived from specific observations</note>, and the production of many noble *works* and *results*. For he hopes, by this means, to fulfill the responsibility for which he takes...

<summary>Rawley explains that Bacon's "Natural History" avoids flashy, decorative science in favor of raw, sometimes "trivial" observations that serve as the necessary foundation for a true, productive scientific philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>Natural History, Great Instauration, scientific method, axioms, Francis Bacon, empiricism, practical science</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface "To the Reader" by William Rawley, Francis Bacon's chaplain and secretary. It elaborates on Bacon’s dedication to the "Advancement of Learning" and his role as a foundational gatherer of data, using the metaphor of a builder who must first do the lowly work of making bricks before the grand structure of science can be built.</meta>

### TO THE READER.

...he considered himself in a way bound; and that is, the advancement of all learning and sciences. For having collected the materials for the building in this present work, and having set down the instruments and directions for the work in his *Novum Organum* <note>original: *Novū Organū*; Latin for "New Instrument," Bacon's famous work on the scientific method</note> (of which his Lordship has yet to publish a second part), people will now fail themselves if they do not raise knowledge to the perfection of which the nature of mortal men is capable. 

In this regard, I have heard his Lordship speak complainingly: that he (who thinks he deserves to be an architect in this building) should be forced to be a workman and a laborer—to dig the clay and burn the brick—and more than that (according to the harsh condition of the *Israelites* toward the end of their captivity), to gather the straw and stubble all over the fields to burn the bricks with. For he knows that unless he does it, nothing will be done; people are so inclined to despise the means of their own good. 

As for the *baseness* <note>humble or lowly nature</note> of many of the experiments: as long as they are God's works, they are honorable enough. And as for their *commonness* <note>original: "vulgarnesse"</note>: true *axioms* <note>general principles or laws of nature</note> must be drawn from plain experience, and not from doubtful experience. His Lordship’s method is to make *wonders plain*, and not to make *plain things into wonders*. Likewise, that experience must be broken down and ground into pieces, and not left whole, or as it grows—

<summary>This page describes Francis Bacon's commitment to the advancement of science, framing his tedious gathering of experimental data as the "manual labor" necessary to build a grand architectural structure of human knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, scientific method, Advancement of Learning, architectural metaphor, experimental philosophy, axioms, empirical data</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface "To the Reader" by William Rawley. It discusses Francis Bacon's distinction between practical and theoretical experiments and his decision to include preliminary explanations of causes to help guide the reader through the vast collection of data.</meta>

...grows. And regarding *use*, his Lordship often mentions the two kinds of *experiments*: *fruit-bearing experiments* <note>original: *Experimenta Fructifera*</note> and *light-bearing experiments* <note>original: *Experimenta Lucifera*</note>—that is, *experiments of use* and *experiments of light*. And he asks himself whether he would not be a strange man to think that light has no *use* just because it has no physical substance. 

Furthermore, his Lordship also thought it good to add to many of the *experiments* themselves some *explanation* <note>original: *glosse*; an interpretive note or commentary</note> of their *causes*, so that in the succeeding work of *interpreting nature* and *framing axioms* <note>general principles or laws of nature</note>, everything may be more prepared. As for the *causes* assigned here, his Lordship is persuaded that they are far more certain than those provided by *others*—not because of any excellence in his own intelligence (as his Lordship is accustomed to say), but because of his continual interaction with *nature* and *experience*. 

He also considered that by adding these *causes*, men's minds (which are so hasty to find out the causes of things) would not think themselves utterly lost in a vast forest of experience. Instead, they might rest upon these *causes* (such as they are) for a little while, until true *axioms* can be more fully discovered. I have also heard his Lordship say that one great reason why he would not put these details into any exact *method* (though anyone who looks attentively at them will find they have a secret...

<meta>This page concludes the "To the Reader" epistle written by William Rawley for Francis Bacon's *Sylva Sylvarum* (Natural History). Rawley explains that the book's lack of a rigid, intimidating structure was intentional to encourage other scientists to contribute their own observations, and he concludes by asserting the work's objective, empirical nature.</meta>

# To the Reader.

<margin>
This letter <note>original: "Epistle"</note> to the reader was placed at the beginning of this book in the first edition.
</margin>

<note>The following text is the conclusion of William Rawley's preface, preserved from the original printing.</note>

(The lack of a rigid order) was because he considered that other men would now think that they could do the same, and so continue with a further collection. If the Author had lived, many would have desired to have had his guidance <note>original: "inducement"</note> regarding his Lordship’s method <note>original: "Order"</note>. For proof of his skill, I can refer anyone to his Lordship's Latin book, *On the Advancement of Learning* <note>original: *De Augmentis Scientiarum*</note>, which (if my judgment is worth anything) is written in the best order of any writing I know. I will conclude with a common saying of his Lordship’s: that this work of his, the *Natural History*, is the world as God made it, and not as man has made it; for it has nothing of mere imagination.

->W. Rawley.<-

->S. P.<-

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page begins the first "Century" (a collection of 100 experiments) of Francis Bacon’s *Sylva Sylvarum*, or *Natural History*. It follows the preface by William Rawley, moving from introductory justifications to the actual scientific observations and experiments Bacon compiled.</meta>

# NATURAL
# HISTORY

---

## First Century
<note>Bacon organized his *Natural History* into "Centuries," which are groups of 100 experiments or observations each.</note>

---

<margin>
1
Related experiments <note>original: "Experiments in Consort"</note> concerning the straining and passing of substances through one another, which is called *percolation*.
</margin>

Dig a pit upon the seashore, somewhat above the high-water mark, and sink it as deep as the low-water mark. As the tide comes in, it will fill with fresh and drinkable <note>original: "potable"</note> water. This is commonly practiced on the coast of Barbary <note>A historical term for the coastal regions of North Africa.</note>, where other fresh water is lacking. Caesar knew this well when he was besieged in Alexandria; for by digging pits in the seashore, he frustrated the laborious works of the enemies, who had turned the seawater into the wells of Alexandria, and so saved his army, which was then in despair. But Caesar mistook the cause; for he thought that all sea sands had natural springs of fresh water. But it is plain that it is actually seawater, because the pit fills according to the measurement of the tide; and the seawater, passing or straining through the sands, leaves the saltiness behind.

<margin>
2
</margin>

I remember to have read that a trial has been made of saltwater passed through earth, through ten vessels, one within another, and yet it has not lost its saltiness enough to become drinkable. But the same author says that (by the report of another) saltwater drained through twenty vessels has become fresh. This experiment seems to contradict that other regarding pits made by the seaside; and yet only in part, if it be true that twenty repetitions produce the effect. But it is worth noting how poor the imitations of nature are in the common course of experiments, unless they are guided by great judgment and some good light of axioms <note>In this context, "axioms" refers to established principles or laws of nature.</note>. For first, there is little difference between a passage

<meta>catchword: passage</meta>

<summary>Bacon begins his natural history by examining "percolation," using the example of how seawater becomes fresh when filtered through coastal sands, a phenomenon noted by Julius Caesar. He contrasts this natural process with less successful man-made attempts to desalinate water using series of vessels.</summary>
<keywords>percolation, desalination, seawater, filtration, Julius Caesar, Alexandria, Barbary, scientific method, axioms</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues Bacon’s discussion of Experiment 2 regarding the desalination of water and proceeds to general observations on "percolation" (straining) in nature and chemistry.</meta>

<header>Natural History:</header>

<margin>2</margin>
...passage of **water** through twenty small vessels, and through such a distance as that between the low-water and high-water marks. Second, there is a great difference between earth and sand. For all earth has in it a kind of nitrous salt <note>original: "Nitrous Salt"; Bacon likely refers to nitrates or salty mineral deposits commonly found in soil.</note>, from which sand is more free; and besides, earth does not strain the **water** as finely as sand does. But there is a third point that I suspect as much as, or more than, the other two: and that is, that in the **experiment** of the **transmission** of **seawater** into **pits**, the **water** rises; but in the **experiment** of the **transmission** of **water** through vessels, it falls. Now, it is certain that the saltier part of **water** (once salted throughout) goes to the bottom. And therefore, it is no marvel if the draining of **water** by descent does not make it fresh. Besides, I somewhat doubt whether the very splashing of the **water** that comes from the sea is more effective at striking off the salt part than when the **water** slides of its own motion.

<margin>3</margin>
It seems that **percolation** or **transmission** (which is commonly called **straining**) is an effective kind of **separation**—not only of thick from thin and coarse from fine, but of more subtle **natures**. This varies according to the body through which the **transmission** is made. For example, if passed through a woolen bag, the liquid leaves behind its fattiness; if through sand, its saltiness; and so on. They speak of separating wine from water by passing it through ivy wood, or through other similar porous bodies; but it is not proven <note>original: "Non Constat"; Latin for "it is not established" or "it does not appear."</note>.

<margin>4</margin>
The **gum** of **trees** (which we see to be commonly shining and clear) is merely a fine passage or **straining** of the juice of the tree through the wood and bark. In the same way, **Cornish diamonds** <note>Clear quartz crystals found in the rocks of Cornwall.</note> and **rock rubies** <note>Likely referring to red garnets or similar translucent stones found in rock fissures.</note> (which are even more radiant than gums) are the fine secretions <note>original: "Exudations"</note> of **stone**.

<margin>5</margin>
**Aristotle** provides a reason, though in vain <note>original: "vainely"; meaning incorrectly or to no purpose.</note>, for why the **feathers** of **birds** are of more lively colors than the **hair** of **beasts**; for no **beast** has any fine azure, carnation, or green **hair**. He says it is because **birds** are in the beams of the sun more than **beasts**. But that is manifestly untrue; for **cattle** are in the sun more than **birds**, which commonly live in the woods or in some cover. The true cause is that the waste moisture <note>original: "Excrementious Moisture"; in early medicine, this referred to surplus fluids the body excreted to form hair, nails, or feathers.</note> of living creatures—which creates the **feathers** in **birds** as well as the **hair** in **beasts**—passes in **birds** through a finer and more delicate strainer than it does in **beasts**. For **feathers** pass through quills, and **hair** through skin.

<margin>6</margin>
The **clarifying** of **liquors** by **adhesion** is an "internal **percolation**." It is achieved when some sticky <note>original: "Cleauing"</note> body is mixed and stirred with the **liquors**, whereby the coarser part of the **liquor** sticks to that sticky body, and so the finer parts are freed from the coarser. Thus, **apothecaries** <note>Historical term for pharmacists.</note> clarify their **syrups** using the whites of eggs beaten with the juices they wish to clarify. These whites of eggs gather all the dregs and coarser parts of the juice to themselves; and afterward, when the **syrup** is set on the fire, the whites of eggs themselves harden, and

<margin>7</margin>
The clarifying of water is an experiment tending toward health, in addition to the pleasure of the eye when water is crystalline. It is achieved by casting in and placing pebbles at the head of a current so that the water may strain through them.

<margin>8</margin>
It may be that **percolation** <note>term: "Percolation"; the process of a liquid slowly passing through a filter or porous substance.</note> causes not only clarity and brilliance but also a sweet scent. For sweetness follows clarity when the finer parts are separated from the coarser ones. Thus, it is found that the sweat of men who are very hot, exercise much, have clean bodies, and fine skin, smells sweet—as was said of **Alexander the Great** <note>original: "Alexander"; historical sources like Plutarch claimed Alexander's skin and breath had a naturally pleasant fragrance due to his "hot" constitution.</note>. We also see commonly that gums <note>term: "Gummes"; natural resins or saps secreted by plants.</note> have sweet odors.

-> **Experiments in concert touching the motion of bodies under pressure.** <-

<margin>9</margin>
Take a glass and put water into it. Wet your finger and draw it around the lip of the glass, pressing somewhat hard. After you have drawn it around a few times, it will cause the water to frisk and sprinkle up in a fine dew. This instance excellently demonstrates the force of compression in a solid body. For whenever a solid body (such as wood, stone, metal, etc.) is pressed, there is an inward tumult in its parts as they seek to deliver themselves from the compression; and this is the cause of all **violent motion**. In this regard, it is strange in the highest degree that this motion has never been observed nor investigated, as it is the most common of all motions and the chief root of all mechanical operations. This motion works in a circle at first—by way of testing and searching for which way to deliver itself—and then moves forward where it finds the easiest escape. In liquids, this motion is visible: all struck liquids create round circles and splash at the same time. But in solids (which do not break), it is so subtle that it is invisible; nevertheless, it reveals itself through many effects, as in this instance of which we speak. For the pressure of the finger—furthered by the wetting because it sticks so much better to the lip of the glass—after some time puts all the small parts of the glass into motion so that they strike the water sharply. That sprinkling comes from that **percussion** <note>term: "Percussion"; the striking of one body against another.</note>.

<margin>10</margin>
If you strike or pierce a solid body that is brittle, such as glass or sugar, it breaks not only where the immediate force is applied but shatters all around into splinters and fragments. The motion, upon the pressure, searches in all directions and breaks where it finds the body weakest.

<margin>11</margin>
The powder in a shot, being expanded into such a flame that it cannot endure compression, moves likewise in a circle (the flame being like a liquid body). This sometimes causes a recoil and sometimes breaks the gun <note>original: "Piece"; a general term for a firearm or cannon.</note>...

<margin>12</margin>
This **motion upon pressure**, and its reciprocal, which is **motion upon tension** <note>original: "Tensure"; the state of being stretched or strained.</note>, we usually call by one common name: **motion of liberty**. This occurs when any **body**, having been forced to an unnatural size or dimension, releases and restores itself to its natural state. Examples include when a **blown bladder**, having been pressed, rises again; or when **leather** or **cloth** that has been stretched springs back. These two motions (of which there are infinite examples) we shall discuss in the proper place.

<margin>13</margin>
This **motion upon pressure** is also excellently demonstrated in **sounds**. For example, when someone strikes a **bell**, it sounds; but as soon as he lays his hand upon it, the **sound** stops. Similarly, the sound of a **virginal** <note>term: "Virginal"; a rectangular keyboard instrument similar to a harpsichord, popular in the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</note> string stops as soon as the **quill** of a **jack** <note>term: "Jack"; the wooden mechanism in a virginal or harpsichord that holds the plectrum (quill) used to pluck the strings.</note> falls upon it. These sounds are produced by the subtle striking of the tiny parts of the bell or string against the air. This is exactly like the way water is made to leap by the subtle striking of the tiny parts of the glass against the water, which we spoke of earlier in the ninth experiment. You must not assume it is the overall **shaking** of the bell or string that causes the sound, as we will fully explain when we come to discuss sounds later.

-> **Experiments in concert touching the separation of bodies by weight.** <-

<margin>14</margin>
Take a glass with a rounded **belly** and a long **neck** <note>original: "Neb"; here referring to the narrow spout or neck of a glass vessel.</note>; fill the belly partially with **water**. Take also another glass and put a mixture of **claret wine** and water into it. Turn the first glass upside down with the belly at the top, blocking the neck with your finger. Then dip the mouth of it into the second glass and remove your finger. Keep it in that position for a while, and it will separate the wine from the water. The wine will rise and settle at the top of the upper glass, and the water will descend and settle at the bottom of the lower glass. This movement is visible to the eye; you will see the wine rising through the water like a small vein. For convenience (since the process takes a little time), it would be good to hang the upper glass from a nail. However, as soon as enough pure and unmixed water has gathered in the bottom of the lower glass so that the mouth of the upper glass is submerged in it, the motion stops.

<margin>15</margin>
If the upper glass contains **wine** and the lower contains **water**, no motion occurs at all. If the upper glass contains pure water and the lower contains colored water (or vice versa), no motion occurs at all. But it has been tested that even if the mixture of wine and water in the lower glass is three parts water and only one part wine, it does not stop the motion. This **separation** of water and wine appears to be caused by **weight**, for it only works with bodies of unequal weight; the heavier body must always be in the upper glass. But also note that since the water is suspended, and there is a great weight of water in the belly of the glass held up...

<margin>Experiments in common regarding judicious and accurate **infusions**, both in liquors and air. 
17.</margin>
In bodies containing fine spirits, which dissipate easily, the rule for making **infusions** is this: a short stay of the **body** <note>In this context, the "body" refers to the physical plant material being soaked.</note> in the **liquor** receives the spirit, but a longer stay ruins it. This is because a longer soak draws out the "earthy" parts as well, which debases the finer spirits. Therefore, it is an error for **physicians** to rely simply on the length of the soak to increase the medicinal strength. If you want a strong **infusion** of those kinds of **bodies** that have fine spirits, your method should not be to give it more time, but to repeat the **infusion** of the **body** more often. Take **violets** and infuse a good handful <note>original: "Pugill"; a handful or a large pinch.</note> of them in a quart of vinegar. Let them stay for three-quarters of an hour and then take them out. Refresh the **infusion** with the same quantity of new **violets** seven times. This will make a vinegar so fresh with the scent of the **flower** that if it is brought to you in a saucer a year later, you shall smell it before it even reaches you. Note that it smells more perfectly of the flower a good while after it is made than it does at first.

<margin>18</margin>
This rule which we have given is of singular use for the preparation of **medicines** and other **infusions**. For example: the leaf of **borage** <note>original: "Burrage"; a herb often used in traditional medicine to treat mood.</note> has an excellent spirit to suppress the sooty <note>original: "Fuliginous"; smoky or soot-like. According to the medical theories of the time, "vapors" from the organs caused mental states.</note> vapor of dark melancholy and so to cure madness. Nevertheless, if the leaf is infused for a long time, it yields only a raw substance of no medicinal value. Therefore, I believe that if **borage** stays for a short time in the "must" <note>unfermented grape juice</note> of wine or the "wort" of beer while it is fermenting (before it is tunned <note>term: "Tunned"; put into a large cask or barrel for storage.</note>), and is often changed for fresh leaves, it will make an excellent drink for melancholy passions. I believe the same would work for **orange flowers**.

<margin>19</margin>
**Rhubarb** clearly has parts within it that perform contrary operations: parts that purge the bowels and parts that bind <note>In medical terms, "binding" refers to causing constipation or stopping diarrhea.</note> the body. The purging parts are more easily released, while the binding parts lie deeper. Thus, if you infuse **rhubarb** for only an hour and crush it well, it will purge better and bind the body less after the purging than if it had stood for twenty-four hours. This has been tested. But I also believe that by repeating the **infusion** of **rhubarb** several times (as was described for violets), letting each batch stay in for only a short time, you may make it as strong a purging medicine as scammony <note>term: "Scammony"; a plant-based resin used as a very powerful and harsh purgative.</note>. It is no small victory in **medicine** if you can make **rhubarb** and other **medicines**...

<header>Natural History:</header>

...medicines that are **gentle** <note>original: "Benedict"</note>, like strong **purgatives**, as those that are not without some **harmfulness** <note>original: "Malignity"</note>.

<margin>20</margin>
**Purging medicines**, for the most part, have their **purgative power** <note>original: "Vertue"</note> in a fine **spirit**. This is shown by the fact that they do not endure boiling without much loss of power. Therefore, it is a good use in **medicine** <note>original: "Physicke"</note> if you can retain the **purging power** and take away the unpleasant taste of the **purgative**; this you may likely do by this method of **infusing** <note>soaking a substance in liquid to extract its qualities</note> often, with only a short soak each time. For it is probable that the horrible and odious taste comes from the coarser <note>original: "Grosser"</note> part of the substance.

<margin>21</margin>
Generally, working by **infusions** is crude and unguided, unless you first test the release <note>original: "Issuing"</note> of the various parts of the substance to see which of them release more quickly and which more slowly. By apportioning the time, you can take or leave that **quality** which you desire. To know this, there are two ways: the one is to test what a long soak and what a short soak produce, as has been said. The other is to test, in order, the succeeding **infusions** of one and the same substance, successively, in several **liquors**. For example: take **orange peels**, or **rosemary**, or **cinnamon**, or whatever you wish. Let them **infuse** for half an hour in **water**. Then take them out and **infuse** them again in other **water**, and then a third time. Then taste and consider the **first water**, the **second**, and the **third**. You will find them differing not only in **strength** and **weakness**, but otherwise in taste or odor. For it may be the **first water** will have more of the scent, being more fragrant, and the **second** more of the taste, being more bitter or biting, and so on.

<margin>22</margin>
**Infusions in air** (for so we may well call **odors**) have the same varieties as **infusions in water**, in that the various **odors** (which are in one flower or other body) come out at different times—some earlier, some later. So we find that **violets**, **honeysuckle** <note>original: "woodbines"</note>, and **strawberries** yield a pleasing scent that comes forth first; but soon after, an ill scent comes that is quite different from the former. This is caused not so much by the flower ripening <note>original: "Mellowing"</note>, as by the later release of the coarser <note>original: "Grosser"</note> spirit.

<margin>23</margin>
Just as we may desire to extract the finest spirits in some cases, so we may desire also to discharge them (as being harmful) in some others. So **mulled wine** <note>original: "Wine burnt"</note>, by reason of the evaporating of the finer spirit, causes less inflammation and is best for **fevers** <note>original: "Agues"</note>. **Opium** loses some of its poisonous quality if it is evaporated out, mingled with **spirit of wine** <note>alcohol</note>, or the like. **Senna** loses some of its "windiness" <note>the quality of causing gas or bloating</note> by **decoction** <note>boiling down a substance</note>. Generally, subtle or "windy" spirits are removed by burning <note>original: "incension"</note> or evaporation. And even in **infusions** of things that have too high a spirit, you were better off pouring off the first **infusion** after a short time and using the latter.

The same reason explains the roundness of the **bubble**, both for the "skin" of the **water** and for the **air** inside; for the **air** likewise avoids **breaking apart** <note>original: "Discontinuance"</note> and therefore shapes itself into a round figure. And as for the fact that the **air** stays trapped for a little while, it shows that the **air** itself has little or no natural desire to rise.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the making of artificial springs. 25</margin>
The number of **experiments** I reject (though it may not seem so) is infinite; yet if an **experiment** seems likely to work and is of great use, I accept it, but present it as doubtful. It was reported by a reliable man that an **artificial spring** may be made as follows: find a piece of sloping ground where there is a strong, fast runoff of rainwater. Lay a stone gutter <note>original: "Halfe-Trough of Stone"</note> of a good length, three or four feet deep within that ground, with one end on the high ground and the other on the low. Cover the trough with a thick layer of ferns <note>original: "Brakes"</note> and throw sand on top of the ferns. You shall see (he says) that after some showers have passed, the lower end of the trough will run like a **spring of water**. This is no miracle as long as the rainwater lasts; but he said it would continue for a long time after the rain has passed, as if the water multiplied itself within the air by the help of the coldness and condensation of the earth, and the attraction of the initial water.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the **transformation** <note>original: "version"</note> **and transmutation of air into water.** 27</margin>

It seems there are likely these ways to **transform** <note>original: "version"</note> **vapors** or **air** into **water** and **moisture**. 

The first is **cold**, which clearly condenses air. We see this in the **contraction of air** in a **thermometer** <note>original: "weather-glass," an early instrument for measuring temperature and pressure</note>, which makes the air one degree closer to becoming **water**. We also see it in the **creation of springs**. The **ancients** thought (very probably) that these were made by the **transformation of air into water**, helped by the **stillness** <note>original: "rest"</note> of the **air** in those places, which prevents it from scattering, and by the **coldness of rocks**, for that is where springs are mainly created. We see it also in the **effects** of the **cold of the middle region** of the **atmosphere** <note>original: "air"</note> (as they call it), which produces **dew** and **rain**. Furthermore, the experiment of turning **water** into **ice** using snow, potassium nitrate <note>original: "nitre"</note>, and salt (which we will discuss later) should be applied to the process of turning **air** into **water**. 

The second way is by **compression**, as seen in **distilling apparatuses** <note>original: "stillatories"</note> where the vapor is turned back upon itself by hitting the sides of the vessel. It is also seen in the **condensation** <note>original: "dew"</note> on the lids of **boiling pots**, and in the moisture that forms on marble and **wood paneling** <note>original: "wainscot"</note> when it is about to **rain**. However, this is unlikely to have much effect except upon vapors and heavy <note>original: "gross"</note> **air** that are already very close to becoming water. 

The third way is something that could be researched but is not yet proven: **mixing moist vapors with air** and testing if they will produce more **water** than there was at first. If so, that increase would be a **transformation of the air**. Therefore, put water into the bottom of a **distilling vessel**, with the spout <note>original: "neb"</note> plugged. Weigh the **water** first. Hang a large **sponge** in the middle of the vessel and see how much **water** you can squeeze <note>original: "crush"</note> out of it, and whether it is more or less than the water used. You must understand that if any **transformation** can be achieved, it will be done most easily in small **pores**, which is why we suggest using a **sponge**. 

The fourth way is also probable, though not yet demonstrated: **receiving air into the small pores of objects**. As has been said, everything in small quantities is easier to **transform**. Tangible objects do not "enjoy" the company of **air** but try to force <note>original: "subact," from Latin *subigere*, meaning to bring under control or subdue</note> it into a more **dense state**. In **solid objects** <note>original: "entire bodies"</note>, this process is blocked because if the **air** were to condense, there would be nothing to fill the empty space. Therefore, it must happen in loose **materials** such as **sand and powder**, which we see gather moisture of their own accord if they are packed tightly.

Onions, as they hang, will often sprout; so will ***pennyroyal*** and an herb called ***orpine*** <note>a succulent plant often called "Livelong"</note>, which people in the country use to decorate their houses by binding it to a lath or stick and setting it against a wall. We see this even more specifically in the larger ***houseleek*** <note>original: "Semper-viue" or "always-living"</note>, which will put out branches for two or three years. However, it is true that people usually wrap the root in a cloth smeared with ***oil*** and renew it once every half-year. Ancient writers reported something similar regarding the ***stalks of lilies***. The cause is that these ***plants*** have a strong, dense, and succulent moisture that does not easily evaporate <note>original: "exhale"</note>; thus, it is able to support the sprouting of the ***plant*** from its own old stores without drawing help from the earth. This sprouting occurs mainly in late spring or early summer, which are the natural times for growth. We also see that ***tree stumps*** lying out of the ground will put forth sprouts for a time. 

But it is a **noble trial** <note>an experiment of great importance</note> of very great consequence to test whether these things increase in ***weight*** while sprouting. This must be tested by weighing them before they are hung up and again after they have sprouted. For if they do not increase in ***weight***, then it is simply that whatever they send out into the sprout, they lose from another part of the plant. But if they gain ***weight***, then it is a **great work of nature** <note>original: "Magnale Naturæ"</note>. For it would show that ***air*** can be condensed enough to be converted into a ***dense body***. Normally, the path and cycle of all things here on Earth is to thin out and turn things into more ***gaseous*** <note>original: "Pneumaticall"</note> and thin states, rather than moving backward from a ***gaseous*** state to something ***dense***. It would also show that ***air*** can ***nourish***, which is another matter of great consequence. Note that to test this, the ***experiment*** with the ***houseleek*** must be done without oiling the cloth; otherwise, the ***plant*** might be receiving nourishment from the oil.

<summary>Bacon discusses how physical manipulation in infancy can alter human anatomy and proposes an experiment to determine if plants growing in air gain weight, which would prove that air can be converted into solid matter.</summary>
<keywords>embryology, physical development, Macrocephali, botany, houseleek, condensation of air, pneumatic matter, scientific method</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Bacon’s exploration of the properties of matter, shifting from the growth of plants out of air to the physical behavior and composition of flame, specifically how it interacts with air in gunpowder and within the "vital spirits" of living beings.</meta>

### Natural History:

<margin>
A solitary experiment concerning the **mixing of flame and air**, and the great force thereof. 30
</margin>

Flame and air do not mingle, except in an instant, or within the **vital spirits** of **plants** <note>original: "Vegetables"</note> and **living creatures**. In **gunpowder**, its force has been attributed to the **rarefaction** <note>the process of a substance becoming less dense, such as a solid turning into a gas</note> of the **earthly substance** into **flame**. Thus far, this is true. Some then claim that it has become another element, the form of which occupies more space, and so, by **necessity**, an **expansion** <note>original: "Dilatation"</note> follows. Therefore, to prevent two bodies from being in one place, there must also follow an **expulsion** of the **pellet** <note>a lead bullet or projectile</note> or the blowing up of a **mine** <note>an explosive charge used in siege warfare</note>. But these are crude and ignorant speculations. 

If there were nothing else but **flame**, unless it were in very great quantity, it would be suffocated by any hard body, such as a **pellet** or the **barrel** of a **gun**. Thus, the **flame** would not expel the hard body; instead, the hard body would kill the **flame** and not allow it to kindle or spread. The cause of such a potent motion is the **nitre** (which we otherwise call **saltpeter**). Because it contains a remarkable **crude** <note>raw or unrefined</note> and windy **spirit**, it first suddenly expands itself by the **heat** of the **fire**. (We know that simple **air**, being unnaturally thinned by **heat**, will make room for itself and break or blow up whatever resists it.) Secondly, when the **nitre** has expanded, it blows the **flame** outward like an internal **bellows**. 

Therefore, we see that **brimstone** <note>sulfur</note>, **pitch**, **camphor**, **wildfire**, and various other **inflammable** matters—though they burn fiercely and are hard to quench—do not create such a fiery wind as **gunpowder** does. On the other hand, we see that **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> (which is a very **crude** and **watery body**), when heated and confined, has a force similar to **gunpowder**. 

As for **living creatures**, it is certain that their **vital spirits** are a **substance compounded** of an **airy** and **flaming matter**. Although **air** and **flame** will not mix well when they are free, they will do so when bound by a **body** that has some stability. You can see this best in those two substances which are their **nutrients** <note>original: "Aliments"</note>, **water** and **oil**. These also will not mix well on their own, but within the **bodies** of **plants** and **living creatures**, they will. It is no marvel, therefore, that a small **quantity** of **spirits** in the **cells** of the **brain** and the **channels** of the **nerves** <note>original: "Sinewes"</note> are able to move the whole **body** (which is of such a great **mass**) with both great **force**, as in **wrestling** and **leaping**, and with great **swiftness**, as in playing a **division** <note>a style of rapid musical ornamentation or "runs"</note> upon the **lute**. Such is the force of these two **natures**, **air** and **flame**, when they combine.

<margin>
A solitary experiment concerning the **secret nature of flame**. 31
</margin>

Take a small **wax candle** and put it in a **socket** made of **brass** or **iron**. Then set it upright in a **bowl** <note>original: "Porringer"</note> full of heated **spirit of wine** <note>high-proof alcohol or ethanol</note>. Set both the **candle** and the **spirit of wine** on fire, and you shall see the **flame** of the **candle** open itself and become four or five times larger than it would otherwise have been. It will appear in a **globular shape** <note>original: "Figure Globular"</note> and not as a **pyramid** <note>original: "Pirammis"</note>. You shall also see that the **inner flame** of the **candle** keeps its **color** and does not turn at all blue like the **outer flame** of the **spirit of wine**. This is a noble instance...

<summary>Bacon argues that the explosive power of gunpowder comes from the expansion of "nitre" rather than just flame, and he compares this interaction of air and fire to the "vital spirits" that power movement in living bodies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the physical properties of flame, specifically how it behaves as a distinct body of matter, and begins a new observation on the nature of gravity and weight within the Earth.</meta>

# Century I.

This is an example where two things are most remarkable. First, one **flame** within another does not extinguish, but remains a distinct body and continues just as **air** or **water** does. Therefore, **flame** would continue to rise upward as one large mass if it were not extinguished on the sides. The larger the **flame** is at the bottom, the higher it rises. Second, **flame** does not mix with other **flame** the way **air** mixes with **air** or **water** with **water**; instead, they remain only adjacent to one another, as happens between solid <note>original: "Consisting"</note> bodies. 

It also appears that the pyramid shape we usually see in **flame** is merely accidental. The surrounding **air**, by extinguishing the sides of the **flame**, crushes it and thins it into that shape; by itself, it would be round. Therefore, **smoke** takes the shape of a reversed pyramid, because the **air** extinguishes the **flame** and receives the **smoke**. Note also that the **flame** of a **candle** placed within the **flame** of **spirits of wine** <note>alcohol, such as brandy or ethanol</note> is agitated. It does not just open and move upward but moves in a waving motion, back and forth. This suggests that **flame**, by its own nature (if it were not extinguished), would roll and turn as well as move upward. 

From all this, it seems that most **celestial bodies** are true **fires** or **flames**, as the **Stoics** <note>an ancient Greek school of philosophy</note> believed, though perhaps more refined and less dense <note>original: "rarified"</note> than our **flame** is. For they are all spherical and distinct; they rotate and have the color and splendor of **flame**. Thus, **flame** in the heavens is long-lasting, solid, and in its natural place. But here on Earth, it is a stranger, momentary <note>original: "momentany"</note>, and impure—like **Vulcan** <note>the Roman god of fire, who was cast out of heaven and walked with a limp (halted)</note> who limped after his fall.

<margin>
A solitary experiment concerning the **different force of flame** in the **middle** and on the **sides**. 32
</margin>

Take an **arrow** and hold it in a **flame** for the duration of ten pulses. When it is removed, you will find that those parts of the **arrow** that were on the outside edges of the **flame** are more burned, blackened, and turned almost into charcoal. Meanwhile, the part in the middle of the **flame** will look as if the **fire** had barely touched it. This is an example of great importance for discovering the nature of **flame**. It clearly shows that **flame** burns more violently toward the sides than in the middle. Furthermore, it shows that **heat** or **fire** is not violent or intense except where it is obstructed or confined. Therefore, the **Peripatetics** <note>followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note>—even though their theory of an "element of fire" above the **air** is rightly rejected—defend themselves well on this point. When challenged that such a **sphere of fire** surrounding the **Earth** would necessarily burn everything up, they respond that pure **elemental fire**, in its own place and not agitated <note>original: "irritate"</note>, produces only a moderate **heat**.

A solitary experiment concerning the **decrease of the natural motion of gravity** away from the Earth, or within some depth of the **Earth**. 33
</margin>

It is frequently stated by many as a common experiment that a **lump of ore** <note>original: "pyre," likely referring to a heavy mass of mineral</note> at the bottom of a **mine** can be moved and tumbled by the strength of two men, whereas if you bring it to the surface of the **Earth**, it requires the strength of at least six men to move it. This is a significant example and deserves to be tested thoroughly. For it is very probable that the **motion** of...

# Natural History:

...of **gravity** works weakly, both far from the Earth and also deep within the Earth. The former occurs because the **desire for union** <note>original: "Appetite of Vnion"</note> of **dense bodies** with the Earth is more sluggish due to distance. The latter occurs because the body has partially achieved its natural state once it is at some depth within the Earth. As for moving toward a specific **point** or place (which was the opinion of the **Ancients**), it is mere foolishness <note>original: "Vanity"</note>.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the **contraction** of **bodies** in **bulk** by mixing a **liquid body** with a more **solid** one.
34
</margin>
It is strange how the **Ancients** accepted **experiments** on trust, yet built great theories upon them. One observation delivered confidently by some of their best authors is that a **vessel** filled with **ashes** will hold the same amount of **water** as it would if it were empty. But this is utterly untrue; the **water** will fail to enter by a **fifth** part. I suspect that this **fifth** part represents the difference between the ashes being packed loosely or tightly. As we see, **ashes** alone occupy less space if they are hard-pressed; likewise, **ashes** with **air** between them lie looser, and with **water**, closer. I have not yet found for certain that **water** itself shrinks or occupies less space when mixed with **ashes** or **dust**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning **making vines** more **fruitful**.
35
</margin>
It is reliably reported that if you place a good amount of **grape seeds** <note>original: "Kernels of Grapes"</note> around the **root** of a **vine**, it will cause the **vine** to sprout earlier and thrive better. This may be tested with other **seeds** placed around the **root** of a **plant** of the same kind, such as **figs**, **apple seeds**, etc. The **cause** may be that the **seeds** draw nutrients <note>original: "iuice"</note> from the earth suited to nourish the **tree**, as if they were going to become **trees** themselves even without a **root**. But the **root**, being stronger, robs and devours the nourishment once the seeds have gathered it, just as great **fishes** devour the small.

<margin>
**Experiments in association** <note>original: "in Confort"; referring to related groups of experiments</note> concerning **purging medicines**.
36
</margin>
The **operation** of **purging medicines** and their **causes** have long been considered a great secret. Consequently, in the lazy manner of men, these effects are attributed to a **hidden property** <note>original: "Hidden Propriety"</note>, a **specific virtue**, or a **fourth quality** <note>Scholastic terms used by medieval and Renaissance philosophers to explain effects when the physical cause was unknown</note>, and similar **excuses for ignorance** <note>original: "Shifts of Ignorance"</note>. The **causes** of **purging** are various; all are plain and clear, and thoroughly supported by **experience**. 

The first cause is that whatever cannot be overcome and digested by the **stomach** is either expelled upward as **vomit** or sent down to the **guts**. Through that **motion of expulsion** in the **stomach** and **guts**, other **parts** of the body (such as the openings of the **veins** and the like) are prompted to expel their contents by **sympathetic reaction** <note>original: "Motion of Consent"</note>. Indeed, nothing is more common in the human body than a **sympathetic reaction**. This overloading of the **stomach** is caused either by the **quality** or the **quantity** of the **medicine**. 

There are three such **qualities**: **extreme bitterness**, as in **aloes**, **colocynth** <note>original: "Coloquintida"; a bitter desert vine used as a powerful laxative</note>, etc.; **loathsomeness** and horrible taste, as in **agaric** <note>a medicinal fungus</note>, **black hellebore**, etc.; and **secret toxicity** <note>original: "Malignity"</note> or incompatibility with **man's body**, which often does not show much in the taste, such as in **scammony** <note>a purgative resin from a vine root</note>, **mechoacan** <note>a root from Mexico used as a purgative</note>, **antimony**, etc. Note well that if there is any **medicine**...

<meta>This page continues Bacon’s discussion on the mechanics of medicine, specifically concluding an entry on why certain substances act as purgatives (laxatives) and beginning a series of numbered observations on the different physical "causes" of purging.</meta>

# Century I.

...that **purges** <note>original: "Purgeth"</note>, and has neither of the first two **manifest** qualities <note>In ancient medicine, "manifest qualities" referred to heat, cold, moisture, or dryness</note>, it is to be held suspected as a kind of **poison**. This is because it works either by **corrosion** or by a **secret malignancy** and **enmity** toward **nature**. Therefore, such **medicines** must be prepared and used cautiously. The third **cause** of purging is when the substance taken causes the body to expel it due to volume; as we see in a great **quantity** of milk swallowed <note>original: "sufted" – likely a transcription error for "sucked" or "stuffed"</note> from the cow, or even a great **quantity** of **meat**. For **surfeits** <note>overindulgence in food or drink</note> many times turn into **purges**, both upwards <note>vomiting</note> and downwards <note>diarrhea</note>. Therefore, we generally see that the working of **purging medicines** begins two or three hours after the **medicines** are taken. This is because the **stomach** must first make a trial to see whether it can digest <note>original: "concoct"</note> them. The same thing happens after **surfeits** or after drinking **milk** in too great a **quantity**.

<margin>37</margin>
A second **cause** is **mordication** <note>biting or stinging irritation</note> of the **orifices** of the **body parts**, especially of the **mesenteric veins**. For example, we see that salt, or any such thing that is sharp and biting, when put into the **rectum** <note>original: "Fundament"</note>, provokes that **part** to expel its contents. Likewise, **mustard** provokes **sneezing**, and any sharp **thing** in the **eyes** provokes **tears**. Therefore, we see that almost all **purgatives** cause a kind of **twitching** and **vellication** <note>a localized irritation or twitching of the nerves/muscles</note>, besides the **griping** <note>sharp abdominal pain</note> which comes from wind <note>gas</note>. If this **mordication** is of an overly high **degree**, it is little better than the **corrosion** of **poison**. This sometimes happens with **antimony** <note>a metallic element used as a powerful emetic and laxative</note>, especially if it is given to **bodies** that are not filled with **humors** <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health</note>; for where **humors** abound, they protect the **internal parts**.

<margin>38</margin>
The third **cause** is **attraction**. I do not deny that **purging medicines** have in them a direct **force** of **attraction**, just as **drawing plasters** do in **surgery**. We see that bruised **sage** or **betony**, **sneezing-powder**, and other **powders** or **liquors** (which **physicians** call **errhines** <note>original: "Erbines" – medicines applied to the nose to clear the head</note>), when put into the **nose**, draw **phlegm** and water from the **head**. It is the same with **antimony** and **gargles** <note>original: "Gargarismes"</note> that draw **rheum** <note>mucus or watery discharge</note> down through the **palate**. By this **virtue** <note>power or characteristic</note>, no doubt, some **purgatives** draw one **humor** more than another, according to the accepted **opinion**: for instance, **rhubarb** draws **choler** <note>yellow bile</note>; **senna** <note>original: "Sean"</note> draws **melancholy** <note>black bile</note>; **agaric** <note>a medicinal fungus</note> draws **phlegm**, and so on. Yet, to a greater or lesser extent, they all draw indiscriminately. Note also that besides **sympathy** <note>natural affinity</note> between the **purgative** and the **humor**, there is another **cause** why some **medicines** draw certain **humors** more than others: it is because some **medicines** work faster than others. Those that act quickly draw only the **lighter** and more **fluid humors**; those that act slowly work upon the more **tough** and **viscous humors**. Therefore, men must be careful about taking **rhubarb** and similar drugs frequently on their own; for it takes only the **lightest** part of the **humor** away and leaves the bulk of the **humors** more stubborn. The same may be said of **wormwood**, which is so highly praised.

<margin>39</margin>
The fourth **cause** is **flatuosity** <note>the state of being gassy</note>. For **wind** (once stirred) moves the body to expel. We find that, in effect, all **purgatives** contain a raw **spirit** or **wind**, which is the **principal cause** of **tortion** <note>twisting or wringing pain</note> in the **stomach** and **belly**. For this reason, most **purgatives** lose their **potency** <note>original: "Vertue"</note> if they are boiled <note>original: "Decoction"</note> over a **fire**; therefore, they are given chiefly as an **infusion**, **juice**, or **powder**. <meta>This page continues Francis Bacon's detailed classification of the seven causes of "purging" (the medical process of expelling waste from the body). <margin>40</margin>
The fifth **cause** is **compression**, or **crushing**: as when water is crushed out of a **sponge**. So we see that **taking cold** moves looseness <note>diarrhea</note> by the contraction of the skin and outward parts. In the same way, **cold** causes **rheums** <note>mucus or discharge</note> and **defluxions** <note>the flow of fluids</note> from the head; and some **astringent plasters** crush out purulent matter. This kind of operation is not found in many **medicines**: **myrobalans** <term>Mirabolanes: dried plum-like fruits used in traditional medicine</term> have it, and perhaps the **barks of peaches**. For this virtue requires an **astringency** <note>original: "Astriction"; the quality of shrinking or constricting body tissues</note>; but such an **astringency** as is not pleasing to the body. (For a pleasing **astringency** tends to bind in the humors rather than expel them.) Therefore, such **astringency** is found in things with a **harsh** <note>original: "Harrish"</note> taste.

---

<margin>41</margin>
The sixth **cause** is **lubrication** <note>original: "Lubrefaction"</note> and **relaxation**. We see this in **emollient medicines** <note>substances used to soften or soothe</note>, such as **milk**, **honey**, **mallows**, **lettuce**, **mercurial** <note>the herb "Mercury" (Mercurialis), not the liquid metal</note>, **pellitory of the wall** <note>a plant in the nettle family</note>, and others. There is also a secret virtue of **relaxation** in **cold**. For the **heat** of the body binds the parts and humors together, which **cold** relaxes. This is seen in **urine**, **blood**, **pottage** <note>thick soup or porridge</note>, or the like; which, if they become **cold**, break and dissolve. By this kind of **relaxation**, **fear** loosens the belly; because the heat retiring inwards toward the **heart**, the guts and other parts are relaxed. In the same manner, **fear** also causes trembling in the **sinews**. Some **medicines** made of **mercury** are of this kind of **purgers**.

---

<margin>42</margin>
The seventh **cause** is **abstertion** <term>Abstertion: the act of cleansing, scouring, or wiping away</term>; which is plainly a scouring off, or **incision** <note>in this context, cutting through or breaking up</note> of the **more viscous humors**, making the **humors** more fluid and cutting between them and the body part. This is found in **nitrous water** <note>water containing nitre or saltpeter</note>, which speedily scours linen cloth of its foulness. But this **incision** must be achieved by a sharpness without **astringency**, which we find in **salt**, **wormwood**, **oxymel** <note>a mixture of honey and vinegar</note>, and the like.

---

<margin>43</margin>
There are **medicines** that move the **stools** but not **urine**, and others that move **urine** but not the **stools**. Those that **purge by stool** are those that enter the **mesenteric veins** <note>veins that drain the intestines</note> only a little or not at all. Instead, they are either not digestible by the **stomach** and therefore move immediately downward to the **guts**, or they are later rejected by the **mesenteric veins** and so likewise turn downward to the **guts**. Most **purgers** are of these two kinds. But those that move **urine** <note>diuretics</note> are those that are well digested by the **stomach** and well received by the **mesenteric veins**. Thus, they come as far as the **liver**, which sends **urine** to the **bladder** as the **whey of blood** <note>the watery part of the blood</note>. These **medicines**, being "opening" and "piercing," strengthen the operation of the **liver** in sending down the watery part of the blood to the **kidneys** <note>original: "Reines"</note>. For **urinary medicines** <note>original: "Urinatiue"</note> do not work by rejection and indigestion, as **laxative** <note>original: "Solutiue"</note> medicines do.

---

<margin>44</margin>
There are various **medicines** which, in a greater **quantity**, move the **stool**, and in a smaller quantity, move **urine**. And conversely, some that in a greater **quantity** move **urine**, and in a smaller quantity, the **stool**. **Rhubarb** and some others are of the former sort. The **cause** is that **rhubarb** is a **medicine** which the **stomach** in a small **quantity** can digest and overcome—since it is not **flatulent** <note>original: "Flatuous"</note> nor loathsome—and so the stomach sends it to the **mesenteric veins**. Because it is "opening," it helps move **urine**. But in a greater **quantity**, the...

<header>Century. I.</header>

The stomach cannot overcome it, and so it goes to the **intestines**. **Pepper**, according to some of the **ancients**, is noted to be of the second sort; in small **quantities**, it moves gas in the **stomach** and **intestines**, and so expels it through a **stool**. But in greater **quantities**, it dissipates the **gas**; it then enters the **mesenteric veins** and reaches the **liver** and **kidneys** <note>original: "Reines"</note>; where, by heating and opening these organs, it causes **urine** to flow more plentifully.

<margin>
Experiments in agreement regarding meats and drinks that are most nourishing.
45
</margin>

WE have spoken of **evacuating** the body; we will now speak of **filling** it using **restoratives** for **consumptions** <note>original: "Consumptions"; wasting diseases such as tuberculosis</note> and **emaciating** diseases. In **vegetables**, one part is more **nourishing** than another; for instance, **grains** and **roots** nourish more than **leaves**. Indeed, the religious **order** of the **Foliatanes** <note>original: "Foliatanes"; a Cistercian sub-order known for extreme fasting, supposedly eating only leaves</note> was suppressed by the **Pope**, as he found **leaves** unable to nourish the human body. Whether there is such a difference in the flesh of **living creatures** has not been well researched—specifically, whether **livers** and other **entrails** are more **nourishing** than the **outward flesh**. We find that among the **Romans**, a **goose's liver** was a great delicacy; they even had artificial means to make it fair and large; but whether it was more **nourishing** is not clear. It is certain that **marrow** is more **nourishing** than **fat**. I believe that some decoction <note>original: "Decoction"; a liquid made by boiling down substances</note> of **bones** and **sinews**, crushed and well-strained, would be a very **nourishing broth**. We also find that **Scotch Shank** <note>original: "Scotch Schincke"; likely referring to a beef hock or shank</note> (which is a pottage of strong nourishment) is made with the **knees** and **sinews** of **beef**, boiled for a long time. **Jelly**, which they use as a **restorative**, is chiefly made from the **knuckles** of **veal**. The **pulp** inside a **crayfish** or **crab**, which they spice and butter, is more **nourishing** than the **flesh** of the **crab** or **crayfish**. The **yolks** of **eggs** are clearly more **nourishing** than the **whites**. So it appears that the parts of **living creatures** that lie further inward nourish more than the outward flesh—except perhaps for the **brain**, which the **animal spirits** prey upon too much to leave it with any great nourishing power. It seems that for the **nourishing** of aged men, or men with **wasting diseases**, some such food should be devised that is already half-converted into **chyle** <term>chyle: the milky fluid formed in the small intestine during digestion</term> before it is put into the **stomach**.

</margin>

Take two large **capons** <term>capon: a castrated rooster, prized for tender meat</term>; parboil them over a soft fire for an hour or more, until in effect all the blood is gone. Add to the liquid the **peel** of a **sweet lemon**, or a good portion of the **peel** of a **citron**, and a little **mace**. Cut off the **shanks** and throw them away. Then, with a good strong chopping knife, mince the two **capons**, bones and all, as small as ordinary minced meat. Put them into a large, clean bolter <term>bolter: a cloth bag or sieve used for straining</term>. Then take a kilderkin <term>kilderkin: a small barrel or cask</term>, sweet and well-seasoned, containing four gallons of beer of "8 shilling" strength <note>a classification of the beer's quality or tax rate</note>, just as it comes from the tunning <note>original: "Tunning"; the process of putting newly brewed beer into casks to ferment</note>. Purposefully make a large bung-hole in the kilderkin. Then thrust the bolter (containing the **capons**) into it, drawn out in length. Let it steep in the beer for three days and three nights with the bung-hole open to allow it to work <note>ferment</note>. Then close the bung-hole, and let it sit for a day and a half. Then draw...

It may also be tried with other meats, such as **pheasant**, **partridge**, **young pork**, **pig**, or **venison** (especially from **young deer**), etc.

<margin>48</margin> A **mortress** <note>a thick pottage of ground meat</note> made with the **meat** <note>original: "Brawne"</note> of **capons**, pounded and strained, and mingled (after it is made) with at least an equal quantity of **almond butter**, is an excellent food to nourish those who are weak. It is better than **blancmange** <note>original: "Blanck-manjar," a creamy medicinal dish</note> or **jelly**. So too is a **cullis** <note>a strong, strained meat broth</note> of **cocks**, boiled thick with a similar mixture of **almond butter**. For the **mortress** or **cullis** by itself is more savory and strong, and not as fit for nourishing weak bodies; but the **almonds**, which do not have as strong a taste as **flesh**, qualify it excellently.

<margin>49</margin> **Indian maize** (corn) certainly has an excellent spirit of nourishment; but it must be thoroughly boiled and made into a **maize-cream** like a **barley-cream**. I judge the same of **rice** made into a **cream**. **Rice** is the primary food in **Turkey** and other countries of the East, but it must be thoroughly boiled because of its hardness, and also because it otherwise causes constipation <note>original: "bindeth the Body"</note> too much.

<margin>50</margin> **Pistachios**, provided they are good and not musty, joined with **almonds** in **almond milk**, or made into a **milk** of themselves (like **almond milk** but greener), are an excellent nourisher. But you would do well to add a little scraped **ginger**, because they are not without some subtle gas <note>original: "windineſſe"</note>.

<margin>51</margin> **Milk** warm from the **cow** is found to be a great nourisher and a good remedy for **consumptions**. But you must put two little bags into it when you milk the **cow**: one of **powdered mint**, the other of **powdered red roses**. These keep the **milk** from turning or curdling in the stomach. Add **sugar** also for the same reason, and partly for the taste. You must drink a large draught so that it stays for less time in the stomach, lest it curdle. Let the cup into which you milk the **cow** be set in a larger cup of hot water, so that you may drink it warm. <header>Century I.</header>

The human body is not a good nourisher of itself, except in **infants**, for whom it is natural.

<margin>52</margin>
**Oil of sweet almonds**, freshly pressed, with **sugar** and a little **spice**, spread upon toasted bread, is an excellent nourisher. However, to keep the oil from overheating <note>original: "frying"</note> in the stomach, you must drink a good draught of mild beer after eating it. To keep it from relaxing the stomach too much, you must add a little powdered cinnamon.

<margin>53</margin>
**Egg yolks** are naturally well-prepared for nourishment by themselves. As long as they are poached or soft-boiled <note>original: "reare boiled"</note>, they need no other preparation or mixture. Yet they may also be taken raw when freshly laid, mixed with **Malmsey** <note>a sweet, strong wine</note> or other sweet wine. You would do well to add a few slices of **eryngium roots** <note>sea holly, often candied and used as a restorative</note> and a little **ambergris** <note>original: "Amber-grice," a rare waxy substance from sperm whales used in medicine</note>. By this means, besides the immediate power of nourishment, such a drink will strengthen the lower back so that it will not draw down the urine too fast, for excessive urination always hinders nourishment.

<margin>54</margin>
**Mincing of meat**, as in pies and **buttered minced meat**, saves the effort of grinding with the teeth. Therefore, it is undoubtedly more nourishing, especially in old age or for those who have weak teeth. However, butter is not as suitable for weak bodies; therefore, it would be good to moisten the meat with a little **claret wine**, lemon or orange **peel** <note>original: "Pill"</note> cut small, sugar, and a very little cinnamon or nutmeg. As for **chewets** <note>original: "Chwets," a type of small savory pie filled with minced meat</note>, which are likewise minced meat, instead of butter and fat, it would be good to moisten them partly with **cream**, or **almond**, **pistachio**, **barley**, or **maize milk** <note>original: "Maiz Creame"</note>, adding a little coriander seed, caraway seed, and a very little saffron. We reserve the more thorough handling of **nutrition** <note>original: "Alimentation"</note> for its proper place.

We have so far handled the specifics which yield the best, easiest, and most plentiful nourishment; now we will speak of the best means of **conveying** and **converting** that nourishment.

<margin>55</margin>
The first method is to ensure that the nourishment is not robbed or drawn away. In this regard, what we have already said is very significant: ensure that the **kidneys** <note>original: "Reines"</note> do not draw an overly large portion of the blood into the urine too strongly. To this, add the precept of **Aristotle**, that wine should be avoided in all **consumptions** <note>wasting diseases</note>. This is because the spirits of the wine prey upon the dewy juices <note>original: "Roscide Iuyce," referring to the body's essential moisture</note> of the body and compete with the body's own spirits, thus deceiving and robbing them of their nourishment. Therefore, if a wasting illness caused by a weak stomach forces you to use wine, let it always be burnt <note>flambéed to remove the harsher alcohol</note> so that the sharper spirits may evaporate, or at the very least "quench" it with two small wedges of gold, repeated six or seven times <note>a traditional medical practice thought to infuse the wine with the restorative "virtue" of gold</note>. Also, take this precaution: let there not be too much loss of nourishment through evaporation and **sweating**. Therefore, if the patient is prone to sweating, it must be gently restrained. But above all, the rule of **Hippocrates** should be followed, who advises the exact opposite of what is commonly practiced: namely, that the **linen** or garment next to the skin should be dry in winter and changed often.

<margin>56</margin>
The second *method* is to send the *nourishment* out into the *body parts* more strongly. To do this, one must work by *strengthening* the *stomach*. Because the *stomach* is chiefly comforted by *wine* and *hot things*—which might otherwise be harmful—it is best to use *external applications* on the stomach. In this regard, it has been found that *padded sachets* <note>original: "quilts"</note> of *roses, spices, mastic, wormwood, mint*, etc., are not nearly as helpful as taking a *cake of new bread* and moistening it with a little *sherry* <note>original: "Sacke"</note> or *Alicante wine* <note>original: "Ale-gant," a sweet Spanish wine</note>. After drying it slightly before a fire, put it inside a clean napkin and lay it on the stomach. For it is certain that all *flour* <note>original: "Flower"</note> has a potent power of *astringency* <term>astriction: the quality of tightening or contracting body tissues</term>, so much so that it hardens a piece of flesh, or even a flower, that is laid in it. Therefore, a *bag padded with bran* is also very good, but it dries the skin somewhat too much, so it must not be left on for long.

<margin>57</margin>
The third *method* (which may be a branch of the previous one) is to send forth *nourishment* more effectively through *sleep*. We see that bears and other *creatures* that *sleep* through the *winter* grow exceedingly *fat*. It is certain (as is commonly believed) that *sleep* provides much *nourishment*, both because the spirits spend less of the nourishment during sleep than when *living creatures* are awake, and because—to the present purpose—it helps push the nourishment out into the body parts. Therefore, in elderly men, weak bodies, and those who do not have an excess of *choler* <term>choler: one of the four "humors" or bodily fluids; an excess was thought to cause a hot, dry temperament and fast digestion</term>, a short *sleep* after dinner helps to *nourish*. In such bodies, there is no fear of an over-hasty digestion, which is the usual drawback of *afternoon naps* <note>original: "Postmeridian sleepes"</note>. *Sleep* in the morning—after taking something easy to digest, such as *milk* from the cow, *nourishing broth*, or the like—also furthers nourishment. But this should be done while sitting upright, so that the *milk* or *broth* may pass more quickly to the bottom of the stomach.

<margin>58</margin>
The fourth *method* is to ensure that the body parts themselves can strongly draw nourishment to them. There is an excellent observation by *Aristotle*: that a great reason why some plants live to a much greater age than *living creatures* is that they put forth new leaves and boughs every year. In contrast, *living creatures* (after their period of growth) put forth nothing young except hair and nails, which are *waste products* <term>excrements: in this context, materials the body casts off, such as hair, nails, or sweat, rather than vital tissue</term> and not functional parts. It is most certain that whatever is young draws nourishment better than that which is old. The "mystery" behind that observation is that as young *boughs* and *leaves* call the sap up to them, that sap nourishes the rest of the body as it passes through. We see this notably proved by the fact that the frequent cutting or *pruning* <note>original: "Polling"</note> of *hedges, trees*, and *herbs* contributes greatly to their longevity. <header>Century I.</header>

Assisting the process of nourishment in *living creatures*: The noblest and most important use of this is for the *prolongation of life*, the *restoration* of some degree of *youth*, and the *softening* <term>inteneration: the process of making tissues tender or soft again</term> of the *body parts*. It is certain that in *living creatures*, there are parts that nourish and repair easily, and parts that nourish and repair with difficulty. You must refresh and renew those that are easy to nourish so that the others may also be refreshed and (as it were) "drink in" nourishment as it passes through. We see that *draught oxen* <note>working oxen used for pulling heavy loads</note>, when put into good pasture, recover the flesh of young beef. Men, after long, emaciating diets, grow plump, fat, and almost new again. Therefore, you may surely conclude that the frequent and wise use of those *weight-loss diets* and *purgings*—and perhaps even some kind of *bloodletting*—is a principal means of *prolonging life* and *restoring* some degree of *youth*. For as we have often said, *death* comes upon *living creatures* like the torture of Mezentius <note>Mezentius was a mythical Etruscan king who famously executed people by tying a living body to a corpse, face to face, until the living person died from the decay</note>.

> ->He even joined dead bodies to the living,<-
> ->Fitting hands to hands and mouths to mouths.<-
> <note>original: "Mortua quin etiam iungebat Corpora viuis. Componens Manibusq; Manus, atq; Oribus Ora." (Virgil, *Aeneid*)</note>

For the parts in a man's body that are easily repairable (such as *spirits*, *blood*, and *flesh*) die in the embrace of the parts that are difficult to repair (such as *bones*, *nerves*, and *membranes*). Likewise, some *internal organs* (which they categorize as *spermatic parts*) are hard to repair, though that division of *spermatic* and *menstrual parts* <note>Spermatic parts were believed to be formed from "seed" (hard, white tissues like bone), while menstrual parts were thought to be formed from "blood" (soft, red tissues like flesh)</note> is merely a theoretical idea. This same *observation* may also be applied to the present purpose of nourishing emaciated bodies. Therefore, *gentle friction* <note>rubbing the skin</note> draws out the nourishment by making the parts a little "hungry" and heating them, which causes them to draw in nourishment better. I recommend this *rubbing* be done in the morning. It is also best done by *hand* or with a piece of *scarlet wool* moistened slightly with *oil of almonds* mixed with a small amount of *bay salt* or *saffron*. We see that the mere brushing and grooming <note>original: "currying"</note> of horses makes them fat and healthy.

<margin>59</margin>
The fifth method is to further the actual *act* of *assimilation* of *nourishment*, which is done by some external *softening agents* <term>emollients: substances used to soften or soothe the skin</term> that make the body parts more ready to *assimilate* <note>absorb and incorporate nutrients</note>. For this purpose, I have compounded an *ointment* of excellent scent, which I call *Roman Ointment*; *see the recipe*. It should be used between periods of sleep, for the body parts chiefly assimilate nourishment during the latter part of sleep.

The method is first to apply a *poultice* <note>original: "pultasse"</note> (*see the recipe*); then a *bath* or *steeping* <term>fomentation: the application of warm, medicinal liquids to the body</term> (*see the recipe*); and then a *plaster* (*see the recipe*). The *poultice* relaxes the pores and makes the "humors" <note>bodily fluids thought to cause disease</note> ready to be released. The *steeping* calls forth the humor by vapors, yet because of the path made by the *poultice*, it draws gently. Therefore, it draws the humor out without drawing more of it to the area; for it...

is a *gentle fomentation* <term>fomentation: the application of warm, medicinal liquids to the body to relieve pain or inflammation</term>, and also has a mixture (though very little) of some *pain-numbing agent* <note>original: "stupefactive"</note>. The *poultice* is to be applied for two or three hours; the *fomentation* for a quarter of an hour, or slightly longer, being used hot and repeated seven or eight times; and the *plaster* is to stay on continuously until the part is fully healed.

Solitary Experiment concerning cure by habit.
61
