There is a secret way of *cure* (currently *unpracticed*) by *habituation* <note>original: "assuetude"</note> to that which in itself is harmful. Some have made *poisons* familiar to their bodies, as has been mentioned before; the *regular caregivers* of those *sick with the plague* are seldom infected. *Enduring torture* has been made easier through *habit*. The *tolerating* of enormous *quantities* of *meat*, and likewise of *wine* or *strong drink*, has been made possible through *habit* without resulting in *overindulgence* <note>original: "surfeit"</note> or *drunkenness*. Generally, *diseases* that are *chronic*, such as *coughs*, *consumptive diseases* <note>original: "phthisicks"; likely referring to tuberculosis</note>, some kinds of *paralysis* <note>original: "palseyes"</note>, *mental illnesses* <note>original: "lunacies"</note>, etc., are most dangerous at the beginning. Therefore, a wise *physician* will consider whether a *disease* is incurable, or whether the actual cure for it is full of peril. If he finds it to be so, let him turn to *palliative care* <term>palliative care: treatment that relieves symptoms without curing the underlying disease</term> and alleviate the *symptoms* without busying himself too much with a perfect *cure*. Many times (if the *patient* is indeed patient), that course of action will exceed all expectations. Likewise, the *patient* himself may strive little by little to overcome the *symptom* during its *worsening* <note>original: "exacerbation"</note>, and so, over time, turn *suffering* into a natural state.

<margin>
Solitary Experiment concerning cure by excess.
62
</margin>

Various *diseases*, especially *chronic* ones (*such as quartan fevers* <note>original: "quartan agues"; a type of fever, often malaria, that recurs every four days</note>), are sometimes cured by *overindulgence* and *excesses*, such as *excessive eating*, *excessive drinking*, *extraordinary fasting*, *extraordinary movement* or *exhaustion*, and the like. The cause is that *long-lasting diseases* gain an acquired strength from *habit*, in addition to their *material cause* from the *humors*. Thus, the *breaking of the habit* leaves them only with their original *cause*; if that cause is at all weak, the disease will fall away. Besides, such *excesses* *excite* and *spur nature*, which then rises up more forcibly against the *disease*.

We see it is a children's game to see if they can rub their chest with one hand and pat their forehead with another; immediately, they will sometimes rub with both hands or pat with both hands. We see that when the *spirits* <term>spirits: in early medicine, these were thought to be subtle fluids or vapors that carried life and sensation through the body</term> that come to the nostrils expel a bad scent, the stomach is ready to expel...

# Century I.

We find that in *consumptions* <note>original: "consumptions of the lungs"; likely tuberculosis or chronic wasting of the lungs</note> of the *lungs*, when nature cannot expel [waste] by a *cough*, people fall into *diarrhea* <note>original: "fluxes of the belly"</note>, and then they die. Similarly, in *pestilent diseases*, if the toxins cannot be expelled by *sweat*, they likewise fall into *looseness* <note>diarrhea</note>, and that is commonly fatal. Therefore, *physicians* should cleverly devise how, through *movements* within their *power*, they may trigger *internal movements* that are not in their power through *physiological resonance* <note>original: "consent"; the idea that one part of the body reacts to stimuli in another</note>. For example, using the *stench of burning feathers* or similar odors, they cure the *rising of the mother* <term>rising of the mother: an old term for hysteria, where the uterus was thought to move upward in the body causing distress</term>.

<margin>
*Solitary Experiment concerning the cure of diseases which are contrary to one's predisposition.*
64
</margin>
**H**ippocrates' *aphorism*, *In diseases [that are] less...* <note>original Latin: "In Morbis minus"</note>, is a profound observation. It suggests that *diseases* which are contrary to a person's *constitution* <term>constitution: original "complexion," referring to the balance of a person's physical traits</term>, *age*, *sex*, *season of the year*, *diet*, etc., are more dangerous than those that align with these factors. One might think it should be the opposite: that when the *sickness* and the *natural disposition* support each other, the *disease* should be more powerful. And no doubt it is, assuming an equal *quantity of matter* (the physical cause of the illness). But what makes the *aphorism* true is that such *diseases* show a greater *buildup of matter*, since they are strong enough to overcome those *natural inclinations* toward the *contrary*. Therefore, in *diseases* of that kind, let the *physician* focus more on *purging* <term>purging: the medicinal evacuation of "humors" or fluids from the body</term> than on *altering* the body's state; because the harm lies in the *quantity* of the illness, and the body's qualities will correct themselves once the excess is removed.

<margin>
*Solitary Experiment concerning preparations before purging, and the settling of the body afterward.*
65
</margin>
**P**hysicians wisely prescribe that *preparations* be used before *proper purges* <note>original: "just purgations"</note>. For it is certain that *purgatives* often do great harm if the body is not prepared both before and after the *purging*. The harm they do for want of *preparation* before *purging* is caused by the *sticking of the humors* <term>humors: bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament</term> and their failure to be expelled cleanly. This causes great *disturbances* and ill *symptoms* in the body during the *purging*, and it also weakens the effect of the *medicine* itself so that it does not purge sufficiently. Therefore, the work of *preparation* is two-fold: to make the *humors fluid* and mature, and to make the *passages* of the body more open; for both of these help the *humors* pass through easily. For the former, *syrups* are most beneficial; and for the latter, *decoctions* <term>decoctions: concentrated herbal broths; original: "apozumes"</term> or *preparing broths*. *Enemas* <note>original: "clisters"</note> also help, lest the *medicine* get stuck in the *guts* and cause griping pains. It is true, however, that *bodies overflowing with humors*, *fat bodies*, and *mild weather* <note>original: "open weather"</note> are *preparations* in themselves because they naturally make the *humors* more fluid. But let a *physician* be careful about purging after hard *frosty weather* or in a *lean body* without *preparation*. As for the harm that may occur after *purging*, it is caused by the *settling of some humors* in *bad places*. It is certain that there are *humors* which are quiet and do little harm when situated in certain parts of the body, but in other *places* (especially *passages*) they cause much mischief. Therefore, it is good after *purging* to use *decoctions* and *broths* that are not as *opening* as those used before, but rather *cleansing* <term>cleansing: original "abstersive"</term> and *purifying* <note>original: "mundifying"</note>.

# Natural History:

Cleansing *enemas* <term>original: mundifying clisters</term> are also good to finish with, in order to draw away the *residues* <note>original: reliques</note> of the *humors* that may have descended to the *lower region* of the *body*.

<margin>Solitary Experiment concerning the *stopping* of *blood*. 66</margin>
**B**lood is stopped <note>original: stanched</note> in various ways. First, by *astringents* and *repelling medicines* <note>original: repercussive</note>. Secondly, by *drawing* the *spirits* and *blood* inward, which is done by *cold*. For example, laying *iron* or a *stone* against the neck stops a *nosebleed*. Also, it has been tested that putting the *testicles* into sharp *vinegar* caused a sudden *withdrawal* <note>original: recesse</note> of the *spirits* and stopped the *blood*. Thirdly, by the *withdrawal* of the *blood* through *sympathy* <note>the theory that like substances attract one another</note>. It has been tested that if the bleeding part is thrust into the body of a *capon* <note>a castrated rooster</note> or *sheep* that has been newly cut open and is still bleeding, it stops the *blood*. The [animal's] *blood*, it seems, sucks and draws up—due to the similarity of the substance—the *blood* it meets, causing the person's own blood to retreat. Fourthly, by habit and time. For instance, when the *Prince of Orange* <note>William the Silent (1533–1584), who survived an assassination attempt in 1582</note> was first wounded by the *Spanish boy* <note>the assassin Jean Jaureguy</note>, he could find no way to stop the *blood* with either *medicine* or *bandages* <note>original: ligament</note>. He was forced to have the *opening* of the wound held shut by *men's thumbs*, with people taking turns, for the space of at least *two days*. Eventually, the *blood* retreated simply by habit <note>the body "learned" to stop the flow over time</note>. There is also a fifth way in use: to *bleed* <term>bloodletting</term> a person in an *opposite part* of the body to create a *diversion* <note>original: revulsion; drawing the blood flow away from the wound to a different area</note>.

<margin>Solitary Experiment concerning the *change* of *foods* and *medicines*. 67</margin>
**I**t helps, in both *medicine* and *food* <note>original: aliment</note>, to change treatments rather than continuing the same ones. The reason is that *nature*, through the constant use of any one thing, develops a *satiety* <note>boredom or fullness</note> and *dullness* in either *appetite* or *function*. We see that *habituation* <note>original: assuetude</note> to harmful things makes them lose their power to hurt—like *poison*, which some people have trained themselves to tolerate through use. Therefore, it is no wonder if helpful things lose their power to help through habit. I consider *intermission* <note>taking a break</note> to be almost the same as *change*, because something that has been paused is, in a way, new again.

<margin>Solitary Experiment concerning *diets*. 68</margin>
**I**t is found by *experience* that in *diets* of *guaiacum* <note>a medicinal wood used to treat syphilis and chronic illnesses</note>, *sarsaparilla* <note>original: sarza</note>, and the like (especially if they are strict), the *patient* is more troubled at the beginning than after some time. This has caused some of the more sensitive *patients* to give up in the middle, assuming that if those *diets* trouble them so much at first, they will not be able to endure them to the end. But the cause is that all those *diets* dry up *humors*, *rheums* <note>watery discharges or mucus</note>, and similar fluids. They cannot dry them up until they have first *thinned* them <note>original: attenuated</note>. While the *humor* is thinned, it is more fluid than it was before and troubles the *body* much more until it is dried up and consumed. Therefore, *patients* must wait for the proper time and not reject the treatment at the start.

### Century I.

**Cold** and **Heat** are **Nature's** two hands, by which she chiefly works. We have **heat** readily available because of **fire**, but for **cold**, we must wait until it comes, or seek it in deep caves or high mountains. Even then, we cannot obtain it in any great degree; for **furnaces** of **fire** are far hotter than a **summer’s sun**, but **vaults** or **hills** are not much colder than a **winter’s frost**.

<margin>69</margin> The first **means** of **producing cold** is that which **nature** presents us with; namely, the **breathing out** of **cold** from the **inward parts** of the **earth** in **winter**, when the **sun** has no power to overcome it. The **earth** is (as has been noted by some) the **primary source of cold** <note>original: "Primum Frigidum"</note>. This has been asserted by both **ancient** and **modern philosophers**. It was the tenet of **Parmenides** <note>a Greek philosopher born c. 515 BCE</note>. It was the opinion of the **author** of the discourse in **Plutarch** (for I believe that book was not **Plutarch's** own) titled **On the Primary Cold** <note>original: "De primo Frigido"</note>. It was also the opinion of **Telesio** <note>Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), an Italian philosopher</note>, who renewed the **philosophy** of **Parmenides** and is the best of the **innovators** <note>original: "Nouellists," meaning modern thinkers who challenged traditional Aristotelian views</note>.

<margin>70</margin> The second **cause** of **cold** is the **contact** of **cold bodies**. For **cold** is **active** and **transferable** into **adjacent** bodies, just as **heat** is. This is seen in things that are touched with **snow** or **cold water**. Therefore, whoever wishes to be an **inquirer** into **nature**, let him resort to an **ice-house** <note>original: "Conseruatory of Snow and Ice"</note>, such as those used for **delicacy** to cool **wine** in **summer**. This is a poor and contemptible use compared to other uses that may be made of such **ice-houses**.

<margin>71</margin> The third **cause** is the **primary nature** of all **tangible bodies**. It is important to note that all things whatsoever that are **tangible** <term>capable of being touched or felt</term> are naturally **cold** of themselves, unless they have an additional **heat** from **fire**, **life**, or **motion**. For even **alcohol** <note>original: "Spirit of wine"</note> or **chemical oils**, which are so hot in their effect, are **cold** to the first touch. Even **air** itself, when compressed and condensed a little by blowing, is **cold**.

<margin>72</margin> The fourth **cause** is the **density** of the **body**. All **dense bodies** are **colder** than most other **bodies**, such as **metals**, **stone**, and **glass**; and they take longer to **heat** than **softer bodies**. It is certain that **earth**, being **dense** and **tangible**, possesses the nature of **cold**. The reason is that since all **tangible matter** is naturally **cold**, it follows that where the **matter** is most concentrated, the **cold** is greater.

<margin>73</margin> The fifth **cause** of **cold** (or rather, of the increase and intensity of **cold**) is a **quick spirit** <term>an active, volatile internal essence</term> enclosed in a **cold body**. This will appear to anyone who attentively considers **nature** in many instances. We see that **saltpeter** <note>original: "Nitre"</note> (which has a **quick spirit**) is **cold**—colder to the **tongue** than a **stone**. Similarly, **water** is **colder** than **oil** because it has a **quick spirit**; for although **oil** has its **tangible** parts better processed <note>original: "digested"</note> than **water**, it has a duller **spirit**. Likewise, **snow** is **colder** than **water** because it has more **spirit** within it. We also see that **salt** added to **ice** (as in the production of **artificial ice**) increases the **activity** of the **cold**. Similarly, some **insects**, which have...

Bodies containing a **spirit of life**, such as **snakes** and **silkworms**, are **cold** to the touch. Similarly, **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> is the **coldest** of **metals** because it is **fullest** of **spirit**.

<margin>74</margin>
The sixth **cause** of **cold** is the **agitating and driving away of spirits** that possess some **degree of heat**. Banishing the **heat** necessarily leaves any body **cold**. We see this in the effects of **opium** and **numbing substances** <term>stupefactives: substances that induce a state of stupor or insensibility</term> on the **spirits** of living creatures. It would be worthwhile to test **opium** by placing it on top of a **weather-glass** <note>an early form of thermometer</note> to see whether it will cause the **air** to contract. However, I doubt it will succeed; for besides the fact that the potency <note>original: "vertue"</note> of **opium** will hardly penetrate through a body like glass, I believe that **opium** and similar substances cause **spirits** to flee because of their **harmful nature** <note>original: "malignity"</note> rather than through actual **cold**.

<margin>75</margin>
Seventhly, the same **effect** must follow from the **evaporating** <note>original: "exhaling"</note> **or drawing out of warm spirits**, just as it does when spirits flee. There is an opinion that the **moon** attracts **heat** (like a magnet), just as the **sun** attracts **cold** and **moisture**. Therefore, it would be useful to test this with **warm water**: expose one container to the beams of the **moon** and place a screen between the moonlight and the other **water** (just as we use shade against the **sun**) to see if the first cools faster. It would also be good to investigate what other means there may be to draw out the **faint** <note>original: "exile," meaning thin or meager</note> **heat** within the **air**, as that could be a powerful secret for **producing cold weather**.

Grouped experiments regarding the conversion and transformation of air into water.

We have previously described the means of turning **air** into **water** in Experiment 27. But because it is a **great work of nature** <note>original: "Magnale Naturæ"</note> and leads to controlling a very significant effect—and is also of many uses—we will add some **grouped examples** that provide further insight.

<margin>76</margin>
Some of the **ancient writers** report that **sailors** used to hang **fleeces of wool** on the sides of their **ships** every night, with the **wool** facing the water, and that they squeezed fresh **water** out of them in the morning for their use. We have tested this ourselves: a quantity of **wool** tied loosely together and lowered into a deep **well**—hanging in the **middle**, about eighteen feet <note>original: "three fathome"</note> above the water for one winter night—increased in weight (as I recall) by a fifth.

<margin>77</margin>
One of the **ancients** reports that in **Lydia**, near **Pergamus** <note>an ancient Greek city in modern-day Turkey</note>, certain **workmen** fled into **caves** during a time of **war**. The enemies blocked the mouths of the **caves**, and the men starved to death. A long time later, their bones were found along with some vessels they had brought with them. The vessels were full of **water**, and that water was thicker and closer to ice than common **water**.

This is a notable example of **condensation** and **hardening** <term>induration: the process of becoming hard</term> caused by being **buried underground** (in **caves**) for a long time. It also seems to be an example of the **conversion** of **air** into **water**, assuming any of those vessels were empty when left there. Therefore, try hanging a small **bladder** in **snow**, another in **saltpeter** <note>original: "nitre"</note>, and similar...

<margin>78</margin>
It is reported by very reliable sources that in the *East Indies*, if you leave an open tub of *water* in a room where *cloves* are stored, the water will be drawn dry within twenty-four hours, even if it stands at some distance from the *cloves*. In the countryside, people often deceitfully place pails of *water* nearby when their *wool* is newly shorn to increase the weight of the *wool*. However, it may be that the heat remaining in the *wool* from the sheep's body, or the heat generated by the *wool* being packed closely together, helps to draw in the watery vapor. But that has nothing to do with the actual transformation <note>original: "version"</note> of air into water.

<margin>79</margin>
It is also credibly reported that newly shorn *wool*, which happened to be laid upon a *container* of *verjuice* <note>original: "veriuyce"; the acidic juice of unripe grapes or other sour fruit</note>, eventually drank up a large portion of the *verjuice*. This occurred even though the container was completely intact without any *flaws* and the bunghole was not open. In this instance, we should also note (in passing) the *filtration* <note>original: "percolation"</note> or *oozing* <note>original: "suing"</note> of the *verjuice* through the wood. Since *verjuice* would never pass through wood on its own, it seems it must first turn into a kind of vapor before it can pass through.

<margin>80</margin>
It is especially important to note the *cause* that helps the *transformation* <note>original: "version"</note> of *air* into *water* when the *air* is not in bulk, but instead subtly mingled with *physical matter* <note>original: "tangible bodies"</note>. As has been partly mentioned before, this happens because *physical matter* has a natural "antipathy" toward *air*. If these bodies find any *liquid body* that is denser nearby, they will draw it in. After they have drawn it in, they will condense it further and essentially incorporate it. 

For we see that a *sponge*, *wool*, *sugar*, or a *woollen cloth*, when only partially placed in *water* or *wine*, will draw the *liquor* upward, beyond the level where the *water* or *wine* reaches. We also see that *wood*, *lute strings*, and similar items swell in *moist seasons*. This is shown by the *breaking* of the *strings*, the *difficulty of turning* the *tuning pegs*, the *sticking* of drawers <note>original: "hard drawing forth of boxes"</note>, and the *sticking* of wooden doors <note>original: "opening of wainscot doores"</note>. This is a kind of *absorption* <note>original: "infusion"</note>, much like soaking wood in water to make it swell—as we see when we fill the *cracks* <note>original: "chops"</note> in wooden bowling balls by laying them in water. However, the part of these *experiments* concerning *attraction* will be reserved for the specific section titled *Attraction*.

<margin>81</margin>
There is also a *transformation* <note>original: "version"</note> of *air* into *water* seen in the *sweating* of *marbles* and other *stones*, and in *wooden paneling* <note>original: "wainscot"</note> before and during moist weather. This must be caused either by some *moisture* the object itself releases, or else by the *moist air* thickening against the hard body. It is clearly the latter. We see that *wood painted with oil colors* will gather droplets on a moist night sooner than bare wood. This is caused by the *smoothness* and *density*, which prevents any of the vapor from entering; instead, it turns the vapor back and thickens it into dew. We also see that *breathing* upon a *mirror* <note>original: "glasse"</note> or any smooth body creates a dew. And on *frosty mornings* (those we call *rime frosts*), you shall find drops of dew upon the...

<margin>Experiments in groups concerning the hardening of bodies.</margin>
*Induration* <note>original: "Induration"; the process of a substance becoming hard</note>, or *Lapidification* <note>original: "Lapidification"; the process of turning into stone</note>, of substances more soft is likewise another degree of *condensation*, and it is a great *alteration* in nature. The achieving and accelerating of this is very worthy to be investigated. It is effected by three means. The first is by *cold*, whose property is to *condense* and compress <note>original: "constipate"; to pack the parts of a substance closely together</note>, as has been said. The second is by *heat*, which is not the cause directly but by consequence; for the *heat* does thin <note>original: "attenuate"</note> a body and, by thinning it, sends forth the *spirit* <note>In early modern science, "spirits" were the volatile, active fluids or gases contained within all matter</note> and moister part of a body. Upon that, the more coarse of the tangible parts do contract and set themselves together—both to avoid a *vacuum* (as they call it) and also to fortify <note>original: "munite"</note> themselves against the force of the *fire* which they have suffered. And the third is by *assimilation*, when a hard body makes a soft one like itself by being touching it.

The examples of *hardening*, taking them as they come, are many: such as the generation of *stones* within the earth, which at the first are but raw earth or clay. The same is true of *minerals*, which no doubt come at first from solidified <note>original: "Concrete"</note> juices which afterward harden. So too of *porcelain*, which is an artificial cement buried in the earth a long time; and so the making of *brick* and *tile*. Also the making of *glass* from a certain sand and fern roots <note>original: "Brake-Roots"</note> and some other matters. Also the *exudations* <note>substances that ooze out</note> of *quartz* <note>original: "Rock-Diamonds"</note> and *crystal*, which harden

<margin>83</margin> Regarding *hardenings* <note>original: "Indurations"</note> caused by *cold*, there are few trials of it. We have no strong or intense *cold* here on the surface of the *earth*, being so near the beams of the *sun* and the *heavens*. The most likely trial is using *snow* and *ice*. Just as *snow* and *ice*—especially when assisted and their *cold* intensified <note>original: "actuated"</note> by *nitre* <note>saltpeter</note> or *salt*—will turn *water* into *ice* within a few hours, so it may be that it will turn *wood* or *stiff clay* into *stone* over a longer time. Therefore, place a piece of *wood* or a piece of *tough clay* into a *conserving pit* <note>a storage pit or ice house</note> of *snow* and *ice* (adding some quantity of *salt* and *nitre*) and let it lie for a month or more.

<margin>84</margin> Another trial is by *mineral waters* <note>original: "Metalline waters"</note>, which have an actual *coldness* in them. Therefore, put *wood* or *clay* into *smith's water* <note>water used by blacksmiths to quench hot iron</note> or other *mineral waters*, and see whether it will not harden in a reasonable amount of time. However, I mean *mineral waters* that come from washing or quenching, and not *strong waters* <note>acids</note> that come by dissolution, for they are too corrosive to solidify <note>original: "consolidate"</note>.

<margin>85</margin> It has already been found that there are some *natural spring waters* that will *turn wood into stone* <note>original: "Inlapidate wood"</note>. You may see a single piece of *wood* where the part above the *water* remains *wood*, while the part under the *water* is turned into a kind of *gravelly stone*. It is likely those *waters* have some *mineral mixture*; however, a more particular inquiry should be made into them. It is certain that an *egg* was found after lying many years at the bottom of a *moat*, where the *earth* had somewhat overgrown it. This *egg* had reached the *hardness* of a *stone*, yet the *colors* of the *white* and *yolk* were perfect, and the *shell* shone in small grains like *sugar* or *alabaster*.

<margin>86</margin> There is another experience of *hardening* <note>original: "Induration"</note> by *cold* that is already well-known: *metals* themselves are hardened by frequent *heating* and *quenching* in *cold water*. This is because *cold* always works most powerfully upon *heat* that came before it.

<margin>87</margin> Regarding *hardening* <note>original: "Induration"</note> by *heat*, it must be considered that *heat*, by evaporating <note>original: "Exhaling"</note> the moister parts, either hardens the body (as in *bricks*, *tiles*, etc.) or, if the *heat* is more fierce, makes the coarser part itself run and melt. We see this in the making of ordinary *glass*, and in the *vitrification* <note>the process of turning into glass</note> of *earth* (as seen in the inner parts of *furnaces*), and in the *vitrification* of *brick* and *metals*. In the former case—hardening by baking without melting—the *heat* has several stages: first, it *hardens*; then it makes the object *fragile*; and lastly, it *turns it to ash* <note>original: "Incinerate"</note> and *burns it to powder* <note>original: "Calcinate"</note>.

But if you desire to achieve *hardening* with *toughness* and less *fragility*, a middle way should be taken. This is something *Aristotle* <note>Ancient Greek philosopher whose theories on the elements and physical properties dominated science until the early modern period</note> noted well, but it should be thoroughly verified. It involves cooking <note>original: "decoct"</note> *bodies*...

For if they are bodies into which the water will enter, then long boiling will <term>soften</term> <note>original: "Seething, will rather Soften than indurate them"</note> rather than harden them, as has been tried with <term>eggs</term>, etc. Therefore, softer bodies must be put into bottles, and the bottles hung in boiling water with the mouths open above the water so that no water may get in. By this means, the "virtual" heat of the water will enter—a heat that will not make the body <term>scorched</term> <note>original: "adust"</note> or fragile—while the substance of the water itself will be shut out. 

We conducted this experiment, and it turned out as follows: It was tried with a piece of <term>limestone</term> <note>original: "Free-stone"</note> and with <term>pewter</term> placed directly into the water. We found the limestone absorbed some water, for it was softer and easier to scrape than a piece of the same stone kept dry. But the pewter, into which no water could enter, became whiter—more like silver—and much less flexible. 

We also put a good pellet of <term>clay</term>, a piece of <term>cheese</term>, a piece of <term>chalk</term>, and a piece of <term>limestone</term> into an earthen bottle, positioned as described before. The clay came out with almost the hardness of stone. The cheese was likewise very hard and difficult to cut, and the chalk and limestone were much harder than they were before. The color of the clay did not shift at all toward the color of <term>brick</term>, but rather toward white, as in ordinary sun-drying. 

Note that all the previous trials were conducted by boiling over a good hot fire, replenishing the water as it evaporated with more hot water. However, the boiling lasted for only twelve hours. It is likely that the experiment would have been more effective if the boiling had continued for two or three days, as we prescribed earlier.

<margin>89</margin>
Regarding <term>assimilation</term> <note>original: "Assimilation"; the process by which a substance transforms surrounding matter into its own likeness or substance</note> (for there is a degree of assimilation even in inanimate bodies), we see examples of it in certain stones in clay soils, lying near the surface where pebbles are found. In these, you can clearly see various pebbles gathered together with a crust of <term>cement</term> or stone between them that is as hard as the pebbles themselves. It would be useful to conduct an intentional trial by taking clay and embedding many pebbles closely together to see whether, over time, it will become harder than another lump of the same clay in which no pebbles are set. We also see that in the ruins of old walls, especially toward the bottom, the <term>mortar</term> becomes as hard as the brick. We see, too, that the wood on the sides of wine vessels gathers a crust of <term>tartar</term> harder than the wood itself, and likewise, <term>scales</term> <note>dental plaque or calculus</note> grow on teeth that are harder than the teeth themselves.

<margin>90</margin>
Hardening by assimilation appears most of all in the bodies of trees and living creatures. For no nourishment that the tree or the living creature receives is as hard as wood, bone, or horn; rather, it is hardened afterward through <term>assimilation</term>.

# Natural History

...we may see great *Axioms of Nature* <note>fundamental principles or laws of the natural world</note> through small and humble *instances*. The *speedy consumption* <note>original: "Depredation"</note> of *watery moisture* by the *air*, and the *transformation* <note>original: "Version"</note> of that moisture into *air*, appears most visibly in the sudden clearing or vanishing of a little *cloud* of *breath* or *vapor* from *glass*, the *blade* of a *sword*, or any such polished body that does not at all retain or soak up the *moisture*. In these cases, the mist scatters and breaks up suddenly. 

But a similar *cloud*, if it were *oily* or *fatty*, will not clear away; not because it sticks faster, but because *air* preys upon *water*, while *flame* and *fire* prey upon *oil*. Therefore, to remove a spot of grease, people use a hot *coal* held over *brown paper* because *fire* works upon grease or *oil* just as *air* does upon *water*. We also see that *paper* or *wood* that has been oiled stays moist for a long time, but if they are *wet* with *water*, they dry or rot much sooner. The cause is that *air* interacts very little with the *moisture* of *oil*.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the *force of union*. 92</margin>

There is an admirable demonstration of the *force of union* <note>the tendency of matter to hold together</note> in that same trifling *instance* of the *little cloud* upon *glass*, *gems*, or *sword blades*. It shows how much this union, even in the smallest quantities and weakest bodies, contributes to preserving the current *form* and resisting a new one. For if you watch the clearing of that *cloud* closely, you shall see it always break up first at the edges and last in the middle. 

We see likewise that a large amount of *water* draws out the juice of a body soaked in it, but a small amount of water is instead soaked up by the body itself. This is a principal cause why, in operations upon *bodies* to *transform* or *alter* them, a trial in large quantities does not match a trial in small quantities. This deceives many people; for, as I said, the larger body resists any alteration of its *form* more strongly and requires far greater strength in the *active body* <note>the substance or force acting upon it</note> that intends to subdue it.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the *production of feathers and hairs of various colors*. 93</margin>

We have spoken before in the fifth *instance* about the cause of *iridescent colors* <note>original: "Orient Colours"</note> in *birds*, which is caused by the fineness of the "strainer" <note>the microscopic structure of the feathers</note>. We will now endeavor to turn that same *axiom* into a practical *work*. For this writing of our *Forest of Materials* <note>original: "Sylva Sylvarum"</note> is, strictly speaking, not just *natural history*, but a high kind of *natural magic*. It is not merely a description of nature, but a way of harnessing nature to create great and strange works. 

Try, therefore, anointing *pigeons* or other *birds* while they are still in their downy stage, or *puppies* <note>original: "Whelpes"</note> after cutting their hair as short as possible, or some other beast, with an ointment that is not harmful to the skin but will harden and stick very closely. Then see whether it will alter the colors of the *feathers* or *hair*. 

It is commonly accepted that *pulling off* the first *feathers* of *birds* entirely will make the new ones come out *white*. It is certain that *white* is a "meager" color, appearing where moisture is scarce. Similarly, *blue violets* and other *flowers* turn pale and *white* if they are starved. *Birds* and *horses* turn *white* from age or scars, and the *grey hairs* <note>original: "Hoare Haires"</note> of men come about for the same reason. Therefore, in *birds*, it is very likely that the *feathers* that...

# Natural History

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the nourishment of living creatures before they are brought forth. 94</margin>

...come first, will many times be of diverse colors, according to the nature of the *bird*; for the skin is more porous. But when the skin is more shut and closed, the feathers will come *white*. This is a good experiment, not only for producing *birds* and *beasts* of strange *colors*, but also for revealing the *nature* of *colors* themselves—identifying which of them require a finer porosity <note>the quality of having tiny spaces or holes</note> and which a coarser one.

It is a work of *Providence* <note>divine care or guidance</note> that has been accurately observed by some: that the *yolk* of the *egg* contributes little to the *generation* <note>the initial formation and shaping</note> of the *bird*, but only to its *nourishment*. For if a *chicken* is opened when it is newly hatched, you shall find much of the *yolk* remaining. It is necessary that *birds*, which are formed outside the female's *womb*, have both the *matter* of *nourishment* and the *matter* of *generation* for the *body* within the *egg*. After the *egg* is laid and severed from the *body* of the *hen*, it receives no more nourishment from the hen, but only a quickening *heat* when she sits upon it. However, *beasts* and *men* do not need the source of *nourishment* within themselves because they are shaped within the *womb* of the *female* and are nourished continually from her *body*.

<margin>Experiments in consort <note>grouped experiments</note> concerning sympathy and antipathy <note>natural attractions or repulsions between things</note> for medicinal use. 95</margin>

It is an ancient <note>original: "inveterate"</note> and accepted opinion that *cantharides* <note>dried beetles, also known as Spanish Fly, used in medicine to cause blistering</note> applied to any part of the *body* affect the *bladder* and cause it to ulcerate if they remain on for long. It is likewise accepted that a kind of *stone* brought out of the *West Indies* <note>likely jade or nephrite, which was historically believed to treat kidney ailments</note> has a peculiar power to move *gravel* <note>small kidney stones or sediment</note> and to dissolve the *stone*. It is so much so that when merely laid against the wrist, it has so forcefully sent down *gravel* that *men* have been glad to remove it, it was so violent.

<margin>96</margin>

It is accepted and confirmed by daily *experience* that the *soles* of the *feet* have a great *affinity* with the *head* and the *opening* <note>original: "mouth"</note> of the *stomach*. As we see, *going wet-shod* <note>walking with wet shoes or feet</note> affects both, for those who are not used to it. *Applications* of hot *powders* to the *feet* first thin and then dry the *rheum* <note>excessive mucus or discharge from the nose and throat</note>. Therefore, a *physician* whom a *man* should consider *mystical* <note>meaning he uses hidden or symbolic knowledge</note> prescribes for the *cure* of *rheum* that a *man* should walk *continually* upon a *chamomile alley*—meaning that he should put *chamomile* within his *socks*. Likewise, *pigeons' bleeding* <note>the application of freshly killed pigeons or their blood to the body, a common folk remedy thought to "draw out" sickness</note> applied to the *soles* of the *feet* eases the *head*. And *soporiferous* <note>sleep-inducing</note> *medicines* applied to them provoke *sleep*.

<margin>97</margin>

It seems that just as the *feet* have a *sympathy* with the *head*, so the *wrists* and *hands* have a *sympathy* with the *heart*. We see the *affects* <note>feelings</note> and *passions* of the *heart* and *spirits* are notably revealed by the *pulse*. It is often tested that the *juices* of *stock-gilliflowers*, *rose-campion*, *garlic*, and other things, when applied to the *wrists* and renewed, have cured long *agues* <note>fevers, especially those involving shivering fits like malaria</note>. I also believe that washing the *palms* of the *hands* with certain *liquors* does much good. In the *heats* of *agues*, it is beneficial to hold *eggs* of *alabaster* and *balls* of *crystal* in the *hands*. We shall speak more of these things when we handle the *title* of *sympathy* and *antipathy* in its proper *place*.

# Century 1.

<margin><insert>Experiment 98: A solitary experiment concerning the secret processes of nature.</insert></margin>

The knowledge of man (up to this point) has been limited by what can be seen. Consequently, whatever is invisible—whether because of the *fineness of the body* itself, the *smallness of its parts*, or the *subtlety of its motion*—is rarely investigated. And yet, these are the very things that principally govern nature. Without understanding them, you cannot make any true *analysis* or provide an accurate account of how nature proceeds. 

The *spirits* or *pneumaticals* <note>original: "Pneumaticals" — Bacon’s term for the active, gaseous, or vaporous substances he believed existed within all solid matter.</note> that exist in all *tangible bodies* are scarcely known. Sometimes people mistake them for *vacuums*, whereas they are actually the most active of bodies. Sometimes they mistake them for *air*, from which they differ greatly—as much as wine differs from water, or wood from earth. Sometimes they claim they are *natural heat* or a *portion of the element of fire*, even though some of them are raw and cold. And sometimes they claim they are merely the *virtues* and *qualities* of the *tangible parts* they can see, whereas these spirits are actually things in their own right. Furthermore, when people observe plants and living creatures, they call these spirits *souls*. Such superficial speculations are like optical toys <note>original: "Prospectives" — early optical devices or perspective paintings that create an illusion of depth.</note> that show internal scenes which are actually just paintings. 

This is not a matter of semantics, but is infinitely important in *nature*. For *spirits* are nothing more than a *natural body*, thinned out to a specific degree and contained within the *tangible parts of bodies* as if in an integument <note>original: "Integument" — a natural outer covering or skin.</note>. These spirits differ as much from one another as the *dense* or *tangible parts* do. They exist in all *tangible bodies* whatsoever, to a greater or lesser degree, and they are almost never at rest. From them and their *motions* proceed most of the *effects of nature*, including *drying, melting, digestion, ripening, rotting, the creation of life*, and more. 

As I have illustrated in my work *The Wisdom of the Ancients* <note>original: "Sapientia Veterum" — Bacon's 1609 book interpreting ancient myths as scientific and philosophical allegories.</note>, using the *fable* of *Proserpina*, in the kingdom of the underworld you will hear very little of the activities of *Pluto*, but much of *Proserpina*. This is because the *tangible parts in bodies* are sluggish things, and the *spirits* (in effect) do everything. 

As for the differences in the *tangible parts of bodies*, the industry of the *chemists* <note>original: "Chymists" — practitioners of alchemy and early chemistry.</note> has provided some insight by separating the *oily, crude, pure, impure, fine,* and *gross parts of bodies*, and so on. *Physicians* are also willing to acknowledge that *herbs* and *drugs* have diverse parts; for instance, that *opium* has a "stupefactive" <note>sleep-inducing</note> part and a heating part (one causing sleep, the other a subsequent sweat), and that *rhubarb* has purging parts and astringent <note>tissue-tightening</note> parts, etc. But this entire *investigation* is handled weakly and negligently. 

As for the more subtle differences in the *minute parts* and their arrangement in the body (which also has great effects), they are not addressed at all. Regarding the *motions of the minute parts of bodies*, which produce such great effects, they have not been observed because they are invisible and are not perceived by the eye; yet they can be grasped through experience. As *Democritus* said well when they accused him of claiming the world was made of the tiny dust motes seen in the sun: "The atom is proved to exist by the necessity of reason and experience, for no one has ever seen an atom" <note>original: "Atomus necessitate Rationis & Experientiae esse convincitur: Atomum enim nemo unquam vidit."</note>. Therefore, the internal commotion in the parts of solid bodies when they are compressed—which is the cause of all—

He critiques contemporary chemistry and medicine for failing to investigate these subtle motions and the arrangement of microscopic parts.</summary>

# Natural History:

The flight of bodies through the air and other **mechanical motions** (as has been partly touched upon before and shall be thoroughly handled in the proper place) are not seen at all. Nevertheless, if you do not know this or do not investigate it attentively and diligently, you will never be able to discern—much less produce—a number of **mechanical motions**. Furthermore, regarding **physical motions** within the enclosures of bodies, whereby the effects (which were mentioned before) pass between the **spirits** and the **tangible parts**—such as **drying** <note>original: "Arefaction" — the process of making something dry.</note>, **melting** <note>original: "Colliquation" — the process of melting or dissolving into liquid.</note>, **digestion** <note>original: "Concoction" — the "cooking" or internal processing of a substance by heat.</note>, **ripening**, etc.—these are not handled at all by current science. Instead, they are dismissed with the names of "Virtues," "Natures," "Actions," "Passions," and other such logical words.

<margin>
Experiment 96: A solitary experiment concerning the power of heat.
</margin>

It is certain that of all **powers in nature**, **heat** is the chief, both in the structure of **nature** and in the works of **art**. It is likewise certain that the effects of **heat** are most advanced when it works upon a body without loss or dissipation of the matter, for that always ruins the results <note>original: "betrayeth the Account" — misleads the calculation or spoils the experimental outcome.</note>. Therefore, it is true that the power of **heat** is best perceived in **distillations** that are performed in closed vessels and receptacles. 

Yet there is a higher degree of heat. Even though **distillations** keep the body in cells and cloisters without letting it escape, they still give space for bodies to turn into vapor, to return into liquid, and to separate one part from another. In this way, nature wanders freely <note>original: "Expatiate"</note>, even if it does not have full liberty, and so the true and **final** <note>original: "Ultime"</note> operations of **heat** are not achieved. 

But if bodies may be altered by **heat**, and yet no such back-and-forth of **thinning** <note>original: "Rarefaction"</note>, **thickening** <note>original: "Condensation"</note>, and **separation** is admitted, then it is likely that this **Proteus** <note>original: "Proteus" — a Greek sea god who could change his shape; used here to represent the fundamental, ever-changing nature of matter.</note> of **matter**, being held by the sleeves, will turn and change into many **transformations** <note>original: "Metamorphoses"</note>. 

Take, therefore, a **square vessel of iron** in the form of a cube, and let it have good thick and strong sides. Put into it a cube of **wood** that may fill it as closely as possible, and let it have a cover of iron at least as strong as the sides. Let it be well **sealed** <note>original: "Luted" — sealed with a clay or cement paste used by early chemists to make vessels airtight.</note> in the manner of the **chemists**. Then, place the **vessel** within burning coals, kept brightly kindled, for the space of a few hours. Then take the **vessel** from the **fire**, take off the cover, and see what has become of the **wood**. 

I suspect that since all **burning** <note>original: "Inflammation"</note> and **evaporation** are utterly prohibited, and the **body** is kept turned in upon itself, one of these two effects will follow: either the **body of the wood** will be turned into a kind of **amalgam** <note>original: "Amalagma" — a soft, paste-like mixture.</note> (as the **chemists** call it), or the finer part will be turned into **air** and the coarser part will stick—as if baked and crusted—upon the sides of the **vessel**, having become a denser matter than the **raw** wood itself. 

And for another trial, take also **water** and put it in a similar **vessel**, stopped as before. But use a gentler **heat**, and remove the vessel sometimes from the **fire**; and again, after some small time when it is cold, renew the **heating** of it. Repeat this **alternation** a few times. If you can once bring it to pass that the **water**, which is one of the simplest of bodies, is changed in color, odor, or taste...

<summary>Bacon criticizes the use of vague logical terms to describe physical processes and proposes an experiment using high heat in a perfectly sealed iron vessel to observe how matter transforms when it cannot escape or evaporate.</summary>

<margin>
Experiment Solitary, touching the impossibility of annihilation. 100

There is nothing more certain in nature than that it is impossible for any **body** <note>original: "Body" — a physical substance or piece of matter.</note> to be utterly **annihilated**. Just as it was the work of God's omnipotence to make **something from nothing**, so it requires the same omnipotence to turn **something into nothing**. 

Therefore, it is well said by an obscure writer of the **sect of the chemists** <note>original: "Chymists" — practitioners of alchemy and early chemistry.</note> that there is no better way to achieve the **strange transmutations** <note>original: "Transmutations" — the changing of one substance into another.</note> of bodies than to strive by all means to reduce them to nothing. In this is also contained a great secret for the **preservation of bodies** from change. For if you can prevent them from turning into **air** (because no air can reach them), and from merging into **adjacent bodies** (because they are utterly different in nature), and from creating a **rotation** and **circulation** within themselves, they will never change—no matter how perishable or mutable they are by nature. 

We see how **flies**, **spiders**, and the like find a **sepulcher in amber** that is more durable than the monument and embalming of the body of any king. And I believe the same would happen to bodies put into **mercury** <note>original: "Quick-siluer".</note>. But then they must be thin, like a leaf, a piece of paper, or parchment; for if they have a greater **thickness** <note>original: "Crassitude" — density or thickness.</note>, they will change within their own bodies even if they do not dissipate. There is nothing more certain in nature than that it is impossible for any **body** <note>original: "Body" — a physical substance or piece of matter.</note> to be utterly **annihilated**. ## Second Century.

<margin>Experiments in group regarding Music.</margin>
<image-desc>Large decorative drop-cap 'M' featuring architectural and floral motifs, with a small human figure visible in the upper scrollwork of the letter.</image-desc>
**Music** in its **practice** has been well pursued and in great variety. But in its **theory**—especially in providing the **causes** behind the practice—it has been very weak, having been reduced to certain mystical subtleties of no use and not much truth. We shall therefore, in our usual manner, join the contemplative and active parts together.

<margin>101</margin>
All **sounds** are either **musical sounds**, which we call **tones**, where there may be **harmony** and which sounds are always **equal** <note>Bacon uses "equal" to mean sounds with a regular, consistent vibration or pitch.</note>; such as singing, the sounds of stringed and wind instruments, the ringing of bells, etc. Or they are **immusical sounds**, which are always **unequal** <note>Meaning irregular vibrations or noise.</note>; such as the voice in speaking, all whisperings, all voices of beasts and birds (except for songbirds), all **percussions** <note>The sound of something being struck.</note> of stones, wood, parchment, or skins (as in drums), and countless others.

<margin>102</margin>
The **sounds** that produce **tones** always come from such **bodies** that are **equal** <note>Meaning uniform or consistent in their physical structure.</note> in their parts and pores—just as the sounds themselves are equal. These include the striking of metal, as in bells; of glass, as in the filling up of a **drinking glass**; of **air**, as in men's voices while they sing, in pipes, whistles, organs, stringed instruments, etc.; and of **water**, as in the **nightingale-pipes** <note>Small organ pipes that used water to create a warbling, bird-like sound.</note> of **regals** <note>A regal is a small, portable pipe organ that was popular in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note> or organs, and other **hydraulic instruments** <note>original: "Hydraulickes" — musical instruments powered or regulated by water.</note>; which

<sig>D 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: which</meta>

<summary>Bacon begins his study of acoustics by distinguishing between musical tones, which possess regular vibrations ("equality"), and non-musical noises. He argues that music theory has focused too much on mysticism and should instead focus on the physical causes of sound.</summary>
<keywords>music theory, acoustics, tones, harmony, percussion, regals, hydraulic organs, physics of sound</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the nature of "equal bodies" and how they produce musical tones. It specifically addresses the physics of stringed instruments and the natural mathematical structure of the musical octave.</meta>

<header>Natural History:</header>

...which the ancients <note>original: *Ancients*</note> had, and Nero valued so highly, but are now lost. And if anyone thinks that the **string** of a bow and the **string** of a viol <note>original: *Viall*; a stringed instrument played with a bow.</note> are not both **equal bodies**, yet still produce musical **tones**, he is mistaken. For the **sound** is not created between the bow or **plectrum** <note>A small tool used to pluck strings, like a pick.</note> and the string, but between the **string** and the **air**. It is no different than the sound created between the finger or quill and the string in other instruments. Thus, in effect, there are only three types of **percussions** <note>The striking of one body against another.</note> that create musical **tones**: the **percussions** of **metals** (including **glass** and similar materials), **percussions** of **air**, and **percussions** of water.

<margin>103</margin>
The **diapason** <note>original: *Diapason*; the interval of an octave.</note>, or **eighth note** in **music**, is the sweetest **concord** <note>A harmonious combination of sounds.</note>. It is effectively a **unison**, as we see in **lutes** that have their bass strings doubled with two strings—one an **octave** above the other—which sound as if they are a single **sound**. Every **eighth note** in an ascending scale (from eight to fifteen, from fifteen to twenty-two, and so on infinitely <note>original: *in infinitum*</note>) is merely a continuation of the **scales** of the **diapason**. The **cause** of this is obscure and has not been explained by anyone; therefore, it deserves deeper contemplation. It seems that air (which is the medium of **sounds**) allows for much variety in **sounds** that are not musical **tones** (which are all **unequal**, as previously mentioned). We see this in the **voices** of **living creatures**, and likewise in the **voices** of different **men** (for we can distinguish different **men** by their **voices**), and in the combination <note>original: *Conjugation*</note> of **letters** from which **articulate sounds** proceed, which are the most varied of all. But in the sounds we call **tones** (which are always **equal**), the **air** cannot take on such variety. Instead, it is forced to return to the same posture or shape, differing only in size and scale. We see that **geometric figures** can be made of **crooked** and **straight** lines in infinite variety where there is inequality. However, **circles**, **squares**, or **equilateral triangles** (which are all **figures** made of equal lines) can only differ in being larger or smaller.

<margin>104</margin>
It should be noted—to prevent anyone from thinking there is something mystical in this number **eight** that creates the **diapason**—that this count of **eight** is a traditional convention rather than a precise mathematical calculation. A true calculation should always involve division into equal portions. Now, in the **rise** of an **octave** (in **tones**), there are two semitones <note>original: *Beemolls* (flats) or *Halfe notes*.</note> involved. So, if you divide the **tones** equally, the **octave** consists of seven whole and equal **notes**. If you subdivide that into **half-notes** (as seen in the frets <note>original: *Stops*</note> of a **lute**), the number becomes **thirteen**.

<margin>105</margin>
Yet this much is true: in the ordinary rising and falling of the **human voice** (not measuring the **tone** by whole notes and half-notes, which is the equal measure), there naturally occur two semitones (as mentioned) between the **unison** and the **diapason**. This variation is natural. For if a man tries to raise or lower his **voice** strictly by **half-notes** (like the frets of a **lute**) or by whole **notes** alone without **halves** for the span of an **octave**, he will not be able to shape his **voice** to do it. This shows that after every three whole **notes**, **nature** requires, for all harmonic use, one **half-note** to be inserted.

<margin>106</margin>
It must be considered that whatever power <note>original: *Vertue*</note> exists in **numbers** for...

<summary>Bacon explores the physics of musical tones, arguing that the octave (diapason) is the most perfect harmony because of the "equal" nature of the air's vibration. He notes that the traditional seven-note scale is a natural necessity of the human voice rather than just an arbitrary mathematical choice.</summary>

<header>Century II.</header>

---

Contributing to the agreement <note>original: *Consent*</note> of **notes**, it should be attributed more to the preceding number than to the entire number itself. For instance, the sound returns after **six** or after **twelve** intervals; thus, the **seventh** or the **thirteenth** is not the primary factor, but rather the **sixth** or the **twelfth**. The **seventh** and the **thirteenth** are merely the limits and boundaries of the **recurrence** <note>original: *returne*</note>.

<margin>107</margin>
The harmonies <note>original: *Concords*</note> in **music** which are **perfect** or **semi-perfect** between the **unison** <note>two notes of the same pitch.</note> and the **octave** <note>original: *Diapaſon*</note> are: the **fifth**, which is the most **perfect**; the **third** next; and the **sixth**, which is harsher. Following the opinion of the ancients <note>original: *Ancients*</note>—as I and some others still do—there is also the **fourth**, which they call the *diatessaron* <note>original: *Diateſſaron*; the musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note>. As for the **tenth**, **twelfth**, **thirteenth**, and so on infinitely <note>original: *in infinitum*</note>, they are merely **recurrences** of the former—namely, of the **third**, the **fifth**, and the **sixth**—being an **octave** <note>original: *Eight*</note> higher than each respectively.

<margin>108</margin>
As for **discords**, the **second** and the **seventh** are the most unpleasant <note>original: *odious*</note> to the sense of **harmony** in all of music. One is just above the **unison**, and the other is just below the **octave**. This may show that **harmony** requires a sufficient <note>original: *competent*</note> distance between **notes**.

<margin>109</margin>
In **harmony**, if there is no **discord** with the **bass** <note>original: *Baſe*</note>, it does not disturb the **harmony**, even if there is a **discord** among the **higher parts**, provided the **discord** is not one of the **two** that are unpleasant. Therefore, the ordinary arrangement <note>original: *Conſent*</note> of **four parts** consists of an **octave**, a **fifth**, and a **third** relative to the **bass**. However, that **fifth** is a **fourth** to the **treble**, and the **third** is a **sixth**. The reason for this is that the **bass**, striking more air, overcomes and drowns out the **treble** (unless the **discord** is very unpleasant) and so hides a small imperfection. For we see that in one of the **lower strings** of a **lute**, the sound of the **treble** does not ring out, nor does any mixed sound; only the sound of the **bass** is heard.

<margin>110</margin>
We have no **music** using **quarter-notes** <note>intervals smaller than a half-step or semitone.</note>, and it may be that they are not capable of **harmony**; for we see that even the **half-notes** themselves are only used occasionally <note>original: *interpoſe ſometimes*</note>. Nevertheless, we have some **slides** or ornaments <note>original: *Reliſhes*</note> of the voice or strings that are, as it were, continued without distinct **notes** from one **tone** to another, rising or falling, which are delightful.

<margin>111</margin>
The causes of what is **pleasing** or **unpleasant** <note>original: *Ingrate*</note> to the **hearing** may be clarified by what is **pleasing** or **unpleasant** to the **sight**. There are two things pleasing to the **sight** (leaving aside **pictures** and **shapes**, which are only secondary objects that please or displease based on memory): these two are **colors** and **order**. The pleasure of **color** corresponds with the **pleasing** of any **single tone** to the ear, but the pleasure of **order** corresponds with **harmony**. Therefore, we see how ornamental garden patterns <note>original: *Garden-knots*</note>, the decorative carvings <note>original: *Frets*</note> of houses, and all equal and well-matched figures (such as **globes**, **pyramids**, **cones**, **cylinders**, etc.) please us, whereas unequal **figures** are merely deformities. Both of these **pleasures**—that of the **eye** and that of the **ear**—are simply the effects of **equality**, **good proportion**, or **correspondence**. So, without question, **equality** and **correspondence** are the **causes** of **harmony**. But to find the **proportion** of that **correspondence** is more difficult <note>original: *abstruse*</note>; nevertheless, we shall say more about it (when we discuss **tones**) during the general inquiry into **sound**.

# Natural History:

<margin>112</margin>
Musical **tones** are not as effective at inducing **sleep** as certain other **sounds**, such as the **wind**, the **purling of water**, the **humming of bees**, or the **sweet voice** of someone reading, and so on. The **cause** of this is that **tones**, because they are steady <note>original: "Equall"</note> and do not fade away <note>original: "slide not"</note>, strike and alert the **senses** more than those other sounds. Excessive **attention** hinders sleep.

<margin>113</margin>
There are in **music** certain **figures or tropes** <note>rhetorical devices or patterns</note> that almost correspond with the **figures of rhetoric**, as well as with the **emotions** <note>original: "Affections"</note> of the **mind** and the other **senses**. First, the **division** <note>a style of melodic decoration involving rapid short notes</note> and **quavering** <note>trills or vibrato</note>, which are so pleasing in **music**, correspond with the **glittering of light**, such as **moonbeams** playing upon a **wave**. Again, the **falling from a discord to a concord**, which creates great **sweetness** in **music**, corresponds with **emotions** that are restored to a better state after some **dislikes**. It also corresponds with the **taste**, which is soon overwhelmed <note>original: "glutted"</note> by that which is only sweet. The **sliding from the close or cadence** <note>avoiding an expected musical resolution</note> corresponds with the **figure in rhetoric** which they call *beyond expectation* <note>original: "Preter Expectatum"</note>; for there is a pleasure even in **being deceived**. The **reports** <note>echo-like repetitions</note> and **fugues** correspond with the **figures in rhetoric** of **repetition and traduction** <note>the repetition of a word in a different form or grammatical case</note>. The **triplas** <note>triple time or rhythms</note> and the **changing of tempos** <note>original: "Times"</note> correspond with **changes of motions**, such as when **Galliard time** <note>a lively dance in triple time</note> and **Measure time** <note>a more stately, slower dance</note> are combined in the **medley** of a single **dance**.

<margin>114</margin>
It has been held and observed since ancient times that the **sense of hearing** and various **kinds of music** have the greatest **influence on character** <note>original: "Operation vpon Manners"</note>. They can **encourage men** and make them **warlike**, or make them **soft and effeminate**, or make them **grave**, or **lighthearted**, or **gentle** and inclined to **pity**, and so on. The **cause** is that the **sense of hearing** strikes the **spirits** <note>In 17th-century science, "spirits" were vaporous substances in the body that carried sensations and governed emotions</note> more immediately than the other **senses**, and more incorporeally than **smelling**. For the senses of **sight, taste, and feeling** have **organs** that do not provide such instant and immediate **access** to the **spirits** as **hearing** does. And as for **smelling**—which indeed also acts immediately upon the **spirits** and is powerful as long as the **fragrant object** <note>original: "Obiect Odorate"</note> is present—it works through the **communication of the breath or vapor of the object**. But **harmony**, entering easily and not mixing with anything else, and arriving with a **perceptible motion**, does (through the habit of frequently **affecting the spirits** and **putting them into a certain posture**) significantly alter the **nature of the spirits**, even after the **object** is removed. Therefore, we see that **tunes** and **airs**, by their very **nature**, have within themselves certain **affinities** with the **emotions**. There are **merry tunes, doleful tunes, solemn tunes, tunes** that incline men's minds to **pity, warlike tunes**, and so on. Thus, it is no wonder if they alter the **spirits**, considering that **tunes** have a **predisposition** for the **motion of the spirits** within themselves. However, it has been noted that although this variety of **tunes** disposes the **spirits** to a variety of **passions** matching them, **music** generally feeds whatever **disposition of the spirits** it already finds. We also see that various **airs and tunes** please different **nations and persons** according to the **sympathy** they have with their specific **spirits**.

*Perspective* <note>The study of optics and how light behaves.</note> has been investigated with some diligence; and so has the *nature of sounds*, in a way, as far as it concerns *music*. But the *nature of sounds* in general has been only superficially observed. It is one of the most subtle parts of nature. Furthermore, I practice as I advise: which is, after a long inquiry into physical things <note>original: "Things, Immerse in Matter"</note>, to introduce some subject that is non-physical <note>original: "Immateriate"</note> or less physical, such as this study of *sounds*. This is done so that the *intellect* may be *corrected* <note>original: "Rectified"</note> and not become biased <note>original: "Partiall"</note> by only considering solid matter.

<margin>115</margin>
It is first to be considered what *great motions* there are in nature that occur without *sound* or *noise*. The *heavens* turn in a most rapid motion without any *noise* perceived by us; though in some *dreams* <note>A reference to the ancient Pythagorean theory of the "Music of the Spheres," which suggested the planets made music as they moved.</note> they have been said to make an excellent *music*. Likewise, the motions of *comets* and *fiery meteors* (such as *shooting stars* <note>original: *Stellæ Cadentes*</note>, etc.) yield no *noise*. And if it is thought that it is the great distance from us that prevents the *sound* from being heard, we see that *lightnings* and *flashes of light* <note>original: "Coruscations"</note>, which are near at hand, yield no *sound* either. And yet in all of these, there is a striking <note>original: "Percussion"</note> and division of the *air*. 

The *winds* in the *upper region* (which move the clouds above—which we call the *drifting clouds* <note>original: "the Racke"</note>—and are not felt below) pass without *noise*. The *lower winds* on a plain make no *noise* unless they are strong; but among *trees*, the *noise* of such *winds* will be perceived. And *winds* (generally) when they make a *noise*, always make it unevenly, rising and falling, and sometimes (when they are violent) trembling at the peak of their blast. *Rain* or *hail* falling (even violently) yields no *noise* while passing through the *air*, until it falls upon the ground, water, houses, or the like. 

*Water* in a *river* (even in a swift stream) is not heard in the channel, but runs in silence if it is of any depth; but the very same *stream* over *shallows* of *gravel* or *pebble* will be heard. And *waters*, when they beat upon the shore, or are restricted <note>original: "straitned"</note> (as in the falls of bridges), or are dashed against themselves by *winds*, give a roaring *noise*. Any piece of *timber* or *hard body* being pushed forward by another touching <note>original: "Contiguous"</note> body without knocking, gives no *noise*. Likewise, *bodies* resting one upon another—though the *upper body* presses the *lower body* down—make no *noise*. 

So the *motion* in the *minute parts* of any *solid body* (which is the principal cause of *violent motion*, though unobserved) passes without *sound*; for that *sound* which is sometimes heard is produced only by the breaking of the *air*, and not by the internal movement <note>original: "Impulsion"</note> of the parts. Thus it is manifest: that where the *leading body* <note>original: "Anteriour Body"</note> gives way as fast as the *following body* <note>original: "Posterior"</note> moves forward, it makes no *noise*, no matter how great or swift the *motion*.

<margin>116</margin>
Open *air* in a large space <note>original: "at Large"</note> makes no *noise* unless it is sharply struck <note>original: "percussed"</note>, as in the sound of a string where *air* is struck by a hard,

...and a stiff body; and with a sharp release <note>original: "loose"</note>. For if the string is not tightened <note>original: "strained"</note>, it makes no **noise**. But where the **air is confined** <note>original: "pent"</note> and constricted, there breath or other blowing (which carries only a gentle **impact** <note>original: "percussion"</note>) suffices to create **sound**, as in **pipes** and **wind instruments**. But then you must note that in **recorders**, which operate with a gentle breath, the **hollow** <note>original: "concave"</note> of the **pipe**—were it not for the **fipple** <term>fipple: the wooden plug in the mouthpiece of a recorder that narrows the airway to create sound</term> that constricts the air much more than a **plain hollow tube**—would yield no **sound**. As for other **wind instruments**, they require a forceful breath, such as **trumpets**, **cornets**, **hunters' horns**, etc. This is evident by the puffed-out cheeks of the person who blows <note>original: "windeth"</note> them. **Organs** also are blown with a strong wind by bellows. And note again that some kinds of **wind instruments** are blown at a small hole in the side, which constricts the breath at the first entrance; this is especially effective because of their **cross-piece** <note>original: "traverse"</note> and **plug** <note>original: "stop"</note> above the hole, which performs the **fipple’s role**. This is seen in **flutes** and **fifes**, which will not produce **sound** by a blast at the end as **recorders**, etc., do. Likewise, in all **whistling**, you contract the mouth; and to make it sharper, men sometimes use their finger. But in **open air**, if you throw a stone or a dart, they give no sound. Neither do **bullets**, unless they happen to be slightly hollowed during casting, which hollow space confines the **air**. Nor do **arrows**, unless their feathers are ruffled, which likewise traps the **air**. As for **small whistles** or shepherds' **oaten pipes**, they give a **sound** because of their extreme narrowness, whereby the **air** is more confined than in a wider **pipe**. Again, the **voices** of **men** and living creatures pass through the throat, which confines the breath. As for the **Jew's harp**, it is a sharp impact; and besides, it has the advantage of confining the **air** in the mouth.

<margin>117</margin>
**Solid bodies**, if they are **struck very softly** <note>original: "very softly percussed"</note>, give no **sound**; as when a man treads very softly upon **floorboards**. Likewise, **chests** or **doors** in fair weather, when they open easily, give no **sound**. And **cartwheels** do not squeak when they are lubricated <note>original: "liquored"</note>.

<margin>118</margin>
The **flame** of **tapers** or **candles**, though it is a swift motion and cuts through <note>original: "breaketh"</note> the **air**, yet passes without **sound**. **Air in ovens**, though (no doubt) it does (as it were) boil and expand <note>original: "dilate"</note> itself and is reflected <note>original: "repercussed"</note>, yet it is without **noise**.

<margin>119</margin>
**Flame struck by air** gives a **noise**, as in blowing a fire with bellows—a greater noise than if the bellows were blowing upon the **air** itself. And likewise, **flame striking the air strongly** (as when a flame suddenly catches and expands) gives a **noise**. Thus, **large flames**, while one pushes against the other, give a bellowing **sound**.

<margin>120</margin>
There is a rumor <note>original: "conceit runneth abroad"</note> that there exists a **white powder** <term>white powder: a legendary "silent" gunpowder often discussed in 17th-century science</term> which will discharge a gun <note>original: "peece"</note> without **noise**. This would be a dangerous discovery <note>original: "experiment"</note> if it were true, for it might allow for secret murders. But it seems impossible to me; for if the **confined air** is driven out and strikes the **open air**, it will certainly make a **noise**. As for the **white powder** (if any such thing exists that might extinguish or deaden the **noise**),

It is likely to be a mixture of **saltpeter** <note>original: "Petre"</note> and **sulfur**, without **charcoal** <note>original: "Coale"</note>. For saltpeter alone will not take fire. And if anyone thinks that the **sound** may be extinguished or deadened by discharging the **compressed air** <note>original: "Pent Aire"</note> before it comes to the **muzzle** <note>original: "Mouth"</note> of the **gun** <note>original: "Peece"</note> and to the **open air**, that is unlikely. For it will make more divided **sounds**; for instance, if you were to make a hollow cross-barrel through the barrel of a gun, it would produce several sounds, both at the muzzle and at the sides. 

But I believe that if it were possible to ensure that no **air was compressed** at the muzzle of the gun, the bullet might fly with little or no **noise**. For first, it is certain there is no **noise** in the impact of the **flame** upon the **bullet**. Next, the **bullet**, in piercing through the **air**, makes no **noise**, as has been said. And then, if there is no **compressed air** that strikes upon **open air**, there is no cause for **noise**; and yet the flying of the **bullet** will not be stopped. For that **motion** (as has been often said) is in the parts of the **bullet** and not in the **air**. Thus, a trial must be made by taking some small **hollow** <note>original: "Concaue"</note> of **metal**, no larger than you intend to fill with powder, and laying the bullet in the opening of it, halfway out into the **open air**.

<margin>121</margin>
I heard it affirmed by a man who was a great dealer in **secrets**—though he was quite boastful—that there was a **conspiracy** (which he himself hindered) to have killed **Queen Mary**, sister to **Queen Elizabeth**, with a **burning glass** <term>burning glass: a large convex lens used to focus the sun's rays to ignite objects</term> while she walked in **Saint James's Park**, from the lead roof of the house. But this much (no doubt) is true: that if **burning glasses** could be brought to a great strength (as people generally talk of **burning glasses** that are able to burn a **navy**), the **impact** <note>original: "Percussion"</note> of the **air** alone by such a **burning glass** would make no **noise**, no more than is found in **flashes of light** <note>original: "Coruscations"</note> and **lightnings** without **thunders**.

<margin>122</margin>
I suppose that the **impression** of the **air** with **sounds** requires a certain amount of time to be conveyed to the **senses**, just like the **impression** of **visual images** <note>original: "Species visible"</note>; otherwise, they will not be heard. And therefore, as the bullet **moves** so **swiftly** that it is **invisible**, so the same **swiftness** of **motion** makes it **inaudible**. For we see that the perception of the **eye** is quicker than that of the **ear**.

<margin>123</margin>
