[Thinkers] have come up with a clever **term** <note>original: "Expression"</note>, by way of a **technical term** <note>original: "Word of Art"</note>; that **term** is commonly accepted, though it is empty of **substance**. This **notion** <note>original: "Conceit"</note> of **elision** <term>elision: the theoretical "cutting" or sudden compression and displacement of air molecules</term> is clearly shown to be false by the fact that the **sound** of a **bell**, **string**, or similar object continues to fade away for some time after the **impact** <note>original: "Percussion"</note>. But it stops immediately if the **bell** or **string** is touched and held still; whereas, if it were the **elision** of the **air** that made the **sound**, it could not be that touching the **bell** or **string** would so suddenly extinguish that motion caused by the **elision** of the **air**. This appears even more clearly when **chiming** with a hammer on the outside of a **bell**; for the **sound** will correspond to the inner hollow of the **bell**, whereas the **elision** or **thinning** <note>original: "Attenuation"</note> of the **air** can only occur between the **hammer** and the outside of the **bell**. Similarly, if it were an **elision**, a broad **hammer** and a **bodkin** <term>bodkin: a small, sharp, pointed tool</term> struck upon metal would produce a **different** <note>original: "diuers"</note> **tone** as well as a different **loudness**. But they do not; for though the **sound** of one is **louder** and the other **softer**, the **tone** is the same. Besides, in **echoes** (some of which are as loud as the **original voice**), there is no new **elision**, but only a **reflection** <note>original: "Repercussion"</note>. But what proves it most of all is that **sounds** are generated where there is no **air** at all. <note>Bacon likely refers here to sound traveling through solid objects or water, though his assertion that no air is present would be scientifically debated today.</note> But these and similar **notions**, once men have cleared their understanding by the light of experience, will scatter and break up like a mist.

<margin>125</margin>
It is certain that **sound** is not produced initially without some **physical movement** <note>original: "Locall Motion"</note> of the **air**, **flame**, or some other **medium**; nor is it produced without some **resistance**, either in the **air** or the **object struck**. For if there is merely a **yielding** <note>original: "Cession"</note>, it produces no **sound**, as has been said. And in this, **sounds** differ from **light** and **colors**, which pass through the **air** or other **bodies** without any **physical movement** of the **air**, either at the start or afterward. But you must carefully distinguish between the **physical movement** of the **air** (which is merely **the carrier of the cause** <note>original: "Vehiculum Causæ"</note>) and the **sounds** themselves conveyed in the **air**. Regarding the former, we see clearly that no **sound** is produced (not even by **air** itself against other **air**, as in **organs**, etc.) except with a perceptible **blast** of **air** and with some **resistance** from the **air** being struck. For even all **speech** (which is one of the gentlest **movements** of **air**) involves the expulsion of a little **breath**. And all **pipes** have a **blast** as well as a **sound**. We also see clearly that **sounds** are carried with the **wind**; therefore, **sounds** will be heard further with the **wind** than against the **wind**, and they likewise rise and fall with the **strengthening** or **weakening** <note>original: "Intention or Remission"</note> of the **wind**. But as for the **impression** of the **sound**, it is quite another thing; it is utterly without any perceptible **physical movement** of the **air**. In that respect, it resembles **visible forms** <note>original: "species visible"</note>. For after a **man** has **shouted** <note>original: "lured"</note> or a **bell** is rung, we cannot discern any perceptible **motion** at all in the **air** as long as the **sound** lasts, except only at the start. Nor does the **wind** (even though it carries a **voice**) confound any of the delicate and articulate **shapes** <note>original: "Figurations"</note> of the **air** in the variety of words by its own **motion**. But these effects are from the **physical movement of the air**, which is an **accompaniment of the sound** <note>original: "Concomitant of the Sound"</note> (as has been said), and not from the **sound** itself.

<margin>128</margin>
It has been anciently reported, and is still believed, that **extreme applause and shouting of people** assembled in great multitudes have so thinned <note>original: "rarified"</note> and broken the **air** that **birds** flying over have fallen down, the **air** being unable to support them. <margin>129</margin>
A very great **sound**, nearby, has struck many **deaf**; and at that **instant** they have felt, as it were, the breaking of a **skin** or **parchment** in their **ear**. And I myself, standing near a **loud** and shrill noise, suddenly felt a hurt as if something had broken or been dislocated in my **ear**; and immediately after, a **loud ringing** (not an ordinary singing or hissing, but far louder and different), so that I feared some **disease**. But after about half a quarter of an **hour**, it vanished. This **effect** may be truly attributed to the **sound**; for (as is commonly accepted) an **over-powerful object** destroys the **sense**. Moreover, **non-material forms** <term>spiritual species: a philosophical term for the way information like light or sound travels through a medium without moving the medium's bulk</term> (both **visible** and **audible**) will act upon the **sensory organs**, even though they do not move any other physical **body**.

<margin>130</margin>
In the **transmission** <note>original: "Delation"</note> **of sounds**, the **enclosure** of them preserves them and causes them to be heard further. The **cause** is that the **sound** spreads and is dissipated in the **open air**; but in such **hollows** <note>original: "Concaues"</note>, it is conserved and concentrated. Similarly, in a **piece of artillery**, if you speak into the **touch-hole** <term>touch-hole: the small vent in a cannon where the fuse is lit</term> and another person puts their **ear** to the **mouth** of the **cannon**, the **sound** passes and is heard far better than in the **open air**.

# Natural History:

It has been tested that in a long **tube** <note>original: "Trunke"</note> of about eight or ten feet, the **sound** is aided, even though both the **mouth** and the **ear** are a handful or more away from the ends of the **tube**. It is somewhat more aided when the **ear** of the **hearer** is near the end than when the **mouth** of the **speaker** is. It is also certain that a **voice** is heard better in a **room** from **outside** than **outside** from within the **room**.

<margin>131</margin>
As an **enclosure** that is **round** and **complete** preserves the **sound**, so does a **semi-concave** (a half-pipe or curved surface), though to a lesser degree. Therefore, if you divide a **tube** or a **cane** in two and one person speaks at one end while you lay your **ear** at the other, it will carry the **voice** further than in the open **air**. Indeed, even further: if it is not a full **half-pipe**, but if you do the same upon the **mast** of a **ship**, a **long pole**, or a **cannon** <note>original: "Peece of Ordnance"</note> (even if one speaks upon the surface of the **cannon** and not at any of the **openings**), the **voice** will be heard further than in the open **air**.

<margin>132</margin>
It should be tested how, and with what degree of disadvantage, the **voice** will be carried in a **horn**, which is an **arched** line; or in a **trumpet**, which is a **curved** <note>original: "Retorted"</note> line; or in some **pipe** that is **winding** <note>original: "Sinuous"</note>.

<margin>133</margin>
It is certain (despite what common opinion says) that **sounds** may be created without **air**, even though **air** is the most favorable **medium** <term>original: "Deferent"; the substance that carries or transmits sound</term> of **sounds**. Take a **vessel** of **water** and strike <note>original: "knap"</note> a pair of **tongs** together some depth within the **water**, and you shall hear the **sound** of the **tongs** well, and not much diminished; and yet there is no **air** present at all.

<margin>134</margin>
Take one **vessel** made of **silver** and another of **wood**, and fill each of them full of **water**. Then strike the **tongs** together as before, about a handful from the **bottom**, and you shall find the **sound** resonates much more from the **vessel of silver** than from that of **wood**. Yet, if there is no **water** in the **vessel** so that you strike the **tongs** in the **air**, you shall find no difference between the **silver** and **wooden vessel**. From this, besides the main point of creating **sound** without **air**, you may conclude two things: first, that the **sound** communicates with the **bottom** of the **vessel**; and second, that such a communication passes far better through **water** than **air**.

<margin>135</margin>
Strike any **hard bodies** together in the middle of a **flame**, and you shall hear the **sound** with little difference from the **sound** in the **air**.

<margin>136</margin>
The **pneumatical part** <term>pneumatical part: in Bacon's theory, the thin, airy, or gaseous substance contained within the pores of all solid matter</term>, which is in all **tangible bodies** and has some affinity with the **air**, performs (to some degree) the role of the **air**. For example, when you knock upon an **empty barrel**, the **sound** is created (in part) by the **air** on the outside and (in part) by the **air** on the inside; for the **sound** will be greater or lesser depending on whether the barrel is more empty or more full. But yet the **sound** also shares in the **spirit** <note>original: "Spirit"; refers to the volatile, active particles Bacon believed inhabited all matter</note> in the **wood** through which it passes from the outside to the inside. This is also what happens in the **chiming** of **bells** on the outside, where the **sound** also passes to the inside; and a number of other...

...other similar instances, which we shall speak of more when we handle the **transmission** <note>original: "Communication"</note> of **sounds**.

<margin>137</margin>
It is a very crude misunderstanding <note>original: "extreme Grossenesse"</note> to think (as we have partly touched upon before) that the **sound** in **strings** is made, or produced, between the **hand** and the **string**, or the **quill** and the **string**, or the **bow** and the **string**. For those are but **vehicles of motion** <note>original: "Vehicula Motus"</note>, mere pathways to the **creation** of the **sound**. The **sound** is actually produced between the **string** and the **air**, and that is not caused by any **shoving** <note>original: "Impulsion"</note> of the **air** from the first **motion** of the **string**, but by the **rebound** <note>original: "Returne or Result"</note> of the **string**—which was stretched by the touch—to its former place. This **motion** of **rebound** is quick and sharp, whereas the first motion is soft and dull. Similarly, the **bow** "tortures" the **string** continually, and thereby holds it in a constant **vibration** <note>original: "Trepidation"</note>.

Experiments in association <note>original: "in Consort"</note> concerning the **volume** <note>original: "Magnitude"</note>, **thinness** <note>original: "Exility"</note>, and **muffling** <note>original: "Damps"</note> of **sounds**.

</margin>
Take a **tube** <note>original: "Trunke"</note>, and let someone whistle at one end while you hold your ear at the other; you shall find the **sound** strikes so sharp that you can scarcely endure it. The cause is that **sound** naturally spreads out in a circle and so exhausts itself; but if the **sound**, which would otherwise scatter in **open air**, is forced to go entirely into a **channel** <note>original: "Canale"</note>, it must necessarily give greater force to the **sound**. Thus, you may note that **enclosures** do not only preserve **sound**, but also increase and sharpen it.

<margin>139</margin>
A **hunter's horn**, being wider at one end than at the other, increases the **sound** more than if the **horn** had a uniform **bore** <note>the hollow internal diameter</note>. The cause is that the **air** and **sound**, being first compressed at the smaller end and afterwards having more room to spread at the wider end, dilate themselves. In coming out, they strike more **air**, whereby the **sound** becomes louder and deeper <note>original: "Baser"</note>. Even **hunters' horns**, which are sometimes straight and not **curved** <note>original: "Oblique"</note>, are always wider at the lower end. This should also be tested with **pipes** made much **wider** at the lower end, or made with a **bulge** <note>original: "Belly"</note> toward the lower end that then narrows into a straight **hollow** <note>original: "Concave"</note> again.

The **cause** is the same as before: all **hollow spaces** <note>original: "Concaves"</note> that move from narrow to broad amplify the **sound** at the exit.

<margin>141</margin>
**Hawks' bells** <note>small round bells attached to a hunting bird's leg</note> that have holes in the sides give a greater ring than if the pellet struck upon brass in the **open air**. The cause is the same as the first instance of the **tube**: namely, that the sound enclosed within the sides of the **bell** comes out through the **holes** unspent and stronger.

# Natural History:

...extended in the open air. The *cause* is the same as the two preceding instances.

<margin>143</margin>
*Sounds* are heard better and at a greater distance in the *evening* or at *night* than at *noon* or during the *day*. The *cause* is that during the *day*, when the *air* is *thinner* <note>Bacon's theory: Heat thins the air, while cool night air is "thicker."</note> (no doubt), the *sound* pierces better; but when the *air* is *thicker* (as in the *night*), the *sound* wastes and spreads abroad less. This serves as a degree of *enclosure*. As for the *night*, it is also true that the general silence helps.

<margin>144</margin>
There are two kinds of *reflections* of *sounds*. The first occurs at a *distance*, which is the *echo*; in this, the *original sound* is heard distinctly, and the *reflection* is also heard distinctly. We shall speak of this later. The other kind occurs in *concurrence*; this is when the reflecting *sound* (the *reflection* being close at hand) returns immediately upon the *original*, and so does not repeat it <note>original: "iterateth it not"</note> but amplifies it. Therefore, we see that *music* sounds louder upon the water; and similarly, *music* is better in rooms that are wood-paneled <note>original: "Wainscotted"</note> than those with wall hangings <note>original: "Hanged"; referring to tapestries which absorb sound.</note>.

<margin>145</margin>
The *strings* of a lute, viol, or virginal <note>A rectangular harpsichord-like keyboard instrument.</note> produce a far greater *sound* because of the *soundhole* <note>original: "Knot"; referring to the decorative "rose" or carved soundhole in the soundboard.</note>, the *bridge* <note>original: "Board"</note>, and the *hollow body* underneath, than if there were only the *flat* of a *board* without that *hollow* and *soundhole* to let the upper air into the lower. The *cause* is the communication of the upper air with the lower, and the penning in of both to prevent them from being spent or dispersed.

<margin>146</margin>
An *Irish harp* has open air on both sides of the *strings*; it has the *hollow body* <note>original: "Concave or Belly"</note> at the end of the *strings* rather than along them. It creates a more resounding *sound* than a bandora, orpharion, or *cittern* <note>These are all various types of plucked, wire-strung instruments similar to guitars or lutes.</note>, which also have *wire strings*. I judge the *cause* to be that the open air on both sides helps, provided there is a *hollow body*, which is therefore best placed at the end.

<margin>147</margin>
In a *virginal*, when the *lid* is down, it makes a more faint <note>original: "exile"</note> *sound* than when the *lid* is open. The *cause* is that any *shutting in of air*, where there is no adequate vent, dampens the *sound*. This also supports the previous *instance*; for the *body* of the *lute* or *viol* does pen in the *air* somewhat.

<margin>148</margin>
There is a *church* at *Gloucester* (and as I have heard, the like is in some other places) where if you speak softly against a wall, another person shall hear your *voice* better a good way off than near at hand. Enquire more particularly into the structure of that place. I suppose there is some vault, hollow, or aisle behind the wall, and some passage to it towards the further end of that wall against which you speak; thus, the *voice* of the speaker slides along the wall and then enters a passage and communicates with the *air* of the *hollow*. The voice is preserved somewhat by the plain wall, but it is too weak to be audible until it has communicated with the *air* behind it.

<margin>149</margin>
Strike a *bowstring* and lay the *horn* of the *bow* near your *ear*; it will increase the *sound* and create a type of *tone*. The *cause* is that the sense organ, by reason of the close contact, is struck <note>original: "percuffed"; the catchword for the next page.</note>

<margin>151</margin>
I remember at *Trinity College* in *Cambridge*, there was an *upper chamber* which was thought to have a weak roof and was supported by an *iron pillar* the size of a man’s arm in the middle of the *room*. <margin>152</margin>
The *sound* made by *buckets* in a *well* when they touch the *water*, strike against the side of the *well*, or clash against each other—these *sounds* are deeper and fuller than if the same impact occurred in the *open air*. The cause is the trapping and enclosure of the air in the hollow of the *well*.

<margin>153</margin>
Barrels placed in a room under the floor of a *chamber* make all noises in that chamber fuller and more resonant.
*Thus, there are five general ways to achieve the amplification <note>original: "Maioration"</note> of sounds: Simple Enclosure; Enclosure with Expansion; Communication <note>Transmission through a solid body.</note>; Concurrent Reflection; and Proximity to the Ear.*

<margin>154</margin>
Regarding the *thinness* <note>original: "Exility"</note> of the *voice* or other *sounds*: It is certain that the *voice* passes through *solid* and *hard bodies* if they are not too thick. It also passes through *water*, which is likewise a very *dense body* <note>original: "Close Body"</note> that does not let in air. But then the *voice* or other *sound* is reduced by such passage to a great *weakness* or *thinness*. Therefore, if you block the *holes* of a *hawk's bell* <note>A small, spherical bell attached to a hunting hawk's leg.</note>, it will not *ring* but only make a flat noise or rattle. The same happens with the *Aëtites* <note>original: "Eagle's Stone"; a hollow geode with a loose stone inside that rattles when shaken.</note>, which has a small *stone* within it.

One would think that the *Sicilian poet* <note>Theocritus, a Greek poet of the 3rd century BCE</note> had knowledge of this *experiment*; for he says that *Hercules' page, Hylas*, went with a *water-pot* to fill it at a pleasant *fountain* near the *shore*, and that the *nymphs of the fountain fell in love with the boy and pulled him underwater*, keeping him alive. And when *Hercules* missed his *page*, he called him by his *name* so loudly that the whole shore rang with it; and *Hylas answered his master from within the water*. <margin>156</margin>
*In lutes and string instruments*, if you stop a *string* high (whereby it has less room to vibrate <note>original: "tremble"</note>), the *sound* is more *treble*, yet more dead.

<margin>157</margin>
Take two *saucers* and strike the edge of one against the bottom of the other within a *bucket of water*. You shall find that as you put the *saucers* lower and lower, the *sound* grows flatter, even while part of the *saucer* is above the *water*. But that *flatness of sound* is joined with a *harshness of sound*, which (no doubt) is caused by the irregularity <note>original: "inequality"</note> of the *sound* coming from the part of the *saucer* under the *water* and from the part above. But when the *saucer* is entirely under the *water*, the *sound* becomes clearer, but far lower, and as if the *sound* came from far away.

<margin>158</margin>
A *soft body* damps *sound* much more than a *hard* one. For instance, if a *bell* has *cloth* or *silk* wrapped around it, it deadens the *sound* more than if it were wrapped in *wood*. Therefore, in keyboard instruments <note>original: "Clericals"; likely referring to clavichords or virginals where the mechanical action or the strings are damped with cloth</note>, the *keys* are lined; and in *colleges*, they usually line the gaming pieces <note>original: "tablemen"; pieces for games like backgammon or checkers, lined with felt to reduce noise on the board</note>.

<margin>159</margin>
A *trial* was made with a *recorder* <note>a common Renaissance woodwind instrument</note> in these several manners: The bottom of it was set against the *palm of the hand*; stopped with *wax* all around; set against a *damask cushion*; thrust into *sand*; into *ashes*; into *water* (half an inch under the *water*); and close to the bottom of a *silver basin*; and in all these, the *tone* remained. But when the *bottom* of it was placed against a *woolen carpet*, a *lining of plush* <note>a rich fabric with a long pile</note>, a *lock of wool* (even if loosely applied), or against *snow*, the *sound* of it was quite deadened and became nothing but *breath*.

<margin>160</margin>
*Hot iron* does not produce as full a *sound* as when it is *cold*. For while it is hot, it appears to be softer and less resonant. Likewise, *warm water* makes a less full *sound* when it falls than *cold water* does. I believe it is softer and closer to the *nature of oil*, for it is more slippery, as may be perceived by the fact that it cleans <note>original: "scowreth"</note> better.

Take a pipe <note>original: "Trunke"; here meaning a hollow tube</note> the length of two *recorders* <note>a common Renaissance woodwind instrument</note>, with holes placed appropriately toward each end. Let two people play the same melody upon it in *unison*. Observe whether the *sound* is blurred <note>original: "confounded"</note>, amplified, or muffled. Similarly, let a *cross* be made of two hollow *pipes*; let two people speak or sing, one along the length and the other across the width. Let two others listen at the opposite ends and note whether the *sound* is blurred, amplified, or muffled. These two *examples* will also clarify the *mixing* of *sounds*, which we shall discuss later.

<margin>162</margin>
If *bellows* are used to blow air into the *hole* of a *drum*, and the *drum* is then struck, it makes the *sound* a little flatter, but there is no other apparent *alteration*. The *cause* is clear: partly because the bellows hinder the *escape* <note>original: "Issue"</note> of the *sound*, and partly because it makes the *air*, being compressed together, less able to move.

<margin>
Experiments in Group concerning the Loudness or Softness of Sounds, and their Travel at longer or shorter Distances.
163
164
</margin>
The *loudness* and *softness* of *sounds* is a thing distinct from the *magnitude* <note>volume or fullness</note> and *thinness* <note>original: "Exilitie"</note> of *sounds*. For a *bass string*, even if struck softly, produces a larger *sound*; but a *treble string*, if struck hard, will be heard much further away. The *cause* is that the *bass string* strikes more *air*, and the *treble* strikes less *air* but with a sharper *impact* <note>original: "percussion"</note>.

Therefore, the *strength* of the *impact* is a principal *cause* of the *loudness* or *softness* of *sounds*, such as in knocking harder or softer, blowing <note>original: "Winding"</note> a *horn* more strongly or weakly, or *ringing* a *hand-bell* harder or softer, etc. The *strength* of this *impact* depends as much, or more, on the *hardness* of the *body* being struck as on the *force* of the *body* doing the striking. For if you strike against a piece of *cloth*, it will produce a smaller *sound*; if against *wood*, a greater one; if against *metal*, a greater one still. Among *metals*, if you strike against *gold* (which is more pliable), it produces a flatter *sound*; if against *silver* or *brass*, it produces a more *ringing sound*. As for *air*, where it is strongly compressed <note>original: "pent"</note>, it acts like a *hard body*. Therefore, we see what a great *noise* is made when discharging a *gun* <note>original: "Peece"</note>. We also see that whether the *charge* is with a *bullet*, with *wet* and hard-packed paper, or with powder alone rammed in hard, it makes no great difference in the *loudness* of the *report* <note>the sound of the explosion</note>.

<margin>165</margin>
The *sharpness* or *quickness* of the *impact* is a major *cause* of *loudness*, as well as the *strength*. For example, if you strike the *air* with a *whip* or a *wand*, the sharper and quicker you strike it, the louder the *sound* it makes. In playing the *lute* or the *virginals* <note>a rectangular keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</note>, a quick stroke or *touch* brings great life to the *sound*. The *cause* is that the *quick strike* cuts the *air* speedily, whereas the *soft strike* tends to beat the air rather than cut it.

<margin>
Experiments in Group concerning the Communication of Sounds.
</margin>
The communication of *sounds* (as in the *bodies* <note>original: "Bellies"</note> of *lutes*, *empty vessels*, etc.) has been mentioned *in passing* <note>original: "obiter"</note> during the discussion on the *amplification* <note>original: "Maioration"</note> of *sounds*. However, it is appropriate to give this its own section <note>original: "Title"</note> as well.

<header>Natural History:</header>

<margin>166</margin> The *experiment* providing the greatest demonstration of the *communication of sounds* is the *chiming of bells*. In this case, if you strike with a hammer upon the upper part, then upon the middle, and then upon the lower, you shall find the *sound* to be more treble or more bass according to the concave <note>the hollow interior</note> on the inside, even though the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> is only on the outside.

<margin>167</margin> When a *sound* is created between the *blast of the mouth* and the *air of the pipe*, it nevertheless has some *communication* <note>interaction or resonance</note> with the matter of the sides of the *pipe* and the spirits <note>Bacon often used "spirits" to refer to the active, invisible gases or energies within matter</note> contained within them. For in a *pipe* or *trumpet* made of wood or brass, the *sound* will be diverse. Similarly, if the *pipe* is covered with *cloth* or *silk*, it will give a different *sound* than it would on its own. Likewise, if the *pipe* is a *little wet* on the inside, it will make a different *sound* than the same *pipe dry*.

<margin>168</margin> A *sound* made within *water* communicates better with a hard body through *water* than a sound made in *air* does with *air*. See *Experiment 134*.

<margin>
Experiments in group touching the equality and inequality of sounds.
</margin>
We have spoken before (in the investigation touching *music*) of *musical sounds*, where there may be a concord or discord between two parts. These sounds we call tones. We have likewise spoken of *unmusical sounds* and have given the *cause*: that the *tone* proceeds from *equality* and the other from *inequality*. We have also explained there what *equal bodies* give *tones* and what *unequal* ones give none. But now we shall speak of such *inequality of sounds* as proceeds not from the nature of the bodies themselves, but is accidental—either from the *roughness* or *obliquity* <note>slant or crookedness</note> of the *passage*, from the *doubling of the striker* <note>original: "percutient"</note>, or from the *trembling* <note>original: "trepidation"</note> of the motion.

<margin>169</margin> A *bell*, if it has a *crack* <note>original: "rift"</note> in it so that the *sound* does not have a clear passage, gives a *hoarse* and *jarring sound*. Likewise, the *voice of man*, when a cold causes the *windpipe* <term>original: "wesill"; the trachea or throat</term> to grow rugged and (as we call it) "furred," becomes hoarse. In these two *instances*, the *sounds* are unpleasant <note>original: "ingrate"</note> because they are merely unequal. But if they are *unequal in equality*, then the *sound* is grateful <note>pleasing</note>, but *purling* <note>having a rippling or vibrating quality</note>.

<margin>170</margin> All *instruments* that have either *returns* <note>u-turns or loops in the tubing</note>, such as trumpets; or *flexions* <note>curves</note>, such as cornets; or are *drawn up* and *pushed out*, such as *sackbuts* <note>an early form of the trombone</note>; have a *purling sound*. But the *recorder* or *flute*, which have none of these inequalities, give a clear *sound*. Nevertheless, the *recorder* itself, or a *pipe* moistened a little on the inside, sounds more solemnly and with a little purling or *hissing*. Again, a *wreathed string*, such as those in the bass strings of *bandoras* <note>a lute-like stringed instrument with wire strings</note>, also gives a *purling sound*.

<margin>171</margin> But a *lute string*, if it is merely *unequal* in its parts, gives a harsh and...

<margin>172</margin>
...and untunable *Sound*; these *Strings* we call *False*, as they are thicker in one place than in another. Therefore, *wire strings* are never *False* <note>Because wire is drawn through a die, it has a perfectly uniform thickness, unlike gut strings</note>. We also see that when we test a *False lute-string*, we usually stretch it tight between the fingers and flick it; if it appears as a double *image* <note>original: "Species"; referring to the visual vibration of the string</note>, it is *True*; but if it appears as a triple image or more, it is *False*.

<margin>173</margin>
*Waters*, in the *noise* they make as they run, represent a *Trembling Noise* to the ear. In *Regals* <note>A small, portable pipe organ popular in the Renaissance</note> (which have a *pipe* they call the *Nightingale-Pipe* containing water), the *sound* has a continual *trembling*. Children also have little toys they call *Cocks* <note>Bird-shaped water whistles</note> that have *water* in them; when they blow or whistle in them, they produce a *Trembling Noise*. This *trembling* of *water* has an affinity with the letter *L*. All these *inequalities* of *vibration* <note>original: "Trepidation"</note> are generally pleasant rather than otherwise.

<margin>174</margin>
All *Bass Notes*, or very high *Treble Notes*, produce a *harsh sound* <note>original: "Asper Sound"</note>. This is because the *Bass* strikes more *air* than it can move equally, and the *Treble* cuts the *air* so sharply that it returns too quickly to make the *sound* equal. Therefore, a *Middle* <note>original: "Meane"</note> or *Tenor* is the sweetest *part*.

We know of nothing that can produce a *musical* or *unmusical sound* at will through voluntary *motion* except the *voice* of *humans* and *birds*. The *cause* (no doubt) lies in the *windpipe* (which we call the *rough artery* <note>original: "Aspera Arteria"; the Latin term for the trachea</note>). When it is well extended, it achieves *equality*—just as a wrinkled bladder becomes smooth when it is stretched. This *extension* is always greater in musical *tones* than in *speech*. Therefore, the *inward voice* or *whisper* can never produce a musical *tone*. In *singing*, there is clearly a greater exertion and labor of the throat than in *speaking*, as is evident in the thrusting out or drawing in of the chin when we sing.

<margin>175</margin>
The *humming* of *bees* is an *unequal buzzing*. Some of the ancients believed it did not come from their mouths but was an *internal sound*. However, it may be neither; it likely comes from the motion of their wings, for it is only heard when they move.

<margin>176</margin>
All *metals* quenched in *water* produce a whistling or hissing *sound* (which has an affinity with the letter *Z*), even though the *sound* is created between the *water* or *vapor* and the *air*. Simmering also, if there is only a small amount of *water* in a vessel, produces a hissing *sound*; but boiling in a full vessel produces a bubbling *sound*, which is somewhat similar to the *water whistles* used by children.

<margin>177</margin>
A trial should be made to see whether an *inequality* or change of the *medium* will produce an *inequality* of *sound*. For example, if three bells were made one inside another with *air* between each, and then the outermost *bell* was struck with a hammer, how would the *sound* differ from a single *bell*? Likewise, take a *plate* of *brass* and a plank of wood, join them closely together, and knock upon one of them to see if they produce an *unequal sound*. Similarly, make two or three *partitions* of wood in a *hogshead* <note>A large wooden cask or barrel</note> with *holes* or *knots* in them, and note the difference between their *sound* and the *sound* of a *hogshead* without such partitions.

<page-num>52</page-num>
# Natural History

<margin>
Experiments in group <note>original: "in Consort"</note> regarding higher **Treble** and lower **Bass Tones**, or **Musical Sounds**.
</margin>

<margin>
178
</margin>
It is evident that the **striking** <note>original: "Percussion"</note> of a **greater quantity** of **air** causes the **lower sound** <note>original: "Baser Sound"</note>, and a **lesser quantity** causes the more **treble sound**. The **striking** of a **greater quantity** of **air** is produced by the **largeness** of the **striking body**; by the **width** <note>original: "Latitude"</note> of the **hollow space** <note>original: "Concave"</note> through which the **sound** passes; and by the **length** of that same **hollow**. Therefore, we see that a **bass string** is thicker than a **treble**; a **bass pipe** has a larger **bore** than a **treble**; and in **pipes** and similar instruments, the lower the **finger holes** are, and the further away from the **mouth** of the **pipe**, the more **bass** a **sound** they yield; and the nearer they are to the **mouth**, the more **treble**. Furthermore, if you strike a **solid object**, such as a **brass fire-dog** <note>original: "Andiron"</note>, at the **top**, it makes a more **treble sound**; and at the **bottom**, a **lower** one.

<margin>
179
</margin>
It is also evident that a **sharper** or **faster striking** of the **air** causes a more **treble sound**, and a **slower** or **heavier** one causes a more **bass sound**. We see this in **strings**: the more they are wound up and tightened <note>original: "strained"</note>—thereby producing a faster snap back—the more **treble** the **sound** is. The slacker they are, or the less they are wound up, the **lower** the **sound**. Therefore, a **thicker string** that is tightened more, and a **thinner string** that is tightened less, may produce the same **tone**.

<margin>
180
</margin>
**Children**, **women**, and **eunuchs** have smaller and shriller **voices** than **men**. The reason is not because **men** have more **heat** (which might make the **voice** stronger, as the strength of a **voice** or **sound** creates a difference in **loudness** or **softness**, but not in **pitch** <note>original: "Tone"</note>). Rather, it is from the **widening** <note>original: "Dilatation"</note> of the **vocal organ**, which is admittedly also caused by **heat**. However, the cause of the **voice changing** at the age of **puberty** is more mysterious. It seems to be because much of the **moisture** of the **body**, which previously nourished <note>original: "irrigate"</note> the parts, is drawn down to the **reproductive organs** <note>original: "Spermaticall vessels"</note>. This leaves the **body** hotter than it was, which causes the **widening** of the **pipes**. We plainly see that all the effects of **heat** appear at that time, such as **hairiness** <note>original: "Pilosity"</note>, **roughness** of the **skin**, **hardness** of the **flesh**, and so on.

<margin>
181
</margin>
The skill of the **musician** has produced two other ways of **tightening** or **increasing the tension** <note>original: "Intension"</note> of **strings**, besides winding them up. One is the **stopping** of the **string** with the **finger**, as seen on the **necks** of **lutes**, **viols**, and similar instruments. The other is the **shortness** of the **string**, as in **harps**, **virginals** <note>A keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</note>, and so on. Both of these share the same reason: they cause the **string** to snap back faster.

<margin>182</margin>
In the **tightening** of a **string**, the further it is stretched, the less **additional stretching** is required to reach a specific **note**. A **string** requires a good deal of **winding** before it will produce any **note** at all; and in the **frets** <note>The ridges on the neck of a stringed instrument</note> of **lutes** and similar instruments, the higher the pitch goes, the less **distance** there is between the **frets**.

<margin>183</margin>
If you fill a **drinking glass** with **water** (especially one that is **tapered** <note>original: "sharpe"</note> at the bottom and **wide** at the top) and **flick** <note>original: "fillip"</note> the **rim** or **outside**, and afterward empty part of the **water**, continuing to empty it bit by bit while testing the **tone** by **flicking** it, you shall find the **tone** drops and becomes more **bass** as the **glass** becomes **emptier**.

He applies these observations to musical instruments, the human voice during puberty, and experiments with water-filled glassware.</summary>

<page-num>53</page-num>
<header>Century II.</header>

<margin>
Experiments in group <note>original: "in Consort"</note>, regarding the proportion of **treble** and **bass tones**.
</margin>

The just and measured **proportion** of the **struck air** <note>original: "Aire Percussed"</note>, in relation to the **bass** or **treble** quality of **tones**, is one of the greatest secrets in the study of **sounds**. For it reveals the true **coincidence** of **tones** into **octaves** <note>original: "Diapasons"</note>, which is the return of the same **sound** at a different pitch. It also reveals the **harmonies** <note>original: "Concords"</note> and **discords** between the **unison** and the **octave**. We have mentioned this before in the **musical experiments**, but we think it is appropriate to resume the topic here as a principal part of our inquiry into the **nature** of **sounds**. This proportion may be found in the **tightening** <note>original: "Winding"</note> of **strings**, in the **distance** between **frets**, and in the **hollow space** <note>original: "Concave"</note> of **pipes**, etc. But it is most easily studied in the last of these.

<margin>184</margin>
Therefore, try **tightening** a **string** by turning the peg once, as soon as it is stretched enough to produce a **tone**; then turn it twice, then three times, and so on. Mark the scale or difference in the **rise** of the **tone**. By doing this, you shall discover two effects in one trial: both the **proportion** of the **sound** relative to the **amount of turning**, and also the **proportion** of the **sound** relative to the **string** as it is more or less tightened. Note that to measure this, the best way will be to take the **length** of the **string** in a straight **line** for every turn of the **peg**.

<margin>185</margin>
As for the **stops** <note>finger positions on a string</note>, you should count the **number** of **frets**. Most importantly, measure the **length** of the **string** <note>original: "Line"</note> from the first stop of the **string** to the stop that produces an **octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> higher than the first stop on that same **string**.

<margin>186</margin>
But this will be most clearly seen (as previously stated) in the **bores** of **wind instruments**. Therefore, have half a dozen **pipes** made that are identical in length and all other aspects, but with a single, double, and so on up to a **six-fold** <note>original: "sextuple"</note> **bore**. Mark what drop in **tone** each one produces. In these last three **examples**, you must diligently observe what **length** of **string**, **distance** of **stop**, or **volume of air** <note>original: "Concave of Aire"</note> produces what **rise** in **sound**. In the last of these—which, as we said, provides the clearest demonstrations—you must record what increase of the **hollow space** is required to make a **note** one step higher, what is required for two **notes**, what for three, and so on up to the **octave**. Then the great secret of **numbers** and **proportions** will be revealed. It is likely that those who make **recorders** and similar instruments already know this, as they make them in **matched sets** <note>original: "Sets"</note>. Similarly, **bell-founders** know this when they tune their **bells**. Therefore, research <note>original: "Enquiry"</note> may save the trouble of an **experiment** <note>original: "Triall"</note>. Certainly, it was observed by one of the **ancients** <note>likely Aristotle</note> that an **empty barrel** tapped with a finger produces an **octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> relative to the sound of a similar **full barrel**. However, I do not fully understand how that could be, for tapping a **barrel**, whether **full** or **empty**, hardly produces a clear **musical tone**.

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon's study of the physical properties of sound, moving from the mathematical proportions of musical notes to a distinction between "Exterior" and "Interior" sounds based on how they move through the air.</meta>

<page-num>54</page-num>
<header>Natural History:</header>

<margin>187</margin>
<margin>Experiments in group <note>original: "in Consort"</note> regarding Exterior and Interior Sounds.</margin>

There is a requirement for some sensible difference in the **proportion** of creating a **note** in relation to the **sound** itself, which is the **passive** <note>The "passive" element refers to the air being acted upon by the instrument.</note> element. This creation must not be too close, but at a distance. For in a **recorder** <note>A type of early flute.</note>, the three uppermost **holes** yield one **tone**, which is a **note** lower than the **tone** of the first three. A similar requirement (no doubt) exists in the **tuning** <note>original: "Winding"</note> or **fingering** <note>original: "Stopping"</note> of **strings**.

<margin>188</margin>

There is another difference in **sounds**, which we will call **Exterior** and **Interior**. This is not a matter of **soft** or **loud**, nor **bass** or **treble**, nor **musical** or **unmusical**. However, it is true that there can be no musical **tone** in an **Interior sound**; whereas in an **Exterior sound**, there may be both **musical** and **unmusical** qualities. We shall list them rather than define them precisely; though (to provide an **outline** <note>original: "Adumbration"</note> of what we mean) the **Interior** is more of a **pushing** <note>original: "Impulsion"</note> or **bruising** <note>original: "Contusion"</note> of the **air**, rather than a **striking** <note>original: "Elision"</note> or **cutting** <note>original: "Section"</note> of it. Thus, the **striking** <note>original: "Percussion"</note> of one against the other differs just as a **blow** differs from a **cut**.

In the **speech** of **humans**, **whispering** (which they call *whisper* <note>original: "Susurrus" in Latin</note>), whether it be louder or softer, is an **Interior sound**. But **speaking out** is an **Exterior sound**. Therefore, you can never produce a musical **tone** nor sing while **whispering**, but in **speech** you can. Likewise, **breathing** or **blowing** by the **mouth**, **bellows**, or **wind** (even if loud) is an **Interior sound**; but **blowing** through a **pipe** or **hollow space** <note>original: "Concave"</note> (even if soft) is an **Exterior** sound. Similarly, the greatest **winds**, if they have no **constriction** <note>original: "Coarctation"</note> or do not blow through a hollow, produce an **Interior sound**. A **whistling** or hollow **wind** yields a **singing** or **Exterior sound**; the former is confined by some other body, while the latter is confined by its own **density**. Therefore, we see that when the **wind** blows "hollow," it is a **sign** of **rain**. A **flame**, as it moves within itself or is blown by a **bellows**, gives a **murmur** or **Interior sound**.

<margin>189</margin>

There is no **hard body** which, when struck against another **hard body**, will not yield an **Exterior sound**, whether greater or lesser. Indeed, if the **striking** <note>original: "Percussion"</note> is too soft, it may result in a **total lack** <note>original: "Nullity"</note> of **sound**, but never an **Interior sound**; such as when one walks so softly that he is not heard.

<margin>190</margin>

Where the **air** is the **striker** <note>original: "Percutient"</note>—whether confined or not—against a **hard body**, it never produces an **Exterior sound**; for example, if you blow strongly with a **bellows** against a **wall**.

<margin>191</margin>

**Sounds** (both **Exterior** and **Interior**) may be made just as well by **suction** <note>Inhaling.</note> as by the **emission** of the **breath**, as seen in **whistling** or **breathing**.

<margin>Experiments in group regarding the Articulation of Sounds.</margin>
<margin>192</margin>

It is evident, and it is one of the strangest **secrets** in **sounds**, that the whole **sound** is not only in the whole body of **air**, but the whole **sound** is also in every small **part** of the **air**. This is why all the complex **diversity** of **artic**ulate...

<margin>193</margin>
The **uneven agitation** of the **winds** and similar factors, though they affect how far **sounds** are carried, do not distort the **articulation** of the sounds at all within the distance they can be heard. However, they may cause sounds to be heard across a shorter distance than in still air, as has been mentioned previously.

<margin>194</margin>
Too great a distance confuses the **articulation** of **sounds**. For instance, you might hear the **sound** of a preacher's voice but not be able to distinguish what he is saying. Additionally, one **articulate sound** will drown out another, as when many people speak at once.

<margin>195</margin>
In the **experiment** of **speaking underwater**, even though the voice is reduced to extreme faintness <note>original: "Exility"</note>, the **articulate sounds** (which are the **words**) are not distorted, as has been noted.

<margin>196</margin>
I believe that an **extremely small** or **extremely loud sound** cannot be **articulate**. Rather, **articulation** requires a **moderate** <note>original: "Mediocrity"</note> level of **sound**. This is because an **extremely small sound** muffles the **articulation** by **contracting** it, while a **loud sound** ruins it by **dispersing** it. And although (as said before) an **articulate sound**, once created, can pass through a small crack, the initial creation of that **articulation** requires more space <note>original: "Dimension"</note>.

<margin>197</margin>
It has been observed that in a **room** or **chapel** with a **vaulted** floor and a **vaulted** roof, a preacher cannot be heard as clearly as in similar places without such vaults. The cause is that **following words** arrive before the **previous words** have faded away. Therefore, the **articulate sounds** become more confused, even though the **total volume** <note>original: "Grosse of the Sound"</note> is greater.

<margin>198</margin>
The **movements** of the **tongue**, **lips**, **throat**, **palate**, etc., which are involved in **making** the various **alphabetical letters**, are worthy of study and relevant to this current **investigation** of **sounds**. However, because they are subtle and take a long time to describe, we will set them aside for now and include them among the **experiments on speech**. The **Hebrews** have been diligent in this and have categorized which **letters** are **labial** (made with lips), which are **dental** (made with teeth), which are **guttural** (made in the throat), etc. As for the **Romans** <note>original: "Latines"</note> and **Greeks**, they have distinguished between **semivowels** and **mutes**. Among the **mutes**, they distinguish between **thin mutes** <note>original: "Mutæ Tenues"</note>, **middle mutes** <note>original: "Mediæ"</note>, and **aspirated mutes** <note>original: "Aspiratæ"</note>. This is not wrong, but it is not detailed enough. They have rarely investigated the specific **strokes** and **motions** that create those **sounds**. For instance, the **letters B, P, F,** and **M** cannot be spoken without **contracting** or **closing** the **mouth**. The **letters N** and **T** cannot be pronounced in certain combinations without the **letter N** turning into an **M**—for example, *Hecatonba* becomes *Hecatomba* <note>original: "Hecatonba, will be Hecatomba"</note>. Similarly, **M** and **T** cannot be pronounced together without a **P** coming between them, as *Emtus* is pronounced *Emptus* <note>original: "as Emtus, is pronounced Emptus"</note>. There are many such examples. If you investigate fully, you will find that fewer **simple motions** are required to create the entire **alphabet** than there are **letters**.

### Third Century.

<margin>

Experiments in group <note>original: "in Consort"</note> concerning the **Motions of Sounds**: in what lines they are **circular**, **oblique**, and **straight**; and how they move **upwards**, **downwards**, **forwards**, and **backwards**.
</margin>
All sounds (of any kind) move in a circle; that is to say, on all sides: upwards, downwards, forwards, and backwards. This is evident in all instances.

<margin>
202
203
</margin>
Sounds do not require being carried to the senses in a **straight line**, as **visible things** <note>original: "Visibles"</note> do, but may be **arched**. Though it is true they move strongest in a **straight line**, this is nonetheless not caused by the **straightness** of the **line**, but by the **shortness** of the distance; a straight line is the shortest path <note>original: "Linea recta brevissima"</note>. And therefore we see that if a **wall** is in between and you speak on one side, you are heard on the other. This is not because the **sound** passes through the **wall**, but because it is **arched** over the **wall**.

If the **sound** is **blocked** and **reflected** <note>original: "Repercussed"</note>, it comes around on the other side in an **oblique line**. For example, if you are in a **coach** and one side of the **boot** <note>original term for the leather side-covers or doors of a carriage</note> is down and the other is up, and a **beggar** asks for money on the **closed side**, you would think that he was on the **open side**. Likewise, if a **bell** or **clock** is (for example) on the north side of a room, and the window of that room is on the south side, a person in the room will think the **sound** came from the south.

<margin>
204
</margin>
Although sounds spread out in a circle (so that there is an **orb** or **spherical area** of the **sound**), they move strongest and go furthest in the **forward lines**, moving away from the first local **impact** <note>original: "Impulsion"</note> of the **air**. Therefore, in **preaching**, you will hear the **preacher's voice** better in front of the **pulpit** than behind it or on the sides, even though the pulpit stands open. Similarly, an **arquebus** <note>original: "Harquebuz"; an early type of portable firearm</note> or **artillery piece** <note>original: "Ordnance"</note> will be heard further forward from the mouth of the **gun** than backward or to the sides.

</margin>

But this may be attributed to the obstructions and obstacles which the voice meets with when one speaks on the same level. Yet there seems to be more to it: for it may be that *sensory images* <note>original: "Spirituall Species"; a scholastic term for the invisible forms of things—like light or sound—that travel through the air to the senses</note>, both of *visible things* and *sounds*, move better *downwards* than *upwards*. It is a strange thing that to men standing below on the ground, those who are on the top of St. Paul's Cathedral seem much smaller than they truly are and cannot be recognized; but to men above, those below do not seem nearly as diminished and may be recognized. Yet it is true that all things seen from above also seem somewhat contracted and better gathered into a shape—just as *ornamental garden beds* <note>original: "Knotts in Gardens"; intricate, formal garden designs meant to be viewed from above</note> show best from an *upper window* or *terrace*.

This may be the most suitable means to judge whether *sounds* descend or ascend better.

<margin>
105
Group of experiments regarding the **persistence** and **fading** of sounds, and regarding the **time** they require for their **creation** or **transmission** <note>original: "Delation"</note>.
207
</margin>
After a *sound* is created (which happens in a moment), we find it continues for a short time, fading away little by little. In this, there is a wonderful error among men, who take this to be a *continuation* of the *first sound*; whereas, in truth, it is a *renewal* <note>original: "Renovation"</note> and not a *continuation*. For the *object struck* has, by reason of the *impact*, a *vibration* <note>original: "Trepidation"</note> produced in its *microscopic parts* <note>original: "Minute Parts"</note>, and so it continually renews the *striking of the air*. This appears clearly because the *fading sound* of a bell or a plucked string—which is thought to be a single continuous sound—stops as soon as the bell or string is touched. For example, in a *virginal* <note>a small harpsichord-like keyboard instrument</note>, as soon as the *jack* <note>the mechanism that plucks the string</note> falls and touches the string, the *sound* stops. And in a *bell*, after you have rung it, if you touch the bell, the *sound* stops. In this, you must distinguish between two types of *vibrations*: one is *obvious and physical* <note>original: "Manifest and Locall"</note>, such as the swinging of the bell when it is hanging; the other is *hidden*, occurring within the *microscopic parts*, such as is described in the ninth instance. But it is true that the *physical* swinging helps the *hidden* vibration greatly. We see likewise that in pipes and other wind instruments, the *sound* lasts no longer than the breath blows. It is true that in *organs* there is a confused murmur for a while after you have played, but that is only while the *bellows* are *deflating*.

<margin>208</margin>
It is certain that in the *noise* of large *artillery* <note>original: "Ordnance"</note>, where many are shot off together, the *sound* will be carried at least twenty miles over land, and much further over water. But then it will reach the ear not at the instant of the shooting, but an hour or more later. This must certainly be a *continuation* of the *first sound*, for there is no *vibration* remaining which should renew it. And

<margin>209</margin>
To test exactly the time in which *sound* is *delayed*, let a man stand in a steeple and have a candle <note>original: "Taper"</note> with him. Let some veil be put before the candle, and let another man stand in a field a mile away. Then let the man in the steeple strike the bell and at the same instant withdraw the veil. Then let the man in the field determine by his pulse <note>using the heartbeat to measure seconds before the invention of the stopwatch</note> what distance of *time* there is between the *light* being seen and the *sound* being heard. For it is certain that the *travel* <note>original: "Delation"</note> of light happens in an instant. This may be tested at much greater distances using larger *lights* and *sounds*.

<margin>210</margin>
It is generally known and observed that *light* and the *object* of *sight* move swifter than *sound*. For we see the *flash* of a gun <note>original: "Peece"</note> sooner than the *noise* is heard. And in chopping wood, if one is some distance away, he shall see the arm lifted up for a second stroke before he hears the noise of the first. The greater the distance, the greater the gap <note>original: "Preuention"; meaning the extent to which one precedes the other</note>, as we see in distant thunder, where the lightning precedes the crack by a good amount of time.

<margin>211</margin>
*Colors*, when they present themselves to the eye, do not fade or melt by degrees but still appear at the same strength. But *sounds* melt and vanish little by little. The cause is that *colors* share nothing with the *motion* of the *air*, but *sounds* do. It is a clear argument that *sound* participates in some *local motion* of the *air* (as an *indispensable cause* <note>original: "Sine quâ non"</note>) because it perishes so suddenly. For in every division or pushing <note>original: "Section, or Impulsion"</note> of the *air*, the *air* suddenly restores and reunites itself—which *water* also does, though not nearly as quickly.

<margin>Experiments in group <note>original: "in Consort"</note> regarding the passage and interception of sounds.</margin>

In the trials of the *passage* or *non-passage* of *sounds*, you must take care that you do not mistake the sound *passing by the sides* of an object for the sound *passing through the object*. Therefore, you must make the *obstructing object* very tight <note>original: "close"</note>, for sound will pass through a small chink.

<margin>212</margin>
Where sound passes through a *hard* or *solid* <note>original: "Close"</note> body (as through *water*, through a *wall*, or through *metal*, as in falconry bells <note>original: "Hawkes Bells"</note> when they are muffled, etc.), the *hard* or *solid* body must be thin and small. Otherwise, it deadens and extinguishes the *sound* utterly. Therefore, in the *experiment of speaking in air under water*, the voice must not be very deep within the *water*, for then the *sound* does not pierce through. Likewise, if you speak on the far side of a *solid wall*, if the *wall* is very thick, you shall not be heard. If there were an empty large barrel <note>original: "Hogshead"</note> with sides two feet thick and the bunghole stopped, I believe the resonating sound (created by the *interaction* of the *outer air* with the *air inside*) would be little or nothing. You would only hear the *noise* of the knock on the outside, as if the vessel were full.

<page-num>60</page-num>
<header>Natural History:</header>

<margin>213</margin> It is certain that in the *passage of sounds* through *hard bodies*, the spirit or pneumatic part <note>original: "Pneumaticall Part"; Bacon's term for the invisible, air-like substance he believed inhabited all matter</note> of the *hard body* itself assists the sound. But it works much better when the sides of that *hard body* are struck than when the impact <note>original: "Percussion"</note> is only within, without touching the sides. Take, therefore, a hawk's bell with the holes stopped up, and hang it by a thread inside a glass bottle. Stop the mouth of the glass very tightly with wax, and then shake the glass to see whether the bell gives any *sound* at all, or how weak it is. But note that you must use a wire instead of the thread, or else ensure the glass has a wide "belly," lest the bell strike the sides of the glass when you shake it.

<margin>214</margin> It is plain that a very *long* and *downward arch* <note>referring to a vaulted or curved architectural structure</note> will completely extinguish the *sound* as it passes. Thus, a *sound* that could be heard over a wall will not be heard over a church; nor will a *sound* that can be heard if you stand some distance from a wall be heard if you stand close under that same wall.

<margin>215</margin> *Soft* and *porous* <note>original: "Foraminous"</note> *bodies* will deaden a *sound* during its initial creation. For striking against cloth or fur will make little *sound*, as has been said. But during the *passage of the sound*, they will permit it to travel better than *harder bodies*. We see this in how curtains and wall-hangings do not stop *sound* much; yet glass windows, if they are very tightly closed, will block a *sound* more than a similar thickness of cloth. We also see, in the rumbling of the belly, how easily *sound* passes through the guts and skin.

<margin>216</margin> It is worthy of inquiry whether *great sounds* (such as those of cannons <note>original: "Ordnance"</note> or bells) become weaker and more *faint* <note>original: "Exile"</note> when they pass through *small cracks*. It may be that the subtleties of *articulate sounds* (like speech) can pass through *small cracks* without becoming confused, while the *magnitude* of a sound perhaps cannot pass as well.

</margin> The *mediums* <note>the materials through which sound travels</note> of *sounds* are *air*, *soft and porous bodies*, and also *water*. *Hard bodies* also do not altogether refuse to be *mediums* of *sounds*. But all of them are dull and unapt *carriers* <note>original: "Deferents"</note>, except for the *air*.
In *air*, thinner or drier *air* does not carry *sound* as well as denser air. This is apparent in *night sounds*, *evening sounds*, and *sounds* in moist weather or during *southern winds*. The reason has already been mentioned in the section on the *increase* <note>original: "Maioration"</note> of *sounds*: because *thin air* is more easily pierced, but *thick air* preserves the *sound* better from wasting away. We have now spoken of the natures of the *mediums*; as for the *disposition* of these *mediums*, it consists in the *penning* <note>original: "Penning"; the confinement or enclosure of air</note> or not *penning* of the air. <margin>Experiments in combination: how the shapes of pipes, hollow spaces, or different objects contribute to sounds.</margin>
### How the *shapes* of *pipes* or *hollow spaces* through which *sounds* pass, or of other different *objects*, contribute to the variety and alteration of *sounds*—either regarding the greater or lesser *quantity* of air which the *hollow spaces* receive, or regarding the carrying of *sounds* a longer or shorter way, or regarding many other *circumstances*—they have been touched upon as they fell under other headings. But those *shapes* we are now to speak of, we intend to be those that concern the *lines* through which *sound* passes, such as *straight*, *crooked*, *angular*, *circular*, and so on.

<margin>221</margin>
The *shape* of a *bell* partakes of the *pyramid* <note>original: "Pyramis"</note>, yet it comes off and widens <note>original: "dilating"</note> more suddenly. The *shape* of a *hunter's horn* and *cornet* is slanted <note>original: "oblique"</note>, yet there are also *straight horns*. If they have the same bore <note>the hollow center of the tube</note> as the *slanted* ones, they differ little in *sound*, except that the *straight* ones require a somewhat stronger blast. The *shapes* of *recorders*, *flutes*, and *pipes* are straight, but the *recorder* has a smaller bore and a larger one, both above and below. The *trumpet* has the *shape* of the *letter S*, which creates that *purling sound* <note>a rippling or murmuring sound</note>, etc. Generally, the *straight line* has the cleanest and roundest *sound*, while the *crooked* is more hoarse and jarring.

<margin>222</margin>
A trial should be made of a *winding pipe* <note>original: "Sinuous Pipe"</note> that might have some four bends <note>original: "Flexions"</note>. Likewise of a *pipe* made like a *cross*, open in the middle. And similarly of an *angular pipe*, to see what the *effects* of these various *sounds* will be. And again of a *circular pipe*: for instance, if you take a perfectly round *pipe* and make a hole into which you shall blow, and another hole not far from that, but with a divider <note>original: "Traverse"</note> or stop between them, so that your breath may go around the *circle* and come out at the second hole. You may also try the *striking* <note>original: "Percussions"</note> of *solid bodies* of several *shapes*, such as *globes*, *flats*, *cubes*, *crosses*, *triangles*, and so on. Also try their combinations, such as *flat* against *flat*, *convex* against *convex*, and *convex* against *flat*, etc., and note well the differences in the *sounds*. Also try the difference in *sound* of several *thicknesses* <note>original: "Crassitudes"</note> of *hard bodies* when struck, and take note of the diversity of the *sounds*. I myself have tried it, and found that a *bell* of *gold* yields an excellent *sound*, not inferior to that of *silver* or *brass*, but rather better. Yet we see that

The **harp** has its **hollow body** <note>original: "Concave"</note> positioned across the **strings**, rather than along them. No instrument has a **sound** so melting and prolonged as the **Irish harp**. You may test this without any **soundboard** along the length, using one only **harp-style** at one end of the **strings**; or finally, with a double **hollow body**, one at each end of the **strings**.

<margin>
Experiments in harmony <note>original: "Confort"</note>, regarding the mixture of sound.
224
</margin>
There is a clear difference between **visible forms** <note>original: "Species Visible"</note> and **audible forms** in this: the **visible** does not mingle in the **medium** <note>the substance, like air, through which a sensation travels</note>, but the **audible** does. For if we look outside, we see the **heaven**, many **stars**, **trees**, **hills**, **men**, and **beasts** all at once, and the **form** of one does not blur <note>original: "confound"</note> the other. But if that many sounds came from different directions, one would utterly drown out the other. So we see that **voices** or **groups** <note>original: "Consorts"</note> of **music** create a **harmony** by **mixture**, which **colors** do not. 

It is true, nonetheless, that a great **light** drowns out a smaller one so that it cannot be seen (just as the **sun** drowns out a **glowworm**), just as a great **sound** drowns out a lesser one. I also suppose that if there were two **glass lanterns**, one **crimson** and the other **azure**, with a **candle** inside each, those **colored lights** would mingle and cast a **purple color** upon a **white paper**. Even among **colors**, they produce a faint and weak **mixture**; for example, white walls make rooms brighter than black ones. 

However, the cause of the **confusion** in **sounds** and the **clarity** <note>original: "Inconfusion"</note> in **visible forms** is because **sight** works in **straight lines** <note>original: "Right Lines"</note> and creates separate **cones** <note>a reference to the "visual cone," an early theory of how light enters the eye</note>; thus, there can be no overlap in the **eye** or **visual point**. But **sounds**, which move in **slanted** <note>original: "Oblique"</note> and **curved** <note>original: "Arcuate"</note> lines, must necessarily encounter and disturb one another.

<margin>225</margin>
The sweetest and best **harmony** occurs when every **part** or **instrument** is not heard by itself, but as a **blending** <note>original: "Conflation"</note> of them all. This requires the listener to stand some distance away. It is just like the **mixture** of **perfumes**, or catching the **scent** of several different **flowers** in the **air**.

<margin>226</margin>
The condition of the **air** in other **qualities** has no great effect upon **sounds**, unless it is joined with **sound** itself. Whether the **air** is bright or dark, hot or cold, quiet or stirring (unless it is stirring with **noise**), sweet-smelling or stinking, it does not matter much; it may only cause some minor alteration or difference.

<margin>227</margin>
But **sounds** do disturb and alter one another: sometimes one drowns out the other so it isn't heard; sometimes one **jars** and discords with the other, creating **confusion**; and sometimes one **mingles** and **combines** with the other, creating a **harmony**.

The cause is profound; but it seems that the **impressions** from the **objects of the senses** do mingle respectively, each with its own kind, but not in the proportions demonstrated earlier. The reason may be because the first **impression**, which is the change from **privation** <note>original: "Priuation"; the absence of a quality</note> to **action** (such as from **silence** to **noise**, or from **darkness** to **light**), is a greater degree of change than moving from **less noise** to **more noise**, or from **less light** to **more light**. And the reason for that, in turn, may be that the **air**, after it has received a **charge** <note>a physical impression or energy</note>, does not receive a surcharge, or greater charge, with the same appetite as it does the first charge. As for the increase of **virtue** <note>original: "Vertue"; here meaning physical power or efficacy</note> generally, and what proportion it bears to the increase of the **matter**, it is a large field and should be handled on its own.

<margin>Experiments in harmony <note>original: "in Consort"</note>, concerning the improvement <note>original: "Melioration"</note> of sounds. 229</margin>

All **concurrent reflections** make **sounds louder**; but if the body that creates either the original **sound** or the **reflection** is clean and smooth, it makes them sweeter. A trial may be made of a **lute** or **viol** with a soundboard <note>original: "Belly"</note> of polished brass instead of wood. We see that even in the open **air**, a **wire string** is sweeter than a string made of **guts**. And we see that for **reflection**, **water** excels, as heard in **music** near the **water** or in **echoes**.

<margin>230</margin>

It has been tested that a **pipe** slightly moistened on the inside—yet so that no drops are left—makes a more solemn **sound** than if the **pipe** were dry; yet it adds a sweet degree of **hissing** <note>original: "Sibillation"</note> or **purling**, as we mentioned before under the heading of **Equality**. The cause is that all **porous** things, being superficially wet and (as it were) between dry and wet, become a little more even and smooth. But the purling (which must necessarily proceed from inequality) I believe is created between the smoothness of the inward surface of the **pipe**, which is wet, and the rest of the wood of the **pipe**, which the wetness does not reach and remains dry.

<margin>231</margin>

In **frosty** weather, **music** sounds better indoors. This may be by reason not of the state of the **air**, but of the wood or **string** of the **instrument**, which is made more **crisp**, and so more porous and hollow. We see that **old lutes** sound better than **new** ones for the same reason, and so do **lute-strings** that have been kept for a long time.

<margin>232</margin>

**Sound** is likewise **improved** by the mingling of **open air** with **trapped air** <note>original: "Pent Aire"</note>. Therefore, a trial may be made of a **lute** or **viol** with a double soundboard <note>original: "Belly"</note>, creating another soundboard with a decorative carving <note>original: "Knot"</note> over the strings—yet so that there is enough room for the strings, and enough room to play below that soundboard. A trial may also be made of an **Irish harp** with a hollow on both sides, whereas it usually has it on only one side. The concern may be that it might make too much resonance <note>original: "Resounding"</note>, whereby one note would overtake another.

<margin>233</margin>

If you sing into the hole of a **drum**, it makes the singing more sweet.

<margin>234</margin>
When a *sound* is created in a *wind instrument*, between the breath and the *air*, if the *sound* is communicated through a more uniform body such as a *pipe*, it *improves* <note>original: "meliorateth"</note> the *sound*. For (no doubt) there would be a different *sound* in a trumpet or *pipe* made of *wood* compared to a *trumpet* or *pipe* made of *brass*. It would be worthwhile to try recorders and hunting horns made of *brass* to see what the *sound* would be.

<margin>235</margin>
*Sounds* are improved by the *focus* <note>original: "Intention"</note> of the *senses*; specifically where the *general awareness* <note>original: "Common Sense"; the faculty that integrates all sensory data</note> is concentrated most on the *particular sense* of *hearing*, and *sight* is suspended. Therefore, *sounds* are sweeter (as well as louder) in the *night* than in the *day*; and I suppose they are sweeter to blind men than to others. It is also manifest that between *sleeping* and *waking* (when all the *senses* are constrained and suspended), *music* is far sweeter than when one is *fully awake*.

Experiments together <note>original: "in Consort"</note> concerning the imitation of sounds.

</margin>
It is a strange thing in nature when it is attentively considered, how *children* and some *birds* learn to *imitate speech*. They take no notice at all of the *motion* of the *mouth* of the person speaking, for *birds* can be taught in the dark as well as in the light. The *sounds of speech* are very intricate and precise, so one would think it was a difficult lesson to learn. It is true that it is done over time, little by little, and with many attempts and efforts; but all this does not explain away the *wonder* of it. It would make a man think (though what we are about to say may seem exceedingly strange) that there is some *transmission of spirits* <note>Bacon's theory that "spirits" were subtle fluids within the body that directed motion and perception</note>; and that the *spirits* of the *teacher*, being put in motion, should trigger a predisposition in the *spirits* of the *learner* to try to *imitate*, thus perfecting the *imitation* by degrees. But regarding *operations* by the *transmission of spirits* (which is one of the highest secrets in nature), we shall speak in the proper place, mainly when we come to inquire about the *imagination*. But as for *imitation*, it is certain that there is a predisposition in men and other creatures to *imitate*. We see how ready apes and monkeys are to *imitate* all motions of man. And in the catching of *dotterels* <note>original: "Dottrells"; a species of bird traditionally believed to be so foolish that it would mimic the movements of a hunter, making it easy to catch</note>, we see how the foolish bird plays the ape in its gestures. Indeed, no man associates with others without learning (before he is aware of it) some gesture, voice, or mannerism of the other.

<margin>237</margin>
In the *imitation* of *sounds*, it is not essential that a man should be the *teacher*; for *birds* will learn from one another, and there is no reward (such as food or the like) given to them for the *imitation*. Besides, you will find parrots that will not only *imitate* voices, but also laughing, knocking, the squeaking of a door on its hinges, or of a cartwheel, and effectively any other noise they hear.

For *speech* must come by *hearing* and *learning*; and *birds* give more heed to and take note of sounds more than *beasts* do, because they are naturally more delighted by them and practice them more, as is apparent in their *singing*. We also see that those who teach *birds* to sing keep them *awake* to increase their *attention*. We see as well that *male birds* <note>original: "Cocke-Birds"</note> among *singing birds* are always the better *singers*; this may be because they are more lively and listen more.

<margin>240</margin>
*Labor* and the *intention* to imitate voices contributes much to *imitation*. Therefore, we see that there are certain *pantomimes* <note>performers who mimic others</note> who will represent the voices of *players* in *interludes* <note>short dramatic plays</note> so lifelike that, if you do not see them, you would think they were those *players* themselves; they do the same with the *voices* of other *men* they hear.

<margin>241</margin>
There have been some who could counterfeit the *distance* of *voices* (which is a *secondary object* of hearing) in such a way that, even when they stand right next to you, you would think the *speech* came from far away in a frightening manner. How this is done may be further investigated. However, I see no great *use* for it except for *imposture*, such as counterfeiting *ghosts* or *spirits*.

<margin>Experiments together <note>original: "in Consort"</note> concerning the reflection of sounds.</margin>
There are three kinds of *reflections* of *sounds*: a *concurrent reflection* <note>one that joins with the original sound to make it louder</note>; an *iterant reflection*, which we call an *echo*; and a *super-reflection*, or an *echo* of an *echo*. The first of these was handled under the *topic* of the *magnitude* of *sounds*; we will now speak of the latter two.

<margin>242</margin>
You can control the *reflection* of *visible images* <note>original: "Species Visible"; the forms or images emitted by objects according to old optical theory</note> using *mirrors*, because they pass in *straight lines* and can be guided to any point. But the *reflection* of *sounds* is hard to master because *sound*, filling great spaces in *curved* <note>original: "Arched"</note> *lines*, cannot be easily guided. Therefore, we see that no means have been practiced to create *artificial echoes*. Furthermore, no already known *echo* returns within a very narrow room.

<margin>243</margin>

# Natural History:
