But there is no doubt that *water* helps the *transmission* <note>original: "Delation"</note> of an *echo*, just as it helps the *transmission* of *original sounds*.

<margin>244</margin>
It is certain (as has been previously mentioned) that if you speak through a *tube* <note>original: "Trunke"</note> that is blocked at the far end, you will feel a blast of air return to your mouth, but no *sound* at all. The reason is that the *enclosure* <note>original: "Closenesse"</note> which preserves the *original sound* is not able to preserve the *reflected sound*. Besides, *echoes* are seldom created except by loud *sounds*. Therefore, there is less hope of creating *artificial echoes* in *air* trapped in a narrow *hollow space* <note>original: "Concave"</note>. Nevertheless, it has been tested that someone leaning over a *well* twenty-five fathoms deep and speaking softly (yet not so soft as a whisper), the *water* returned a clearly *audible echo*. It should be tested whether speaking in *caves* with no exit except where you speak will yield *echoes* as *wells* do.

<margin>245</margin>
The *echo comes* just as the *original sound* does, in a *spherical wave of air* <note>original: "Round Orbe of Aire"</note>. It would be useful to try creating an *echo* where the *reflecting* <note>original: "Repercuffing"</note> body creates an *angle*, such as against the corner <note>original: "Returne"</note> of a wall, etc. Also, we see that in *mirrors* there is a similar *angle of incidence* from the *object* to the *glass* and from the *glass* to the eye. And if you strike a *ball* sideways, not directly against the surface, the rebound will be just as far the opposite way. Whether there is any such *rebound* <note>original: "Resilience"</note> in *echoes* (that is, whether a person will hear better if they stand to the side of the *reflecting* body than if they stand where they speak, or anywhere in a straight line between) should be tested. Trials should also be made by standing closer to the place of *reflection* than the person speaking, and again by standing further away; and so knowledge would be gained as to whether *echoes*, as well as *original sounds*, are strongest when nearby.

<margin>246</margin>
There are many places where you shall hear a number of *echoes* one after another. This happens when there is a variety of *hills* or *woods*, some nearer and some further away; so that the return from the furthest, being created last, will likewise be heard last.

<margin>247</margin>
As the *voice travels* in a circle, moving toward the back as well as toward the front of the speaker, so too does the *echo*. For you have many *back-echoes* returning to the place where you stand.

<margin>248</margin>
To make an *echo* that will repeat three, four, or five *words* distinctly, it is necessary that the *reflecting body* be a good distance away. For if it is near, and yet not so near as to make a *simultaneous echo*, it *interrupts* <note>original: "choppeth"</note> you suddenly. It is also necessary that the *air* not be too *confined* <note>original: "pent"</note>. For *air* at a great distance that is *confined* produces the same effect as *open air* <note>original: "Aire, at large"</note> at a short distance. Therefore, in the trial of speaking in the *well*, although the *well* was deep, the *voice* came back suddenly and would only carry the report of two *words*.

As for *echoes upon echoes*, there is a rare instance of this in a place which I will now accurately describe. It is about three or four miles from *Paris*, near a town called *Pont-Charenton*, located roughly the distance of a bird-bolt shot <term>a short-range, blunt-headed arrow</term>, or a bit more, from the River *Seine*. The room is a *chapel* or small *church*. The walls are all standing, both at the sides and at the ends. Two rows of pillars, built in the style of church *aisles*, are also standing; however, the roof is entirely open, with not even a bit of the arched vaulting <note>original: "embowment"</note> left near any of the walls. Against every pillar was a stack of *logs* <term>billets: thick pieces of wood cut for fuel</term> taller than a man’s height, which the boatmen who bring wood down the *Seine* in stacks (rather than in boats) had laid there, it seems, for their convenience. Speaking at one end, I heard it return the voice thirteen separate times; and I have heard from others that it would return it sixteen times. I was there about three o’clock in the afternoon, and echoes are best in the evening, as all others are. It is clear that these are not *echoes* from several different places, but rather a *tossing of the voice* back and forth like a ball. This is similar to *reflections* in *mirrors*; if you place one *mirror* in front and another behind, you shall see the *mirror* behind with the *image* inside the *mirror* in front; and again, the *mirror* in front inside that one, and various such *super-reflections*, until the *image of the image* <note>original: "species speciei"</note> finally dies out. For every return is weaker and fainter. In the same way, the *voice* in that *chapel* creates an *image of the image* and makes succeeding *super-reflections*. It melts away by degrees, and every *reflection* is weaker than the one before. So, if you speak three words, it will (perhaps) report the whole three words back to you about three times; then it will report the last two words for a few times; and finally, only the last word alone for a few times, still fading and growing weaker. And whereas in *echoes* of only one return it is a great feat to hear four or five words, in this *echo* of so many returns, you effectively hear over twenty words for every three spoken.

<margin>250</margin>
A similar *echo upon echo*, though with only two reports, has been observed to occur if you stand between a *house* and a *hill* and shout loudly <term>lure: to call out or shout</term> toward the *hill*. For the *house* will give a *back-echo*, one taking the sound from the other, with the latter being the weaker of the two.

Where *echoes* come from several different parts at the same distance, they must necessarily create (as it were) a choir of *echoes*, and so make the report louder, and even a *continued echo*; you shall find this in certain *hills* that stand enclosed, theater-like.

<margin>254</margin>
It does not yet appear that there is *refraction* in *sounds* as there is in *visible forms* <note>original: "species Visible"</note>. For I do not think that if a *sound* should pass through different *mediums* (such as *air*, *cloth*, or *wood*), it would deliver the *sound* in a different place from where it was directed; which is the specific effect of *refraction*. But *amplification* <note>original: "Maioration"</note>, which is also the work of *refraction*, appears plainly in *sounds* (as has been discussed in full); but it is not caused by a diversity of *mediums*.

<margin>
Experiments in group <note>original: "in Consort"</note> concerning the agreement and disagreement between things seen and things heard <note>original: "Visibles and Audibles"</note>.
</margin>
We have *incidentally* <note>original: "obiter"</note>, for the sake of demonstration, used in various *instances* the examples of *sight* and *visible things* to illustrate the *nature* of *sounds*. But we think it good now to pursue that *comparison* more fully.

---

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal border composed of repeating circular and floral patterns.</image-desc>

## AGREEMENT OF THINGS SEEN,
## and Things Heard,

<margin>255</margin>
Both of them spread themselves in a *circle* <note>original: "Round"</note> and fill a whole floor or *area* <note>original: "Orbe"</note> up to certain limits; and they are carried a long way; and they fade and lessen by degrees according to the distance of the objects from the *senses* <note>original: "Sensories"</note>.

<margin>256</margin>
Both of them have the entire *image* <note>original: "Species"</note> in every *small portion* of the *air* or *medium*; so that the *images* pass through small crannies without confusion. As we see ordinarily in *vistas* <note>original: "Levels"</note> regarding the *eye*, and in *crannies* or *chinks* regarding *sound*.

<margin>257</margin>
Both of them are of a *sudden* and *easy creation* and *transmission* <note>original: "Generation and Delation"</note>; and likewise *perish swiftly* and *suddenly*; as when you remove the *light*, or touch the *bodies* that give the *sound*.

<margin>258</margin>
Both of them *receive* and *carry exquisite* and *accurate distinctions*; such as colors, figures, motions, and distances in *visible things*; and articulate voices, tones, songs, and *vibrations* <note>original: "Quauerings"</note> in *audible things*.

<margin>259</margin>
Both of them, in their power and operation, do not appear to *emit* any *physical substance* <note>original: "Corporall Substance"</note> into their *mediums*, or the *sphere* of their influence; nor again do they raise or stir any *evident physical motion* in their *mediums* as they pass; but only carry certain *non-material forms* <note>original: "Spirituall Species"</note>. The perfect knowledge of the cause of this, having been until now scarcely attained, we shall search for and handle in the proper place.

<margin>260</margin>
Both of them seem not to *generate* or *produce* any other *effect* in *nature*,

<page-num>69</page-num>
<header>Century 3.</header>

nature, but such as pertain to their proper objects and senses, and are otherwise barren.

<margin>261</margin>
But **both** of them in their own proper **action** produce three manifest **effects**. The first is that the **stronger species** <note>original: "Species" — in this context, the sensory form or signal of light or sound</note> drowns out the **lesser**; just as the light of the sun drowns the light of a glow-worm, or the **report** of an **ordnance** <note>original: "Ordnance" — a large piece of artillery or a cannon</note> drowns out the voice. The second is that an **object** of surcharge or **excess** destroys the sense; just as the light of the sun destroys the eye, or a violent **sound** (near the ear) destroys the hearing. The third is that **both of them will be reverberated**; as in **mirrors** and in **echoes**.

<margin>262</margin>
Neither of them **destroys** or **hinders the species of the other**, even though they encounter one another in the same **medium** <note>the substance through which the light or sound travels, such as air</note>; for light or color do not hinder sound, nor on the contrary <note>original: "è contrà"</note>.

<margin>263</margin>
**Both** of them affect the senses in **living creatures** and yield **objects of pleasure and dislike**. Yet, nevertheless, the **objects** of them also (if it be well observed) affect and work upon dead **things**; namely, those things that have some conformity with the **organs** of the two **senses**. For example, **visibles** work upon a **looking-glass**, which is like the pupil of the eye; and **audibles** work upon the places of **echo**, which resemble, in some way, the cavity and structure of the ear.

<margin>264</margin>
**Both** of them **work diversely** as they have their **medium diversely disposed**. So, a trembling **medium** (such as smoke) makes the **object** seem to tremble; and a rising or falling **medium** (such as winds) makes **sounds** rise or fall.

<margin>265</margin>
**To both**, the **medium** which is the most favorable and conducive is **air**; for glass or water, etc., are not comparable.

<margin>266</margin>
**In both** of them, where the **object** is **fine and accurate**, it helps much to have the **sense intentive** <note>intently focused</note> and **erect**. Thus, you contract your **eye** when you would see sharply, and erect your **ear** when you would hear attentively; which is most manifest in beasts that have movable ears.

<margin>267</margin>
**The beams of light**, when they are multiplied and gathered together, generate **heat**, which is a different **action** from the **action of sight**. And the **multiplication and gathering together of sounds** generate an extreme **rarefaction of the air** <note>a thinning of the air's density</note>, which is a physical <note>original: "materiate"</note> action, differing from the **action of sound**. This may be true if it is as anciently reported: that **birds**, at the sound of great shouts, have fallen down dead.

# DIFFERENCES BETWEEN VISIBLES,
## and Audibles.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut footer border matching the scrolling floral design of the header.</image-desc>

---

<margin>268</margin>
The **forms** of **visibles** <note>original: "species" — the sensory images or physical forms of things seen</note> seem to be **emissions** of **beams** from the object seen; almost like **odors**, except that they are more **incorporeal** <note>without physical body or substance</note>. But the **forms** of **audibles** <note>original: "species" — things heard</note> seem to participate more in **local motion**, like **percussions** <note>impacts or strikes</note> or **impressions** made upon the **air**. So, while all bodies seem to work in two ways—either by the **communication** of their **natures**, or by the **impressions** and **signatures** of their **motions**—the **diffusion** of **visible forms** seems to partake more of the former **operation**, and the **audible forms** of the latter.

<margin>269</margin>
The **forms** of **audibles** seem to be carried more clearly through the **air** than the **forms** of **visibles**. For I believe <note>original: "conceive"</note> that a strong headwind will not hinder the sight of **visibles** as much as it will the **hearing** of **sounds**.

<margin>270</margin>
There is one **difference**, above all others, between **visibles** and **audibles** that is the most remarkable, as many smaller **differences** depend upon it: namely, that **visibles** (except for **lights**) are carried in **straight lines** <note>original: "right lines"</note>, and **audibles** in **curved lines** <note>original: "arcuate lines"</note>. Because of this, it happens that **visibles** do not intermingle and confuse one another, as has been said before, but **sounds** do. This is also why the **solidity** of bodies does not much hinder sight, provided the bodies are clear and the pores are in a **straight line**, as in **glass**, **crystal**, **diamonds**, **water**, and so on. But a thin **scarf** or **handkerchief**, even though they are bodies that are not nearly as solid, hinders sight. In contrast, these porous bodies do not much hinder **hearing**, while solid bodies almost stop it, or at least weaken <note>original: "attenuate"</note> it. This is also why small **mirrors** <note>original: "glasses"</note> are sufficient for the **reflection** of **visibles**, but for the **reverberation** <note>the echoing or bouncing back</note> of **audibles**, larger **spaces** are required, as has likewise been said before.

<margin>271</margin>
**Visibles** are seen from further away than **sounds** are heard, provided we account for the **ratio** of their **size** <note>original: "rate of their bigness"</note>. Otherwise, a great **sound** will be heard from further away than a **small body** can be seen.

<margin>272</margin>
**Visibles** generally require some **distance** between the **object** and the **eye** to be better seen, whereas with **audibles**, the closer the **sound** is to the **sense**, the better. But in this, there may be a double error. The first is because **seeing** requires **light**, and anything that touches the pupil of the **eye** entirely excludes the **light**. For I have heard from a very credible person (who himself was cured

And yet, nevertheless, some **distance** is required for both.

<margin>273</margin>
**Visibles** <note>things seen</note> are carried more swiftly to the **sense** than **audibles** <note>things heard</note>, as appears in **thunder** and **lightning**, **flame** and the report of a **gun** <note>original: "peece"</note>, or the motion of the **air** in **chopping** <note>original: "hewing"</note> **wood**. All of these have been set down before, but they are appropriate for this **heading**.

<margin>274</margin>
I also believe <note>original: "conceiue"</note> that the **forms** <note>original: "species" — the sensory images or physical manifestations of a sound</note> of **audibles** hang longer in the **air** than those of **visibles**. For although even those of **visibles** hang for some time—as we see in **spinning rings** that look like **spheres**, in **lute-strings** when plucked <note>original: "fillipped"</note>, a **firebrand** carried along which leaves a **trail** of **light** behind it, and in the **twilight**, and the like—yet I believe that **sounds** stay longer because they are carried up and down with the **wind**, and because of the delay in time when **cannons** <note>original: "ordnance"</note> are discharged and heard 20 **miles** away.

<margin>275</margin>
Among **visibles**, there are no **objects** found that are as odious and unpleasant to the **sense** as there are among **audibles**. For foul **sights** displease more because they trigger the memory of foul things than because of the immediate **objects** themselves. Therefore, in **pictures**, those foul **sights** do not offend much. But among **audibles**, the **grating** of a **saw** when it is sharpened offends so much that it **sets the teeth on edge**. And the **ear** immediately rejects any of the **harsh discords** in **music**.

<margin>276</margin>
Among **visibles**, after a great **light**, if you suddenly enter the **dark**, or conversely, go from the **dark** into a **glaring light**, the **eye** is dazzled for a time and the **sight** confused. But whether any such **effect** occurs after great **sounds** or after a **deep silence** could be better investigated. It is an old tradition that those who dwell near the **cataracts of the Nile** <note>original: "Cataracts of Nilus"</note> are struck deaf, but we find no such **effect** in **cannoneers**, nor **millers**, nor those who dwell upon **bridges** <note>Bacon refers to the constant roar of water under bridges, such as the Old London Bridge</note>.

<margin>277</margin>
It seems that the **impression** of **color** is so weak that it only works through a cone of **direct beams** or **straight lines**, where the **base** <note>original: "basis"</note> is at the **object** and the **vertex** <note>original: "verticall point"</note> is in the **eye**. Thus, there is a **co-radiation** <note>the meeting of rays</note> and conjunction of **beams**. And those **beams** sent forth are not strong enough to produce similar borrowed or second **beams**, except by **reflection**, which we are not discussing here. For the **beams** pass through and give little **stain** <note>original: "tincture"</note> to the adjacent **air**; if they did, we would see **colors** outside of a **straight line**. But while this is true for **colors**, it is different for the **body** of **light**. For when there is a **screen** between the **candle** and the **eye**, the **light** still passes to the **paper** where one is writing, so that the **light** is seen where the **body** of the **flame** is not...

<margin>
278
Experiments in concert, regarding the sympathy or antipathy of sounds with one another.
</margin>
ALL *concords* and *discords* of *music* are (no doubt) *sympathies* and *antipathies* of *sounds*. And so likewise in that *music* which we call ***broken music*** <note>original: "Broken Musicke" — music played by a "mixed consort" of different families of instruments, such as strings and woodwinds together</note> or ***consort music***; some *combinations* <note>original: "Consorts"</note> of *instruments* are sweeter than others (a thing not yet sufficiently observed). For instance, the *Irish harp* and *bass viol* <note>original: "Bafe Viall"</note> agree well; the *recorder* and *stringed music* agree well; *organs* and the *voice* agree well, and so on. But the *virginals* <note>a keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</note> and the *lute*, or the *Welsh harp* and *Irish harp*, or the *voice* and *pipes* alone do not agree so well. For the *improvement* <note>original: "Melioration"</note> of *music*, there is still much left to try and investigate regarding these *exquisite concerts*.

<margin>279</margin>
There is a common observation that if a *lute* or *viol* is laid upon its back with a small straw upon one of the *strings*, and another *lute* or *viol* is laid by it, and in that other *lute* or *viol* the *unison* <note>the same pitch</note> to that string is struck, it will make the string move. This will appear both to the eye and by the straw falling off. The same will happen if the *diapason* <note>original: "Diapason" — the interval of an octave</note> or *eighth* to that string is struck, either in the same *lute* or *viol* or in others lying nearby. But in none of these is there any audible *sound* <note>original: "Report of Sound"</note> that can be discerned, only motion.

<margin>280</margin>
It was devised that a *viol* should have a layer of wire strings below, placed as close to the belly <note>the soundboard or front of the instrument</note> as a *lute*, and then the *strings* of gut mounted upon a bridge as in ordinary *viols*. The intention was that by this means, the upper strings when struck should make the lower ones resound by *sympathy*, and so make the *music* better. If this works as intended, then *sympathy* operates by the *sound* itself as well as by *motion*. But I conceive this device to be of no use, because the upper *strings* (which are fingered <note>original: "stopped" — pressed against the fingerboard to change pitch</note> in great variety) cannot maintain an *octave* or *unison* with the lower strings, which are never fingered. But if it were to be of any use at all, it must be in *instruments* that have no fingerboards <note>original: "Stops"</note>, such as *virginals* and *harps*, where a trial may be made of two rows of strings placed at a distance from one another.

<margin>281</margin>
The *experiment of sympathy* may perhaps be transferred from *stringed instruments* to other *instruments of sound*. For example, one could try if there were two *bells* of *unison* in one steeple, whether the striking of one would move the other more than if it were a different harmony <note>original: "Accord"</note>. And likewise in *pipes* (if they are of equal bore and *sound*), whether a little straw or feather would move in one *pipe* when the other is blown at a *unison*.

It seems that in both the *ear* and *eye*, the *instrument* of *sense* has a *sympathy* or *similarity* with that which provides the *reflection* (as has been mentioned before). <margin>
Experiments in concert, regarding the hindering or helping of hearing.
283
284
</margin>
When a man yawns, he cannot *hear* as well. The *cause* is that the *membrane* of the *ear* is stretched; and so it deflects the *sound* rather than drawing it in.
We *hear* better when we *hold our breath* than otherwise; indeed, in all listening to catch a *sound* from far away, men *hold their breath*. The *cause* is that in all *exhalation*, the motion is outward, and therefore it pushes away the voice rather than drawing it in. Furthermore, we see that in any *effort* to do something with strength, we *hold our breath*; and listening for a *sound* that is heard with difficulty is a kind of *effort*.

<margin>285</margin>
To *help hearing*, let a trial be made (and I believe it is likely to succeed) of making an *instrument* like a *tunnel* <note>Bacon is describing an early version of an ear trumpet</note>. The narrow part should be the size of the hole of the *ear*, and the broader end much larger, like the flare of a *bell*. It should be half a foot long or more. Let the narrow end be set close to the *ear*, and observe whether any *sound* out in the open *air* is heard more distinctly from a further distance than without that *instrument*. It would be, as it were, an *ear-spectacle*. I have heard there is an *instrument* in use in *Spain* to be set to the *ear* that somewhat *helps* those who are *hard of hearing* <note>original: "Thicke of Hearing"</note>.

If the *mouth* is shut tight, a *murmur* is nevertheless produced by the *roof* of the *mouth*, such as is used by those who cannot speak. But if the *nostrils* are also stopped, no such *murmur* can be made, except in the back of the *palate* toward the *throat*. By this, it appears clearly that a *sound in the mouth* (except for the one just mentioned) passes from the *palate* through the *nostrils* if the *mouth* is stopped.

<margin>
Experiments in concert, regarding the spiritual and refined nature of sounds.

</margin>
The reflection of *sounds* (which we call *echo*) is a great argument for the *non-physical nature of sounds* <note>original: "Spirituall Essence of Sounds." In this context, "spiritual" refers to things that are invisible, weightless, or active forces rather than solid matter</note>. For if sound were *physical* <note>original: "Corporeall"</note>, the reflection would have to be created in the same manner and by similar *instruments* as the *original sound*. But we see what a number of refined *organs* <note>original: "Instruments" — referring here to the lips, tongue, and throat</note> must work together to speak words, whereas there is no such thing involved in the returning of them—only a plain *stop* and *reflection*.

<margin>288</margin>

<margin>289</margin>
All *sounds* are suddenly made and suddenly perish. But neither that, nor the *exquisite differences* between them, is a matter of such great wonder. For the *quaverings* and *warblings* in lutes and pipes are just as swift; and the tongue (which is not a very refined instrument) makes no fewer motions during speech than there are letters in all the words being uttered. But that *sounds* should not only be so speedily generated, but carried so far in every direction in such a momentary time, deserves more wonder. For example, if a man stands in the middle of a field and speaks aloud, he shall be heard a furlong in every direction <note>a furlong is about 201 meters</note>. That speech will consist of *articulate sounds*, and those sounds shall be entire in every little portion of the *air*, and all this happens in less than a minute.

<margin>290</margin>
The *sudden generation* and *perishing* of *sounds* must happen in one of two ways. Either the *air* suffers some force by the *sound* and then restores itself, just as water does—which, when divided, makes many circles until it restores itself to its natural stillness—or otherwise, the *air* willingly absorbs the *sound* as something pleasing but cannot maintain it. It would seem the *air* has a secret and hidden appetite for receiving the *sound* at first, but then other coarse and more *material* <note>original: materiate</note> qualities of the *air* immediately suffocate it. This is like a *flame*, which is generated with eagerness but is immediately quenched by the hostility of the *air* or other surrounding bodies.

->There are these *differences* (in general) by which *sounds* are divided: 1. *Musical*, *unmusical*; 2. *Treble*, *bass*; 3. *Flat*, *sharp*; 4. *Soft*, *loud*; 5. *Exterior*, *interior*; 6. *Clear*, *harsh* or *rippling* <note>original: purling</note>; 7. *Articulate*, *inarticulate*.<-

We have labored diligently (as may appear) in this *investigation* <note>original: inquisition</note> of *sounds*, both because *sound* is one of the most hidden portions of *nature* (as we said at the beginning) and because it is a *power* <note>original: vertue</note> which may be called *incorporeal* and *immaterial*, of which there are few in *nature*. Besides, we were willing (now in these our first *centuries* <note>Bacon's book is organized into "centuries," or groups of 100 observations/experiments</note>) to create a pattern or *precedent* <note>original: president</note> of an *exact investigation*. We shall do the same hereafter in other subjects that require it. For we desire that men should learn and perceive how rigorous a thing the true *investigation* of *nature* is, and should accustom

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the radiant <note>original: orient</note> colors in the dissolution of metals. 291</margin>
Metals give radiant and fine colors in dissolutions; as gold gives an excellent yellow; **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> an excellent green; tin gives an excellent azure. Likewise in their **putrefactions** or **rusts**, such as **vermilion**, **verdigris**, **bice** <note>original: Bisse; a blue or green pigment</note>, **ceruse** <note>original: Cirrus; likely ceruse, a white lead pigment</note>, etc. And likewise in their **vitrifications** <note>the process of turning into glass</note>. The cause is that, by their strength of body, they are able to endure the **fire** or **strong waters** <note>acids, like nitric acid</note>, and to be put into an **equal posture**, and again to retain part of their principal **spirit**. These two things (equal posture and quick spirits) are required chiefly to make colors bright.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the prolongation of life. 292</margin>
It contributes to **long life** and to the more **peaceful** <note>original: placide</note> **motion** of the **spirits**, which thereby less prey upon and consume the **juice of the body**, if either **men's actions are free and voluntary**—that nothing be done "against the grain" <note>original: *Invitâ Minervâ*; literally 'with Minerva unwilling'</note> but "according to one's natural inclination" <note>original: *Secundum Genium*</note>—or, on the other side, that the **actions of men be full of regulation and commands** within themselves. For then the **victory and performing of the command** gives a good disposition to the spirits, especially if there is a proceeding from degree to degree, for then the **sense of victory** is the greatest. An example of the former of these is in a **country life**, and of the latter, in **monks** and **philosophers**, and such as continually enjoin themselves <note>impose strict rules or discipline upon themselves</note>.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the appetite for union in bodies. 293</margin>
It is certain that in all **bodies**, there is an **appetite for union** and an **avoidance** <note>original: evitation</note> **of the breaking** <note>original: solution</note> **of continuity**. Of this **appetite**, there are many **degrees**, but the most **remarkable** and fit to be distinguished are three. The first is in **liquors**; the second in **hard bodies**; and the third in **bodies that are clinging** <note>original: cleaving</note> or **tenacious**. In **liquors**, this **appetite** is weak. We see in **liquors** the **threading** of them in **drippings** <note>original: stillicides</note> (as has been said), the **falling** of them in **round drops** (which is the form of **union**), and the **staying** of them for a little time in **bubbles** and **froth**. In the second **degree** or **kind**, this **appetite** is strong, as in **iron**, in **stone**, in **wood**, etc. In the third, this **appetite** is in a **middle state** <note>original: medium</note> between the other two, for such **bodies** partly follow the **touch** of another **body** and partly stick and continue to themselves; and therefore they "rope" and draw themselves into **threads**, as we see in **pitch**, **glue**, **birdlime**, etc. But note that all **solid bodies** are **clinging**, more or less, and that they prefer the **touch** of something **tangible** rather than of **air**. For **waters** in small quantity cling to any **thing** that is **solid**, and so would **metal** too if the weight did not draw it off. And therefore **gold leaf** <note>original: Gold Foliate</note>, or any **metal leaf**, clings. But those **bodies** which are noted to be **clammy** and **clinging** are such as have a more indifferent **appetite** (at once) to follow another **body** and to hold to themselves.

# Natural History

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the similar effects <note>original: Operations</note> of heat and time.
294
</margin>
Time and *heat* are partners in many effects. *Heat* dries bodies that easily evaporate <note>original: expire</note>, such as parchment, leaves, roots, clay, etc. And so does *time* or *age* dry them out <note>original: arefy</note>, as in those same bodies, etc. Heat dissolves and melts bodies that keep in their spirits <note>the internal gases or vital essences believed to animate matter</note>, as seen in various *liquefactions*. And so does *time* in some bodies of a softer consistency: as is manifest in honey, which by *age* becomes more liquid; and the like in sugar; and so in old oil, which is always clearer and "hotter" <note>more chemically active or pungent</note> in medicinal use. *Heat* causes the spirits to seek some exit from the body, as in the *volatility* of *metals*. And so does *time*, as in the *rust* of *metals*. But generally, *heat* does in a short time what *age* does over a long period.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the differing effects of fire and time.
295
</margin>
Some things that pass through the *fire* are softest at first and by *time* grow hard, such as the crumb of bread. Some are harder when they come from the *fire* and afterwards soften <note>original: give again</note> and grow soft, such as the crust of bread, biscuit, sweetmeats, salt, etc. The cause is that in those things which grow hard with *time*, the work of the *fire* is a kind of *melting*. And in those that grow soft with *time* (on the contrary), the work of the *fire* is a kind of *baking*. And whatever the *fire* bakes, *time* dissolves to some degree.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning movements by imitation.
296
</margin>
Movements pass from one man to another, not so much by exciting the *imagination* as by invitation—especially if there is a readiness <note>original: aptness</note> or inclination beforehand. Therefore *gaping*, or *yawning*, and *stretching* do pass from man to man. For what causes *yawning* and *stretching* is when the spirits are a little heavy due to any vapor or the like. For then they strive (as it were) to wring out and expel that which loads them. So people who are drowsy and desirous to sleep, or who are about to suffer a fit of fever <note>original: Ague</note>, usually yawn and stretch; and they likewise produce a *voice* or *sound*, which is an involuntary sound <note>original: interjection</note> of expulsion. So if another person is ready and prepared to do the same, he follows by the sight of the other. Similarly, the *laughing* of another person makes one *laugh*.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning infectious disease.
297
</margin>
There are some known diseases that are *infectious*, and others that are not. Those that are *infectious* are: First, those that exist chiefly in the *spirits* <note>vital or animal spirits</note> and not so much in the *humors* <note>the four primary bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note>, and therefore pass easily from body to body. Such are *plagues* <note>original: Pestilences</note>, *eye inflammations* <note>original: Lippitudes</note>, and such like. Secondly, those that *taint* the *breath*, which we see passes clearly from man to man—and invisibly, as the influences <note>original: affects</note> of the spirits do. Such are *consumptions of the lungs* <note>tuberculosis</note>, etc. Thirdly, those that come out to the *skin*, and therefore taint the *air* or the *body adjacent*.

...adjacent; especially if they consist of an *unctuous substance* <note>original: "Vnctious"; an oily or greasy matter</note>, which is not likely to dissipate. Such are *scabs* and *leprosy*. Fourthly, some infections are merely in the *humors* <note>the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament</note>, and not in the *spirits*, *breath*, or *exhalations*. Therefore, they never infect except by *touch* only; and even then, it must be a *touch* that penetrates beneath the *epidermis* <note>the outer layer of skin</note>, such as the venom of the *French Pox* <note>a historical name for syphilis</note> and the *biting of a mad dog* <note>rabies</note>.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the incorporation of powders and liquids.
298
</margin>
Most powders grow more close and coherent by being mixed with *water* than by being mixed with *oil*, even though *oil* is a thicker substance—as seen with *meal* <note>flour or ground grain</note>, etc. The reason is the "congruity" of bodies; if there is more compatibility between substances, it allows for a more perfect absorption and incorporation. In most powders, this compatibility is greater between *them* and *water* than between them and *oil*. However, *painter's colors* when ground, and *ashes*, do incorporate better with *oil*.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning exercise of the body.
299
</margin>
Much motion and exercise is good for some bodies, while *sitting* and less *motion* are better for others. If the body is hot and lacks superfluous moisture, too much *motion* is harmful; it is an error for *physicians* to insist too much upon *exercise*. Likewise, men ought to beware of using *exercise* and a *restricted diet* at the same time. Instead, if one does much *exercise*, they should have a *plentiful diet*; and if they have a *restricted diet*, they should do little *exercise*. 

The benefits that come from *exercise* are: *first*, it sends *nourishment* into the parts of the body more forcibly; *secondly*, it helps to *excrete* <note>original: "Excerne"; to separate or discharge waste</note> through *sweat*, and so makes the body parts assimilate nutrients more perfectly; *thirdly*, it makes the *substance* of the *body* more *solid* and *compact*, and so less likely to be *consumed* and *preyed upon* <note>original: "Depredated"</note> by the *spirits* <note>the internal gases or vital essences believed to animate and "burn through" the body's moisture</note>. 

The *evils* that come from *exercise* are: *first*, it makes the *spirits* more *hot* and *predatory*; *secondly*, it also absorbs and thins <note>original: "attenuate"</note> the *moisture* of the *body* too much; *thirdly*, it causes too great a *concussion* <note>shaking or jarring</note> (especially if it is violent) of the *internal parts*, which delight more in *rest*. Generally, however, much *exercise* is no friend to the *prolongation of life*; this is one reason why *women* live longer than *men*, because they move around less.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning foods that induce satiety.
300
</margin>
Some food we may eat for a long time and in large amounts without *glutting* <note>becoming sickened or overly full</note>, such as *bread* or *meat* that is not fat or rancid. Some other foods (though pleasant) cause satiety sooner, such as *sweetmeats*, *fat meats*, etc. The *cause* is that *appetite* consists in the *emptiness* of the *opening* <note>original: "Mouth"</note> of the *stomach*, or in filling it with something that is *astringent* and therefore *cold* and *dry*. 

But things that are *sweet* and *fat* are more *filling*; they linger and "swim" more around the *opening* of the *stomach* and do not go down as quickly. Furthermore, they turn more quickly into *choler* <note>yellow bile, associated with heat and bitterness</note>, which is hot and always reduces the *appetite*. We also see that another *cause* of *satiety* <note>feeling full or satisfied</note> is *over-custom* <note>habit or repetition</note>, whereas *novelty* creates *appetite*. Therefore, if the same foods are taken continually, they induce *loathing*. To give the reason for the *distaste* of *satiety*, and of the *pleasure*...

### IV. Century.

<margin>Experiments in collaboration regarding the **clarification** of liquors and the **acceleration** of that process.</margin>
The acceleration of **time** in the **works of nature** may well be esteemed **among the great wonders of nature** <note>original: *Inter Magnalia Naturæ*</note>. And even in **divine miracles**, the **accelerating of time** is next in importance to the **creating of matter**. We will now, therefore, proceed to the **investigation** <note>original: "Enquiry"</note> of it. As for the **acceleration of germination** (the sprouting of seeds), we will refer that to the section where we shall handle the **subject of plants** in general; we will now begin with other types of acceleration.

---

<margin>301</margin>
**Liquors** are, many of them, at first thick and cloudy <note>original: "troubled"</note>: such as **must** <note>unfermented grape juice</note>, **wort** <note>infusion of grain used in brewing beer</note>, the **juices of fruits**, or **pressed** <note>original: "expressed"</note> **herbs**, and so on. Over **time**, they settle and **clarify**. But to make them clear before their natural time is a great **feat** <note>original: "Worke"</note>; for it is a **spur to nature** and puts her out of her normal pace. Besides, it is very useful for making **drinks** and **sauces** drinkable and ready for use quickly. However, to know the **means of accelerating clarification**, we must first know the **causes of clarification**. The first **cause** is the **separation** of the **coarser parts** <note>original: "Grosser Parts"</note> of the liquor from the **finer**. The second is the **equal distribution** of the **spirits** <note>the active, volatile essences or gases within a substance</note> of the liquor throughout the **tangible parts**; for that always makes **substances** <note>original: "Bodies"</note> appear clear and unclouded,

...enabled. The third way is by the **refining** of the **spirit** itself, which thereby gives to the **liquor** more **splendor** and more **luster**.
First, regarding **separation**: it is achieved by **weight**, as in the ordinary settling <note>original: "Residence"</note> of **liquors**; by **heat**; by **motion**; by **precipitation** or **sublimation** (which is a drawing of the various parts either up or down, acting as a kind of **attraction**); by **adhesion**, as when a more **viscous** <note>thick or sticky</note> body is mingled and stirred with the **liquor**, which **viscous** body (after being separated) draws the grosser parts of the **liquor** with it; and lastly, by **percolation** <note>filtering</note> or passage.

<margin>303</margin>
Secondly, regarding the **even distribution** of the **spirits**: it is achieved by **gentle heat** and by **agitation** or **motion**. (We do not mention **time**, because time is exactly what we wish to anticipate and represent.) It is also achieved by the **mixture** of some other **body** which has the power to open the **liquor** and allow the **spirits** to pass through more easily.

<margin>304</margin>
Thirdly, regarding the **refining** of the **spirit**: it is likewise achieved by **heat**, by **motion**, and by the **mixture** of some **body** which has the **virtue** <note>natural power or efficacy</note> to thin it. Having shown the **causes**, take these **instances** and **trials** for the **accelerating** and **inducing** of **clarification** in general.

<margin>305</margin>
It is common **practice** to draw **wine** or **beer** away from the **lees** <note>the sediment at the bottom of the barrel</note>, which we call **racking**. By this, it will **clarify** much sooner; for the **lees**, though they keep the **drink** "in heart" <note>vigorous or flavorful</note> and make it last longer, also throw up some **thickness** <note>original: "Spiffitude"</note>. This **instance** is categorized under **separation**.

<margin>306</margin>
On the other hand, it would be good to test what **adding** more **lees** than the liquor’s own would do. For though the **lees** make the **liquor** cloudy <note>original: "turbide"</note>, they also refine the **spirits**. Take, therefore, one **vessel** of **new beer** and another **vessel** of **new beer**. Rack the first **vessel** from its **lees**, and pour those **lees** into the **unracked vessel**, and observe the **effect**. This **instance** is categorized under the **refining** of the **spirits**.

<margin>307</margin>
Take **new beer** and put a quantity of **stale beer** into it, and see whether it will not accelerate the **clarification** by **opening** the **body** of the **beer** and **cutting** <note>breaking down</note> the grosser parts, so that they may fall down into the **lees**. This **instance** is again categorized under **separation**.

<margin>308</margin>
The longer **malt**, **herbs**, or similar items are infused in **liquor**, the thicker and more troubled the **liquor** becomes. But the longer they are decocted <note>boiled</note> in the **liquor**, the clearer it becomes. The reason is plain: in **infusion**, the longer it lasts, the greater the portion of the **gross body** that enters the **liquor**. But in **decoction**, though more comes out, it either purges at the top or settles at the bottom. Therefore, the most exact way to **clarify** is first to **infuse**, then take off the **liquor** and **boil** it; as they do with **beer**, where **malt** is first infused in the **liquor** and then boiled with the **hop**. This is also categorized under **separation**.

Note that when emptying one bottle into another, you must do it quickly so the drink does not go flat. It would also be good to try this in a bottle with a little air below the neck without emptying it. This experiment refers to the even distribution and refining of the spirits by motion.

<margin>311</margin>
As for percolation <note>filtration through a porous substance</note>, both internal and external (which belongs to the process of separation), a trial should be made of clarifying by adhesion. This could be done with milk put into new beer and stirred with it; for it may be that the coarser part of the beer will stick to the milk. The doubt is whether the milk will separate well again, which is easily tested. It is common when clarifying hypocras <note>original: "Ippocraſſe"; a spiced wine</note> to put in milk, which afterward separates and carries with it the coarser parts of the wine, as has been mentioned elsewhere. Also, for better clarification by percolation, when they barrel <note>original: "tun"</note> new beer, they usually let it pass through a strainer; and typically, the finer the strainer is, the clearer the beer will be.

### ->We will now enquire into the speeding up of maturation.<-

And regarding maturation <note>ripening or aging</note> itself: it is of three natures. The maturation of fruits, the maturation of drinks, and the maturation of abscesses <note>original: "Impostumes"</note> and ulcers. This last one we refer to another place, where we shall handle medicinal experiments. There are also other maturations, such as those of metals, etc., of which we will speak as the occasion serves. But we will begin with that of drinks, because it has such a closeness <note>original: "Affinity"</note> with the clarification of liquors.

<margin>312</margin>
For the maturation of drinks, it is achieved by the gathering together <note>original: "Congregation"</note> of the spirits, whereby they process <note>original: "digest"</note> the coarser parts more perfectly. It is effected partly by the same means that clarification is (of which we spoke before). But note that an extreme clarification does...

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon’s observations on the maturation of liquids and fruits, focusing on how the movement and preservation of "spirits" (the active, volatile essences within matter) affect the freshness and ripening process.</meta>

<page-num>82</page-num>

...spread the *spirits* so smoothly that they become dull and the *drink* goes flat <note>original: "dead"</note>, whereas it ought to have a little foaming <note>original: "flouring"</note>. This is why all your clear *amber-colored drinks* are flat.

<margin>313</margin> We see the *degrees of maturation in drinks*: in *grape juice* <note>original: "must"</note>, in *wine* (as it is drunk), and in *vinegar*. In *grape juice*, the *spirits* are not well gathered together <note>original: "congregated"</note>; in *wine*, they are well united, making the liquid somewhat more oily. In *vinegar*, they are gathered together but are more meager <note>original: "jeiune"</note> and in smaller quantity, because the greatest and finest *spirit* and part has evaporated <note>original: "exhaled"</note>. We see that *vinegar* is made by setting the vessel of *wine* in the hot sun; therefore, *vinegar* will not burn because much of the finer parts have evaporated.

<margin>314</margin> The *refreshing* and *reviving* <note>original: "quickening"</note> of *drink* that has gone flat <note>original: "palled"</note> or dead is achieved by *forcing the motion of the spirit*. We see that *mild weather* <note>original: "open weather"</note> relaxes the *spirit* and makes its *motion* more lively. We also see that *bottling* *beer* or *ale* while it is new and full of *spirit*—so that it squirts out when the stopper <note>original: "stopple"</note> is removed—makes the *drink* more lively and carbonated <note>original: "windy"</note>. A *pan of coals* in the *cellar* also helps, making the *drink* ferment <note>original: "work"</note> again. *New drink* added to *drink* that is *dead* encourages it to ferment again; in fact, as some claim, *a brewing of new beer* placed near *old beer* makes it ferment again. It would also be good to *force* the *spirits* by some *mixtures* that may excite and revive them, such as putting *saltpeter* <note>original: "nitre"</note>, *chalk*, *lime, etc.* into the *bottles*. We see that *cream* is *matured* and made to rise more quickly by adding *cold water*, which seemingly forces the *whey* to settle.

<margin>315</margin> It has been tested that the *burying of bottles of drink* well-stopped, either deep in *dry earth* or at the *bottom of a well under water*—and best of all, the *hanging* of them in a *deep well* somewhat *above the water* for about two weeks—is an excellent *way* of making *drink* fresh and lively. This is because the *cold* does not cause any *evaporation* <note>original: "exhaling"</note> of the *spirits* at all, as *heat* does (even though it thins the remaining liquid). Instead, *cold* makes the *spirits* vigorous and stimulates <note>original: "irritateth"</note> them, causing them to blend <note>original: "incorporate"</note> perfectly with the *liquor*.

<margin>316</margin> Regarding the *maturation of fruits*: it is achieved by *drawing the spirits of the body outward* and spreading them more smoothly, and also by *breaking down* <note>original: "digesting"</note>, in some degree, the *coarser parts*. This is accomplished by *heat*, *motion*, *attraction*, and by the *beginnings of rot* <note>original: "a rudiment of putrefaction"</note>. Indeed, the *beginning of rotting* <note>original: "inception of putrefaction"</note> involves a process of *maturation*.

The results of these *experiments* were as follows:

<margin>318</margin> After a month’s time, the *apple* enclosed in *wax* was as green and fresh as when it was first put in, and the *seeds* <note>original: "kernels"</note> remained white. <header>Century IV.</header>

<margin>319</margin>
The disadvantage <note>original: "conuenience"</note> is that it tastes a little of the *wax*. I suppose that in a *pomegranate* or some other thick-coated *fruit*, this would not happen.

The *apple hung* in the *smoke* turned into something like an *old mellow apple*: wrinkled, dry, soft, sweet, and yellow inside. The *cause* is that this specific degree of *heat* neither melts nor scorches. (We see that in great *heat*, a *roasted apple* softens and melts; and "pigs' feet" <note>A historical culinary term for pears quartered and stewed into a specific shape</note> made of quarters of *Wardens* <note>A variety of large baking pear</note> scorch and develop a blackened skin.) This heat mellows the fruit rather than burning <note>original: "adure"</note> it. The *smoke* also leaves the *apple* as if sprinkled with *soot*, which helps it to *ripen*. We see a similar process in the *drying* of *pears* and *prunes* in an oven, where they are frequently moved as they begin to "sweat," though that involves a much more intense degree of *heat*.

<margin>320</margin>
The *apples covered in lime and ashes* were well *ripened*, as shown by both their yellowness and sweetness. The *cause* is that the *degree of heat* found in *lime* and *ashes* (being a smothering heat) is the most appropriate of all. It neither liquefies the fruit nor dries it out <note>original: "arefie"</note>, and that is true *ripening*. Note that the taste of those *apples* was good, making this the most practical *experiment* for actual *use*.

<margin>321</margin>
The *apples covered with crab apples* <note>original: "crabs"</note> and *onions* were likewise well *ripened*. The cause is not any *heat*, but rather that the *crab apples* and the *onions* draw out the *spirits* <note>The active, volatile essences within the fruit</note> of the *apple* and spread them equally throughout its *body*, which removes the hardness. Thus we see that one *apple ripens* against another. For this reason, when making *cider*, they first pile the *apples* in a heap. Similarly, one *cluster of grapes* that touches another while growing ripens faster; as the saying goes, "a cluster of grapes matures faster against another cluster" <note>original Latin: *Botrus contra Botrum citius maturescit*</note>.

<margin>322</margin>
The *apples* kept in *hay* and *straw* ripened visibly, though not as much as the *others*; however, the *apple in the straw* ripened more. The *cause* is that *hay* and *straw* have a very low degree of *heat*, yet it is contained and smothering, and does not dry the fruit out.

<margin>323</margin>
The *apple* in the *closed box* was also ripened. The *cause* is that any air kept enclosed has a degree of *warmth*, as we see with *wool, fur, plush*, and so on.

Note that all of these were compared with *another apple of the same kind* that sat by itself. In comparison to that one, these were sweeter and more yellow, appearing to be more ripe.

<margin>324</margin>
Take an *apple*, *pear*, or other similar *fruit* and *roll* it firmly upon a table. We know from common experience that *rolling* softens and sweetens the *fruit* immediately. This is simply due to the *smooth distribution* of the *spirits* into all its parts, for it is the *unequal distribution* of the *spirits* that causes hardness. However, this *hard rolling* falls somewhere between *ripening through heat* <note>original: "concoction"</note> and a *simple ripening*. Therefore, if you were to *roll* them gently, perhaps twice a day, and continue for about seven days, it is likely they would *ripen* more delicately and in a way that resembles *natural ripening*.

<margin>325</margin>
Take an *apple* and cut a piece out of the top, then cover it to see whether that *physical break* <note>original: "solution of continuity"</note> will hasten *ripening*. We see that

<margin>*Solitary Experiment regarding the Making of Gold.*</margin>
The world has been much deceived <note>original: "abused"</note> by the belief in the *making of gold*. I judge the work itself to be possible; but the *means* (proposed until now) to achieve it are, in practice, full of error and *fraud* <note>original: "Imposture"</note>; and in theory, full of unsound imaginations. For to say that *Nature* intends to make all metals *gold*, and that if she were freed from obstacles, she would complete her own work; and that if the rawness, impurities, and "leprosies" <note>original: "Leprosities"; an alchemical term for the perceived corruptions or "diseases" of base metals compared to gold</note> of *metals* were cured, they would become *gold*; and that a small *quantity* of the medicine, in the work of *projection* <note>original: "Projection"; the final stage of alchemy where a "catalyst" is added to transform base metal into gold</note>, will turn a sea of *base metal* into *gold* by *multiplying*—all these are but dreams. So are many other foundations of *alchemy*. To help the matter, the *alchemists* also call upon many vanities from *astrology*, *natural magic*, superstitious interpretations of *Scriptures*, oral traditions <note>original: "Auricular Traditions"</note>, fabricated <note>original: "Fained"</note> testimonies of *ancient authors*, and the like. 

It is true, on the other side, that they have brought to light quite a few profitable *experiments*, and thereby made some amends to the world. But we, when we come to handle the *transformation* <note>original: "Version"</note> and *transmutation* of *substances* <note>original: "Bodies"</note>, and the experiments concerning *metals* and *minerals*, will reveal the true ways and paths of *nature* which may lead to this great *result* <note>original: "Effect"</note>. And we commend the wit of the *Chinese*, who despair of *making gold* but are obsessed with the *making of silver*. For it is certain that it is more difficult to make *gold* (which is the heaviest <note>original: "most Ponderous"</note> and most substantial <note>original: "Materiate"</note> among *metals*) from other *metals* that are less heavy and less substantial, than it is (*vice versa*) <note>original: "viâ versâ"</note> to make *silver* from *lead* or *quicksilver* <note>original: "Quick-Siluer"; mercury</note>. Both of these are heavier than *silver*, so that they...

<header>Century IV.</header>

...need a further degree of *fixation* <note>original: "Fixation"; in alchemy, the process of turning a volatile substance into a solid or stable form</note> rather than any *condensation*. Meanwhile, because we are discussing the *axioms* <note>original: "Axiomes"; established principles or self-evident truths</note> regarding *maturation*, we will propose a *trial* concerning the *maturation of metals*, and thereby *turning* some of them into *gold*. For we truly believe that a perfectly successful *concoction*, *digestion*, or *maturation* of certain *metals* will produce *gold*. 

And here we recall that we knew a *Dutchman* who had convinced a high-ranking person of his ability to make *gold*. His argument was that *gold* could indeed be made, but that the *alchemists* applied too much heat to the process <note>original: "Ouer-fired the Worke"</note>. For (he said) the *making of gold* required a very moderate *heat*, since in *nature* it is a *subterranean* work where little *heat* reaches; yet it requires more heat to *make gold* than any other *metal*. Therefore, he intended to do it using a large *lamp* that would provide a moderate and steady heat, and he claimed it was a work of many months. The invention of the lamp was foolish; however, his points regarding the excessive heat currently used, the need for a steady heat, and the requirement that it be a lengthy process are sound arguments.

Therefore, we return to our *axioms* of *maturation*, which were briefly mentioned earlier. 

The first is that a *moderate heat* must be used, for it is always *moderate heats* that *digest* and mature substances. By *moderate*, we mean relative to the *nature of the subject*; for what may be *moderate* for *fruits* and *liquors* will have no effect at all upon *metals*. 

The second is that the *spirits of the metal* must be activated <note>original: "quickened"</note> and the *tangible parts opened*. Without these two operations, the *spirit of the metal* being acted upon will not be able to "digest" or transform its parts. 

The third is that the *spirits should spread themselves evenly and not move erratically* <note>original: "subsultorily"; jumping or pulsing unsteadily</note>; for this will make the parts dense and flexible. This requires a heat that does not fluctuate, but continues as *steadily as possible*. 

The fourth is that *no part of the spirit should be released, but instead kept inside*. For if there is a *release of spirit*, the body of the *metal* will remain hard and brittle <note>original: "Churlish"</note>. This will be achieved partly by the moderation of the fire and partly by the airtightness of the vessel.

The fifth point is that a **choice** should be made of the most likely and best **prepared metal** for the **conversion** <note>original: "Version"</note>, as this will make the work easier. The sixth point is that you must give **time** enough for the **work**—not to keep **hopes** alive (as the **alchemists** do), but to give **nature** a suitable **amount of time** to operate. These **principles** are most certain and true. We will now derive a method of **trial** based on them, which may perhaps be improved by further **reflection**.

<margin>327</margin>
Let a **small furnace** be made with a **temperate heat**. The **heat** should be such that it may keep the **metal perpetually molten** and nothing more; for that is the most important factor for the **work**. For the **material**, use **silver**, which is the **metal** that naturally **corresponds** <note>original: "Symbolizeth"</note> most closely with **gold**. Also add a tenth part of **mercury** <note>original: "Quick-siluer"</note> and a twelfth part of **saltpeter** <note>original: "Nitre"</note> by weight. Both of these serve to activate and open the "body" of the **metal**. Let the **work** continue for at least **six months**. I also recommend that, from time to time, there be an **injection** of some **oily substance**, such as those used in the **recovery** of **gold** that has become **brittle** <note>original: "Churliſh"; difficult to work with</note> after being agitated by chemical **separations**. This is done to make the parts more **compact** and **smooth**, which is the **main objective**. For **gold** (as we see) is the **densest** (and therefore the heaviest) of **metals**, and it is also the most **flexible** and **ductile** <note>original: "Tensible"</note>. Note that trying to make **gold** out of **mercury** just because it is the heaviest is a hopeless task, as **mercury** cannot withstand the **management** of the **fire**. After **silver**, I believe **copper** would be the most suitable **material**.

The **inducing** and **accelerating** of **decay** <note>original: "Putrefaction"</note> is a subject of universal investigation. For **corruption** <note>decay</note> is the **counterpart** <note>original: "Reciprocall"</note> to **generation** <note>the creation or growth of new things</note>. These **two** are like **nature's two boundaries**, and the **guides** to **life** and **death**. **Decay** is the work of the **spirits** <note>internal gaseous or active forces</note> within **bodies**, which are always **restless** to **escape**, gather with the **air**, and enjoy the **sunbeams**. The **escape** or **spreading** of the **spirits** (spreading being a partial degree of escape) involves five **different operations**. It

<page-num>87</page-num>
<header>Century IV.</header>

If the *Spirits* <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to active, invisible, vaporous agents within all matter that drive physical changes.</note> are held within the body and move more violently, *liquefaction* <note>original: "Colliquation"; the process of melting or turning to liquid</note> follows, as seen in *metals*, etc. If they move more mildly, *ripening* or *maturation* <note>original: "Digestion"</note> follows, as in *drinks* and *fruits*. 

If the *Spirits* are not merely held but push outward a little, and that motion is confused and disorderly, *putrefaction* <note>decay or rotting</note> follows. This always dissolves the consistency of the body into great irregularity, as seen in *flesh, rotten fruits, glowing wood* <note>original: "Shining Wood"; bioluminescent rotting wood, often called foxfire</note>, etc., and also in the *rust* of *metals*. 

But if that motion occurs in a certain order, *vivification* <note>the process of coming to life</note> and *figuration* <note>the formation of a specific shape or organized body</note> follow. This is seen both in *living creatures* born from *putrefaction* <note>a reference to the then-common belief in "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter</note> and in *perfect living creatures*. 

But if the *Spirits* leave the body entirely, *desiccation* <note>drying out</note>, *hardening* <note>original: "Induration"</note>, and *decay* <note>original: "Consumption"</note> follow, as seen in the making of *brick*, the evaporation of *liquid bodies*, and similar processes.

<margin>329</margin>
The means to *induce* and *accelerate putrefaction* are: First, by *adding some raw or watery moisture*, such as *wetting* any *flesh, fruit,* or *wood* with water, etc. Conversely, *greasy* and *oily substances* preserve them.

<margin>330</margin>
The second way is by *invitation* or *excitation*. This occurs when a *rotten apple* lies close to another *apple* that is *sound*, or when *dung* (which is a substance already putrefied) is added to other bodies. This is also notably seen in *churchyards* where many are buried; there, the earth will consume the *corpses* in a much shorter time than other earth will.

<margin>331</margin>
The third way is by *confinement and sealing*, which keeps the *Spirits* "imprisoned" more than they naturally would be. This provokes them to seek an exit, as seen in *grain* <note>original: "Corne"</note> and *clothes* which grow *musty*. Therefore, open *air* (which they call *flowing air* <note>original Latin: "Aer perflabilis"</note>) preserves things. This is also clearly seen in *fevers* <note>original: "Agues"</note>, most of which come from *obstructions* and the *trapping* of the *humors* <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health</note>, which then *putrefy*.

<margin>332</margin>
The fourth way is by the *breaking of a surface* <note>original: "Solution of Continuity"; a physical break or wound</note>. As we see, an *apple* will rot sooner if it is *cut or pierced*; the same happens to *wood*, etc., and to the *flesh* of living creatures where they have received a *wound*.

<margin>333</margin>
The fifth way is either by the *evaporation* <note>original: "Exhaling"</note> or by the *driving back* of the principal *Spirits* that maintain the consistency of the *body*. When their control is dissolved, every *part* returns to its own nature or *original state* <note>original: "Homogeny"</note>. This also appears in *urine* and *blood* when they cool and thereby separate <note>original: "breake"</note>. It also appears in *gangrene* or the *mortification* of *flesh*, caused either by *opiates* or by *intense cold*. I also believe the same effect occurs in *plagues* <note>original: "Pestilences"</note>, because the *malice* of the *infecting vapor* daunts the *principal spirits* and makes them flee and abandon their *rule* <note>original: "Regiment"</note>. Then the *humors, flesh,* and *secondary spirits* dissolve and break down, as if in a state of anarchy.

<margin>334</margin>The sixth cause is when a **foreign spirit** <note>original: "Forraine Spirit"; an external active force or substance</note>, stronger and more **aggressive** than the **spirit** of the body, enters the **body**, such as in the **stinging of serpents**. This is generally the **cause** of the **swelling** that follows all **poisons**. We see that **swelling** also follows when the **spirits** of the body itself **gather** <note>original: "Congregate"</note> too much, as from **blows** and **bruises**, or when they are **trapped** <note>original: "Pent"</note> too tightly, as in **swelling** caused by **cold**. We also see that the **spirits** arising from the **putrefaction** <note>decay or rotting</note> of **humors** <note>bodily fluids</note> in **fevers** <note>original: "Agues"</note>, etc.—which may be counted as **foreign spirits** even though they are bred within the body—**snuff out** and **smother** the **natural spirits** and **heat**.

<margin>335</margin>The seventh cause is a **low level of heat** that sets the **spirits** into a slight **motion** but is not able either to **mature** the **parts** or to **release** the **spirits**. This is seen in **meat** <note>original: "Flesh"</note> kept in a **room** that is not **cool**, whereas in a **cool** and **damp larder**, it will keep longer. We see also that **vivification** <note>the process of coming to life</note> (of which **putrefaction** is the **bastard brother**) is brought about by such **gentle heats**, like the **hatching** of **eggs**, the **heat** of the **womb**, etc.

<margin>336</margin>The eighth cause is the **releasing of the spirits**, which were previously kept enclosed by the **solidity** of their **covering**, thereby checking their **tendency** <note>original: "Appetite"</note> to **escape**. This is seen in the **chemically induced rusts** <note>original: "Artificiall Rusts"</note> created by **strong acids** <note>original: "strong Waters," such as nitric acid</note> in **iron, lead**, etc. Therefore, **wetting** hastens **rust** or the **decay** of anything because it softens the **crust**, allowing the **spirits** to come out.

<margin>337</margin>The ninth cause is the **alternation of heat and cold**, or **wet and dry**. We see this in the **crumbling of soil** <note>original: "Mouldring of Earth"</note> during **frosts** and **sun**, and in the faster **rotting of wood** that is sometimes **wet** and sometimes **dry**.

<margin>338</margin>The tenth cause is **time** and the **work** and **process** of the **spirits** themselves, which cannot remain still—especially if they are left to themselves and there is no **agitation** or **physical movement**. This is seen in **grain** <note>original: "Corne"</note> that is not stirred and in human **bodies** that are not exercised.

<margin>339</margin>All **molds** are the **beginnings of decay** <note>original: "Inceptions of Putrefaction"</note>, such as the **molds** on **pies** and **meat**, or the **molds** on **oranges** and **lemons**. These **molds** later turn into **maggots** <note>original: "Wormes"</note> or more foul **putrefactions**, and therefore usually produce a bad **odor**. If the body is **liquid** and not prone to **decaying** entirely, it will produce a **film** <note>original: "Mother"; a thick, cloudy substance like the "mother" in vinegar</note> on the **top**, like the **films** found in **distilled waters**.

<margin>340</margin>**Moss** is a **kind of mold** of the **earth** and **trees**. However, it might be better classified as an **early stage of growth** <note>original: "Rudiment of Germination"</note>, which is where we shall categorize it.

<page-num>89</page-num>
<header>Century IV.</header>

Regarding the **bodies** of **men** and **living creatures** (as in **fevers** <note>original: "Agues"</note>, **worms**, **lung consumption**, **abscesses** <note>original: "Impostumes"</note>, and **ulcers** both **internal** and **external**), these are a major **part** of **medicine** and **surgery**. Therefore, we will reserve the **study** of them for their proper **place**, where we shall handle **medicinal experiments** of all **sorts**. For the rest, we will now begin an **inquiry**. Much insight may be gained here from what has already been said about the **means** to **induce** or **accelerate putrefaction**; for **removing** that which caused **putrefaction** does **prevent** and **avoid putrefaction**.

<margin>341</margin>
The first means of **prohibiting** or **checking putrefaction** is **cold**. We see that **food** and **drink** will last longer without **rotting** or **souring** in **winter** than in **summer**. We also see that **flowers** and **fruits** kept in **snow houses** <note>original: "Conseruatories of Snow"</note> stay fresh. This works by **holding in** the **spirits** and by the **tightening** <note>original: "Constipation"; here meaning the contraction or compression of physical matter</note> of the **tangible parts**.

<margin>342</margin>
The second is **astringency** <note>original: "Astriction"; the quality of shrinking or contracting body tissues</note>. For **astringency** prohibits the **breaking apart** <note>original: "Dissolution"</note> of a substance. We see this generally in **medicines**, where **astringents** inhibit **putrefaction**. By the same principle of **astringency**, a small **quantity** of **sulfuric acid** <note>original: "Oile of Vitrioll"</note> will keep fresh **water** from **rotting** for a long time. This **astringency** exists in a **substance** that has a **hidden coldness** <note>original: "Virtuall Cold"</note>, and it works partly by the same **means** that actual **cold** does.

<margin>343</margin>
The third is the **exclusion of air**—and conversely, the **exposure to air**. For these **opposites** (as often happens) produce the same **effect**, depending on the **nature** of the **subject matter**. So we see that **beer** or **wine** in tightly stopped **bottles** lasts a long time; that **underground granaries** <note>original: "Garners"</note> keep **grain** longer than those above **ground**; and that **fruit** sealed in **wax** stays fresh. Likewise, **bodies** placed in **honey** and **flour** stay fresher, and **liquors**, **drinks**, and **juices** stay fresh with a little **oil** poured on the **top**. On the other hand, we see that **cloth** and **clothing** breed **moths** and **mold** if they are not **aired out**. The **difference** is that in **bodies** that need to **keep in** their **spirits**, the **exclusion** of the **air** is beneficial, as in **drinks** and **grain**. But in **bodies** that need to **release spirits** to discharge some of the superfluous **moisture**, excluding air does hurt, for they require **airing**.

<margin>344</margin>
The fourth is **motion** and **stirring**. For **putrefaction** requires **rest**. The **subtle motion** that **putrefaction** requires is disturbed by any **agitation**. All **physical motion** keeps **bodies intact** <note>original: "Integrall"</note> and their **parts** together. We see that **turning** over **grain** in a **granary**—or **letting** it run like an **hourglass** from an upper **room** into a **lower** one—keeps it **sweet**. **Running waters** do not rot. In **human bodies**, **exercise** hinders **putrefaction**. Conversely, **rest** and a lack of **motion** or **blockages** <note>original: "Stoppings"</note>—where the **flow** of **humors** <note>bodily fluids</note> or the **motion** of **perspiration** is stopped—further **putrefaction**, as we touched upon briefly before.

<summary>This page explores four primary methods for preventing decay: cold temperatures, astringent substances, the regulation of air exposure, and physical motion. Bacon argues that these methods work by either trapping vital "spirits" within a body or allowing harmful moisture to escape.</summary>
<keywords>putrefaction, preservation, cold, astringency, oil of vitriol, air exposure, ventilation, motion, humors, Francis Bacon</keywords>
