<page-num>90</page-num>
<header>Natural History;</header>

<margin>345</margin> The fifth method is the **venting of external moisture** <note>original: "Breathing forth of the Adventitious Moisture"</note> **from bodies**. Just as **wetting** hastens **decay**, **proper drying** (which keeps only the more **essential moisture** <note>original: "Radicall Moisture"</note> inside) holds back **decay**. Thus, we see that **herbs** and **flowers** keep best if they are dried in the shade, or dried in the hot sun for a short time. For the **releasing** of the **loose** and **external moisture** protects the **essential moisture**, while allowing it to remain would draw the essential moisture out along with it.

<margin>346</margin> The sixth is the **strengthening of the internal spirits of bodies** <term>Spirits</term> <note>In early modern science, "spirits" were invisible, active substances within matter thought to govern its vitality and preservation.</note>. Just as **intense heat** keeps **bodies** from **decay**, while a **lukewarm heat** <note>original: "Tepide Heat"</note> inclines them toward it, so too a **strong spirit** preserves a body, while a **weak** or **faint spirit** makes it prone to **corruption**. Thus, we find that saltwater does not decay as quickly as freshwater, and the **salting** of oysters and the **curing** <note>original: "Powdring"</note> of meat keeps them from **decay**. It should also be tested whether **chalk** put into **water** or **drink** preserves it from **decaying** or quickly souring. Similarly, we see that **strong beer** will last longer than **weak beer** <note>original: "small"</note>, and all things that are hot and **aromatic** help to preserve liquids or powders. They do this both by strengthening the **spirits** and by soaking up the loose **moisture**.

<margin>347</margin> The seventh is the **removal of coarser components** <note>original: "Separation of the Cruder Parts"</note>, thereby making the body **more uniform**. This is because any **imperfect mixture** is likely to **decay**, and watery substances are more prone to **decay** than oily ones. Thus, we see distilled waters will last longer than **raw waters**, and things that have been processed by fire last longer than those that have not, such as **dried pears**.

<margin>348</margin> The eighth is the **continuous removal of that part where decay begins**, which is commonly the **loose** and **watery moisture**. This is not only for the reason given before—that it draws the **essential moisture** out with it—but because if it is kept in the body, the **decay** taking hold of it infects the rest. We see this in the **embalming of dead bodies**, and the same logic applies to **preserving herbs**, **fruits**, or **flowers** in **bran** or **meal**.

<margin>349</margin> The ninth is the **mixing in of anything that is more oily or sweet**. Such **bodies** are least prone to **decay**, as the **air** has little effect on them, and because they do not decay themselves, they preserve the rest. Therefore, we see that **syrups** and **ointments** will last longer than **juices**.

<margin>350</margin> The tenth is the **mixing in of something dry**. **Decay** begins first from the **spirits** and then from the **moisture**, and that which is dry is not prone to decay. Therefore, **smoke** preserves meat, as we see in **bacon**, **ox tongues** <note>original: "Neats-Tongues"</note>, and **winter-salted beef** <term>Martlemas Beef</term> <note>Beef slaughtered and salted around St. Martin's Day in November for winter storage.</note>.

<margin>351</margin> The opinion held by some of the **ancients**—that **compressed air** <note>original: "Blowne Aires"</note> preserves bodies longer than other **air**—seems probable to me. This is because **compressed air**, being over-charged and squeezed, can hardly receive the vapors exhaled from an object, but rather repels them. This was tested using a **blown-up bladder** into which meat and a flower were placed, but it did not work; for **dry bladders** will not **inflate**, and **new bladders** rather...

<margin>A solitary experiment concerning wood that shines in the dark. 352</margin>
We have diligently conducted and pursued the experiment of wood that **shines** in the **dark**. We did so because, of all things that give off light here on earth, it is the most long-lasting and has the least visible movement. **Fire** and **flame** are constantly consuming fuel; **sugar** shines only while it is being scraped; and **saltwater** glows only while it is splashing. **Glow-worms** shine while they are alive or shortly after. Only the **scales** of (decaying) **fish** seem to be of the same nature as **shining wood**. It is true that all **decay** <note>original: "Putrefaction"</note> involves an internal motion, just as **fire** or **light** does. The trial results were as follows:

1.  The **shining** is **brighter** in some pieces and **dimmer** in others, but even the **brightest** does not reach the light of a **glow-worm**.
2.  The woods tested for shining are mainly **sallow** <note>a species of willow</note> and **willow**, as well as **ash** and **hazel**. It may also occur in others.
3.  Both the **roots** and the **main trunks** <note>original: "Bodies"</note> shine, but the **roots** shine better.
4.  In daylight, the **color** of the **shining part** is **white** in some pieces and reddish in others, which in the countryside they call **"white garret"** and **"red garret"** <note>"Garret" or "Goret" was a regional term for the decaying heartwood of a tree.</note>.
5.  The part that shines is usually somewhat **soft** and **moist** to the touch, though some was found to be **firm** and **hard**, enough that it could be carved into a cross or into beads, etc. However, you should not expect to see a clear image or likeness in anything that emits light. Even a face in red-hot iron cannot be seen, as the light blurs the small differences between light and dark areas that define a shape.
6.  When the **shining part was shaved off** until the non-shining wood was reached, the **adjacent part** also began to **shine** within two days when left outside in the dew. Thus, it seems the decay spreads.
7.  Other dead wood of the same kind was **placed outside**; it did not **shine** at first, but after one night outside, it began to **shine**.
8.  Other **wood** that **initially shone** lost its **glow** within five or six days when kept dry indoors, but recovered the **glow** when placed outside again.
9.  **Shining woods** lost their light within a week when kept in a **dry room**, but kept **shining** when placed in a **cellar** or **damp room**.
10. **Boring holes** in that kind of wood and then placing it outside seems to help it **shine**. The cause is that any **break in the structure** <term>solution of continuity</term> <note>original: "solution of Continuity"; a physical break or interruption in the substance of an object.</note> helps promote **decay**, as mentioned before.
11. No **wood** cut down while **alive** has yet been found to **shine**; only wood that **rotted** in both the trunk and root while it was still growing.
12. Part of the **wood that shone** was soaked in **oil** and kept its **glow** for two weeks.
13. The same occurred with wood **soaked in water**, and much better.
14. It has not yet been tested how long the **glow** will continue if the **wood is placed outside every night** and brought in and **sprinkled with water during the day**.

<margin>
Experiment 353:
A solitary experiment concerning the acceleration of birth.
</margin>

The delivery of **living creatures** may be **accelerated** <note>original: "speeded up"</note> in two ways: one, if the **embryo matures** and reaches perfection sooner; the other, if there is some cause from the **mother's body** for **expulsion** or delivery. The former is good and suggests strength; the latter is bad and happens by accident or disease. Therefore, the ancient **observation** is true: a **child born in the seventh month** usually does well, but one **born in the eighth month** (for the most part) dies. However, the **cause** assigned to this is a myth <note>original: "fabulous"</note>. They say that in the eighth month, the reign of the **planet Saturn** returns, which is considered a **harmful planet** <note>original: "Planet Maligne"</note>, whereas in the seventh month, the **moon** reigns, which is a **favorable planet** <note>original: "Planet Propitious"</note>. The true **cause** is that when there is such a great anticipation of the ordinary time, it is due to the **vigor** <note>original: "lustiness"</note> of the child. But when the time is closer to the full term (like the eighth month), the early birth is caused by some **ailment** <note>original: "indisposition"</note> of the mother.

<margin>
Experiment 354:
A solitary experiment concerning the acceleration of growth and stature.
</margin>

To accelerate **growth** or **stature**, it must proceed from one of three things: a **plenty of nourishment**, the **nature of the nourishment**, or the **quickening** and exciting of the **natural heat**. Regarding the first, an **excess of nourishment** is harmful; it makes the child corpulent, growing in width rather than height. You can see an experiment of this in **plants**, which, if they spread out much, are seldom tall. 

As for the **nature of the nourishment**: first, it must not be too **dry**. Therefore, children in **dairy** regions grow taller than those where they feed more on bread and meat. There is also a common tale that boiling **daisy roots** in **milk**—which are certainly great drying agents—will make **dogs** small. However, this much is true: an **over-dry nourishment** in childhood stunts stature. 

Secondly, the **nourishment** must be of an **opening nature** <note>tending to clear blockages or stimulate the flow of fluids</note>, for that thins the juices <note>original: "attenuateth the juice"</note> and encourages the movement of the "spirits" <note>the vital energies believed to drive bodily functions</note> upward. It is not without cause that **Xenophon**, in his account of the **upbringing** <note>original: "nouriture"</note> of **Persian children**, so highly commends their feeding on **cardamon**. He says it made them grow better and have a more **active habit** <note>physical constitution</note>. **Cardamon** in Latin is ***nasturtium*** <note>original: "Nasturtium"</note> and for us is **watercress**. It is certainly an herb that, while young, is healthy <note>original: "friendly to life"</note>. 

As for the **quickening** of **natural heat**, it must be done chiefly with **exercise**. Therefore, no doubt, spending much time at school, where children sit so much, hinders the **growth of children**. In contrast, country people who do not go to school are commonly of better stature. Furthermore, men must be careful not to give **children** anything that is **cold in its effect** <note>original: "cold in operation"</note>. Even **long-term breastfeeding** <note>original: "long-sucking"</note> hinders both **intelligence** <note>original: "wit"</note> and **stature**. It has been tested that a puppy <note>original: "whelp"</note> fed with **nitre** <note>potassium nitrate, or saltpeter</note> in **milk** has become...

## Century IV.

...become very small, but extremely lively: for the *Spirit of Nitre* <note>original: "Spirit of Nitre"; a substance like saltpeter or nitric acid believed to have cooling and life-extending properties</note> is *cold*. And though it is an excellent medicine in the prime of life for the prolongation of life, it is an enemy to *growth* in children and young creatures. This is for the same reason: *heat* is required for growth, but after a man reaches middle age, *heat* consumes the *spirits*; the coldness of the *Spirit of Nitre* helps to condense and correct this.

<margin>
Experiments in grouping regarding Sulphur and Mercury, two of Paracelsus's principles
</margin>

There are two *Great Families of Things*. You may call them by several names: *Sulphurous* and *Mercurial*, which are the *chemists' words* <note>original: "Chymists Words"; referring to the followers of the physician and alchemist Paracelsus</note>. (As for their *salt* <note>original: "Sal"</note>, which is their third principle, it is a *compound* of the other two). These families are also called *inflammable* and *not inflammable*; *mature* and *crude*; *oily* and *watery*. For we see that in *subterranean things* <note>original: "Subterranies"; minerals and metals found underground</note> there are, as the fathers of their *tribes*, *brimstone* and *mercury*. In *vegetables* and *living creatures*, there is *water* and *oil*. In the *inferior order* of <term>gases</term> <note>original: "Pneumaticals"; substances relating to air or spirit</note> there is *air* and *flame*. And in the *superior order*, there is the *body of the star* and the *pure sky*. 

These pairs, though they are unlike in the *primary differences* of matter, seem to have many correspondences <note>original: "Consents"</note>. For *mercury* and *sulphur* are the main materials of *metals*; *water* and *oil* are the main materials of *vegetables* and *animals*, and seem to differ only in *ripening* <note>original: "Maturation"</note> or *processing* <note>original: "Concoction"</note>. *Flame* (in common opinion) is merely *ignited air* <note>original: "Aire Incensed"</note>, and they both have a similar quickness of motion and ability to yield <note>original: "Facility of Cession"</note>. And the *interstellar sky* (though the opinion is false that the *star* is the *denser part of its orbit*) has so much affinity with the *star* that there is a rotation of the sky as well as of the star. Therefore, it is one of the greatest <term>wonders of nature</term> <note>original: "Magnalia Naturæ"; great works or mysteries of nature</note> to turn *water* or *watery juice* into *oil* or *oily juice*. This is greater in nature than turning *silver* or *quicksilver* into *gold*.

# Natural History

...living creatures, though much of their **fat** and **flesh** comes from **oily nourishment** (such as **meat** and **bread**), yet they also **assimilate** <note>original: "Assimilate"; to absorb and incorporate into the body</note> to some degree their **drink** of **water**, and so on. But these two ways of **conversion** <note>original: "Version"</note> of **water** into **oil** (namely by **mixture** and by **assimilation**) occur through many passages and filterings, by the long continuation of gentle **heats**, and over long cycles of time.

<margin>357</margin> The third way is at the **beginning** of **decay** <note>original: "Inception of Putrefaction"</note>, as seen in contaminated water and the "mothers" <note>original: "Mothers"; the dregs or sediment</note> of distilled waters; both of which have a kind of **fatness** or **oiliness**.

<margin>358</margin> The fourth is in the **refining** <note>original: "Dulcoration"; literally "sweetening," but here referring to a chemical process</note> of some **metals**, such as **Sugar of Lead** <note>original: "Saccharum Saturni"; lead acetate, a sweet but toxic chemical compound</note>.

<margin>359</margin> The goal of the **conversion** of **water** into a more **oily substance** is achieved by **maturation** <note>original: "Digestion"</note>. For **oil** is almost nothing else but **matured water**; and this **maturation** is principally caused by **heat**. This **heat** must be either **external** or **internal**. Furthermore, it may be achieved by **provocation** or **stimulation**, which is caused by mixing in bodies that are already **oily** or **matured**; for they will communicate some of their nature to the rest. **Maturation** is also strongly affected by the direct **assimilation** of **raw bodies** into **matured bodies**, as seen in **plants** and **living creatures**, whose nourishment is far rawer than their own bodies. But this **maturation** takes place over a great **duration** <note>original: "Compasse"</note>, as has been said. As for the fuller handling of these two principles, of which this is but a taste (the study of which is one of the deepest inquiries into nature), we leave it for the **section** on the **Conversion of Bodies**, and also for the **section** on the **Primary Groupings of Matter**, which, like a general **parliamentary assembly** <note>original: "Assemblie of Estates"</note>, gives laws to all physical bodies.

<margin>
Solitary experiment regarding chameleons.
360
</margin>

A **chameleon** is a creature about the size of an ordinary **lizard**. His head is disproportionately large and his eyes are great. He moves his head without turning his neck (which is inflexible), just as a **pig** does. His back is crooked, and his skin is spotted with little bumps <note>original: "Tumours"</note> which are less prominent near the belly. His tail is slender and long. On each foot he has five fingers: three on the outside and two on the inside. His tongue is of a marvelous length in proportion to his body and hollow at the end; he will **dart it out** <note>original: "launch out"</note> to prey upon **flies**. 

His color is green and a dusky yellow, becoming brighter and whiter toward the belly, yet spotted with blue, white, and red. If he is placed on green, the green predominates; if on yellow, the yellow. This is not the case if he is placed on blue, red, or white; on those, only the green spots receive a more **brilliant** <note>original: "Orient"</note> luster. Placed on black, he looks entirely black, though not without a mixture of green. He feeds not only upon air (though that is his principal sustenance), for sometimes he catches **flies**, as was mentioned. Yet some who have kept **chameleons** for a whole year together could never perceive that they ever fed upon anything else but air. They observed their bellies swell after they had **inhaled** <note>original: "exhausted"</note> the air and closed their jaws, which they open commonly...

# Century IV

...commonly against the rays of the sun. There is a foolish tradition in **magic** <note>original: "Magicke"</note> that if a **chameleon** <note>original: "Chamelion"</note> is burnt on the top of a house, it will raise a tempest. This is based on their vain dreams of **sympathies** <note>original: "Sympathies"; the occult belief that things with similar properties can influence each other</note>; they suppose that because it nourishes itself with air, its body should have great power to affect the air.

<margin>Solitary experiment regarding subterranean fires. 361</margin>
It is reported by one of the **ancients** <note>original: "Ancients"; likely referring to Greek or Roman writers like Pliny the Elder</note> that in parts of **Media** <note>an ancient region in modern-day Iran</note>, there are **eruptions of flames out of plains**. These flames are clear and do not cast forth smoke, ashes, or pumice as **volcanic flames** <note>original: "Mountaine Flames"</note> do. The reason, no doubt, is because the flame is not trapped as it is in mountains or earthquakes that cast flame. There are also some **hidden fires** <note>original: "Blind Fires"</note> under stone that do not flare up, but if oil is poured upon them, they burst into flame. The cause seems to be that the fire is so smothered that it is unable to move the stone; it is heat rather than flame, which is nevertheless sufficient to ignite the oil.

<margin>Solitary experiment regarding nitre. 362</margin>
It is reported that in some lakes, the water is so **nitrous** <note>original: "Nitrous"; containing nitre or saltpeter (potassium nitrate), though here likely referring to alkaline salts like natron</note> that if dirty clothes are put into it, it cleans them by itself. If they stay in the water for any length of time, they crumble away. This cleaning power of **nitre** is especially noteworthy because it is a **cold substance** <note>original: "Body Cold"</note>, and we usually see that warm water cleans better than cold. The cause is that it has a subtle spirit which separates and divides anything that is dirty or sticky and clings to an object.

<margin>Solitary experiment regarding the congealing of air. 363</margin>
Take a bladder, the largest you can find. Fill it full of air and tie it at the neck with a waxed silk thread. Apply wax very closely over the tie so that when the neck of the bladder dries, no air can possibly get in or out. Then bury it three or four feet under the earth in a vault, or in a **snow house** <note>original: "Conservatory of Snow"; a structure for storing ice or snow</note>, making a hollow in the snow for the bladder. After about two weeks, see whether the bladder has shrunk. If it has, then it is clear that the coldness of the earth or snow has **condensed** the air and brought it a degree nearer to becoming water. This is an experiment of great significance.

<margin>Solitary experiment regarding the congealing of water into crystal. 364</margin>
It is a report of good credit that in deep caves, there are **hanging crystals** <note>original: "Pensile Crystall"; stalactites</note> and **formations of crystal** <note>original: "Degrees of Crystall"; likely stalagmites</note> that drop from above, and in some others (though more rarely) that rise from below. Although this is chiefly the work of cold, it may also be that water passing through the earth acquires a more sticky nature, making it better suited to congeal and become solid than ordinary water. Therefore, a trial should be made: during a heavy frost, lay a heap of earth over a hollow vessel, placing a piece of canvas between them so the earth does not fall in. Pour water upon the earth in such a quantity that it is sure to soak through, and see whether it creates a harder ice at the bottom of the vessel,

# Natural History

Solitary experiment regarding preserving rose leaves in both color and smell.
365
</margin>
Take **damask roses** <note>original: "Damaske Roses"; a highly fragrant variety of rose</note> and pluck them. Then dry them on the roof of a house, upon a lead surface or **terrace** <note>original: "Tarras"</note>, in the hot sun on a clear day, only between the hours of twelve and two, or thereabouts. Then put them into a clean, dry earthenware bottle or a glass with a narrow mouth, stuffing them closely together without bruising them. Seal the bottle or glass tightly, and these roses will retain not only their perfect scent but also their fresh color for at least a year. Note that nothing destroys any plant or other body—whether by **decay** <note>original: "Putrefaction"</note> or **drying out** <note>original: "Arefaction"</note>—as much as the **external moisture** <note>original: "Adventitious Moisture"</note> that hangs loosely in the body if it is not drawn out. For this external moisture betrays and lures out the **natural and fundamental moisture** <note>original: "Innate and Radical Moisture"</note> along with it when it leaves. Therefore, in living creatures, moderate sweating preserves the fluids of the body. Note also that these roses have little or no smell when you take them from drying; thus, the fragrance is a secondary scent that emerges from the flower afterward.

<margin>
Experiments in group regarding the duration of flame.
366.
</margin>
The duration of a flame, depending on the variety of the **burning material** <note>original: "Body Enflamed"</note> and other circumstances, is worthy of investigation. This is primarily because although a flame lasts almost only a moment, it can be made to last longer or shorter durations. We will first speak in detail about materials that are burned entirely and immediately, without any **wick** to help the combustion. 

*   A spoonful of **alcohol** <note>original: "Spirit of Wine"</note>, slightly heated, was taken and it burned for a duration of 116 **heartbeats** <note>original: "Pulses"; used as a primitive timer before the invention of reliable stopwatches</note>. 
*   The same quantity of alcohol mixed with a sixth of a spoonful of **saltpeter** <note>original: "Nitre"</note> burned for only 94 heartbeats. 
*   Mixed with the same quantity of **sea salt** <note>original: "Bay salt"</note>, 83 heartbeats. 
*   Mixed with the same quantity of **gunpowder** (which dissolved into black water), 110 heartbeats. 
*   A cube or pellet of **yellow wax**, half the size of the alcohol, was placed in the middle; it burned for only 87 heartbeats. 
*   Mixed with a sixth of a spoonful of milk, it burned for 100 heartbeats, and the milk curdled. 
*   Mixed with a sixth of a spoonful of water, it burned for 86 heartbeats. 
*   With an equal quantity of water, it burned for only 4 heartbeats. 
*   A small pebble was laid in the middle, and the alcohol burned for 94 heartbeats. 
*   A piece of wood, the size of an arrow and about a finger’s length, was set up in the middle, and the alcohol burned for 94 heartbeats. 

Thus, the pure alcohol lasted the longest, while the alcohol mixed with sea salt or an equal amount of water lasted the shortest time.

### Century IV.

...is caused either by the **Greater Vigor** of the **Flame** in **Burning**, or by the resistance of the mixed substance and its **aversion** <note>original: "Auersion"; reluctance or opposition</note> to catching **fire**. This will be shown by the quantity of the **spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spirit of wine"; high-proof alcohol or ethanol</note> that remains after the **flame** goes out. It clearly seems to be the latter, because the mixture of things least likely to burn is the quickest to go out. And note, by the way, that **spirit of wine** burned until it goes out by itself will not burn again. It no longer tastes as hot in the mouth as it did before. It is not even sour—as if it had moved toward becoming **vinegar** <note>original: "Vineger"</note>, as **burnt wine** <note>original: "Burnt Wine"; wine that has been boiled or distilled</note> does—but instead tastes flat and dead.

<margin>368</margin>
Note that in the experiment with **wax** mentioned before, the wax dissolved during the burning but did not blend with the **spirit of wine** to produce a single **flame**. Instead, wherever the **wax** floated, the **flame** avoided it, until finally the wax spread over the whole surface and put the **flame** out entirely.

<margin>369</margin>
These experiments on mixtures of inflamed **spirit of wine** are for the sake of **discovery** and not for practical **use**. But now we will speak of the **duration of flames**, such as those used for **candles**, **lamps**, or **tapers**. These consist of **flammable materials** and a **wick** <note>original: "wieke"</note> that causes **ignition** <note>original: "Inflamation"</note>. This subject involves not only **discovery** but also **use** and **profit**, for it offers a great saving in all such lights if they can be made as bright as others yet last longer. **Pure wax** made into a **candle**, and **wax mixed** separately with various substances—namely **water**, **aqua-vitae** <note>original: "Aqua-vitæ"; a strong distilled spirit, literally "water of life"</note>, **milk**, **sea salt** <note>original: "Bay-salt"; coarse salt produced by evaporation of seawater</note>, **oil**, **butter**, **saltpeter** <note>original: "Nitre"</note>, **sulfur** <note>original: "Brimstone"</note>, and **sawdust**—were tested. Each of these additives made up a sixth part of the wax. Every one of these mixed candles had the same weight and wick as the **pure wax** candle. They performed as follows in their **burning** and lasting:

The quickest to be consumed was the candle with **sawdust**. It burned brightly at first until part of the candle was used up and the **dust** gathered around the **wick tip** <note>original: "Snafte"; the burnt part of a candle wick or the charred remains</note>. But then it made the **wick tip** big and long, causing it to burn dimly, and the candle was used up in half the time of the **pure wax**. The next fastest were the **oil** and **butter**, which were consumed one-fifth faster than the **pure wax**. Then followed the **clear wax** itself. After that was the **sea salt**, which lasted about an eighth longer than the **clear wax**. Then followed the **aqua-vitae**, which lasted about a fifth longer than the **clear wax**. Then followed the **milk** and **water**, which were very similar to the **aqua-vitae**, though the **water** was the slowest. In these last four, the wick would spit out little sparks. As for the **saltpeter**, it would not stay lit for more than about twelve **pulses** <note>original: "Pulses"; heartbeats, used here as a measure of time</note>. All the while, it would spit out bits of **flame**, which would then turn into vapor. The **sulfur** stayed lit for about the same time as the **saltpeter**, but after a little while, it would harden and form a crust around the **wick tip**. Therefore, mixing **sea salt** with wax adds an eighth to its lasting time, and **water** adds a fifth.

<margin>370</margin>
After the different **materials** were tried, tests were also made on several **wicks**, such as **ordinary cotton**, **sewing thread**, **rush**, **silk**, **straw**, and **wood**. The **silk**, **straw**, and **wood** would flame a little until they...

...they reached the **wax**, and then went out. Of the **other three**, the **thread** burned faster than the **cotton** by a sixth of the time. The **cotton** was next. Then the **rush** burned slower <note>original: "flower"; a common printing error for "slower"</note> than the **cotton** by at least a third of the time. Regarding the size of the **flame**, the **cotton** and **thread** produced flames that were very similar, while the **rush** produced a much smaller and dimmer flame. **Question**: whether wood and wicks together, as in **torches**, burn faster than **simple wicks**.

<margin>371</margin>
We have spoken of the different **materials** and the various **wicks**. But the **duration** <note>original: "lasting"</note> of the **flame** depends not only on what the material is, but also on whether that same material is hard, soft, old, or new. To make their **candles** burn longer, good **housewives** usually lay them (one by one) in **bran** or **flour**, which makes them harder and causes them to burn more slowly. In fact, by this means, they will outlast other candles made of the same material by almost double the time. Both **bran** and **flour** have the power to harden the wax; therefore, both aging and lying in bran help with longevity. We also see that **wax candles** last longer than **tallow candles** <note>original: "Tallow Candles"; candles made from rendered animal fat</note> because wax is firmer and harder.

<margin>372</margin>
The **duration** of the **flame** also depends on the ease of **drawing fuel** <note>original: "Drawing of the Nourishment"</note>. As we see in the **Court of England**, there is a service they call an "**All-night**" <note>A large candle or cake of wax designed to burn throughout the night</note>, which is essentially a great cake of **wax** with the **wick** in the middle. Because of this, the wick draws its fuel from a greater distance. We also see that **lamps** last longer because the vessel is much broader than the width of a **taper** or **candle**.

<margin>373</margin>
Take a **turreted lamp** made of **tin**, shaped like a <term>square</term> <note>original: "Squire"; a carpenter's square or L-shape</note>. Let the height of the **turret** be three times the length of the lower part where the **lamp** stands. Make only one hole in it, at the end of the horizontal section furthest from the **turret**. Turn it over and fill it full of **oil** through that hole; then set it upright again, put a **wick** in the hole, and light it. You will find that it burns slowly and for a long time. This is because (as mentioned previously) the **flame** draws its **fuel** from a distance. You will also find that as the **oil** is used up and its level drops, the top of the **turret** gradually fills with **air**. This is caused by the expansion <note>original: "Rarefaction"</note> of the oil due to heat. It would be worth observing—by making a hole in the top of the **turret**—whether the "air" created from the oil will ignite if you hold a candle flame to it as it is released. It would also be good to have the lamp made of **glass** instead of **tin**, so you can see how the vapor or **air** gradually gathers at the top.

<margin>374</margin>
A fourth point that affects the **duration** of the **flame** is the **confinement of the air** in which the flame burns. We see that if **wind** blows on a **candle**, it wastes away quickly. We also see that it lasts longer in a **lantern** than in the **open air**. There are also legends of **lamps** and **candles** that have burned for a very long time in **caves** and **tombs**.

# Century IV.
99

...of the **air** where the **flame** burns: whether it is hot or cold, moist or dry. If the **air** is very **cold**, it irritates the **flame** and makes it burn more fiercely (just as fire scorches more in frosty weather), and so it hastens the **consumption** <note>original: "Consumption"; the process of the fuel being used up</note>. Once the **air** is heated, I believe it makes the **flame** burn more mildly, and so helps it **last longer** <note>original: "Continuance"</note>. If the **air** is **dry**, it is neutral <note>original: "indifferent"</note>. If the **air** is **moist**, it quenches the **flame** to some degree (as we see **lights** go out in the **damp** <note>original: "Damps"; pockets of suffocating or toxic gas found in mines</note> of **mines**); regardless, moisture makes it burn more dully and thus helps it **last longer**.

<margin>Experiments in combination <note>original: "in Confort"; experiments performed together or in relation to one another</note> concerning the burial of various bodies in the earth. 376</margin>
**Burials** in the **earth** serve for **preservation**, **condensation** <note>original: "Condensation"; the process of making a substance more dense</note>, and the **hardening** <note>original: "Induration"</note> of **bodies**. If you intend to **condense** or **harden** them, you may bury the **bodies** so that the **earth** touches them, such as if you wish to make **artificial porcelain** <note>European scientists at this time were experimenting with burying mixtures to replicate Chinese porcelain</note>, etc. You may do the same for **conservation** if the **bodies** are hard and solid, such as clay, wood, etc. But if you intend to **preserve** **bodies** that are more soft and tender, then you must do one of two things: either you must put them in **cases** so they do not touch the **earth**, or else you must **vault** the earth so it hangs over them without touching. For if the **earth** touches them, it will do more harm by its moisture (causing them to rot) than good by its natural coldness (to conserve them)—unless the **earth** is very dry and sandy.

<margin>377</margin>
An **orange**, **lemon**, and **apple** wrapped in a **linen cloth** were buried four feet deep in the earth for two weeks. Even though the location was moist and the weather rainy, they came out not at all moldy or rotten, but had become a little harder than they were before. Otherwise, they remained fresh in their color, though their juice was somewhat flat. However, after being buried for two weeks more, they became rotten.

<margin>378</margin>
A **bottle of beer**, buried in the same way as described before, became more lively, better-tasting, and **clearer** than it was. A **bottle of wine** reacted in the same way. A **bottle of vinegar**, so buried, came out more lively and more **fragrant** <note>original: "Odoriferous"</note>, smelling almost like a violet. After a whole month of **burial**, all three came out as fresh and lively, if not better, than before.

<margin>379</margin>
It would be a profitable **experiment** to preserve **oranges**, **lemons**, and **pomegranates** until **summer**, for then their price will be greatly increased. This may be done if you put them in a pot or vessel, well-covered so the moisture of the earth does not reach them, or else by putting them in a **conservatory of snow** <note>An early ice-house or snow-pit used for refrigeration</note>. Generally, whoever wishes to perform **experiments involving cold** should be provided with three things: a **conservatory of snow**, a large vault at least twenty feet underground, and a **deep well**.

<margin>380</margin>
There has been a tradition that **pearls**, **coral**, and **turquoise** <note>original: "Turchois-Stone"</note> that have lost their color may be recovered by **burying** them in the **earth**. This would be a very profitable thing if it worked, but after a trial of six weeks of **burial**, there was no effect. It would be good to try it in...

Solitary experiment concerning the effects on men’s bodies from various winds.
381
</margin>
**Men's bodies** are heavier and less inclined to move when **southern winds** blow than when **northern** ones do. The **cause** is that when the **southern winds** blow, the **humors** <note>original: "Humours"; the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—once believed to govern health</note> do (to some degree) melt and become fluid, and so flow into the **limbs** <note>original: "Parts"</note>. This is seen in **wood** and other **objects** which swell when the **southern wind** blows. Besides, the motion and activity of the body consist chiefly in the **sinews** <note>original: "Sinewes"; here referring to tendons or nerves</note>, which are more relaxed when the **southern wind** blows.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning winter and summer illnesses.
382
</margin>
It is commonly seen that more people are **sick in the summer**, and more **die in the winter**, except in the case of **pestilential diseases** <note>original: "Peſtilent Diſeaſes"; infectious diseases like the plague</note>, which commonly prevail in **summer** or **autumn**. The reason is that **diseases** are indeed bred chiefly by **heat**, but then they are cured most by **sweating** and **purging**, which occur or are induced more easily in the **summer**. As for **pestilential diseases**, the reason why most people die of them in **summer** is because they are mostly bred in the **summer**; otherwise, those who are afflicted <note>original: "touched"</note> are in the most danger in the **winter**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning seasons of plague.
383
</margin>
The general opinion is that **years that are hot and moist** are the most **pestilential**, based on the superficial reasoning that **heat** and **moisture** cause **decay** <note>original: "Putrefaction"</note>. In **England**, this is found to be untrue; for many times, there have been great **plagues in dry years**. The **cause** of this may be that **drought** in the **bodies of islanders**, who are accustomed to **moist air**, irritates the **humors** and makes them more likely to decay or become inflamed. Besides, drought commonly taints the **waters** and makes them less wholesome. Furthermore, in **Barbary** <note>The Barbary Coast of North Africa</note>, the **plagues** cease <note>original: "breake vp"; in hot climates, the plague often dissipated during the peak heat of summer</note> in the **summer months** when the weather is **hot** and **dry**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning a common error about epidemic diseases.
384
</margin>
Many diseases (both **epidemic** and others) break out at **particular times**. The **cause** is falsely attributed to the **condition of the air** at the time they break out or prevail; whereas it actually proceeds from a **preceding sequence** and **series of the seasons** of the year. Therefore **Hippocrates**, in his ***Prognostics*** <note>original: "Prognoſticks"; a work by the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates concerning the prediction of the course of diseases</note>, makes good observations regarding the **diseases** that follow from the **nature** of the **four preceding seasons** of the year.

<margin>Experiment Solitary regarding stuttering <note>original: "Stutting"</note>. 386</margin>
We see that various people **stutter**. The **cause** may be (in most cases) the **chilling** <note>original: "Refrigeration"</note> of the **tongue**, which makes it less able to move. Therefore we see that those with intellectual disabilities <note>original: "Naturalls"</note> generally **stutter**; and we see that in those who **stutter**, if they drink **wine** moderately, they **stutter** less because it provides heat. We also see that those who **stutter** do so more at the first **attempt** <note>original: "Offer"</note> to speak than in **continued speech**, because the **tongue** is somewhat heated by **motion**. In some it may also be caused (though rarely) by the **dryness** of the **tongue**, which likewise makes it less able to move, just as **cold** does. For it is a **condition** <note>original: "Affect"</note> that happens to some **wise** and **great men**, as it did to **Moses**, who was **slow of speech** <note>original Latin: "Lingua præpedita"; literally "impeded tongue"</note>. We find that many **stutterers** are very **hot-tempered** <note>original: "Cholericke"</note> men, as **anger** <note>original: "Choler"; one of the four humors, associated with a hot and dry temperament</note> **induces a dryness** in the **tongue**.

<margin>Experiments in concert <note>original: "in Confort"; a group of related experiments</note> regarding smells. 387</margin>
Smells and other **odors** are sweeter in the **air** at some **distance** than they are near the **nose**, as has been mentioned briefly before. The **cause** is twofold. First, there is a finer **mixing** or **blending** <note>original: "Incorporation"</note> of the **smell**; for we see that with **sounds** likewise, they are sweetest when we cannot hear every **individual part** by itself. The other **reason** is that all **sweet smells** have joined with them some **earthy** or **raw** <note>original: "Crude"</note> **odors**; at some distance, the **sweetness**—which is more **refined** <note>original: "Spirituall"</note>—is perceived, while the **earthy** odor does not reach so far.

<margin>388</margin>
**Sweet smells** are strongest in **dry substances** when they are **broken**. Likewise, in **oranges** or **lemons**, **nipping** <note>squeezing or pinching</note> their **rind** releases their **smell** more. Generally, when **objects** <note>original: "Bodies"</note> are **moved** or **stirred**, even if they are not **broken**, they smell more—such as when a **sachet of perfume** <note>original: "Sweet-Bagge"</note> is waved. The **cause** is twofold. First, there is a **greater release** <note>original: "Emission"</note> of the **essence** <note>original: "Spirit"</note> when a path is opened; this applies to **breaking, nipping,** or **crushing**. It also applies (to some degree) to **moving**, but in that case, there is the **cooperation** <note>original: "Concurrence"</note> of a **second cause**: the **movement** <note>original: "Impulsion"</note> of the **air**, which brings the **scent** to us faster.

<margin>389</margin>
The most delicate **smells** of **flowers** come from those **plants** whose **leaves have no scent**, such as **violets, roses, wallflowers, carnations** <note>original: "Gilly-flowers"</note>, **pinks** <note>a type of Dianthus</note>, **honeysuckle** <note>original: "woodbines"</note>...

# Natural History:

<margin>390</margin>
**Vine-flowers**, **Apple-blooms**, **Lime-tree blooms**, **Bean-blooms**, etc. The cause is that where there is enough heat and strength in the **plant** to make the **leaves fragrant** <note>original: "Odorate"</note>, the **smell** of the **flower** is rather **fading** <note>original: "Euanide"</note> and weaker than that of the **leaves**; as it is in **rosemary flowers**, **lavender flowers**, and **sweet-briar roses**. But where there is less heat, the **spirit** of the **plant** is digested and refined, and separated from the thicker <note>original: "grosser"</note> juice, during the **flowering** <note>original: "Efflorescence"</note>, and not before.

Most **odors** smell best when **broken** or **crushed**, as has been said. But **flowers**, when **pressed** or **beaten**, lose the freshness and sweetness of their **odor**. The cause is that when they are **crushed**, the thicker <note>original: "grosser"</note> and more **earthy spirit** comes out with the finer one and disturbs it; whereas in **stronger odors**, there are no such different levels in how the **smell** is released.

<margin>
Experiments in Groups <note>original: "in Consort"</note> concerning the quality <note>original: "Goodnesse"</note> and choice of water.
391
</margin>
It is very useful to discover the **quality** of **waters**. The **taste** is somewhat helpful to those who drink **water** only, but other **experiments** are more certain. First, test **waters** by **weight**; you may find some difference, though not much, and you may consider the **lighter** water to be the **better** one.

<margin>392</margin>
Second, test them by **boiling** over an **equal fire**; the one that boils away <note>original: "consumeth away"</note> the fastest, you may consider the **best**.

<margin>393</margin>
Third, test them in **separate** <note>original: "Seuerall"</note> **bottles** or open **vessels** that are identical in every other way, and see which of them **lasts longest** without stench or **decay** <note>original: "Corruption"</note>. The one that stays **pure** <note>original: "Vnputrified"</note> longest, you may likewise consider the **best**.

<margin>394</margin>
Fourth, test them by **making drinks stronger** or **weaker** <note>original: "Smaller"</note> using the same **quantity** of **malt**. You may conclude that the **water** which makes the **stronger drink** is the more **processed** <note>original: "Concocted"</note> and **nourishing**, though perhaps it is not as good for **medicinal use**. Such **water** is commonly the **water** of **large** and **navigable rivers**, and likewise from **large** and **clean ponds** of **standing water**; for the **sun** has more power over both of these than over **springs** <note>original: "Fountaines"</note> or **small rivers**. I believe that **chalky water** <note>original: "Chalke-water"</note> is the next best for making **drink** go furthest, for that also helps **digestion** <note>original: "Concoction"</note>, provided it comes from a **deep well**. In that case, the depth cures the rawness of the **water**; but **chalky water** near the surface <note>original: "Top of the Earth"</note> is too **abrasive** <note>original: "fretting"</note>, as is seen in the **laundering** of **clothes**, which wear out quickly if you use such **waters**.

<margin>395</margin>
Fifth, **housewives** find a **difference** in **waters** regarding whether they "carry" <note>original: "Bearing"</note> **soap** or not. It is likely that the more **rich** <note>original: "Fat"</note> **water** will carry **soap best**, for "**hungry**" **water** kills the **oily** <note>original: "Vnctuous"</note> **nature** of the **soap**.

<margin>396</margin>
Sixth, you may judge **waters** according to the **place** from which they spring or come. **Rainwater** is esteemed by **physicians** as the finest and the best; yet it is said to decay <note>original: "putrifie"</note> soonest, which is likely because of the refinement <note>original: "Finenesse"</note> of its **spirit**. And in reser- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; catchword indicates "reservatories" or water tanks.</note>

# Century IV.

[Re]servoirs of **rainwater** (such as they have in **Venice**, etc.) are not found to be **choice waters**; they are perhaps worse because they are covered from above and kept from the sun. **Snow water** is considered unwholesome, so much so that the people who dwell at the foot of **snowy mountains**, or on their slopes (especially the women), develop great bags hanging under their throats from drinking **snow water** <note>This refers to goiters, a swelling of the thyroid gland once common in Alpine regions due to iodine deficiency, though here attributed to the water source</note>. **Well water**, unless it is found in **chalk** or from a very plentiful spring, makes meat turn red, which is a bad sign. **Springs** on the **tops of high hills** are the best; for they seem to have a lightness and a natural tendency to rise, and besides, they are the most pure and unmixed. Again, they are better filtered <note>original: "Percolated"</note> through a great distance of earth. For **waters in valleys** effectively join underground with all **waters** of the same level, whereas **springs on the tops of hills** pass through a great deal of pure **earth** with less mixture from other **waters**.

<margin>397</margin>
Seventhly, judgment may be made of waters by the **soil** <note>original: "Soyle"</note> over which the water runs. **Pebble** beds produce the cleanest and best-tasted water; next to that is **clay water**; thirdly, **water over chalk**; fourthly, that over **sand**; and worst of all is water over **mud**. Neither should you trust **waters** that **taste sweet**, for they are commonly found in the rising grounds of great **cities**, which must necessarily absorb a great deal of filth <note>The "sweetness" here likely refers to contamination from organic waste or sewage</note>.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the temperate heat under the Equator <note>original: "Æquinoctiall"</note>.
398
</margin>
In **Peru** and various parts of the **West Indies**, though they are directly under the **Equator** <note>original: "the Line"</note>, the **heats** are not as intolerable as they are in **Barbary** <note>North Africa</note> and the edges of the **Torrid Zone**. The **causes** are, first, the great **breezes** <note>original: "Brizes" — referring to steady trade winds</note> produced by the motion of the air in great circles (such as those under the **girdle of the world**); these provide cooling, and therefore in those parts, noon is not nearly as hot when the **breezes** are strong as it is around nine or ten o'clock in the morning. Another **cause** is that the **length of the night** and the **dews** it brings compensate for the **heat of the day**. A third **cause** is the duration of the sun's presence; not in terms of day and night (which was mentioned before), but in terms of the **season**. Under the **Equator**, the sun crosses the **line** and creates two summers and two winters; but at the edges of the **Torrid Zone**, it turns back <note>at the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn</note> and so creates one long summer.

Solitary experiment concerning the coloration of Black and Tawny Moors <note>The author uses "Moors" as a general historical term for people with dark skin</note>.

The **reason** may be because **fire** dries up the **spirits** and blood of the body so that they evaporate <note>original: "Exhale"</note>; thus, it always makes **men** look pale and sallow. But the **sun**, which provides a gentler heat, only draws the blood to the **outward parts**; it ripens <note>original: "Concocteth"</note> the blood rather than draining <note>original: "Soaketh"</note> it. ### Natural History:

Black people <note>original: "Negroes"</note> are bred in countries that have plenty of water, by rivers or otherwise. For Meroe, which was the capital <note>original: "Metropolis"</note> of Ethiopia, was upon a great lake. And Congo, where Black people live, is full of rivers. And the borders of the River Niger, where Black people also live, are well watered. And the region around Cape Verde is likewise moist, so much so that it is plague-ridden <note>original: "pestilent"</note> because of the moisture. But the countries of the Abyssinians <note>original: "Abyllenes"</note>, and Barbary [North Africa], and Persia, where the people are tawny, olive-colored <note>original: "Oliuafter"</note>, and pale, are generally more sandy and dry. As for the Ethiopians, as they are plump and fleshy, so (it may be) they are sanguine <note>In the theory of the four humors, "sanguine" refers to being red-blooded and healthy</note> and ruddy-colored, if their black skin would allow it to be seen.

<column-break/>

<margin>Experiment 400: Solitary experiment regarding motion after the moment of death.</margin>

Some creatures move for a good while after their head is off, such as *birds*. Some move for a very little time, such as *men* and all *beasts*. Some move even though cut into several pieces, such as *snakes, eels, worms, flies*, etc. First, therefore, it is certain that the *immediate cause* of death is the dissolution <note>original: "Resolution"</note> or extinguishing of the *spirits* <note>In 17th-century science, "spirits" were subtle vapors or fluids thought to animate the body and transmit sensations from the brain</note>. The destruction or corruption of the *organs* is only the *indirect cause* <note>original: "Mediate Cause"</note>. However, some *organs* are so essentially necessary that the extinguishing of the *spirits* follows quickly—but even so, there is a short *interval* of time. It is reported by one of the *ancients* of good reputation that a *sacrificed beast* has bellowed <note>original: "lowed"</note> after the *heart* has been removed. It is also a report of good reputation that the *head* of a *pig* has been opened, and the *brain* placed into the palm of a man's hand, trembling, without breaking any part of it or severing it from the spinal cord <note>original: "Marrow of the Backe-bone"</note>. During this time, the *pig* appeared in all appearance entirely dead and without motion. Yet, after a short time, the *brain* was replaced, the *skull* of the *pig* closed, and the *pig* walked around shortly after. And it is certain that an *eye*, plucked out in an act of revenge, has been thrust out so that it hung a significant distance by the *small nerves*; and during that time the *eye* had no power of *sight*; yet after being replaced, it recovered *sight*. Now, the *spirits* are chiefly in the *head* and the cavities <note>original: "Cells"</note> of the *brain*, which in *men* and *beasts* are large; therefore, when the *head* is off, they move little or nothing. But *birds* have small *heads*, and therefore the *spirits* are a little more dispersed in the nerves <note>original: "Sinewes"</note>, so that *motion* remains in them a little longer. This is so well known that it is recorded in history that a *Roman Emperor* <note>This refers to the Emperor Commodus, who was famous for his archery feats in the arena</note>, to show the accuracy of his aim, shot a great forked arrow at an *ostrich* <note>original: "Eſtrich"</note> as she ran swiftly upon the stage and struck off her head; and yet she continued the race for a little way without her head. As for *worms, flies*, and *eels*, the *spirits* are spread almost all over, and therefore they move in their individual pieces.

# NATURAL HISTORY
## Fifth Century <note>original: "V. Century"; Bacon’s work is organized into ten "centuries," each containing 100 observations or experiments</note>

<margin>Experiments in combination <note>original: "in Confort"</note> regarding the acceleration of growth <note>original: "Germination"</note>.</margin>
We will now investigate *plants* or *vegetables*, and we shall do so with diligence. They are the principal part of the *Third Day's Work* <note>A reference to the biblical creation story in Genesis, where plants were created on the third day</note>. They are the first *product* <note>original: "Producat," referencing the Latin command *producat terra* ("let the earth bring forth") from Genesis</note> which carries the word of *animation* <note>In this context, the power of life or growth</note>, for the other words were only words of *existence* <note>original: "Essence"</note>. They are of excellent and general use for food, medicine, and a number of mechanical crafts.

<margin>401</margin>
There were sown in a *bed*, *turnip seed*, *radish seed*, *wheat*, *cucumber seed*, and *peas* <note>original: "Pease"</note>. The *bed* we call a *hotbed*, and the manner of it is this: we took *horse dung* that was old and well-rotted; this was laid upon a bank half a foot high and supported all around with planks. Upon the top, we spread sifted earth about two fingers <note>A traditional unit of measurement, approximately 1.5 to 2 inches</note> deep. Then the *seed* was sprinkled upon it, having been soaked <note>original: "steeped"</note> all night in *water* mixed with *cow dung*. The *turnip seed* and the *wheat* came up half an inch above the ground within two days, without any watering. The rest came up on the third day. The *experiment* was made in *October*; and (perhaps) in the *spring*, the *acceleration* would have been even speedier. This is a noble *experiment*; for without this help, they would have

It may be tried also with *cherries*, *strawberries*, and other fruit, which are most expensive when they arrive early.

<margin>402</margin>
There was *wheat* steeped in *water* mixed with *cow dung*; other wheat in *water* mixed with *horse dung*; other in *water* mixed with *pigeon dung*; other in the *urine* of *man*; other in *water* mixed with powdered *chalk*; other in *water* mixed with *soot*; other in *water* mixed with *ashes*; other in *water* mixed with *bay salt*; other in *claret wine* <note>A dry red wine from Bordeaux</note>; other in *Malmsey* <note>A sweet, fortified Greek wine</note>; other in *spirit of wine* <note>original: "Spirit of wine"; high-proof distilled alcohol or brandy</note>. The proportion of the mixture was one-fourth part of the ingredients to the *water*, except that there was no more than an eighth part of the *salt*. The *urine*, the *wines*, and the *spirit of wine* were *simple* <note>In this context, "simple" means pure or undiluted</note> without the mixture of *water*. The time of the steeping was twelve hours. The time of the year was *October*. There was also other *wheat* sown *unsteeped*, but *watered* twice a day with *warm water*. There was also other *wheat* sown *simple* to compare it with the rest.

The result was that those in the mixture of *dung*, *urine*, *soot*, *chalk*, *ashes*, and *salt* came up within six days. And those that afterwards proved the highest, thickest, and most vigorous <note>original: "Lusty"</note> were: first, the *urine*; then the *dungs*; next the *chalk*; next the *soot*; next the *ashes*; next the *salt*; next the *wheat simple* of itself, unsteeped and unwatered; next the one *watered twice a day* with warm water; and next the *claret wine*. So, these last three were slower than the ordinary wheat on its own, and this cultivation did rather delay <note>original: "retard"</note> than advance growth. As for those that were steeped in *Malmsey* and *spirit of wine*, they did not come up at all. 

This is a *profitable experiment* <note>original: "Rich Experiment for Profit"</note>: for most of the steeping liquids are cheap things, and the quality of the crop is a matter of great gain—if the quality of the crop matches the earliness of its arrival, as it likely will, both being caused by the vigor of the *seed*. This also partly appeared in the former *experiments*, as has been said. This *experiment* should be tried in other *grains*, *seeds*, and *kernels*, for it may be that some *steeping* will agree best with specific *seeds*. It should be tried also with *roots* steeped as before, but for a *longer time*. It should also be tried in *several seasons* of the *year*, especially the *spring*.

<margin>403</margin>
*Strawberries* watered every now and then (such as once in three days) with *water* in which *sheep dung* or *pigeon dung* has been steeped, will ripen and arrive early. And it is likely the same effect would follow in other *berries*, *herbs*, *flowers*, *grains*, or *trees*. And therefore it is an *experiment* which, though common for *strawberries*, is not yet brought into general use. For it is usual to help the *ground* with *manure* <note>original: "Mucke"</note>, and likewise to refresh it sometimes with *manure* applied to the *roots*; but to water it with *manure water*, which is likely to be more powerful, is not practiced.

<header>Century. V.</header>
<sig>K 3</sig>

Roots of *trees*, does set them forward. But to do it to *herbs*, without a mixture of *water* or *earth*, it may be these helps are too hot.

<margin>405</margin> The former *means of helping germination* are achieved either by the *goodness* and *strength* of the *nourishment*, or by the *comforting* and *exciting* of the *spirits* <note>original: "Spirits"; in the 17th century, "spirits" referred to the vital internal forces or "breath of life" believed to animate living things</note> in the *plant* to draw the *nourishment* better. And of this latter kind, concerning the *comforting* of the *spirits* of the *plant*, are also the experiments that follow, though they are not applications to the *root* or *seed*. The *planting* of *trees* warmly against a *wall* facing the south or southeast sun does hasten their *coming on* and ripening. The southeast is found to be better than the southwest, even though the southwest is the hotter direction <note>original: "Coast"</note>. But the cause is chiefly because the heat of the *morning* follows the cold of the night, and partly because (many times) the southwest sun is too parching. Similarly, the *planting* of them on the *back* of a *chimney* where a *fire* is kept does hasten their *coming on* and ripening. Nay, more, the *drawing* of the *boughs* into the *inside* of a *room* where a *fire* is continually kept produces the same effect; this has been tried with grapes, so much so that they will arrive a month earlier than the grapes grown outside.

<margin>406</margin> Besides the two *means of accelerating germination* formerly described—that is to say, the *improving* <note>original: "Mending"</note> of the *nourishment* and the *comforting* of the *spirit* of the *plant*—there is a third. This is the *making way* for the *easy arrival* to the *nourishment* and the *drawing* of it. Therefore, *gentle digging* and *loosening* of the *earth* about the *roots* of *trees*, and the *moving* of *herbs* and *flowers* into new earth once every two years (which is the same thing, for the new earth is always looser), greatly furthers the *prosperity* and *earliness* of *plants*.

<margin>407</margin> But the most remarkable *acceleration* achieved by *making the nourishment easier* is that of *water*. For a *standard* <note>A plant or shrub grown on a single tall stem</note> of a *Damask rose* <note>A variety of rose known for its fragrance and pale pink or red color</note> with the *root* still attached was set in a room where no *fire* was. It was placed upright in an *earthen pan* full of *clean water* <note>original: "Faire Water"</note> without any mixture, half a foot under the *water*, with the *standard* being more than two feet high above the *water*. Within the space of ten days, the *standard* put forth a beautiful green leaf and some other little buds, which remained unchanged <note>original: "stood at a stay"</note> without any sign of decay or withering for more than seven days. Afterward, that leaf faded, but the young buds continued to sprout; these afterward opened into beautiful *leaves* in the space of three months and continued so for a while after, until we ended the trial upon moving. But note that the *leaves* were somewhat paler and lighter-colored than *leaves* usually are outdoors. Note that the first *buds* appeared at the end of *October*. It is likely that if it had been in the *springtime*, it would have put forth with greater strength and (perhaps) would have grown enough to bear flowers. By this means, you may (it seems) have *roses* set in the middle of a *pool*, supported by some stay; this is a matter of rarity and pleasure, though of little practical use. # Natural History:

Strange, because a similar *rose-bush* <note>original: "Rose-standard"</note> was placed, at the same time, into *water* mixed with *horse dung*—the *horse dung* being about a fourth part of the *water*—and in four months' space (while it was being observed) it did not produce any leaves, though it had several buds at the first, just like the other.

A *Dutch flower* <note>Likely a tulip or hyacinth bulb</note> that had a *bulbous root* was likewise placed at the same time entirely under *water*, some two or three fingers deep. Within seven days it sprouted and continued growing for a long time afterward. There were also put in a *beet root*, a *borage root*, and a *radish root*, which all had their leaves cut almost close to the *roots*. Within six weeks, they had beautiful *leaves* and continued so until the end of *November*.

<margin>409</margin>
Note that if *roots*, *peas*, or *flowers* can be *accelerated* in their *emergence* and *ripening*, there is a double profit. The first is the high *price* that those things command when they arrive early; the other is the *speed* of their *returns* <note>The turnover rate of the crop</note>. For in some grounds which are strong, you shall have a *radish*, etc., arrive in a month, whereas in other grounds it will not arrive in two; thus making double the *returns*.

<margin>410</margin>
*Wheat* was also put into the *water* and did not come forth at all. So it seems there must be some strength and bulk in the body put into the *water*, as there is in *roots*; for with *grains* or *seeds*, the cold of the *water* will kill <note>original: "mortifie"</note> them. However, by chance, some *wheat* lay under the pan and was somewhat moistened by the seepage <note>original: "Suing"; the exuding or leaking of liquid</note> of the pan; in six weeks (as mentioned before) it looked moldy to the eye, but it had sprouted forth half a finger's length.

<margin>804</margin>
<margin>411</margin>
It seems by these *examples* of *water* that, for nourishment, *water* is almost everything, and that the *earth* only keeps the *plant* upright and saves it from overheating and over-cooling. Therefore, this is a comforting *experiment* for those who enjoy a drink <note>Bacon humorously suggests that if plants thrive on liquid alone, humans might too</note>. It also proves our former *opinion* that *drink* combined with *meat* or *roots* (as in *capon-beer* <note>original: "Capon-Beere"; a restorative drink made by boiling a chicken in ale with spices</note>, etc.) will nourish more easily than meat and drink taken separately.

<margin>504</margin>
<margin>412</margin>
The *housing* <note>Keeping plants indoors or in a greenhouse-like environment</note> of *plants* (I believe) will both *accelerate germination* and produce *flowers* and *plants* in the *colder seasons*. Just as we *house* *hot-country plants* like *lemons*, *oranges*, and *myrtles* to save them, so we may *house* our own *country's plants* to push them forward and make them arrive in the cold seasons. In such a way, you may have *violets*, *strawberries*, and *peas* all *winter*, provided that you sow or transplant them at appropriate times. This *experiment* is to be attributed to the *comforting* of the *spirit* of the *plant* by *warmth*, as well as the *housing* of their boughs, etc. So then, the *means* to *accelerate germination* are specifically eight, and generally three.

# Century V.

But they will not come out exactly on the tops where they were cut, but out of those shoots which were (as it were) *water-boughs* <term>Water-boughs: Weak or non-fruiting shoots that grow from the main trunk or branches, often drawing away sap.</term>. <margin>414</margin>
The second method is the *pulling off the buds of the rose* when they are *newly knotted* <term>Knotted: The stage when a flower bud first begins to form into a distinct, tight lump.</term>. For then the side-branches will bear flowers. The *cause* is the same as the former: for *cutting off the tops* and *pulling off the buds* work the same effect in retaining the sap for a time and diverting it to the sprouts that were not as far forward in their growth.

<margin>415</margin>
The third is the *cutting off some few of the top branches* in the *springtime*, but allowing the lower branches to grow on. The *cause* is that the branches do help to draw up the sap more strongly; and we see that in pollarding <note>original: "Powling"</note> <term>Pollarding: A pruning technique where the upper branches of a tree are removed to promote a dense head of foliage and branches.</term> trees, many people use to leave a branch or two on the top to help draw up the sap. It is also reported that if you graft upon the branch of a tree and cut off some of the old branches, the new scions <note>original: "Cions"</note> <term>Scion: A young shoot or twig of a plant, especially one cut for grafting.</term> will perish.

<margin>416</margin>
The fourth is by *laying the roots bare* for some days around *Christmas*. The *cause* is plain: it arrests the sap from going upward for a time. This arrest is afterward released by the covering of the root again with earth; and then the sap rises, but later.

<margin>417</margin>
The fifth is the *removing of the tree* about a month before it *buds*. The *cause* is that some time will be required after the *removal* for resettling before it can draw the juice <note>Here meaning sap or nutrients</note>. Since that time is lost, the blossom must necessarily come forth later.

<margin>418</margin>
The sixth is the *grafting of roses* in *May*, which gardeners commonly do not do until *July*. In that case, they do not bear until the *next year*; but if you graft them in *May*, they will bear the same year, but late.

<margin>419</margin>
The seventh is the *girding of the body of the tree* with some packthread <term>Packthread: Strong thread or twine used for tying up bundles.</term>. For that also, to a degree, restrains the sap and makes it come up later and more slowly.

<margin>420</margin>
The eighth is the *planting of them in a shade* or in a *hedge*. The *cause* is partly the keeping out of the sun, which hastens the sap to rise, and partly the robbing of them of nourishment by the other growth <note>original: "Stuffe"</note> in the hedge. These means may be practiced upon other trees and flowers, *making the necessary changes* <note>original: "Mutatis Mutandis"</note>.

<margin>421</margin>
Men have entertained a concept <note>original: "Conceit"</note> that seems clever: namely, that if you graft a *late-maturing fruit* upon a stock of a *fruit tree* that *matures early*, the graft will bear *fruit early* (such as a peach upon a cherry). Conversely, if an *early-maturing fruit* is grafted upon a stock of a *fruit tree* that *matures late*, the graft will bear *fruit late* (such as a cherry upon a peach). But these are merely fantasies and are untrue. The *cause* is that the scion <note>original: "Cions"</note> completely overrules the stock; and the stock is only passive and provides nourishment <note>original: "Aliment"</note>, but gives no biological impulse <note>original: "Motion"</note> to the graft.

<summary>This page details eight practical methods for delaying the blooming and fruiting of plants, such as pruning, root exposure, and shading, to control harvest times. It also debunks the theory that the timing of a fruit's maturation is determined by the rootstock it is grafted onto.</summary>

# Natural History:

<margin>
Experiments in association, concerning the improvement <note>original: "Melioration"</note> of fruits, trees, and plants.
</margin>

We will speak now about how to make *fruits*, *flowers*, and *roots* larger, more plentiful, and sweeter than they usually are. We will also discuss how to make the *trees* themselves taller, more spreading, and faster-growing <note>original: "more Hastie and Sudden"</note> than they usually are. There is no doubt that the previous *experiments* regarding *acceleration* (speeding up growth) will serve these purposes well. Furthermore, the *experiments* we will now describe also help with *acceleration*, because both effects come from increasing the vigor of the tree. However, to avoid confusion, and because some methods are better suited for one effect than the other, we will handle them separately.

<margin>422</margin> It is a proven experience that a *heap of flints* or *stones* placed around the *base* of a *wild tree* (such as an oak, elm, ash, etc.) when it is first planted makes it thrive twice as much as it would without them. The *cause* is that the stones retain the moisture that falls on the *tree* and prevent it from being evaporated <note>original: "exhaled"</note> by the sun. Additionally, they keep the tree warm, protecting it from cold blasts and frosts as if it were inside a house. It may also be that the stones help keep the tree steady during its initial growth. *Inquire* <note>original: "Quære"</note> whether laying straw to a certain height around the trunk <note>original: "Body"</note> of a *tree* will make the *tree grow faster* <note>original: "forwards"</note>. For though the root provides the sap, it is the trunk that draws it up. However, you must note that if you place *stones* around the stalks of lettuce or other softer plants, it will over-moisten the roots, causing worms to eat them.

<margin>423</margin> A *tree*, when first *planted* <note>original: "Setting"</note>, should not be *shaken* until it has *fully taken root*. For this reason, some people place two small forks around the base of their *trees* to keep them upright. However, after a year of rooting, shaking the *tree* is beneficial by loosening the earth and perhaps by "exercising" and stirring the tree's sap.

<margin>424</margin> Generally, *cutting away branches* and *suckers* <term>Sucker: A shoot that grows from the roots or the main stem of a plant, often drawing energy away from the main plant.</term> at the *root* and *trunk* makes *trees* grow tall. Conversely, pollarding <note>original: "Powling"</note> and cutting the top makes them grow wide and bushy, as seen in *pollards* <term>Pollard: A tree that has had its top branches cut back to the trunk to encourage a dense head of new shoots.</term> and similar trees.

<margin>425</margin> It is reported that to create *fast-growing coppice-woods* <term>Coppice-wood: An area of woodland in which the trees or shrubs are periodically cut back to ground level to stimulate growth and provide wood.</term>, the method is to take *willow*, *sallow* <note>original: "Sallow" – a type of willow tree</note>, *poplar*, or *alder* of about seven years' growth. Plant them not upright, but at an angle <note>original: "a-slope"</note> at a reasonable depth underground. Instead of one root, they will put forth many, and thus produce more shoots on a single stem.

<margin>426</margin> When you would have **many new roots for fruit trees**, take a *low tree* and bend it, laying all its branches flat upon the ground, and cover them with earth. Every twig will then take root. This is a very profitable *experiment* for *costly trees*, as the branches will become new rootstocks <note>original: "Stockes"</note> <term>Rootstock: The part of a plant, often a root or stem, which provides the root system for a grafted plant.</term>.

It also describes a method for propagating new trees by burying the branches of a low-growing tree so they take root.</summary>
