<header>Century V.</header>

<margin>427</margin> Rootstocks without the need for grafting <note>original: "without charge"</note>; such as *apricots*, *peaches*, *almonds*, *Cornelians* <note>original: "Cornelians" - likely Cornelian cherries (Cornus mas)</note>, *mulberries*, *figs*, etc. The same is continually practiced with *vines*, *roses*, *musk-roses*, etc.

->From *May* to *July*, you may take off the *bark* of any *bough* that is about three or four *inches* thick. Cover the bare place, somewhat above and below, with loam well-mixed with horse-dung, binding it down fast. Then, around *Allhallowtide* <note>original: "Alholtide" - the season of All Saints' Day, early November</note>, cut off the bough at the bare place and set it in the ground; it will grow to be a fine *tree* in one *year*. The benefit is that stripping the *bark* keeps the *sap* from descending toward *winter*, and so holds it in the *bough*. It may also be that the *loam* and *horse-dung* applied to the bare place moisten and nourish <note>original: "cherish"</note> it, making it more ready to put forth a *root*. *Note* that this may be a general *means* for keeping up the *sap* of *trees* in their *boughs*, which may serve other purposes.<-

<margin>428</margin> It has been practiced with *trees* that look healthy but do not bear fruit, to bore a hole through the *heart* of the *tree*, after which it will bear. This may be because the *tree* previously had too much *repletion* <note>original: "repletion" - an over-abundance of sap</note> and was oppressed by its own *sap*; for *repletion* is an *enemy* to *generation* <note>original: "generation" - the process of reproduction or bearing fruit</note>.

<margin>429</margin> It has been practiced with *trees* that do not bear to split two or three of the *chiefest roots* and put a small *pebble* into the cleft to keep it open; then the tree will bear. The *cause* may be that a *root* of a *tree* can be "hide-bound" <note>original: "Hide-bound" - a condition where the skin or bark is too tight, restricting growth</note> just as much as the *body* of the *tree*; however, it will not stay open without something placed inside it.

<margin>430</margin> It is usually practiced to plant *trees* that require much *sun* upon walls facing the *south*, such as *apricots*, *peaches*, *plums*, *vines*, *figs*, and the like. This has a double *advantage* <note>original: "Commodity"</note>: first, the *heat* of the *wall* by *reflection*, and second, the *removal* of the *shade*. For when a *tree* grows in a round shape, the upper *boughs* overshadow the lower ones; but when it is spread upon a *wall*, the *sun* reaches the upper and lower *branches* equally.

<margin>431</margin> It has also been practiced by some to pull off some *leaves* from the *trees* spread this way so that the *sun* may reach the *bough* and *fruit* better. There has also been a *curiosity* <note>original: "Curiosity" - a refined or experimental technique</note> practiced to plant a *tree* on the *north side* of a wall and, at a small height, draw it through the *wall* and spread it upon the *south side*. The idea was that the *root* and lower *part* of the *trunk* should enjoy the *freshness* of the *shade*, while the upper *boughs* and *fruit* enjoyed the *comfort* of the *sun*. But it did not work <note>original: "it sorted not"</note>. The *cause* is that the *root* requires some *comfort* from the *sun*, even under the *earth*, as well as the *body*; and the *lower part* of the *body* requires it more than the *upper*, as we see when we mulch <note>original: "Composting"</note> a *tree* below with *straw*.

<margin>432</margin> The *lowness* of the *bough* where the *fruit* grows makes the *fruit* larger and helps it ripen better; for you shall always see in *apricots*, *peaches*...

### Natural History:

Peaches, or *peach-quinces* <note>original: "Melo-Cotones"; a variety of peach grafted onto quince stock, prized in the 17th century for its size and flavor</note>, grown against a wall produce the largest fruit toward the bottom. In *France*, the *grapes* used for *wine* grow on low vines tied to small stakes, whereas vines raised on arbors produce only *verjuice* <note>original: "Veriuyce"; the tart, acidic juice of unripe grapes</note>. It is true that in *Italy* and other *countries* with a hotter sun, they raise vines on *elms* and other trees; however, I believe that if the *French* method of planting low were used there, their *wines* would be stronger and sweeter. But this would be more expensive <note>original: "chargeable"</note> due to the cost of the props. It would be worth testing whether a *tree* grafted near the ground—where only the lower boughs are maintained and the higher ones are continually pruned off—would produce larger *fruit*.

<margin>433</margin>
To have *fruit* in *greater plenty*, the method is to graft not only onto young *stocks* but onto various *boughs* of an old *tree*. These boughs will bear a great number of fruits, whereas if you graft onto only one stock, the *tree* can bear only a few.

<margin>434</margin>
The annual *digging* around the *roots* of *trees*, which is an excellent way to both *accelerate* growth and *improve* <note>original: "Melioration"</note> the *fruit*, is practiced only with *vines*. If this were applied to other *trees* and *shrubs* (such as *roses*, etc.), I believe it would benefit them as well.

<margin>435</margin>
It has been known for a *fruit tree* to be blown nearly out of the *roots* by the wind and then set upright again, after which it bore fruit exceedingly well the next year. The *cause* of this was simply the *loosening* of the *earth*, which benefits any *tree*. This should be practiced more than it currently is with *fruit trees*, for *trees* cannot be moved into new soil as easily as *flowers* and *herbs* can.

<margin>436</margin>
To revive an *old tree*, the best method is digging around the *roots* and applying new soil <note>original: "Mould"</note> to them. We see a similar effect when *draft oxen* are put into fresh pasture and develop new and tender flesh. In all things, better nourishment than what was previously used helps to renew life—especially if the nourishment is not only better, but also changed and different from the former kind.

<margin>437</margin>
If an *herb* is cut off at the *roots* at the beginning of winter, and the earth is then trodden and beaten down hard with the foot and spade, the *roots* will grow to a very large size by summer. The reason is that because the moisture is prevented from rising into the plant, it stays longer in the root and expands it. *Gardeners* often tread down any loose ground after they have sown *onions*, *turnips*, etc.

<margin>438</margin>
If *millet* <note>original: "Panicum"; a type of quick-growing cereal grass</note> is placed below and around the bottom of a *root*, it will cause the root to grow to an excessive size. The cause is that the millet, being of a spongy substance, draws the moisture of the earth to itself and thereby feeds the root. This is most useful for *onions*, *turnips*, *parsnips*, and *carrots*.

<margin>439</margin>
The *shifting* of *ground* <note>the practice of transplanting or crop rotation</note> is a means to improve the *tree* and fruit, but with this caution: all things prosper best when they are moved to a better environment. Your *nursery* of *stocks* ought to be in a more barren...

...barren ground than the ground to which you move them. In the same way, all *graziers* <note>original: "Grafiers"; farmers who raise or fatten cattle for market</note> prefer to move their cattle from poorer pastures to better ones. We also see that hardship in youth lengthens life, because it leaves a reserve of vitality for the body in old age. Indeed, in exercises, it is good to begin with the hardest tasks, such as dancing in heavy shoes, and so on.

<margin>440</margin>
It has been observed that *hacking the bark of trees*, both vertically and horizontally—making slices rather than continuous gashes—does great good to *trees*. Especially, it prevents them from being *hide-bound* <term>hide-bound: a condition where a tree's bark is too tight or thick, restricting its growth</term> and kills their *moss*.

<margin>441</margin>
For some *plants*, shade is more conducive to making them large and healthy than the *sun*, as seen in *strawberries* and *bay trees* <note>original: "Bayes"; laurel trees</note>, etc. Therefore, among *strawberries*, sow some *borage seed* here and there; you shall find the *strawberries* under those leaves grow much larger than their fellows. *Bay trees* must be planted to the *north*, or protected from the *sun* by a hedgerow. When you sow the *berries*, do not weed the *borders* for the first half-year, for the weeds provide them with shade.

<margin>442</margin>
To increase the *yield of plants*, one should consider not only *increasing the fertility of the earth* or of the *plant*, but also saving that which is usually wasted. For example, they have lately conducted a trial *to plant wheat by hand* <note>original: "to set wheat"; the practice of "dibbling" or planting individual seeds in holes rather than scattering them</note>, which was nevertheless abandoned because of the trouble and effort. Yet it is true that much is saved by *planting* compared to what is *sown* <note>original: "Sowen"; referring to broadcasting seeds by scattering them over a field</note>, both by keeping it from being picked up by *birds* and by avoiding shallow placement, which prevents much of the sown seed from taking root.

<margin>443</margin>
It is prescribed by some of the *ancients* that you should take *small trees* on which *figs* or other *fruit* are growing but are still unripe, and cover the *trees* in the *middle of autumn* with dung until the spring. Then, take them up on a warm day and replant them in good ground; by that means, the previous year's *fruit* will be ripe, as if by a new birth, when other *trees* of the same kind are only just blossoming. But this seems to have no great probability <note>original: "Pobability"</note>.

<margin>444</margin>
It is reported that if you take *nitre* <note>original: "Nitre"; saltpeter or potassium nitrate, considered a "mineral spirit" in early science</note> and mix it with *water* to the thickness of *honey*, and coat the *bud* with it after the *vine* is pruned, it will sprout within eight days. The cause is likely (if the *experiment* is true) the opening of the *bud* and the surrounding parts by the spirit of the *nitre*; for *nitre* is, as it were, the life-force of *vegetables*.

<margin>445</margin>
Take the seeds or kernels of *apples*, *pears*, or *oranges*, or a *peach* or *plum stone*, etc., and put them into a *squill* <note>original: "Squill"; the sea onion (*Drimia maritima*), which grows from a large bulb</note> (which is like a great onion), and they will grow much earlier than in the *earth* itself. I conceive this to be a kind of *grafting in the root*; for just as the stock of a graft yields better-prepared nourishment to the graft than the raw earth does, so the *squill* does the same for the *seed*. I suppose the same could be done by putting kernels into a turnip or the...

# Naturall History:

...and the like; except that the *squill* <note>original: "Squill"; a type of sea onion (Drimia maritima) often used in medicine or as a hardy plant</note> is more vigorous and hot. This may also be tried by putting *onion seed* into an *onion head*, which (perhaps) will produce a larger and earlier *onion*.

<margin>446</margin>
*Pricking* a *fruit* in several places when it is almost at its full size and before it ripens has been practiced successfully to make the *fruit* ripen more quickly. We see the example of *wasps* or *worms* biting a *fruit*, which clearly makes it ripen sooner.

<margin>447</margin>
It is reported that *seaweed* <note>original: "Alga Marina"</note> placed under the roots of *coleworts* <note>original: "Coleworts"; cabbage-like plants</note>, and perhaps other *plants*, will promote their growth. The benefit (no doubt) relates to the *salt*, which is a great aid to fertility.

<margin>448</margin>
<margin>X</margin>
People have practiced cutting off the stalks of *cucumbers* close to the ground immediately after they have finished *bearing fruit*. Then, by covering the remaining *plant* with a good amount of earth, they will bear fruit the next year much earlier than usual. The *cause* may be that the sap goes down sooner and is not wasted in the stalks or leaves that remain after the fruit is gone. Note here that the *death* of the *roots* of *annual* plants in winter seems to be partly caused by the over-expenditure of sap into the stalks and leaves; if this is prevented, they will *survive for more than a year* <term>super-annate: to live or last longer than a year; to become perennial</term> if they are kept warm.

<margin>449</margin>
*Pulling off* many of the *blossoms* from a *fruit tree* makes the *fruit* more beautiful. The *reason* is obvious: the sap has fewer things to nourish. It is also a *common experience* that if you do not pull off some *blossoms* the first time a tree blooms, it will "blossom itself to death."

<margin>450</margin>
It would be worth testing what the *effect* would be if all the blossoms were pulled from a *fruit tree*, or the *acorns* and *chestnut buds*, etc., from a *wild tree* for two years in a row. I suspect that in the third year, the *tree* would either produce larger and more plentiful *fruit*, or in those same years, it would produce larger leaves because of the stored-up sap.

<margin>451</margin>
It has been generally accepted that a *plant* watered with *warm water* will grow sooner and better than with cold water or rain showers. However, our *experiment of watering wheat with warm water* (as previously mentioned) did not succeed. This may be because the trial was conducted too late in the year—specifically, at the end of *October*. The cold arriving then might have harmed the seed after it had been made more tender by the warm water.

<margin>452</margin>
There is no doubt that *grafting* (for the most part) improves the *fruit*. The *reason* is clear: the nourishment is better prepared within the stock <note>the parent plant or stem onto which a graft is made</note> than in the *raw earth*. Yet, note carefully that some *trees* are said to grow more successfully from the *seed* <note>original: "Kernell"</note> than from a *graft*, such as the *peach* and the *melocotone* <note>original: "Melocotone"; an old variety of peach grafted onto a quince</note>. I suppose the *cause* is that these *plants* require very moist nourishment, and though the nourishment from the stock is more refined,

...and better prepared, yet it is not so moist and plentiful as the *nourishment* of the *earth*. And indeed, we see those *fruits* are very cold *fruits* in their nature.

<margin>453</margin>
It has been accepted that a smaller *pear*, grafted onto a *stock* <note>original: "Stocke"; the rooted plant onto which a scion is grafted</note> that bears a larger *pear*, will become great. But I think it is as true as the theory of the *early-fruiting scion* upon the *late-fruiting stock*—and *conversely* <note>original: "e converso"</note>—which we rejected before: for the *scion* <note>original: "Cions"; a young shoot or twig of a plant, especially one cut for grafting</note> will determine the nature of the plant. Nevertheless, it is probable enough that if you can get a *scion* to grow upon a *stock* of another kind that is much moister than its own *stock*, it may make the *fruit* larger because it will yield more plentiful *nourishment*; though it is likely it will make the *fruit* of poorer quality <note>original: "Baser"</note>. But generally, *grafting* is done upon a drier *stock*, such as an *apple* upon a *crabapple*; a *pear* upon a *hawthorn* <note>original: "Thorne"</note>, and so on. Yet it is reported that in the *Low Countries* <note>The coastal region of northwestern Europe, including the Netherlands and Belgium</note> they will graft an *apple scion* upon the *stock* of a *cole-wort* <note>original: "Cole-wort"; a type of cabbage or kale</note>, and it will bear a great, flimsy *apple*. The *seed* <note>original: "Kernell"</note> of this apple, if planted, will produce a *cole-wort* and not an *apple*. It would be good to test whether an *apple scion* will thrive if it is grafted upon a *sallow* <note>original: "Sallow"; a species of willow</note>, or upon a *poplar*, or upon an *alder*, or upon an *elm*, or upon a *horse-plum*, which are the moistest of *trees*. I have heard that it has been tried upon an *elm* and succeeded.

<margin>454</margin>
It is manifest by experience that *flowers* grow larger when they are *moved* <note>transplanted</note> because the nourishment is more easily obtained in the loose *earth*. It may be that frequently re-grafting the same *scion* may likewise make *fruit* larger; as if you take a *scion* and graft it upon a *stock* the first year, and then cut it off and graft it upon another *stock* the second year, and so for a third or fourth year, and then let it rest, it will yield afterward, when it bears, the larger *fruit*.

*Concerning grafting, there are many experiments worth noting, but those we reserve for a proper place.*

<margin>455</margin>
It makes *figs* better if a *fig tree*, when it begins to put forth *leaves*, has its top cut off. The cause is plain, for the *sap* has less to feed and a shorter distance to climb. But it may be the *fig* will ripen somewhat later, as was formerly mentioned. The same may be tried likewise in other *trees*.

<margin>456</margin>
It is reported that *mulberries* will be finer and the *trees* more fruitful if you bore through the *trunk* of the *tree* in several places and thrust into the bored holes wedges of some "hot" *trees*, such as *turpentine*, *mastic-tree*, *guaiacum* <note>original: "Guaiacum"; a tropical tree known for its very hard, resinous wood</note>, *juniper*, and so on. The *cause* may be that the *added* <note>original: "Adventive"</note> heat stimulates the *natural juice* of the *tree*.

<margin>457</margin>
It is reported that *trees* will grow larger and bear better *fruit* if you put *salt*, or *lees of wine* <note>original: "Lees of Wine"; the sediment at the bottom of a wine cask</note>, or *blood* to the *root*. The *cause* may be the increasing of the *vitality* or *energy* <note>original: "Lust or Spirit"</note> of the *root*; these things being more powerful than ordinary *composts*.

<margin>458</margin>
It is reported by one of the ancients that *artichokes* will be less prickly and more tender if the *seeds* have their tops dulled or ground off against a stone.

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon's observations on plant cultivation, moving from grafting techniques to methods for improving the quality, taste, and behavior of herbs, vegetables, and trees through transplanting, specialized watering, and physical alterations.</meta>

# Natural History:

<margin>459</margin> Herbs will be more tender and attractive if you take them out of their garden beds when they have newly sprouted and transplant them into pots with better soil. The practice of moving plants from bed to bed was mentioned previously, but that occurred over several years; this method is done suddenly. The reason is the same as with other transplants formerly mentioned.

<margin>460</margin> Cole-worts <term>cabbage or kale</term> are reported by one of the ancient writers to thrive exceptionally well and have a better flavor if they are occasionally watered with salt water, and even more so with water mixed with nitre <term>saltpeter or potassium nitrate</term>. The essence of nitre is less caustic <note>original: "Adurent"; burning or scorching</note> than salt <note>original: "Sals"</note>.

<margin>461</margin> It is reported that cucumbers will prove more tender and delicate if their seeds are soaked for a short time in milk. The cause may be that the seed, being softened by the milk, will be too weak to draw the coarser juices of the earth and will only take in the finer ones. The same experiment may be performed with artichokes and other seeds when you wish to remove either their tastelessness <note>original: "Flashinesse"</note> or their bitterness. It is also said that a similar effect follows from soaking seeds in water mixed with honey, but that seems less probable to me because honey has too active a quality <note>original: "quicke a Spirit"</note>.

<margin>462</margin> It is reported that cucumbers will be less watery and more like melons if you fill the hole where you plant them halfway up with chaff or small sticks and then pour earth over them. For cucumbers, it seems, crave moisture extremely and "over-drink" themselves, which this chaff or wood prevents. Furthermore, it is reported that if you place a pot of water five or six inches away from a growing cucumber, it will grow so much in twenty-four hours that it will touch the pot. If this is true, it is an experiment of a higher order than belongs to this section; for it reveals a sense of perception in plants <note>original: "Perception in Plants"</note>—moving toward that which should help and comfort them even though it is at a distance. The ancient tradition regarding the vine is far more strange: it is said that if you set a stake or prop some distance from it, the vine will grow in that direction. This is considered much stranger than the water experiment; for water may work by a natural attraction <note>original: "Sympathy of Attraction"</note>, but moving toward the stake seems like a logical decision <note>original: "Reasonable Discourse"</note>.

<margin>463</margin> It has been mentioned before that the drilling of holes <term>terebration</term> into trees makes them thrive better. But it is also found that it makes the fruit sweeter and better. The reason is that, despite the drilling, they still receive sufficient nourishment, yet no more than they can well process and digest; at the same time, they "sweat out" the coarsest and most useless sap. This is exactly as it is in living creatures, which attain the healthiest state of body through moderate eating, exercise, and sweating.

<margin>464</margin> Just as drilling holes improves <note>original: "Meliorate"</note> fruit, so for a similar reason does the "blood-letting" of plants. This involves pricking vines or other trees after they have reached a certain growth, thereby letting out gum or "tears" <note>sticky resins or sap</note>. Unlike drilling, this is not meant to be a permanent condition but is done only at certain seasons. It is reported that by this technique, bitter almonds have been turned into sweet ones.

<summary>Bacon explores various methods for improving plant quality, including transplanting, using additives like milk or nitre, and physical interventions like drilling holes (terebration) to purge "unprofitable" juices. He also notes the curious way plants like cucumbers and vines seem to move toward water or supports, suggesting a form of vegetable perception.</summary>

<header>Century 5.</header>

<margin>465</margin>
The ancients, for the **sweetening** <note>original: "Dulcorating"</note> of **fruit**, recommend **pig manure** <note>original: "Swines-dung"</note> above all other manure. This may be because of the moisture of that beast, which results in the **excrement** having less acrimony <term>bitterness or harshness</term>; for we see that the flesh of **swine** and **pigs** is the moistest of all meats.

<margin>466</margin>
It is observed by some that all **herbs** grow sweeter, both in smell and taste, if they are cut after they have grown for a reasonable time, so that you take the later sprout. The **cause** may be that the longer the juice stays in the root and stalk, the better it **matures** <note>original: "concocteth"; the process of ripening or "digesting" nutrients within the plant</note>. Indeed, one of the chief causes why **grains**, **seeds**, and **fruits** are more nourishing than **leaves** is the length of time in which they grow toward **maturity**. It would not be a bad idea to hold back the sap of **herbs** or similar plants by some appropriate means until the end of summer; by doing so, they may perhaps become more nourishing.

<margin>467</margin>
Just as **grafting** generally advances and **improves fruits** beyond what they would be if they were grown from **seeds** or **pits**—because the **nourishment** is better matured—so, no doubt, even in **grafting**, the choice of the **stock** <term>the rooted plant onto which a graft is joined</term> matters much for the same reason. It must always be ensured that the stock is somewhat inferior to the **scion** <term>a young shoot or twig of a plant, especially one cut for grafting</term>; otherwise, it dulleth it. They highly recommend **grafting pears** or **apples** upon a **quince** tree.

<margin>468</margin>
Besides the **means of improving fruits** mentioned before, it is recorded as a proven method that a **mixture of bran** and **pig manure**, or **chaff** and **pig manure** (especially if laid up together for a month to rot), is a very great nourisher and strengthener to a **fruit tree**.

<margin>469</margin>
It is reported that **onions** grow larger if they are taken out of the earth and laid out to dry for twenty days, and then planted again. They grow larger still if the outermost **skin** <note>original: "Pill"</note> is taken off entirely.

<margin>470</margin>
It is reported by some that if one takes the **bough** of a **low fruit tree** that has newly budded and draws it gently, without hurting it, into an **earthen pot** perforated at the bottom to let in the **plant**, and then covers the **pot** with earth, it will yield a very large **fruit** inside the ground. This **experiment** is nothing but the **potting of plants** without moving them, and leaving the **fruit** in the earth. The same effect, they say, will be achieved by putting an empty **pot** without earth over a **fruit** while it hangs upon the **tree** (propped up with a **stake**); it works even better if some few **openings** <note>original: "Perfusions"; likely meaning small holes or vents to allow air and light</note> are made in the **pot**. In this case, besides defending the **fruit** from the extremes of sun or weather, some give the reason that the **fruit**, loving and desiring the open air and sun, is invited by those openings to spread and move as near the open air as it can, and so it increases in **size**.

<margin>471</margin>
All **trees** in **high and sandy grounds** are to be planted deep, and in **watery grounds**, more shallow. In all **trees**, when they are moved (especially **fruit trees**), care ought to be taken that the sides of the **trees** are **oriented** <note>original: "coasted"</note> toward the **North** and **South**, etc., just as they stood before. The same is said of **stone** taken out of a **quarry** to make it more durable; though that

<margin>472</margin>
**Timber trees** in a **coppice** <term>a thicket of small trees or shrubs grown for periodic cutting</term> grow better than in an **open field**. This is both because they do not tend to spread out as much, but instead continue to grow upwards in **height**, and primarily because they are sheltered from too much sun and wind, which hinder the growth of all **fruit**. Similarly, there is no doubt that **fruit trees** or **vines** planted against a **wall** facing the sun, between "elbows" or stone buttresses, ripen more than on a plain **wall**.

<margin>473</margin>
It is said that if **potato roots** <note>original: "Potado Roots"</note> are planted in a **pot** filled with earth, and that pot is then placed into the ground about two or three inches deep, the **roots** will grow larger than usual. The **cause** may be that they have enough earth within the **pot** to nourish them, and then, being prevented by the bottom of the **pot** from sending roots <note>original: "strings"</note> downward, they must necessarily grow larger in **breadth** and **thickness**. It may also be that all **seeds** or **roots** that are **potted** and then set into the **earth** will thrive better.

<margin>474</margin>
The **cutting off** of the **leaves** of **radishes** or other **root vegetables** at the beginning of winter, before they wither, and then covering the **root** again quite high with earth, will preserve the **root** all winter and make it larger in the following **spring**, as was briefly mentioned before. Thus, there is a double benefit to this **cutting off** of the **leaves**: for **plants** where the **root** is the **edible part** <note>original: "esculent"</note>, such as **radishes** and **parsnips**, it will make the **root** larger; it will do the same for the **heads** of **onions**. And where the **fruit** is the **edible part**, by strengthening the **root**, it will also make the **fruit** larger.

<margin>475</margin>
It is an **experiment** of great pleasure to make the **leaves** of **shade trees** larger than usual. It has been proven (for certain) that a **scion** <term>a shoot or twig used for grafting</term> of a **wych elm** <note>original: "witch-Elme"</note> grafted onto the **trunk** <note>original: "stocke"</note> of an **ordinary elm** will produce **leaves** almost as broad as the brim of a hat. It is very likely that just as in **fruit trees** the **graft** produces larger **fruit**, so in **trees** that bear no **fruit**, it will produce larger **leaves**. Therefore, this should be tried primarily with trees of that kind, such as **birch**, **aspen** <note>original: "Aspe"</note>, **willow**, and especially the **shining willow**, which they call **"swallow-tail"** because of the attractive shape of the **leaf**.

<margin>476</margin>
The **barrenness** of trees by **accident**—aside from the **weakness** of the soil, seed, or root, and the **damage** <note>original: "iniury"</note> of the **weather**—comes either from being **overgrown** with **moss**, or being **"hide-bound"** <term>a condition where the bark is so tight it restricts the growth of the tree</term>, or being **planted** too deep, or by the **sap** flowing **too much** into the **leaves**. For all of these, there are **remedies** mentioned previously.

<header>Century 5</header>

->L 3<-

monsters, though they are more rare. And it is held that the proverb, "Africa always produces something monstrous" <note>original: *Africa semper aliquid Monstri parit*</note>, comes from the fact that because water springs are rare there, various kinds of beasts come from different parts to drink. Being refreshed, they mate, often with different species. The compounding or mixture of species in **plants** has not yet been discovered; nevertheless, if it is possible, it is more under our control than that of living creatures, because the mating of animals requires a voluntary movement. Therefore, it would be one of the most noble experiments regarding **plants** to discover how to do this. For in that way, you might have a great variety of new **fruits** and **flowers** as yet unknown. **Grafting** does not achieve this: that improves the **fruit** or doubles the **flowers**, etc., but it does not have the power to create a new **species**. For the **scion** <term>a young shoot or twig of a plant, especially one cut for grafting</term> always overrules the **stock** <term>the root or stem of a plant onto which a graft is made</term>.

<margin>477</margin>
It has been set down by one of the **ancients** that if you take two twigs of different **fruit trees**, flatten them on the sides, bind them close together, and set them in the ground, they will grow up into one **stock**. However, they will still put forth their individual **fruits** without any mixing in the **fruit** itself. Note here (by the way) that **unity of continuity** <note>physical joining</note> is easier to achieve than **unity of species** <note>biological merging into a new kind</note>. It is also reported that **vines** of **red** and **white grapes**, when set in the ground with their upper parts flattened and bound close together, will produce **grapes** of both colors on the same branch, and **grape seeds** of different colors within the same **grape**. This effect increases after a year or two as the union (it seems) grows more perfect. This process will also be helped if they are frequently watered from the first **uniting**, for all moisture helps with **union**. It is also recommended to bind the **bud** as soon as it emerges, as well as the **stock**, at least for a time.

<margin>478</margin>
They report that various **seeds**, placed into a **cloth** <note>original: "clout"</note> and laid in earth that is well-fertilized with dung, will produce **contiguous plants** which, after being bound together, will have their **shoots incorporate**. The same is said of **kernels** placed into a **bottle** with a narrow mouth filled with earth.

<margin>479</margin>
It is reported that young **trees** of various kinds, set close together without any binding and watered very often in **fruitful ground**, will incorporate and grow together through the very vigor <note>original: "luxury"</note> of the **trees**. This seems to me the most likely method that has been proposed; for **binding** hinders the natural swelling of the **tree**, which unites better while it is in motion.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into how plants interact with one another, debunking mystical ideas of "sympathy" and "antipathy" in favor of a nutritional explanation based on how plants extract "juices" from the soil.</meta>

<header>Natural History:</header>

For some plants will thrive best growing near others, which people attribute to *Sympathy*; and some grow worse, which they attribute to *Antipathy*. But these are idle and ignorant notions, and they ignore the true evidence of the causes, just as most experiments concerning *sympathies* and *antipathies* do. For regarding *plants*, there is no such *secret friendship* or hatred as people imagine. Even if we were willing to use the terms *sympathy* and *antipathy*, they are completely misunderstood; for what they call *sympathy* is actually a form of *antipathy*, and their *antipathy* is a *sympathy*. It works like this: whenever one *plant* draws a specific juice out of the earth, it conditions the soil so that the juice remaining is suitable for another plant; in that case, the neighborhood is beneficial because their nutritional needs are contrary or distinct. But where two *plants* draw (for the most part) the same juice, their neighborhood is harmful, for one deprives <note>original: "deceiueth"</note> the other of nourishment.

<margin>480</margin>
First, therefore, all *plants* that draw much nourishment from the *earth*, and so drain and exhaust it, hurt all things that grow near them. This includes large *trees* (especially *ash trees*) and trees that spread their *roots* near the surface of the ground. Likewise, the *colewort* <note>original: "Colewort"; a type of cabbage or kale</note> is not an enemy only to the *vine* (as was anciently believed), but it is an enemy to any other *plant* because it strongly draws the richest juice from the earth. And if it is true that a *vine* will turn away when it creeps near a *colewort*, this may be because it finds worse nourishment there; for though the *root* remains where it was, I suspect the *plant* will bend toward where it is best nourished.

<margin>481</margin>
Where *plants* are of different natures and draw different juices out of the earth, then (as has been said) one planted by the other is helpful. As several of the ancients have recorded, *rue* <note>original: "Rew"; a bitter medicinal herb</note> prospers greatly and becomes stronger if it is planted by a *fig tree*. This (we believe) is caused not by any *friendship*, but by the *extraction* of a contrary juice: the one drawing juice that results in sweetness, the other drawing bitter juice. They have likewise recorded that a *rose* planted near *garlic* is sweeter. This also may be because the more fetid <note>stinking</note> juice of the earth goes into the *garlic*, while the more fragrant <note>original: "Odorate"</note> juice goes into the *rose*.

<margin>482</margin>
We see this clearly in certain *wildflowers* <note>original: "Corne-Flowers"</note> that seldom or never appear in other places unless they are planted, but grow only among *corn* <term>in this period, "corn" refers to cereal grains like wheat, barley, or rye</term>. These include the *bluebottle* <note>the cornflower, Centaurea cyanus</note>, a kind of *yellow marigold*, *wild poppy*, and *fumitory*. This cannot be due to the cultivation of the ground by plowing or furrowing, in the way that some *herbs* and *flowers* will only grow in newly dug ditches; for if the ground lies fallow and unsown, these flowers will not appear. Thus, it would seem to be the *corn*...

<summary>Bacon argues that "sympathy" and "antipathy" between plants are actually caused by whether neighboring plants compete for the same soil nutrients or extract different ones. He provides examples like roses growing sweeter near garlic and specific wildflowers that only thrive among grain crops.</summary>

### Century 5.

...that qualifies the earth and prepares it for their growth.

This observation, if it holds true (as is very probable), is of great use for the **improving of taste** <note>original: "Meliorating of Taste"</note> in **fruits** and **edible herbs** <note>original: "Esculent Herbes"</note>, and for the **scent** of **flowers**. For I do not doubt that if the **fig tree** makes **rue** <note>original: "Rew"</note> stronger and more bitter (as the **ancients** have noted), then a good amount of **rue** planted around a **fig tree** will make the **figs** sweeter. Now, the tastes that most offend in **fruits**, **herbs**, and **roots** are **bitter**, **harsh**, **sour**, and **watery** or **tasteless** <note>original: "Flashy"</note>. It would be beneficial, therefore, to conduct the following **trials**.

<margin>483</margin>
Take **wormwood** or **rue** and plant it near **lettuce**, **cauliflower** <note>original: "Coleflory"</note>, or **artichoke**, and see whether the lettuce or the cauliflower, etc., becomes sweeter.

<margin>484</margin>
Take a **service tree**, a **cornelian cherry tree**, or an **elder tree**—which we know have **fruits** with harsh and binding juice—and plant them near a **vine** or **fig tree**, and see whether the **grapes** or **figs** will not be sweeter.

<margin>485</margin>
Take **cucumbers** or **pumpkins** <note>original: "Pumpions"</note> and plant them (here and there) among **muskmelons**, and see whether the **melons** will not be more **vinous** <note>original: "Winy"; having a flavor like wine</note> and better-tasting. Likewise, plant **cucumbers** among **radishes** and see whether the **radishes** will not be made more **biting**.

<margin>486</margin>
Take **sorrel** and plant it among **raspberries** <note>original: "Raspes"</note>, and see whether the raspberries will not be sweeter.

<margin>487</margin>
Take the **common briar** and plant it among **violets** or **wallflowers**, and see whether it will not make the violets or wallflowers sweeter and less earthy in their smell. Similarly, plant **lettuce** or **cucumbers** among **rosemary** or **bay trees**, and see whether the rosemary or bay will not be more **fragrant** <note>original: "Odorate"</note> or **aromatic**.

<margin>488</margin>
Conversely, you must take care how you plant **herbs** together that draw very similar juices. Therefore, I think **rosemary** will lose its sweetness if it is planted with **lavender**, **bay**, or the like. But yet, if you wish to correct the strength of an **herb**, you shall do well to plant other similar herbs by it to "take it down." For example, if you should plant **tansy** near **angelica**, it may be that the angelica would become weaker and more suitable for mixing in perfume. And if you should plant **rue** by **common wormwood**, it may be that the wormwood would turn out more like **Roman wormwood** <note>a milder variety</note>.

<margin>489</margin>
This **axiom** is of wide application and therefore should be separated and refined by **trial**. Neither must you expect to see a **massive difference** from this kind of cultivation, but only **further perfection**.

<margin>490</margin>
**Trials** should also be made in **poisonous** and **purgative herbs**, whose harmful qualities (perhaps) may be discharged or tempered by planting stronger poisons or purgatives by them.

<margin>491</margin>
It is reported that the **shrub** called **Our Lady’s Seal** (which is a kind of **bryony**) and **coleworts** <note>original: "Coleworts"; a type of cabbage or kale</note>, if planted near each other, one or both will die. The cause is that they are both great **depredators** <note>original: "Depredatours"; plants that heavily deplete the soil's nutrients</note> of the earth, and one starves the other. 

<margin>492</margin>
The same is said of a **reed** and a **brake** <note>original: "Brake"; a fern or bracken</note>; both of which are succulent, and therefore the one de- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page with "deprives" (original: "deceiueth")</note>

<summary>Bacon proposes experiments in companion planting, suggesting that planting bitter or pungent herbs near fruits and flowers can improve their flavor and scent by drawing undesirable nutrients out of the soil. He also warns that plants with similar nutritional needs will compete and harm each other.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how plants interact with one another by drawing specific nutrients or "juices" from the soil. It concludes the previous point regarding hemlock and rue before moving on to the physical causes of plant movement.</meta>

...receives the other. The same is true of *hemlock* <note>original: "Hem-locke"</note> and *rue* <note>original: "Rew"</note>, both of which draw strong juices.

<margin>493</margin>
Some of the **ancients**, and likewise various **modern writers** who have worked in *natural magic*, have noted a *sympathy* between the *sun*, *moon*, and some principal *stars*, and certain *herbs* and *plants*. They have even labeled some *herbs "solar"* and others *"lunar"*, and similar fancies expressed in grand language. It is clear that there are some flowers that react to the *sun* in two ways: one by *opening* and *shutting*, and the other by *bowing* and *inclining* the *head*. For *marigolds*, *tulips* <note>original: "Tulippa's"</note>, *pimpernel*, and indeed most *flowers* open or spread their leaves wide when the *sun* shines serenely and fair. Conversely, they close them—or at least gather them inward—either toward nightfall or when the sky is overcast. There is no need to assign such a solemn reason for this, such as saying they "rejoice" in the presence of the *sun* and "mourn" in its absence. It is actually nothing more than a slight weighing down of the leaves and a swelling at their base caused by the moisture of the air, whereas dry air causes them to extend. They also consider it a wonder that *garden clover* <note>original: "Garden Claver"</note> will hide its *stalk* when the *sun* shows bright, which is nothing but the full expansion of the leaves. As for the *bowing* and *inclining* of the *head*, this is found in the great "flower of the sun" <note>the sunflower</note>, in *marigolds*, *wartwort* <note>original: "wart-wort"</note>, *mallow flowers*, and others. The *cause* is somewhat more *obscure* than the former, but I believe it is simply that the part of the stalk which the *sun* beats against becomes more faint and flaccid, and is therefore less able to support the *flower*.

<margin>494</margin>
What a small amount of moisture can do to *vegetables*, even when they are dead and severed from the earth, is clearly shown in an *experiment of magicians* <note>original: "Experiment of Juglers"; here meaning a magic trick or illusion</note>. They take the "beard" <note>an "awn" or bristle</note> of an *oat*, which (if you observe it closely) is twisted at the bottom and consists of one smooth, entire straw at the top. They take only the twisted part and cut off the rest, leaving the *beard* about half a finger's width in length. Then they make a little *cross* out of a *quill*. The long part of the cross is made from the part of the *quill* that contains the *pith*, and the cross-piece is made from a piece of *quill* without *pith*. The whole *cross* is about a finger's width high. They then prick the bottom where the *pith* is and insert the *oat-beard*, leaving half of it sticking out of the *quill*. 

Then they take a small white wooden box to deceive people, as if something inside the box were performing the feat. In this box, they use a pin to make a small hole—large enough to hold the *beard*, but not so large that the *cross* sinks down, allowing it to stay upright. Then, as part of the trick, they ask a question, such as: "Who is the fairest woman in the company?" or "Who has a specific glove or card?" They have someone else name various people, and upon every naming, they place the *cross* in the box. Before doing so, they bring it toward their mouth as if they were casting a spell on it. The *cross* does not move; but when they reach the person they intend to pick, as they hold the *cross* to their mouth, they...

<margin>
Related Experiments concerning the making of herbs and fruits medicinal. 
499
</margin>

The altering of the *scent*, *color*, or *taste* of *fruit* by *infusing*, *mixing*, or *inserting* into the *bark* or *root* of the *tree*, *herb*, or *flower* any *colored*, *aromatic*, or *medicinal substance* are nothing but *fancies* <note>original: "Fancies"; myths or unfounded beliefs</note>. The reason is that those substances have passed their peak and do not provide nourishment. All *alteration* of *vegetables* <note>original: "Vegetables"; a general term for all plant life</note> in those qualities must be achieved by something that is likely to be incorporated into the nourishment of the *plant*. 

But this is true: where *cows* feed upon *wild garlic*, their *milk* tastes plainly of the *garlic*; and the flesh of *mutton* is better flavored where the *sheep* feed upon *wild thyme* and other wholesome *herbs*. *Galen* <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> also speaks of the curing of a *scirrhus* <note>original: "Scirrus"; a hard, cancerous tumor or swelling</note> of the liver by the *milk* of a *cow* that feeds only upon certain *herbs*. And *honey* in *Spain* smells (clearly) of the *rosemary* or *orange* from which the bee gathers it. There is also an old tradition of a *maiden* who was fed with *monkshood* <note>original: "Napellus"; a highly toxic plant, also known as wolfsbane</note>, which is considered the strongest poison of all *plants*. Through gradual use, it did not hurt the *maiden*, but it poisoned some who had *sexual* relations with her. 

So it is observed by some that there is a potent *bezoar* <note>A stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, believed to have medicinal properties</note> and another without potency, which appear the same to the eye. But the potent one is taken from the beast that feeds upon the mountains where there are *healing herbs* <note>original: "Theriacall Herbs"; herbs used to create "theriac," a famous universal antidote</note>, and the one without potency comes from those that feed in the valleys where no such *herbs* are. Thus far, I am of the opinion that just as steeped wines and beers are very *medicinal*, and likewise bread mixed with various powders, so too with *meat* (such as *flesh*, *fish*, *milk*, and *eggs*). These may be made of great use for *medicine* and *diet* if the *beasts*, *fowl*, or *fish* are fed with a special kind of food suited for a particular disease. This could also be a dangerous method for secret poisonings. But whether it may be applied to *plants* and *herbs*, I doubt more, because their nourishment is a more common sap <note>original: "Iuyce"</note> which is hardly capable of holding any special quality until the *plant* incorporates it into its own substance.

<margin>500</margin>

But lest our disbelief hinder any profitable operations of this kind (especially since many of the ancients have recorded them), we think it good briefly to propose the four *methods* which they have devised for making *plants medicinal*. 

The first is by *slitting* the *root* and *infusing* the *medicine* into it—such as *hellebore*, *opium*, *scammony* <note>A plant resin used as a strong purgative</note>, *antidote* <note>original: "Triacle"; theriac, a universal medicinal compound</note>, etc.—and then binding it up again. This seems to me the least probable because the *root* draws nourishment immediately from the earth, and so the nourishment is more general and less specialized; besides, it takes a long time to travel up before it reaches the *fruit*. 

The second way is to *perforate* <note>pierce or drill</note> the *body* of the *tree* and there *infuse* the *medicine*. This is somewhat better, for if any potency is received from the *medicine*, it has a shorter distance and less time to travel upward. 

The third is the *steeping* of the *seed* or *kernel* in some *liquid* wherein...

334 The sixth cause is when a *foreign spirit* <note>original: "Forraine Spirit"; in this context, a "spirit" refers to an active, volatile force or gaseous substance within a body</note>, stronger and more aggressive than the *spirit* of the *body*, enters that *body*; as seen in the *stinging* of *serpents*. This is generally the *cause* why *swelling* follows all *poisons*. We also see that *swelling* occurs when the *spirits* of the *body* itself *congregate* too much, as happens with *blows* and *bruises*; or when they are *trapped* <note>original: "Pent"</note> in too much, as in *swelling* caused by *cold*. We also see that the *spirits* resulting from the *putrefaction* of *fluids* <note>original: "Humours"</note> in *fevers* <note>original: "Agues"</note>, which may be considered *foreign spirits* even though they are bred within the *body*, do *extinguish* and *suffocate* the *natural spirits* and *heat*.

335 The seventh cause is by such a *weak degree* of *heat* that it sets the *spirits* into a slight *motion* but is not strong enough to either *mature* <note>original: "disgest"</note> the *parts* or to *release* the *spirits*. This is seen in *flesh* kept in a *room* that is not *cool*, whereas in a *cool* and *wet larder*, it will keep longer. We also see that *life-creation* <note>original: "Vinification"; Bacon uses this to describe the generation of life or spirit, of which "putrefaction is the bastard brother"</note> is effected by such *soft heats*, such as the *hatching* of *eggs*, the *heat* of the *womb*, and so on.

336 The eighth cause is the *releasing* of the *spirits* which were previously kept enclosed by the *solidity* of their *covering* <note>original: "Couerture"</note>, thereby checking their *appetite* for *escaping*. This is seen in *artificial rusts* induced by *acids* <note>original: "strong Waters"</note> in *iron*, *lead*, and other metals. Therefore, *wetting* hastens *rust* or the *putrefaction* of anything because it *softens* the *crust*, allowing the *spirits* to come forth.

337 The ninth cause is the *alternation* <note>original: "Enterchange"</note> of *heat* and *cold*, or *wet* and *dry*; as we see in the *mouldering* of *earth* during *frosts* and *sunshine*, and in the more rapid *rotting* of *wood* that is sometimes *wet* and sometimes *dry*.

338 The tenth cause is *time*, and the *work* and *process* of the *spirits* themselves, which cannot remain still <note>original: "keepe their Station"</note>; especially if they are left to themselves and there is no *agitation* or *local motion*. This is seen in *grain* <note>original: "Corne"</note> that is not stirred and in men's *bodies* that are not exercised.

339 All *molds* are the *beginnings* <note>original: "Inceptions"</note> of *putrefaction*, such as the *molds* on *meat pies* and *flesh*, or the *molds* on *oranges* and *lemons*. These *molds* afterwards turn into *worms* <note>likely referring to maggots or larvae</note> or more foul *putrefactions*, and therefore usually have a bad *odor*. If the *body* is *liquid* and not prone to *rotting* entirely, it will produce a *film* <note>original: "Mother"</note> on the *top*, such as the *mothers* found in *distilled waters*.

340 *Moss* is a *kind* of *mold* of the *earth* and *trees*. However, it may be better classified as a *rudiment* of *germination* <note>the very beginning of plant growth</note>, to which we refer it later.

# NATURAL HISTORY

## VI. Century
<note>In this context, a "century" refers to a group of one hundred experiments or observations.</note>

<margin>Experiments in association regarding *curiosities about fruits and plants.*</margin>
We take care that our experiments are (as we have often said) either *fruit-bearing experiments* <note>original: "Experimenta Fructifera"; experiments that yield practical or profitable results</note> or *light-bringing experiments* <note>original: "Experimenta Lucifera"; experiments that provide theoretical knowledge or enlightenment</note>; that is, aimed at either *utility* or *discovery*. For we hate *impostures* and despise *mere curiosities* <note>original: "Curiosities"; here Bacon refers to trivial or ornamental experiments that lack scientific substance.</note>. Yet, because we must accommodate ourselves somewhat to the interests of others, we will set down some *curiosities* regarding *plants*.

<margin>501</margin>
It is a *curiosity* to have *several different fruits upon one tree*. This is even more notable when some of them ripen *early* and some ripen *late*, so that you may have ripe *fruits* on the same *tree* all *summer*. This is easily done by grafting several *scions* <note>original: "Cions"; a young shoot or twig of a plant, especially one cut for grafting</note> onto the various branches of a single trunk <note>original: "Stock"</note> in good, well-nourished soil. In this way, you may have all kinds of *cherries*, and all kinds of *plums*, *peaches*, and *apricots* on one *tree*. However, I believe the *diversity* of *fruits* must be limited to those species that are compatible enough to graft onto the same *rootstock*. Therefore, I doubt whether you can have *apples*, *pears*, or *oranges* on the same *stock* upon which you graft *plums*.

<margin>502</margin>
It is a *curiosity* to have *fruits* of *various shapes* and *figures*. This is easily achieved by molding them while the *fruit* is young, using molds made of clay or wood. Thus, you may have *cucumbers*, and so forth, as long

You may even have **fruit** in more precise shapes, such as the figures of **humans**, **animals**, or **birds**, depending on how you make the molds. In this, you must understand that the mold must be large enough to contain the whole **fruit** when it has grown to its maximum size. Otherwise, you will stifle <note>original: "choake"</note> the growth of the **fruit**, which would otherwise expand to fill the hollow space and thus take the desired **shape**, just as it happens when molding liquid materials. Some doubt may be raised that keeping the sun from the **fruit** might harm it, but there is common experience of **fruit** that grows while covered. <note>original: "Quære"; Latin for "inquire" or "investigate"</note> Investigate also whether some small holes might be made in the wood to let in the sun. Note that it would be best to make the molds in pieces that are glued or cemented together so that you may open them when you take out the **fruit**.

<margin>503</margin> It is a **curiosity** to have **inscriptions** or **engravings** in **fruit** or **trees**. This is easily done by writing with a **needle**, a **bodkin** <note>a small pointed tool for piercing holes in cloth or leather</note>, a **knife**, or something similar when the **fruit** or **trees** are young. <margin>504</margin> You may have **trees** clothed with **flowers** or **herbs** by **boring holes** in their trunks and filling them with **soil enriched with manure** <note>original: "Earth holpen with Mucke"</note>, then **planting seeds** or **cuttings** <note>original: "Slips"</note> of **violets**, **strawberries**, **wild thyme**, **chamomile**, and the like in that soil. In these holes, they grow in the **tree** just as they do in **pots**, though perhaps with some nourishment from the **trees**. This should also be tested with **shoots** of **vines** and **roots** of **red roses**; for it is possible that, being of a more woody <note>original: "Ligneous"</note> nature, they will merge with the **tree** itself.

<margin>505</margin> It is a common **curiosity** to **force trees** and **shrubs** (such as **rosemary**, **juniper**, and the like) into **various shapes**. This is done by training them within a mold and pruning them on the outside. But these are often unsatisfactory <note>original: "lame Things"</note>, being too small to keep their shape. Great **castles** made of **trees** grown upon **timber frames**, complete with **turrets** and **arches**, were considered works of great magnificence.

<margin>506</margin> Among **curiosities**, I shall include **coloring**, though it is a somewhat better pursuit, for **beauty** in **flowers** is their highest distinction. It is observed by some that **gillyflowers** <note>clove-scented flowers like carnations</note>, **Sweet Williams**, and **violets** that are colored will turn **white** if they are neglected and neither watered, given new soil, nor transplanted. It is probable that **white** flowers, with much cultivation, may become **colored**. For it is certain that the **white color** comes from a scarcity of nourishment, except in flowers that are naturally **white** and do not accept other colors.

<margin>507</margin> It is useful, therefore, to see what **natures** accompany certain **colors**; for by doing so, you will gain insight into how to produce **colors** by encouraging those **natures**. **White** flowers are, for the most part, more scentless <note>original: "Inodorate"</note>...

...than **flowers** of the same kind that are **colored**; as is found in **single white violets**, **white roses**, **white gillyflowers** <note>a clove-scented flower, often a carnation or wallflower</note>, **white stock gillyflowers**, etc. We also find that **blossoms** of **trees** that are **white** are commonly **odorless** <note>original: "Inodorate"</note>, such as **cherries**, **pears**, and **plums**; whereas those of **apples**, **crabapples**, **almonds**, and **peaches** are pinkish <note>original: "Blushy"</note> and smell sweet. The **cause** is that the substance that makes the **flower** is the thinnest and finest part of the **plant**, which is also why **flowers** have such delicate **colors**. If this substance is too scarce and thin, it does not attain any strength of scent—unless it is in **plants** that are very **succulent**. In those cases, the plants need to be limited <note>original: "scanted"</note> in their nourishment rather than overfed to make them sweet. We see this in the **white satyrian** <note>a type of orchid</note>, which has a delicate smell, and in **bean flowers**, etc. On the other hand, if a **plant** is of such a nature that it only produces **white flowers**, and those flowers are not thin or dry, they are commonly of a rank and unpleasant smell, such as **mayflowers** and **white lilies**.

<margin>508</margin>
On the contrary, in **berries**, the **white** variety is commonly more delicate and sweet in taste than the **colored** ones, as we see in **white grapes**, **white raspberries** <note>original: "Raspes"</note>, **white strawberries**, **white currants**, etc. The **cause** is that the **colored** ones are juicier, and their juice is coarser; therefore, they are not as well or as equally **ripened** <note>original: "concocted"; in early science, this referred to the process of "digestion" or maturing by heat</note>. But the **white** berries are better suited to the "digestion" or internal processing of the **plant**.

<margin>509</margin>
But in **fruits**, the **white** variety is commonly inferior <note>original: "meaner"</note>, as in **pear plums**, **damsons** <note>original: "Damafins"</note>, etc. The choicest **plums** are black. The **mulberry** (which, though they call it a **berry**, is a **fruit**) is better when it is **black** than when it is **white**. The **harvest white plum** is a low-quality plum, and the **verdoccio** <note>a green Italian plum</note> and **white date plum** are not very good plums. The **cause** is that they are all over-watery, whereas a higher degree of **ripening** <note>original: "concoction"</note> is required for sweetness or a pleasant taste. Therefore, all your choice plums are a little dry and are **freestones** <note>original: "come from the Stone"; meaning the flesh separates easily from the pit</note>, such as the **mussel plum**, the **damson plum**, the **peach**, the **apricot**, etc. Yet some **fruits** that do not grow to be **black** are like **berries** in nature, being sweetest when they are paler. For example, the **heart cherry** <note>original: "Cœur-Cherry"</note>, which tends toward **white**, is sweeter than the **red**; but the **sour cherry** <note>original: "Egriot"</note> is more tart.

Take **gillyflower seed** from one kind of **gillyflower** (such as the **clove gillyflower**, which is the most common) and sow it. **Gillyflowers** will come up—some of one **color** and some of another—by chance, depending on what nourishment the **seed** meets with in the earth. Thus, **gardeners** find that they may have two or three roots among a hundred that are rare and highly prized, such as **purple** or **carnation** with various **stripes**. The **cause** is (no doubt) that in the **earth**, even if it is side-by-side <note>original: "contiguous"</note> and in one bed, there are very different **juices**; and as the **seed** by chance meets with them, it develops accordingly. It is especially noted that those which come up **purple** always come up as single flowers; the **juice**, it seems, is not able to provide enough nourishment for both a rich <note>original: "succulent"</note> **color** and a **double flower** <note>original: "Double Leafe"</note>. Few **fruits** are colored **red** inside. The **Queen apple** is, as is another **apple** called the **rose apple**; **mulberries** are as well, and **grapes** (though their color is mostly near the skin). There is also a **peach** that has a circle of **red** near the stone, and the **sour cherry** <note>original: "Egriot-Cherry"</note> is somewhat **red** inside. However, no **pear**, nor **warden pear** <note>a large, firm cooking pear</note>, nor **plum**, nor **apricot**—even though they often have **red** skins—are colored **red** inside. The **cause** of this may be investigated.

<margin>512</margin>
The general **color** of **plants** is **green**, which is a **color** no flower possesses. There is a **greenish primrose** <note>original: "Prime-Rose"</note>, but it is **pale** and hardly a **green** at all. The **leaves** of some **trees** turn a little **dark red** <note>original: "Murry"</note> or **reddish**; these are commonly **young leaves**, as seen in **oaks**, **vines**, and **hazel** <note>original: "Hasle"</note> trees. **Leaves** rot into a **yellow** color, and some **hollies** have parts of their **leaves** that are **yellow**, which (to all appearances) are as fresh and shining as the **green** ones. I also suppose that **yellow** is a less juicy <note>original: "Succulent"</note> **color** than **green**, and one degree closer to **white**. For it has been noted that those **yellow leaves** of holly always face the **north** or **northeast**.

<margin>802</margin>
Some **roots** are **yellow**, such as **carrots** <note>original: "Carrets"</note>, and some **plants** are **blood-red**—stalk, leaf, and all—such as **amaranth** <note>original: "Amaranthus"</note>. Some **herbs** incline toward **purple** and **red**, as a kind of **sage** and a kind of **mint** do, along with **sundew** <note>original: "Rosa Solis"</note>, etc. Some have **white leaves**, like another kind of **sage** and another kind of **mint**; but **bright blue** <note>original: "Azure"</note> and a **true purple** are never found in **leaves**.

<margin>903</margin>
This shows that **flowers** are made from a refined juice of the earth, as are **fruits**; but **leaves** are made from a coarser <note>original: "Course"</note> and more common juice.

<margin>513</margin>
It is also a point of interest <note>original: "Curiosity"</note> to make **flowers double** <note>flowers with more than the usual number of petals</note>. This is achieved by **frequently transplanting** <note>original: "Often Remouing"</note> them into **new soil**. Conversely, **double flowers** will become **single** again if they are neglected and not **transplanted**. The way to do this quickly is to sow or plant **seeds** or **cuttings** <note>original: "Slips"</note> of **flowers**, and as soon as they sprout, move them into **new ground** that is good. Investigate also whether **grafting** <note>original: "Inoculating"</note> flowers (such as **stocks** <note>original: "Stock-Gilly-Flowers"</note>, **roses**, **musk roses**, etc.) makes them **double**. There is a **cherry tree** that has **double blossoms**, but that **tree** bears no **fruit**.

<margin>812</margin>
And it may be that the same methods which, when applied to the **tree**, extremely accelerate the rising of the sap and its bursting forth, would cause the **tree** to spend all its energy on **flowers**, making them **double**. This would be a great pleasure to see, especially in **apple trees**, **peach trees**, and **almond trees**, which have **pinkish** <note>original: "Blush-Coloured"</note> **blossoms**.

<margin>514</margin>
Producing **fruits** without a **core** or **stone** is likewise a **point of interest** and somewhat more useful, because whatever makes them so is likely to make them more **tender** and **delicate**. If a **scion** <note>original: "Cions"</note> or shoot that is ready to be planted has its **pith** carefully removed (not entirely, but with some left to preserve its life), it will bear a **fruit** with little or no **core** or **stone**. The same is said to happen by splitting a **living tree** <note>original: "Quick-Tree"</note> down to the ground, taking out the **pith**, and then binding it up again.

<summary>This page explores why most fruits are not red inside and why leaves are green while flowers are multi-colored. It also provides early horticultural advice on creating double-petaled flowers through frequent transplanting and producing seedless fruits by removing the pith from saplings.</summary>

<page-num>131</page-num>
<header>Century VI.</header>

<margin>515</margin>
It is also reported that a **citron** <note>a large, thick-skinned citrus fruit</note> grafted upon a **quince** will have small seeds or none at all. It is very probable that any **sour fruit** grafted upon a **stock** <note>the rooted part of a plant onto which another is grafted</note> that bears a **sweeter fruit** may both make the fruit sweeter and more free of the harsh material of **kernels** or **seeds**.

<margin>516</margin>
It is reported that not only the **removal** of the **pith** <note>the spongy central tissue of a plant stem</note>, but the **stopping** of the **juice** of the pith from **rising** in the **middle**, and **directing** it to rise on the **outside**, will make the **fruit** grow without a **core** or **stone**. This might be done, for example, by boring a hole clean through a **tree** and inserting a wedge. It is true that there is some **affinity** <note>natural relationship or similarity</note> between the **pith** and the **kernel**, because they are both of a harsh **substance** and both are placed in the **middle**.

<margin>517</margin>
It is reported that **trees** watered perpetually with **warm water** will produce **fruit** with little or no **core** or **stone**. The **rule** is general: whatever will turn a **wild tree** into a **garden tree** will also cause a **garden tree** to have less **core** or **stone**.

<margin>
<insert>
Grouped experiments concerning the degenerating of plants, and the transmutation of one kind into another.
</insert>
</margin>

<margin>518</margin>
The rule is certain: **plants**, for want of **cultivation** <note>original: "culture"</note>, degenerate and become baser versions of the same **kind**, and sometimes change so far as to turn into another **kind** <note>species</note> entirely. 1. **Standing long** in one place and not being **replanted** makes them **degenerate**. 2. **Drought** does the same, unless the **earth** is naturally moist. 3. So does **moving** them into **worse earth**, or **failing** to **compost** <note>fertilize</note> the **earth**. We see, for example, that **water-mint** turns into **field-mint**, and **colewort** <note>a type of wild cabbage</note> turns into **rape** <note>a plant of the mustard family, like a turnip</note> through neglect, and so on.

<margin>519</margin>
Whatever **fruit** is usually grown from a **root** or a **cutting** <note>original: "slip"</note>, if it is instead sown from seed, it will degenerate. **Grapes** sown; **figs**, **almonds**, and **pomegranate kernels** sown—all make the **fruits** degenerate and become **wild**. Furthermore, most of those **fruits** that are usually grafted will degenerate if they are planted from **kernels** or **stones**. It is true that **peaches** (as mentioned before) do better when **planted from stones** than when **grafted**. The **rule** for this exception seems to be this: whatever **plant** requires much **moisture** prospers better from the **stone** or **kernel** than from a **graft**. This is because the **stock**, though it provides a more refined **nourishment**, provides a more limited <note>original: "scanter"</note> amount than the earth at large.

<margin>520</margin>
**Seeds**, if they are very **old** and yet still have enough strength to produce a **plant**, will make that **plant degenerate**. Therefore, skillful **gardeners** test the **seeds** before they buy them to see if they are good by putting them into **water** that has been gently **boiled**. If they are good, they will sprout within **half an hour**.

<margin>521</margin>
It is strange what is reported: that **basil**, if too much exposed to the **sun**, turns into **wild thyme**. Although those two **herbs** seem to have little **affinity**, **basil** is almost the only "hot" **herb** that has **thick** and **succulent leaves**. If that **oiliness** is drawn out by the **sun**, it is likely to cause a very great **change**.

<margin>522</margin>
There is an old **tradition** that **branches** of **oak** put into the **earth** will produce **wild vines**. If this is true, it is undoubtedly not the **oak** turning into a **vine**, but the **rotting oak branch** conditioning the **earth** to produce a **vine** on its own.

<page-num>132</page-num>
<header>Natural History:</header>

<margin>523</margin>
It is not impossible, and I have heard it verified, that upon cutting down an old **timber tree**, the **stump** <note>original: "stub"</note> has sometimes put out a **tree** of another **kind**; such as a **beech** putting forth **birch**. If this is true, the **cause** may be that the old stump is too low on juice to produce the original tree, and therefore puts forth a tree of a smaller kind that requires less nourishment.

<margin>524</margin>
There is a common belief in the countryside that if the same **ground** is often sown with the same **grain** <note>original: "corne"</note> that grew upon it, the crop will eventually grow into a baser or lower-quality kind.

<margin>525</margin>
It is certain that in very sterile years, **grain** sown will grow into another **kind**.

> ->Often in the furrows to which we have entrusted the large barley, the miserable darnel and sterile wild oats dominate. <note>original Latin: *Grandia sæpè quibus mandauimus Hordea sulcis, Infelix Lolium, & steriles dominantur Auenæ*</note><-

And generally, it is a rule that **plants** which are produced by **cultivation** <note>original: "culture"</note>, such as **grain**, will change into other **species** more quickly than those that grow wild. This is because **cultivation** provides only an **acquired nature** <note>original: "adventitious nature"</note>, which is more easily shed.

This work of the **transmutation** <note>the changing of one substance or species into another</note> of **plants** into one another is among the **Great Works of Nature** <note>original: *Magnalia Naturæ*</note>. In the **common philosophy** <note>original: "vulgar Philosophy," referring to the standard academic teachings of the time</note> of the day, the **transmutation** of **species** is pronounced **impossible**. Certainly, it is a difficult thing that requires a deep search into **nature**; but seeing that some manifest **instances** of it appear, the opinion of **impossibility** is to be rejected and the means of achieving it found. We see that in **living creatures** arising from **decay** <note>original: "putrefaction"; Bacon refers to the then-common belief in spontaneous generation</note>, there is much **transmutation** of one into another, such as **caterpillars** turning into **flies**, etc. It seems probable that whatever **creature** possessing life is generated without **seed**, that **creature** will change from one **species** into another. For it is the **seed** and its specific **nature** which locks and bounds the **creature** so that it does not **stray from its type** <note>original: "expatiate"</note>. So, we may well conclude that since the **earth** itself puts forth **plants** without **seed**, **plants** may well undergo a **migration of species** <note>original: "transmigration of Species"</note>. Therefore, lacking the **instances** that usually occur, we shall provide **directions** for the most likely **trials**. Generally, we would not want those who read this **work** of ours, *Sylva Sylvarum* <note>Latin: "A Forest of Forests"</note>, to think it strange or a result of **over-haste** that we have set down **particulars** that are as yet untried. On the contrary, in our own **estimation**, we consider such **suggestions** more worthy than those that are already...
<meta>catchword: ready</meta>

<summary>Bacon explores the "transmutation of species" in plants, arguing that while traditional philosophy deems it impossible, evidence from spontaneous generation and agriculture suggests that one plant can indeed turn into another under the right conditions.</summary>
