<meta>This page continues Bacon's investigation into the "transmutation" of plants, proposing specific experimental rules to test how soil and surrounding vegetation might force one species to change into another.</meta>

# Century VI.

...already tried and known. For these latter ones must be accepted as you find them; but the others aim directly at the **invention of causes and axioms** <note>scientific principles or laws</note>.

<margin>526</margin>
First, therefore, you must keep in mind that if you want one **plant** to change into another, the **nourishment** <note>the nutrients in the soil</note> must dominate the **seed**. Therefore, you should practice this using **nourishments** as contrary as possible to the **nature** of the **herb**, as long as the **herb** can still grow. Use **seeds** of the weakest kind with the least vigor. You would do well, therefore, to take **marsh herbs** and plant them upon the tops of hills and open plains <note>original: "Champaignes"</note>, and take such **plants** as require much moisture and plant them upon sandy and very dry grounds. For example, plant **marshmallows** and **sedge** upon hills; plant **cucumber**, **lettuce seeds**, and **cabbages** <note>original: "Coleworts"</note> upon a **sandy plot**. Conversely, plant **bushes**, **heath**, **heather** <note>original: "Ling"</note>, and **ferns** <note>original: "Brakes"</note> upon wet or **marshy ground**. I also believe that all **edible** <note>original: "Esculent"</note> and **garden herbs** set upon the tops of hills will prove more **medicinal**, though less **edible**, than they were before. Likewise, you may turn some **wild herbs** into **salad herbs** <note>original: "Sallet-Herbs"</note>. This is the first rule for the **transmutation of plants**.

<margin>527</margin>
The second rule shall be to bury a few **seeds** of the **herb** you wish to change among other **seeds**. Then you shall see whether the juice of those other **seeds** modifies the earth enough to alter the **seed** you are working on. For example: put **parsley seed** among **onion seed**; or **lettuce seed** among **parsley seed**; or **basil seed** among **thyme seed**; and observe any change of taste or other qualities. However, you would do well to put the **seed** you wish to change into a small linen cloth so that it does not physically mix with the **foreign seed**.

<margin>528</margin>
The third rule shall be the **making of a medley** or **mixture** of earth with other **plants** that have been **crushed** <note>original: "bruised"</note> or **shaved**, using either the leaf or the root. For example, prepare earth with a mixture of **cabbage leaves** that have been **pounded** <note>original: "stamped"</note>, and plant **artichokes** or **parsnips** in it. Similarly, take earth mixed with **marjoram**, **oregano** <note>original: "Origanum"</note>, or **wild thyme** that has been **crushed** or **pounded**, and plant **fennel seed**, and so on. In this operation, I believe the process of nature will still be that the **herb** you are working on does not draw the juice of the foreign **herb** directly (for we have previously rejected that opinion). Instead, there will be a new **mixture of soil** <note>original: "Confection of Mould"</note> that perhaps will alter the **seed**, yet without turning it into the same kind as the previous **herb**.

<margin>529</margin>
The fourth rule shall be to note what **herbs** certain soils produce on their own, and to take that earth and put it in a pot or **container** <note>original: "Vessell it"</note>. In that soil, plant the **seed** you wish to change. For example, take the earth from under walls or similar places where **nettles** grow in abundance—ensuring you have only the earth without any **fibers** <note>original: "String"</note> or **roots** of the **nettles**—and pot that earth. Then plant **stock-gilliflowers** <note>a fragrant garden flower</note> or **wallflowers**, etc., or sow their **seeds** in it, and see what the outcome will be. Or use earth that you have prepared to produce **mushrooms**.

<summary>Francis Bacon outlines four experimental rules for the "transmutation" of plants, suggesting that extreme changes in nourishment, proximity to other seeds, or specific soil compositions can force one species to transform into another.</summary>
<keywords>transmutation of plants, botany, Francis Bacon, experimental science, soil composition, plant nourishment, agriculture, medicinal herbs</keywords>

Natural History:

...comes, of itself, (of which you shall find some examples following); and sow in it **purslane seed**, or **lettuce seed**. For in these **experiments**, it is likely enough that the earth, being accustomed to send forth one kind of nourishment, will alter the new **seed**.

<margin>530</margin>
The fifth rule shall be to make the **herb grow contrary to its nature**, such as making **ground-creeping herbs** rise in **height**. For example, grow **chamomile**, or **wild thyme**, or the **green strawberry** upon **sticks**, as you do **hops** upon **poles**, and see what the **outcome** <note>original: "Event"</note> will be.

<margin>531</margin>
The sixth rule shall be to make **plants grow out of the sun or open air**, for that is a great **mutation** <note>change</note> in **nature** and may induce a change in the **seed**. For instance, place **earth** in a barrel and sow some **seed** in it, and put it at the bottom of a pond; or put it in some great hollow **tree**. Try also the sowing of **seeds** in the bottoms of **caves**; and pots with **seeds** sown, hung up in wells some distance from the water, and see what the **outcome** will be.

<margin>
Experiments in a group <note>original: "in Consort"</note> concerning the **procerity** <term>procerity</term> <note>original: "procerity" - tallness or height</note>, and shortness, and artificial dwarfing of trees.
532
</margin>
It is certain that **timber trees** in **coppice woods** <note>original: "Coppice woods" - a thicket or grove of small trees or shrubs that are periodically cut back to stimulate growth</note> grow more upright and are more free from **lower branches** <note>original: "Under-Boughes"</note> than those that stand in the **fields**. The cause of this is that **plants** have a natural motion to reach toward the sun. Besides, they are not oversated <note>original: "glutted"</note> with too much **nourishment**, because the **coppice** shares it with them; and **repletion** <term>repletion</term> <note>original: "repletion" - being overly full of nutrients</note> always hinders height. Lastly, they are kept warm, and warmth in **plants** always helps them grow upward.

<margin>533</margin>
**Trees** that are naturally full of **heat** (which **heat** is shown by their **flammable resins** <note>original: "Inflammable Gummes"</note>), such as **firs** and **pines**, grow tall of their own accord without side branches until they reach the top. The cause is partly heat and partly the **thinness of their juice** <term>tenuity of juice</term> <note>original: "Tenuity of Iuyce" - the thin or watery consistency of the plant's sap</note>; both of these send the sap upwards. As for **juniper**, it is but a **shrub** and does not grow large enough in its trunk to sustain a tall **tree**.

<margin>534</margin>
It is reported that a good strong **canvas** spread over a **tree** grafted low, soon after it begins to grow, will dwarf it and make it spread. The cause is plain: all things that grow will grow as they find **room**.

<margin>535</margin>
**Trees** are generally planted from **roots** or **kernels** <note>seeds</note>; but if you plant them from **slips** <note>original: "Slips" - cuttings taken from a plant to be grown into a new one</note> (as you may with some **trees**, namely the **mulberry**), some of the **slips** will take root. And those that do (as it is reported) will be **dwarf trees**. The cause is that a **slip** draws nourishment more weakly than either a **root** or a **seed**.

<margin>536</margin>
All **plants** that release their **sap** quickly have bodies that are not proportional to their length; therefore they are **winders** and **creepers**, such as **ivy**, **bryony**, **hops**, and **woodbine** <note>honeysuckle</note>. In contrast, **dwarfing** requires a slow growth and less vigor in climbing.

<meta>This page continues Bacon’s observations on the nature of plant life, specifically focusing on moss as a "rudiment" or primitive form of a plant. # Century VI.

<margin>Rudiments of Plants, and the Excrescences of Plants, or Super-Plants.</margin>
For so the best *translations* have it. And it is true that *moss* is but the *rudiment of a plant*; and (as it were) the *mold of the earth or of bark*.

<margin>537</margin>
*Moss* grows chiefly upon the *ridges of houses*, whether tiled or thatched, and upon the *crests of walls*. That *moss* is of a bright and pleasant green. Its growth upon *slopes* is caused by the fact that, while *moss* comes from moisture and water on the one hand, on the other hand the *water* must slide off and not stand or pool. Its *growth* upon *tiles*, or *walls*, etc., is caused because those dried earths, lacking sufficient moisture to produce a *plant*, instead attempt *germination* by putting forth *moss*. However, when by *age* or otherwise they begin to soften <note>original: "relent"</note> and dissolve <note>original: "resolve"</note>, they sometimes produce *plants*, such as *wallflowers*. Almost all *moss* has little stalks here and there, in addition to the low, carpet-like *tufts* <note>original: "Thrumme" — a fringe of threads or a shaggy mass</note>.

<margin>538</margin>
*Moss* grows upon *alleys*, especially those that lie cold and face the *north*, as in various *terraces*. It also grows if they are much trodden upon, or if they were originally graveled; for wherever *plants* are kept down, the earth puts forth *moss*.

<margin>539</margin>
*Old ground* that has long been unbroken gathers *moss*. Therefore, farmers <note>original: "Husbandmen"</note> usually cure their *pasture grounds* when they become mossy by *tilling* them for a year or two. This also depends upon the same *cause*: the more *meager* <note>original: "Sparing"</note> and *impoverished* <note>original: "Starving"</note> *juice* <note>the nutrient-rich fluid or sap of the earth</note> of the earth, being insufficient for *plants*, breeds *moss*.

<margin>540</margin>
*Old trees* have far more *moss* than *young* ones. This is because the sap is not vigorous <note>original: "francke"</note> enough to rise all the way to the boughs; instead, it tires along the way and puts out *moss*.

<margin>541</margin>
*Fountains* have *moss* growing upon the *ground* around them:
->*Mossy fountains*;<- <note>original: "Muscosi Fontes"</note>
The *cause* is that the *fountains* drain the *water* from the *adjacent ground*, leaving only enough moisture to breed *moss*. Additionally, the *coldness* of the *water* contributes to this.

<margin>542</margin>
The *moss of trees* is a kind of *hair*; for it is the juice of the *tree* that is excreted <note>original: "Excernd"</note> and does not transform <note>original: "Assimilate"</note> into the tree's own substance. Upon great *trees*, the *moss* takes on a shape like a *leaf*.

<margin>543</margin>
The *moister types of trees* yield little *moss*, as we see in *aspen trees, poplars, willows, beeches*, etc. This is partly caused by the reason already given—the vigorous <note>original: "francke"</note> pushing up of the *sap* into the *boughs*—and partly because the *bark* of those *trees* is *closer* and *smoother* than that of *oaks* and *ashes*, making it harder for the *moss* to break through.

<margin>544</margin>
In *clay soils*, all *fruit trees* grow full of *moss* on both their *trunks* <note>original: "Body"</note> and *boughs*. This is caused partly by the *coldness* of the *ground*, which causes the *plants* to receive less nourishment, and partly by the *toughness* of the *earth*, which shuts in the *sap* and prevents it from rising and spreading as vigorously <note>original: "franckly"</note> as it should.

<summary>This page discusses the nature and causes of moss growth, characterizing it as a primitive "rudiment" of a plant that emerges when moisture or nutrients are insufficient for more complex vegetation. Bacon observes how moss thrives on roofs, old ground, and trees, linking its presence to poor sap circulation or specific soil conditions like clay.</summary>
<keywords>moss, botany, plant germination, sap, soil quality, tilling, tree bark, Francis Bacon, natural history</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Bacon’s investigation into "imperfect plants," moving from the causes of moss growth to the nature and spontaneous generation of mushrooms, which he views as products of "fat" or "concocted" moisture.</meta>

<page-num>136</page-num>
# Natural History:

<margin>545</margin>
We have said before that if *trees* are *hide-bound* <note>A condition where the bark is too tight, restricting the tree's growth</note>, they become less fruitful and gather *moss*. Therefore, they are helped by *hacking* <note>original: "Hacking" — the practice of cutting slits in the bark to relieve tension</note>, etc. Consequently, by the principle of opposites, if *trees* are bound in with *cords* or some *external bands*, they will produce more *moss*. This (I think) happens to *trees* that stand *exposed* <note>original: "Bleake"</note> to the cold winds. It should also be tested whether covering a *tree* somewhat thickly on the top after its *pollarding* <note>original: "Powling" — pruning the top branches of a tree to encourage a thick head of new foliage</note> will cause it to gather more *moss*. I also think that the *watering* of *trees* with *cold fountain water* will make them grow full of *moss*.

<margin>546</margin>
There is a *moss* that *perfumers* use, which comes from *apple trees*, that has an excellent *scent*. *Inquire* <note>original: "Quære"</note> particularly into the *manner of its growth* and its *nature*. For the sake of this *experiment*, it being a valuable thing, I have set down the previous *experiments* on how to multiply and encourage the growth of *mosses*.

Next to *moss*, I will speak of *mushrooms*, which are likewise an *imperfect plant*. These *mushrooms* have two strange properties: one, that they yield such *delicious food*; the other, that they grow so quickly, even in a single night, and yet they are *unsown*. Therefore, those who are social upstarts in the state are reproachfully called *mushrooms*. It must be, therefore, that they are made of *much moisture*, and that moisture must be *rich* <note>original: "Fat"</note>, coarse, and yet somewhat *processed by heat* <note>original: "Concocted"</note>. Indeed, we find that *mushrooms* cause the condition which we call *incubus* <note>original: "Incubus" — a nightmare or a feeling of heavy pressure on the chest during sleep</note>, or the *nightmare* <note>original: "the Mare"</note>, in the *stomach*. Therefore, overindulging in them may *suffocate* and *poison*. This shows that they are "windy" (gassy), and that gas is thick and swelling, not sharp or griping. For the same reason, *mushrooms* are an *aphrodisiac food* <note>original: "venereous Meat"</note>.

<margin>547</margin>
It is reported that the *bark* of *white or red poplar* (which are among the moistest of *trees*), cut small and cast into *furrows* that are well dunged, will cause the ground to produce *mushrooms* fit to be eaten at all *seasons of the year*. Some add to the mixture *leaven* of *bread* dissolved in water.

<margin>548</margin>
It is reported that if a *hilly field*, where the *stubble* is still standing, is set on *fire* during a *showery season*, it will produce a great abundance of *mushrooms*.

<margin>549</margin>
It is reported that *hart's horn* <note>Deer antler</note>, *shaved* or in *small pieces*, mixed with dung and *watered*, produces *mushrooms*. We know that *hart's horn* is of a *fat and sticky substance*, and it is possible that *ox horn* would do the same.

There is no known substance, except for *earth* and things produced from *earth* (as *tile, stone, etc.*), that yields any *moss* or *herbal substance*. A trial may be made by putting some *seeds*, such as *fennel seed, mustard seed*, and *rapeseed*, into some little *holes* made in the *horns* of *stags or oxen* to see if they will grow.

<margin>551</margin>
There is also another *imperfect plant* that (in appearance) is like a great *mushroom*. It is sometimes as broad as one's *hat*, which people call a *toadstool*. But it is not *edible* <note>original: "Esculent"</note>; and it grows (commonly) by a dead *stump* <note>original: "Stub"</note> of a *tree*, and likewise around the *roots* of *rotting trees*. Therefore, it seems to take its juice from *decayed* <note>original: "Putrified"</note> wood. This shows, by the way, that *decayed wood* yields an abundant *moisture*.

<margin>552</margin>
There is a *cake-like growth* that grows upon the side of a *dead tree* that has no specific *name*, but it is large, of a *chestnut* color, hard, and pithy. This suggests that even *dead trees* do not forget their habit of *sprouting* <note>original: "Putting forth"</note>, no more than the *corpses* of *human bodies* continue to produce *hair* and *nails* for a *time*.

<margin>553</margin>
There is a *pod* <note>original: "Cod"</note> or *bag* that grows commonly in the *fields* which at first is hard like a *tennis ball* and white; afterward, it grows to a *mushroom color* and is full of light *dust* upon *breaking*. It is thought to be dangerous for the *eyes* if the *powder* gets into them, and to be good for treating *chilblains* <note>original: "Kibes" — painful, itchy sores on the feet or hands caused by exposure to cold</note>. Likely it has a *caustic* and *irritating* nature.

<margin>554</margin>
There is an *herb* called *Jew's Ear* <note>A type of jelly fungus, Auricularia auricula-judae, commonly found on elder trees</note> that grows upon the *roots* and *lower parts* of the *trunks* of *trees*, especially of *elders*, and sometimes *ashes*. It has a strange property: for in *warm water*, it swells and opens extremely. It is not green, but of a dusky brown color. It is used for *quinsy* <note>original: "Squinancies" — an inflammation of the throat or tonsils</note> and *inflammations* in the *throat*, which suggests it has a *softening* and *soothing* <note>original: "Mollifying, and Lenifying"</note> quality.

<margin>555</margin>
There is a kind of *spongy growth* which grows chiefly upon the *roots* of the *larch tree* <note>original: "Laser-Tree" — likely the Larch, the source of medicinal agaric</note>, and sometimes upon *cedar* and other *trees*. It is very *white*, *light*, and *crumbly* <note>original: "Friable"</note>; we call this *agaric*. It is famous in *medicine* <note>original: "Physicke"</note> for the *purging* of *thick phlegm*. It is also an excellent *remedy* for opening the *liver*, but it is *upsetting* to the *stomach*. In *taste*, it is sweet at first and afterward *bitter*.

<margin>556</margin>

There is a foolish *tradition* that there is a *bird* called a *mistle-thrush* <note>original: "Missel-bird"</note> that feeds upon a *seed* which she often cannot digest, and so excretes it whole with her *droppings*. When this falls upon a *branch* of a *tree* that has some *crack* <note>original: "Rif"</note> in the bark, it sprouts the *mistletoe*. But this is a *myth* <note>original: "Fable"</note>; for it is not probable that *birds* would feed upon something they cannot digest. But even if we allowed that, it cannot be true for other *reasons*: for first, it is found only upon certain *trees*, and those *trees* bear no such *fruit* as would attract that *bird* to sit and feed upon them. It may be that the *bird* feeds upon the *mistletoe berries* and so is often found there, which may have given rise to the story. But the point that settles the ques-

<header>Natural History:</header>

The observation is that *mistletoe* has been found to sprout from under the *boughs*, and not only on top of the *boughs*. Therefore, it cannot be caused by anything that simply falls onto the *bough* <note>The author is arguing against the common contemporary belief that mistletoe was generated from bird droppings falling on trees.</note>. *Mistletoe* grows chiefly upon *crab-apple trees*, *apple trees*, and sometimes upon *hazels*; it grows only rarely upon *oaks*. The *mistletoe* of the oak is considered very *medicinal*. It is evergreen in both winter and summer and bears a white, *glistening berry*. It is a *plant* that is utterly different from the *plant* upon which it grows. Two things, therefore, may be certainly established: First, that *superfetation* <note>original: "Super-fetation"; here meaning a secondary growth or a "plant upon a plant."</note> must be caused by an *abundance* of sap in the *bough* that produces it. Secondly, that the sap must be of a kind that the *tree* excretes <note>original: "excerne"</note> and cannot incorporate into itself; otherwise, the sap would turn into a normal *bough*. Furthermore, this sap seems to be more fatty and oily <note>original: "Vnctuous"</note> than the ordinary *sap* of the *tree*, which is shown both by the *berry*, which is sticky, and by the fact that it remains green in winter and summer, whereas the *tree* does not.

<margin>557</margin>
This *experiment* regarding *mistletoe* may provide insight into other *practices*. Therefore, a *trial* should be made by slicing into the *bark* of a *crab-apple tree* bough and watering the wound every day with *warm water mixed with dung*, to see if it would produce *mistletoe* or any similar *thing*. However, it would be even more likely to succeed if tried with some other *watering* or *anointing* substance that is not as *natural* to the *tree* as *water* is—such as *oil* or *yeast* <note>original: "Barme of Drinke"</note>, etc.—provided they are substances that do not kill the *bough*.

<margin>558</margin>
It would be good to test what *plants* would produce if they are forbidden from sprouting their *natural boughs*. Therefore, prune <note>original: "Poll"</note> a *tree* and cover the top with a layer of *clay*, and see what it will sprout. I suspect it will sprout *roots*, for a *shoot* <note>original: "Cions"</note> will do so when turned down into *clay*. Therefore, in this *experiment* as well, the *tree* should be sealed with something that is not as *natural* to the *plant* as *clay* is. Try it with *leather*, *cloth*, or *paint*, as long as it is not harmful to the *tree*. It is certain that a *brake* <note>A type of fern or thicket.</note> has been known to grow out of a *pollard* <note>A tree that has been heavily pruned or "topped" to encourage a thick head of new branches.</note>.

<margin>559</margin>
One may consider the *prickles* of *trees* to be a kind of *outgrowth* <note>original: "Excrefcence"</note>, for they will never become *boughs* nor bear *leaves*. The *plants* that have *prickles* on their *boughs* are *thorns* (both black and white), *briar*, *rose*, *lemon trees*, *crab-apple trees*, *gooseberry*, and *barberry*. The *plants* that have *prickles* on their *leaves* are *holly*, *juniper*, *whin-bush* <note>Also known as gorse or furze.</note>, and *thistle*. *Nettles* also have a small, venomous *prickle*, as does *borage* <note>original: "Burrage"</note>, though its prickles are harmless. The *cause* of these must be a *hasty sprouting*, a *lack* of *moisture*, and the *tightness* of the *bark*. Because the internal "spirit" is in a hurry to sprout, but there is a *lack* of *nourishment* to form a full *bough*, and the *bark* is too *tight*, *prickles* are formed on the *boughs*. This is why they are always shaped like a *pyramid* <note>original: "Pyramis"</note>, as the *moisture* is exhausted after only a little *sprouting*. As for *prickles* on *leaves*, they also come from *pushing more juice* into the *leaf* than can spread out *smoothly*; therefore, such *leaves* are otherwise *rough*, as *borage* and *nettles* are. In the case of *holly leaves*, they are *smooth* but never *flat*, appearing instead with *folds* for the same *reason*.

<header>Century VI.</header>

<margin>560</margin>
There are also *plants* that, though they have no prickles, yet they have a kind of *downy* or *velvet rind* <note>original: "Rine"; the outer skin or surface of the leaf</note> upon their *leaves*, such as *rose campion, stock flowers*, and *coltsfoot*. This down, or *nap*, comes from a subtle spirit within a *soft* or *fatty substance*. For it is certain that both *stock flowers* and *rose campions*, when crushed, have been successfully applied to the *wrists* of those who have had *tertian* or *quartan fevers* <note>original: "Agues"; fevers characterized by paroxysms that return every third or fourth day</note>. And the vapor of *coltsfoot* has a healing virtue for the *lungs*; the *leaf* is also healing when used in *surgery* <note>original: "Surgery"; here referring to the treatment of external wounds or sores</note>.

<margin>561</margin>
Another kind of *growth* <note>original: "Excrescence"</note> is an *exudation* of *plants* joined with *decay* <note>original: "Putrefaction"</note>, as we see in *oak apples* <note>original: "Oake-Apples"; galls produced on oak trees by the larvae of gall wasps</note>, which are found chiefly upon the *leaves* of *oaks*, and similarly upon *willows*. *Country* people have a kind of *prediction* that if the *oak apple*, when broken, is full of *worms*, it is a sign of a *year of pestilence*. This is a likely thing, because they grow from corruption.

<margin>562</margin>
There is also upon *sweet-briar*, or other *briars*, a fine *tuft* or *brush* of *moss* of various colors; if you cut it, you shall always find it full of little white *worms*.

It is certain that *earth* taken out of the *foundations* of *vaults* and *houses*, and the *bottoms* of *wells*, and then put into *pots*, will produce various kinds of *herbs*. But some *time* is required for the *germination*; for if it is taken from only a *fathom* deep <note>original: "Fathome"; a unit of length equal to six feet</note>, it will sprout the *first year*. If much deeper, it will not sprout until after a *year* or *two*.

<margin>564</margin>
The *nature* of the *plants* growing out of *earth* so taken up follows the *nature* of the *soil* <note>original: "Mould"</note> itself. If the *soil* is *soft* and fine, it produces *soft herbs*, such as *grass, plantain*, and the like. If the *earth* is *harder* and *coarser*, it produces *herbs* that are more *rough*, such as *thistles, firs, etc*.

<margin>565</margin>
It is common *experience* that where *garden paths* <note>original: "Alleyes"</note> are closely *graveled*, the *earth* produces *knot-grass* in the first year, and afterward *spire-grass*. The *cause* is that the *hard gravel* or *pebbles*, when first *laid*, will not allow the *grass* to grow upright, but force it to find its way where it can; but after the *earth* is somewhat loosened at the *top*, the ordinary *grass* comes up.

<margin>566</margin>
It is reported that *earth* taken from some depth in *shady* and *watery woods* and potted will produce *herbs* of a *fat* and *juicy* substance, such as *pennywort, purslane, houseleek* <note>original: "Mouselecke"; a succulent plant, likely the common houseleek or a related species</note>, *pennyroyal, etc*.

<margin>567</margin>
The *water* also sends forth *plants* that have no *roots* fixed in the *bottom*; but they are less *perfect plants*, being almost nothing but *leaves*, and small ones at that. Such is the plant we call *duckweed*, which has a leaf no bigger than a *thyme leaf* but of a fresher green, and puts out a little *string* into the *water* far from the *bottom*. As for the *water-lily*, it has a *root* in the *ground*, as do a number of other *herbs* that grow in *ponds*.

# Natural History:

They are thought to grow from a solidifying <note>original: "Concretion"</note> of slime from the **water**, in places where the **sun** beats hot and where the **sea** moves very little. **As for** ***Alga Marina*** (**Sea-weed**) and ***Eryngium*** (**Sea Thistle**), both have **roots**; however, the **sea-weed** grows under the water, while the **sea-thistle** grows only upon the **shore**.

<margin>569</margin> The ancient authors have noted that there are some **herbs** that grow out of **snow** that has been packed close together and **decayed** <note>original: "Putrified"</note>; and these plants are all **bitter**. They specifically name one called ***Flomus*** <note>original: "Flomus"; likely referring to *Phlomis* or *Verbascum* species</note>, which we call **moth-mullein**. It is certain that **worms** are commonly found in **snow**, similar to **earth-worms**; therefore, it is not unlikely that snow may also produce **plants**.

<margin>570</margin> The **ancients** have claimed that there are some **herbs** that grow out of **stone**. This may be possible, as it is certain that **toads** have been found inside the middle of a block of **freestone** <note>original: "Free-Stone"; a fine-grained stone like limestone or sandstone that can be easily cut in any direction</note>. We also see that **flints** lying above **ground** gather **moss**, and **wall-flowers** and some other **flowers** grow upon **walls**. However, whether they grow upon the **solid brick** or **stone**, or whether they grow out of the **mortar** <note>original: "Lime"</note> or **cracks**, has not been well observed. **Elder** and **ash** trees have been seen growing out of **steeples**, but they clearly grow out of **fissures**; indeed, when they grow large, they will actually break the **stone** apart. Furthermore, it is uncertain whether the **mortar** itself produces the plant, or whether some **seeds** were dropped there by **birds**. There are likewise **rock-herbs**, but I suspect those grow where there is some **mold** or **earth**. It has also been found that great **trees** growing upon **quarries** have pushed their **roots** down into the **stone**.

<margin>571</margin> In some **mines** in **Germany**, as is reported, **vegetables** grow at the bottom. The **workers** say they have **magical powers** <note>original: "Magicall Vertue"</note> and will not allow **men** to gather them.

<margin>572</margin> **Sea-sands** seldom bear **plants**. The **cause** given for this by some of the **ancients** is that the **sun** evaporates the **moisture** before it can mix with the **earth** and provide nourishment for the **plant**. It is also claimed that sand always has its **roots** in **clay**, and that there are no **veins** of **sand** found at any great depth within the **earth**.

<margin>573</margin> It is certain that some **plants** grow for a time using their own **reserves** <note>original: "Store"</note>, without any **nourishment** from **earth**, **water**, **stone**, etc. Regarding this, *see Experiment 29*.

# Natural History:

...of the **hotter countries** translated into the **colder**, will be more advanced <note>original: "forward"</note> than the ordinary **grain** of the **cold country**. It is likely that this will prove better in **grains** than in **trees**; because **grains** are only **annuals**, and so the **vitality** <note>original: "Vertue"</note> of the **seed** is not worn out; whereas in a **tree**, it is weakened <note>original: "embased"</note> by the **ground** to which it is moved.

<margin>576</margin>
Many **plants** that grow in the **hotter countries**, being set in the **colder**, will nevertheless—even in those **cold countries**—emerge and last most part of the **summer** if sown from **seeds** late in the **spring**. We find this in **orange** and **lemon seeds**, etc. Their **seeds**, sown at the end of **April**, will bring forth excellent **salads** <note>original: "Sallets"</note> mixed with other **herbs**. And I do not doubt that the **seeds** of **clove trees** and **pepper seeds**, etc., if they could arrive here **fresh** <note>original: "Greene"</note> enough to be sown, would do the same.

<margin>
Experiments in collaboration <note>original: "in Consort"</note>, concerning the seasons in which plants emerge.
577
</margin>
There are some **flowers, blossoms, grains**, and **fruits** which come more **early**, and others which come more **late** in the **year**. The **flowers** that come early among us are: **primroses, violets, anemones, water-daffodils, spring crocuses** <note>original: "Crocus Vernus"</note>, and some early **tulips**. And they are all **cold plants**; which therefore (as it would seem) have a quicker **perception** of the **increasing heat** of the **sun** than the **hot herbs** have; just as a **cold hand** will sooner feel a little **warmth** than a **hot** one. And those that come next after are **wallflowers, cowslips, hyacinths, rosemary flowers**, etc. And after them, **pinks, roses, irises** <note>original: "Flower deluces"</note>, etc. And the latest are **gillyflowers, hollyhocks, larkspur** <note>original: "Larks-Foot"</note>, etc. The earliest **blossoms** are the **blossoms** of **peaches, almonds, Cornelian cherries** <note>original: "Cornelians"</note>, **mezereon** <note>original: "Mezerious"</note>, etc. And they are from such **trees** that have much **moisture**, either **watery** or **oily**. And therefore the **spring crocus** <note>original: "Crocus Vernus"</note> also, being an **herb** that has an **oily juice**, puts forth early. For those also find the **sun** sooner than the **drier trees**. The **grains** are: first **rye** and **wheat**; then **oats** and **barley**; then **peas** and **beans**. For though **green peas** and **beans** are eaten sooner, the **dry ones** that are used for **horse feed** <note>original: "horse-meat"</note> are ripe last; and it seems that the **richer grain** <note>original: "Fatter Graine"</note> comes first. The earliest **fruits** are: **strawberries, cherries, gooseberries, currants**; and after them, **early apples, early pears, apricots, raspberries** <note>original: "Rasps"</note>; and after them **damsons** and most kinds of **plums, peaches**, etc. And the latest are **apples, warden pears** <note>original: "Wardens"</note>, **grapes, nuts, quinces, almonds, sloes, blackberries** <note>original: "Brier-Berries"</note>, **rosehips** <note>original: "Heps"</note>, **medlars, service-berries** <note>original: "Seruices"</note>, **Cornelian cherries**, etc.

<margin>578</margin>
It is to be noted that (commonly) **trees** that ripen latest blossom earliest: such as **peaches, Cornelian cherries, sloes, almonds**, etc. And it seems to be a work of **Providence** that they blossom so soon; for otherwise, they could not have the **sun** long enough to ripen.

The **violet** also, among **flowers**, comes twice a year—especially the **double white**; and that also...

# Natural History:

<margin>580</margin>
...is a **plant** full of **moisture**. **Roses** bloom twice, but it is not without **pruning** <note>original: "Cutting"</note>, as has been said previously.

In **Russia** <note>original: "Muscovia"</note>, although the **grain** <note>original: "Corne"</note> does not come up until late **spring**, yet their **harvest** is as early as ours. The cause is that the **fertility** <note>original: "Strength"</note> of the **ground** is kept in by the **snow**. We see among us that if it is a long winter, it is commonly a more **plentiful year**. After those kinds of winters, the **flowers** and **grain**, which normally come earlier or later, often come all at once at the same time. This frequently troubles the **farmer** <note>original: "Husbandman"</note>, for you shall have **red roses** and **damask roses** bloom together, along with the **harvest** of **wheat** and **barley**. But this happens because the **earlier** plants wait for the **later** ones, not because the **later** ones arrive sooner.

<margin>581</margin>
There are various **fruit trees** in **hot countries** which have **blossoms**, **young fruit**, and **ripe fruit** almost all year round, succeeding one another. It is said the **orange tree** does the same here for a great part of the summer, and so does the **fig tree**. No doubt, the **natural tendency** <note>original: "Naturall Motion"</note> of **plants** is to do so, but they either lack **sap** <note>original: "Iuyce"</note> to spend or they encounter the **cold** of **winter**. Therefore, this **cycle of ripening** can only happen in **moist** <note>original: "Succulent"</note> **plants** and **hot countries**.

<margin>582</margin>
Some **herbs** are only **annuals** and die, root and all, once a year—such as **borage**, **lettuce**, **cucumbers**, **muskmelons**, **basil**, **tobacco**, **mustard seed**, and all kinds of **grain**. Some continue for many years, such as **hyssop**, **germander**, **lavender**, **fennel**, etc. The cause of their dying is twofold: first is the **tenderness** and **weakness** of the **seed**, which finishes its **lifespan** <note>original: "Period"</note> in a short time, as with **borage**, **lettuce**, **cucumbers**, **grain**, etc. Therefore, none of these are **warm** <note>In the medical theory of the time, plants were classified as "hot" or "cold" based on their perceived effect on the body's humors.</note> in nature. The other cause is that some **herbs** cannot endure the cold as well, such as **basil**, **tobacco**, and **mustard seed**; and all of these have much **heat**.

<margin>
Experiments in collaboration <note>original: "in Consort"</note>, concerning the longevity <note>original: "Lasting"</note> of herbs and trees.
583
</margin>
The **longevity** of **plants** is greatest in those that have the **largest bodies**, such as **oaks**, **elms**, **chestnuts**, the **lote tree** <note>original: "Loat-Tree"; likely the European Nettle Tree</note>, etc. This holds true for **trees**, but in **herbs** it is often the opposite. For **borage**, **cabbage** <note>original: "Colewort"</note>, and **pumpkins** <note>original: "Pompions"</note>—which are **herbs** of the **largest size**—are of short **duration** <note>original: "Durance"</note>. Whereas **hyssop**, **winter savory**, **germander**, **thyme**, and **sage** will last a long time. The cause is that **trees** last according to the **strength** and **quantity** of their **sap**, being well **fortified** <note>original: "munited"</note> by their **bark** against the **harshness** <note>original: "Iniuries"</note> of the **air**. But **herbs** draw a **weak sap** and have a **soft stalk**; therefore, those among them which last longest are **herbs** with a **strong smell** and a **woody** <note>original: "Sticky"</note> **stalk**.

<margin>584</margin>
**Trees** that bear **nuts** <note>original: "Mast, and Nuts"</note> are commonly longer-lasting than those that bear **fruit**, especially the **moister fruits**. Thus **oaks**, **beeches**, **chestnuts**, **walnuts**, **almonds**, and **pine trees** last longer than **apples**, **pears**, **plums**, etc. The cause is the **richness** <note>original: "Fatnesse"</note> and **oiliness** of the **sap**, which always dissipates <note>original: "wasteth"</note> less than a more **watery** sap.

<margin>585</margin>
**Trees** that bring forth their **leaves** late in the **year** and shed them late as well are more long-lasting than those that sprout their **leaves early** or shed...

<header>Century 6.</header>

...shed them early <note>original: "betimes"</note>. The cause is that the late emergence shows a more stable <note>original: "fixed"</note> moisture, while the other is more unstable <note>original: "loose"</note> and more easily dissipated <note>original: "resolved"</note>. The same cause explains why wild trees last longer than garden trees; and within the same species, those whose fruit is acidic last longer than those whose fruit is sweet.

<margin>586</margin>
Nothing promotes the longevity <note>original: "Lasting"</note> of trees, bushes, and herbs so much as frequent pruning <note>original: "Cutting"</note>. For every pruning causes a renewal <note>original: "Renovation"</note> of the sap <note>original: "Iuyce"</note> of the plant, so that it neither travels as far nor rises as weakly as when the plant is not pruned. Consequently, annual plants—if you prune them at the right time and refrain from using them, allowing them to remain young—will last for more than one year. This has been mentioned previously regarding plants such as lettuce, purslane, cucumber, and the like. As for great trees, we see that almost all overgrown trees in churchyards or near ancient buildings are pollards <note>trees with their tops cut off to encourage a thick head of foliage</note> or dottards <note>old, decaying trees that have lost their tops or branches</note>, rather than trees at their full height.

<margin>587</margin>
An experiment should be conducted to see how by art we might make plants last longer than their natural lifespan, such as making a stalk of wheat, etc., last a whole year. You must always assume that you handle it so that the winter does not kill it, for we speak only of prolonging its natural period of life. I believe that the rule will hold: whatever makes the herb emerge later than its usual time will make it last for a longer time. It would be good to try this with a stalk of wheat, etc., set in the shade and surrounded by a wooden case (not touching the straw) to keep out the open air.

As for the preservation of fruits and plants, whether on the tree or stalk or once gathered, we shall handle that under the title of "The Conservation of Bodies."

### Experiments in Common regarding the various shapes of plants.
<margin>588</margin>
We leave the specific shapes of plants to their individual descriptions, but we will observe a few general points. Trees and herbs, in the growth of their boughs and branches, do not follow a set shape and keep no specific order. The cause is that the sap, being confined within the rind and bark, does not break forth at all (as seen in the trunks of trees and stalks of herbs) until they begin to branch. Then, when they erupt, they break out randomly wherever they find the easiest path through the bark or rind. It is true that some trees have more scattered boughs, such as willow trees <note>original: "Sallow-Trees"</note>, warden pear trees, quince trees, medlar trees, lemon trees, etc. Some are shaped more like a pyramid <note>original: "Pyramis"</note> and almost come to a point at the top, such as the pear tree (which critics claim borrows its name from the Greek word for "fire" <note>original: "πῦρ" (pyr)</note> because of its shape). Others include orange trees, fir trees, service trees, lime trees, etc. And some are more spread and broad, such as beeches, hornbeams, etc. The rest are more varied <note>original: "indifferent"</note>. The cause of the scattering of boughs is the rapid eruption of the sap; therefore, those trees do not rise with a trunk of any great height but branch near the ground. The cause of the pyramid shape is the containment of the sap for a long time before it branches, and then the gradual spending of it once it begins to branch. The...

# Natural History:

...spreading is caused by the carrying up of the sap, plentifully, without waste <note>original: "Expence"</note>; and then putting it forth speedily, and all at once.

<margin>589</margin>
There are various herbs, but no trees, that may be said to have a kind of "order" in how they put forth their leaves. For they have joints or knuckles, which act as stops in their germination; such as gillyflowers <note>original: "Gilly-Flowers"; a member of the carnation family</note>, pinks, fennel, grain <note>original: "Corne"</note>, reeds, and canes. The cause of this is that the sap rises unequally and, as it were, tires and stops along the way. It also seems they have some density <note>original: "Closenesse"</note> and hardness in their stalks, which hinders the sap from rising until it has gathered into a knot, and is then forced to push outward. Therefore, most of them are hollow when the stalk is dry, such as fennel stalks, stubble, and canes.

<margin>590</margin>
Flowers all have exquisite shapes <note>original: "Figures"</note>. The number of petals <note>original: "Flower-Numbers"</note> are chiefly five and four. For example, primroses, briar roses, single musk roses, single pinks, and gillyflowers have five petals <note>original: "Leaues"</note>. Lilies, fleurs-de-lis <note>original: "Flower-de-Luces"</note>, borage, bugloss, etc., have four petals. But some put forth petals that are not specifically numbered, though these are always small, such as marigolds and trefoil <note>original: "Trifoile"</note>. We also see that the sockets and supports of flowers have specific shapes, such as the "five brethren of the rose" <note>a traditional name for the five sepals at the base of a rose bud</note> and the sockets of gillyflowers. Leaves also have specific shapes: some are round, some are long, but none are square. Many are jagged on the sides, though the petals of flowers seldom are. I consider the jagged edges of pinks and gillyflowers to be like the unevenness of oak or vine leaves; they rarely have small decorative fringes <note>original: "Purles"</note>.

<margin>Experiments in Progress regarding some Principal Differences in Plants. 591</margin>
Of plants, some few put forth their blossoms before their leaves, such as almonds, peaches, Cornelian cherries <note>original: "Cornelians"</note>, and blackthorn. But most put forth some leaves before their blossoms, such as apples, pears, plums, cherries, and whitethorn. The cause is that those that blossom first have either a sharp essence <note>original: "Acute and Sharpe Spirit"</note> (and therefore they usually emerge early in the spring but ripen very late, like most of the examples mentioned before), or else an oily juice, which is more prone to produce flowers than leaves.

<margin>592</margin>
Of plants, some are green all winter, while others shed their leaves. Those that remain green all winter include holly, ivy, box, fir, yew <note>original: "Eugh"</note>, cypress, juniper, bays <note>laurel</note>, and rosemary. The cause of them staying green is the dense and compact substance of their leaves and their stalks <note>original: "Pedicles"</note>. The cause of that density is either the tough and sticky <note>original: "Viscous"</note> juice of the plant, or its inherent strength and heat. Of the first sort is holly, which has such a sticky juice that they make bird-lime <note>a sticky substance used for trapping birds</note> from its bark. The stalk of ivy is tough and not brittle <note>original: "Fragile"</note>, as we see in other small dry twigs. Fir yields pitch. Box is a dense <note>original: "fast"</note> and heavy wood, as we see when it is used for lawn bowls. Yew is a strong and tough wood, as we see in bows. Of the second sort is juniper, which is a fragrant <note>original: "Odorate"</note> wood and makes a hot fire. Bays are likewise a hot and aromatic wood, and so is rosemary for a shrub. As for the leaves, their density is apparent because they are smooth and...

<header>Century VI.</header>

...and shining, as in **laurel** <note>original: "Bayes"</note>, **holly**, **boxwood**, etc. Or in that they are hard and pointed like a spire, as in the others. And an **experiment** <note>original: "Tryall"</note> should be made of **grafting** **rosemary**, **laurel**, and **boxwood** upon a **holly tree trunk** <note>original: "Holly-Stocke"</note>, because they are all **plants** that thrive throughout the **winter**. It would be beneficial to try this also with **grafts** of other **trees**, either **fruit trees** or **wild trees**, to see whether they might yield their **fruit** or bear their **leaves** later and longer into the **winter**, because the **sap** of the **holly** flows most actively in the **winter**. It is possible that a **mezereon tree** <note>original: "Mezerion-Tree"; a species of flowering shrub</note> grafted upon a **holly** will turn out to be both an **earlier** blooming and a **larger tree**.

<margin>593</margin> There are some **plants** that bear no **flowers** and yet bear **fruit**; there are some that bear **flowers** and no **fruit**. There are some that bear neither **flowers** nor **fruit**. Most of the great **timber trees** (such as **oaks**, **beeches**, etc.) bear no visible **flowers**. A few of the **fruit trees** (likewise), such as the **mulberry**, **walnut**, etc., and some **shrubs** (such as **juniper**, **holly**, etc.), bear no **flowers**. Various **herbs** also bear **seeds** (which serve as the **fruit**) and yet bear no **flowers**, such as **purslane** <note>original: "Purflane"</note>, etc. Those that bear **flowers** but no **fruit** are few, such as the **double cherry**, the **willow** <note>original: "Sallow"</note>, etc. But regarding the **cherry**, it is uncertain whether this is not caused by **human skill** <note>original: "Art"</note> or **cultivation**. For if it is done by **art**, then an **experiment** should be made to see whether the **blossoms** of **apples** and other **fruits** may also be doubled. There are a few that bear neither **fruit** nor **flower**, such as the **elm**, **poplars**, **boxwood**, **ferns** <note>original: "Brakes"</note>, etc.

<margin>594</margin> There are some **plants** that always shoot upwards and can support themselves, as do the majority of **trees** and **plants**. There are others that **creep** along the **ground** or **wind** around other **trees** or **supports** <note>original: "Props"</note> and cannot support themselves, such as **vines**, **ivy**, **briars**, **bryony**, **honeysuckle** <note>original: "woodbines"</note>, **hops**, **clematis** <note>original: "Climatis"</note>, **chamomile**, etc. The cause (as has been partly mentioned) is that all **plants** naturally move upwards. However, if the **sap** rises too quickly, it creates a slender **stalk** that cannot support the weight. Therefore, these latter types are all **fast** and **quick growers** <note>original: "Hasty Commers"</note>.

<margin>Experiments in grouping regarding all manners of composts and helps for the ground. 595</margin> The first and most common help for soil is **fertilizing with manure** <note>original: "Stercoration"</note>. **Sheep's dung** is one of the best, followed by the **dung** of **cattle** <note>original: "Kine"</note>, and thirdly, that of **horses** (which is considered to be somewhat too "hot" or potent unless it is mixed). The dung of **pigeons** is excellent for a **garden** or a small **amount** of **ground**. The **method of using** <note>original: "Ordering"</note> **manure** is: if the **ground** is **plowed for crops** <note>original: "Arable"</note>, spread it immediately before **plowing** and **sowing**, and then **plow** it in. For if you spread it long before, the **sun** will draw out much of the **richness** <note>original: "Fatnesse"</note> of the **manure**. If the **ground** is **pasture** <note>original: "Grazing Ground"</note>, spread it somewhat late, toward **winter**, so that the **sun** may have less **power** to dry it up. As for special **composts** for **gardens** (such as a **hotbed**, etc.), we have discussed them previously.

<margin>596</margin> The **second kind of compost** is the **spreading** of various **kinds of soils** <note>original: "Earths"</note>, such as **marl** <note>a lime-rich mud or mudstone used as fertilizer</note>, **chalk**, **sea-sand**, **soil** upon **soil**, **pond-soil**, and **mixtures** of these. **Marl** is thought to be the best, as it has the most **richness** <note>original: "Fatnesse"</note>.

# Natural History:

<margin>595</margin> And not heating the **ground** too much. The next is **sea-sand**, which (no doubt) obtains a special virtue from the **salt**; for **salt** is the first element <note>original: "rudiment"</note> of life. **Chalk** overheats the **ground** a little. Therefore, it is best used upon **cold clay grounds** or **moist grounds**. However, I heard a great **farmer** <note>original: "Husband"; referring to a practitioner of husbandry or agriculture</note> say that it was a common error to think that **chalk** helps **arable grounds** <note>land suitable for plowing and crops</note> but does not help **grazing grounds**. In fact, it helps **grass** as well as **corn** <note>general term for grain</note>. The reason for this error is that after **chalking** the **ground**, people wear it out with many **crops** without giving it any rest; and then, afterward, it will indeed bear little **grass** because the **ground** is tired out.

<margin>596</margin> It would be good to try laying **chalk** upon **arable grounds** a little while before **plowing**, and then to **plow** it in, just as they do with **manure** <note>original: "Dung"</note>. But it must first be made crumbly <note>original: "Friable"</note> by rain or by lying out. As for **earth**, it **fertilizes** <note>original: "Compaſſeth"</note> itself. For I knew of a **great garden** that had a field (in a manner of speaking) poured upon it, and it bore **fruit** excellently in the first year of planting; for the **surface** of the **earth** is always the most fruitful. **Earth** prepared in this way has a double **surface**. But it is true, as I understand it, that **earth** which has **saltpeter** <note>original: "Salt-Petre"; potassium nitrate, used historically as a powerful fertilizer</note> bred in it excels all others, if you can procure it without too much expense. The way to hasten the **breeding of saltpeter** is to block the sun and the growth of **vegetables**. Therefore, if you build a large, thatched **shed** <note>original: "Houell"</note> over a **quantity** of ground—or even if you just cover the ground with planks—it will breed **saltpeter**. As for **pond earth** or **river earth**, it is a very good **compost**, especially if the **pond** has gone a long time without being cleaned, so that the water is not too **lacking in nutrients** <note>original: "Hungry"</note>. I judge it will be even better if there is some **mixture of chalk**.

<margin>597</margin> The third **help of ground** is by using other **substances** that have the power to make **ground fertile**, even though they are not strictly **earth**. In this, **ashes excel**. To such an extent, the countries around **Mount Etna** and **Mount Vesuvius** receive a kind of compensation <note>original: "Amends"</note> for the mischief the eruptions often do by the exceeding **fruitfulness** of the soil caused by the **ashes** scattered about. **Soot** also, though spread thinly in a field or **garden**, is proven to be a very good **compost**. As for **salt**, it is too costly. However, it has been tested that when mixed with **seed-corn** and sown together, it does good. I am also of the opinion that **chalk** in powder form, mixed with **seed-corn**, would do good—perhaps as much as **chalking** the **ground** all over. As for the **steeping of seeds** in several **mixtures** with **water** to give them vigor, or **watering grounds** with **compost-water**, we have spoken of those before.

<margin>598</margin> The fourth **help of ground** is the **allowing of vegetables to die into the ground** and so fatten it. For example, the **stubble of corn**, and especially **pea stalks** <note>original: "Peaſe-Brakes"</note> cast upon the **ground** at the beginning of **winter**, will make it very fruitful. It would also be good to try whether **leaves of trees**, swept together and mixed with some **chalk** and **manure** to give them more **richness** <note>original: "Heart"</note>, would not make a good **compost**. Currently, nothing is wasted so much as **leaves of trees**; when they lie scattered and without being mixed, they tend to make the **ground sour** <note>acidic or unproductive</note> rather than helping it.

# Natural History:
### Century VI.

<margin>599</margin>
The fifth **help for the soil** is **heat and warmth**. Since ancient times, it has been a practice to burn **heath**, **heather** <note>original: "Ling"</note>, and **sedge** on the ground, taking advantage of the **wind**. We see that the **warmth** provided by **walls** and **enclosures** improves the ground. We also see that **sloping toward the south** <note>original: "Lying open to the South"</note> improves the ground. We see again that the **folding of sheep** <note>the practice of confining sheep in portable pens to fertilize and warm a specific area</note> helps the ground through both their **warmth** and their **manure** <note>original: "Compost"</note>. It is also possible that the **covering of the ground with ferns** <note>original: "Brakes"</note> at the beginning of the **winter** (which we mentioned in the last **experiment**) helps the soil because of the **warmth** it provides. Indeed, some very skilled **farmers** <note>original: "Husbands"</note> suspect that **gathering up flints** in **flinty ground** and piling them in **heaps** (which is a common practice) is poor **farming** <note>original: "Husbandry"</note>, because the stones help to keep the **ground warm**.

<margin>600</margin>
The sixth **help for the soil** is through **watering** and **irrigation**, which is done in two ways. The first is by **letting in** and **shutting out water** at the right times. Water at certain seasons, if left too long, does harm; but at other seasons, if left for a reasonable time, it does good. This method serves only for **meadows** located along a **river**. The other way is to bring **water** from **sloping grounds** <note>original: "Hanging Grounds"</note> where there are **springs** down into the **lower grounds**, carrying it through long **furrows**, and from those **furrows**, drawing it across the land to spread the **water**. This creates an excellent **improvement** for both **grain** <note>original: "Corne"</note> and **grass**. It is even more effective if those **sloping grounds** are fertile, because the water washes off some of the **richness** <note>original: "Fatnesse"</note> of the earth. Regardless, it is very profitable. Generally, where there are great **floods** in **fens** <note>low-lying, marshy land</note> or similar areas, drowning them in the **winter** makes the following **summer** more fruitful. The **reason** for this may be that it keeps the **ground warm** and nourishes it. However, the **fen-men** <note>people who lived in and managed the marshlands</note> maintain that the **drainage channels** <note>original: "Sewers"</note> must be managed so that the **water** does not stay too long in the **spring** until the **weeds** and **sedge** have grown up. For then the ground will be like a **forest**, which blocks out the **sun** and keeps the ground **wet**. Because of this, it will never be suitable for **grazing** that year. So much for **irrigation**. As for the **removal** and **drainage of water** where there is too much, and the **methods of helping** the ground in that regard, we shall discuss them in another place.

# Natural History
## Century V.

<margin>447</margin>
The fifth help for the soil <note>original: "Ground"</note> is **heat** and manure <note>original: "Manure," here referring broadly to any substance used to enrich the soil</note>. It has been a common practice to burn heath, heather <note>original: "Ling"</note>, and sedge along with the top layer of turf. Then, upon the earth that has been burnt—using the ashes and the soil itself—wheat and other grains are sown. This improves the ground for a few years. The reason is that it turns the plants into ashes, which helps the soil through both the salt and the organic remains <note>original: "Chaff"</note>. It is also debated whether the burning <note>original: "censing"</note> of the plants at the beginning of winter (instead of summer) helps the ground by providing warmth. In some very skilled farming practices <note>original: "husbandries"</note>, they suspect that leaving the top layer of the ground bare and exposed to the sun is poor farming <note>original: "Husbandry"</note>, because they prefer to keep the ground warm.

<margin>448</margin>
The sixth help for the soil is through stirring and turning it over <note>original: "inversion"</note>, which is done in two ways: one by tilling and sowing in furrows, and the other by digging. Digging the ground with a spade loosens it more than tilling with a plow. Digging is better for herbs that have long and deep roots because the plow does not go deep enough; furthermore, it is more gentle on the earth. While the plow tears the soil, the spade breaks it more gently.

<margin>449</margin>
The seventh help for the soil is by letting in water, and this creates an excellent **improvement** for both **grass** and **grain** <note>original: "Corn"</note>. For sloping ground <note>original: "Water-Hanging Ground"</note>, this is fruitful because it washes away the "hunger" or barrenness of the earth <note>original: "Famine of the Earth"</note>. However, it is very profitable regardless, especially where there are great overflows in the wintertime, by drawing the water into the furrows following the slope of the land. The reason may be that it prevents the ground from becoming mossy. Regarding the "water-thistle" <note>likely referring to land damaged by standing water</note>, if the water stays too long in any place, it will rot the **grass**; any plants that do grow will have leaves like a water-weed, which will persist in that **pasture**. Such land will never produce good **grass** for its intended purpose that year. This is even more true for summer-watering; but in winter-watering, where there is too much water, the top layer of the ground at that depth will likely perish.

<margin>450</margin>
The eighth help for the soil is the "housing" of it, such as by sheltering the earth or covering it with boards or similar materials. This keeps off the sun and the cold air, whereas if the earth is left open to the weather, it will be <unclear>...</unclear>

# NATURAL HISTORY.

## Seventh Century.

<margin>
Collective experiments regarding the differences between plants and inanimate bodies. 601
</margin>

<image-desc>A decorative square initial 'T' with ornate floral and foliage patterns, featuring small human figures integrated into the design.</image-desc>

The differences between *animate* <note>living</note> and *inanimate* <note>non-living</note> bodies, we shall handle fully under the title of *Life*, *Living Spirits*, and *Powers*. We shall, therefore, make only a brief mention of them in this place. The main *differences* are two. All *bodies* have *spirits* and *pneumatic* <term>pneumatic: relating to air, gas, or wind; in Bacon's science, these are the subtle, invisible substances within all matter</term> *parts* within them. But the main *differences* between *animate* and *inanimate* are these: The first is that the *spirits* of *animate things* are all connected to themselves <note>original: "Continued with themselves"</note> and are *branched in veins* and secret *channels* <note>original: "Canales"</note>, just as *blood* is. And in *living creatures*, the *spirits* have not only *branches*, but certain *cells* or *seats* where the principal *spirits* reside and where the rest gather <note>original: "resort"</note>. But the *spirits* in *inanimate* things are shut in and cut off by the *tangible parts*, and they are not accessible <note>original: "pervious"</note> to one another, just as *air* is trapped within *snow*. 

The second main *difference* is that the *spirits* of *animate bodies* are all, to some degree (more or less), kindled and inflamed; they possess a fine *mixture* <note>original: "Commixture"</note> of *flame* and an *aerial substance*. But *inanimate bodies* have their *spirits* not at all *inflamed* or *kindled*. And this *difference* does not consist in the *heat* or *coolness* of *spirits*; for *cloves* and other *spices*, *naphtha*, and *petroleum* have exceedingly *hot spirits* (much hotter than *oil*, *wax*, or *tallow*, etc.), but they are not *inflamed*. And when any of those weak and temperate *bodies* come

# Natural History:

...to be inflamed <note>caught fire or energized</note>, they then gather a much greater *heat* than others have when *un-inflamed*; besides their *light*, and *motion*, etc.

<margin>602</margin>
The *differences* which are *secondary* and proceed from these two *radical* <term>radical: fundamental or root-level</term> *differences* are: First, *plants* are all *figurate* and *determinate* <term>figurate and determinate: having a specific, set shape and size</term>, which *inanimate* <note>non-living</note> *bodies* are not. For however far the *spirit* is able to *spread* and *continue* itself, so far goes the *shape* or *figure*, and then it is *determined* <note>fixed or ended</note>. Secondly, *plants* nourish themselves; *inanimate bodies* do not. They have an *accretion* <term>accretion: growth by external addition, like a snowball</term>, but no *alimentation* <term>alimentation: the internal processing of nutrients to grow</term>. Thirdly, *plants* have a *period of life* <note>a lifespan</note>, which *inanimate bodies* do not. Fourthly, they have a *succession* and *propagation* of their *kind* <note>reproduction</note>, which is not found in *inanimate bodies*.

<margin>603</margin>
The *differences* between *plants* and *metals* or *fossils* <note>at this time, "fossil" referred to anything dug out of the earth</note>, besides those four mentioned before (for I consider *metals* to be *inanimate*), are these: First, *metals* are more *durable* than *plants*. Secondly, they are more *solid* and *hard*. Thirdly, they are wholly *subterranean* <note>original: "Subterrany"</note>, whereas *plants* are part above the *earth* and part under the *earth*.

<margin>604</margin>
There are very few *creatures* that share the *nature* of both *plants* and *metals*. *Coral* is one of the *nearest* to both *kinds*. Another is *vitriol* <note>a metal sulfate, usually iron or copper, which can form crystal structures</note>, for that is most likely to sprout when exposed to *moisture*.

<margin>605</margin>
Another special *affinity* <note>similarity</note> is between *plants* and *mold* or *putrefaction* <note>decay</note>. For all *putrefaction* (if it does not dissolve through *arefaction* <term>arefaction: the process of drying out completely</term>) will in the end result in *plants* or *living creatures* bred from *putrefaction*. I consider *moss*, *mushrooms*, *agaric* <note>a type of fungus used in medicine</note>, and others of those kinds to be merely the *molds* of the *ground*, *walls*, *trees*, and the like. As for *flesh*, *fish*, and *plants* themselves, and a number of other things, after a period of *moldiness*, *rottenness*, or *corrupting*, they will begin to breed *worms*. These *putrefactions* which have an *affinity* with *plants* have this *difference* from them: they have no *succession* or *propagation* <note>they do not reproduce themselves</note>, though they *nourish* themselves, have a *period of life*, and also have some *figure* <note>shape</note>.

<margin>606</margin>
By chance, I once left a *citron* <note>a large citrus fruit</note> cut open in a closed room for three summer months while I was away. Upon my return, there had grown out of the cut pith *tufts of hair* an inch long, with little black heads, as if they were intended to be some kind of *herb*.

<margin>
Collective experiments regarding the affinities and differences between plants and living creatures; and the intermediate forms that share characteristics of both. 607
</margin>
The *affinities* and *differences* between *plants* and *living creatures* are as follows. They both have *spirits* that are *continuous* <note>unbroken or connected throughout the body</note>, *branched*, and also *inflamed* <note>active or "on fire" with life</note>. But first, in *living creatures*, the *spirits* have a *cell* or *seat* <note>a central location like a brain or heart</note> which *plants* do not have, as was said before. Secondly, the *spirits of living creatures* are more like *flame* than the *spirits of plants* are. And these two are the *radical differences*. As for the *secondary differences*, they are as follows. First, *plants* are all *fixed* to the *earth*, whereas all *living creatures* are separate and independent. Secondly, *living creatures* have *local motion* <note>the ability to move from place to place</note>; *plants* do not. Thirdly, *living creatures* take nourishment from their *upper parts*, chiefly by the *mouth*; *plants* take nourishment from below, namely from the *roots*. Fourthly, *plants* have their *seed* and *seminal parts* at the top; *living creatures* have...

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon's comparison between plants and animals (which he calls "living creatures"). He is concluding a list of eight primary differences begun on the previous page.</meta>

...have them lowest. And therefore it was said, not only elegantly but philosophically: *Man is an inverted plant* <note>original Latin: *Homo est Planta inuerfa*</note>; for the *root* in *plants* is like the *head* in *living creatures* <note>Bacon suggests the root is the "head" because it is the primary organ for taking in nourishment</note>. Fifthly, *living creatures* have a more precise *form* than *plants*. Sixthly, *living creatures* have a greater *diversity* of *organs* within their *bodies*, and (so to speak) *internal forms*, than *plants* have. Seventhly, *living creatures* have *senses*, which *plants* do not. Eighthly, *living creatures* have *voluntary motion*, which *plants* do not.

<margin>608</margin>
Regarding the *difference* of *sexes* in *plants*, they are often distinguished by name, such as *male peony* and *female peony*; *male rosemary* and *female rosemary*; *he-holly* and *she-holly*, etc. But *reproduction* <note>original: "generation"</note> by *sexual intercourse* <note>original: "copulation"</note> certainly does not extend to *plants*. The nearest approach to it is between the *male palm* and the *female palm* <note>the Date Palm</note>; which (as they report), if they grow nearby, incline toward one another. In fact (what is even stranger), they do not hesitate to report that to keep the *trees* upright from bending, they tie *ropes* or *lines* from one to the other, so that the *contact* might be enjoyed through the *contact* of an *intermediary body* <note>original: "middle body"</note>. But this may be fabricated, or at least exaggerated. Nevertheless, I am inclined enough to think that this same *pairing* <note>original Latin: *Binarium*</note> of a stronger and a weaker, similar to *masculine* and *feminine*, holds in all *living bodies*. It is sometimes confused, as in some *creatures* born of *decay* <note>original: "putrifaction"; refers to the obsolete theory of spontaneous generation where insects were thought to arise from rotting matter</note>, in which no *marks* of *distinction* appear. And it is sometimes doubled, as in *hermaphrodites*; but generally, there is a *degree* of *strength* <note>meaning sexual differentiation</note> in most *species*.

<margin>609</margin>
The *intermediaries* <note>original: "Participles or Confiners"; organisms that seem to belong to two categories at once</note> between *plants* and *living creatures* are chiefly those that are *fixed* and have no *local motion* to *move* from place to place, though they have *motion* in their *parts*. These include *oysters*, *cockles*, and the like. There is a fabulous story that in the *northern countries* there is an *herb* that grows in the likeness of a *lamb* <note>the "Vegetable Lamb of Tartary," a legendary plant-animal once believed to grow sheep as fruit</note>, and feeds upon the *grass* in such a way that it will bare the *grass* all around it. But I suppose that the *shape* creates the *fable*; for as we see, there are *bee flowers* <note>orchids that look like bees</note>, etc. As for the *grass*, it seems the *plant*, having a large *stalk* and *top*, preys upon the *grass* for a good distance around by drawing the *juice* of the *earth* from it.

The *Indian fig* <note>the Banyan tree, *Ficus benghalensis*</note> bows its *roots* down so low in one year that it takes *root* again by itself. Thus it multiplies from *root* to *root*, making a kind of *wood* <note>a grove or thicket</note> out of one *tree*. The *cause* is the *abundance* of the *sap* and the *softness* of the *stalk*, which makes the *bough*—being overloaded and not stiffly upheld—weigh down. It has *leaves* as broad as a little *shield* <note>original: "target"</note>, but the *fruit* is no bigger than *beans*. The *cause* is that the continual *shade* increases the *leaves* and diminishes the *fruit*, which nevertheless has a pleasant *taste*. That (no doubt) is caused by the *suppleness* and *mildness* of the *juice* of that *plant*, which is also what makes the *boughs* so *flexible*.

# Natural History:

[A] tree having few but very large *leaves*, three cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> long and two broad; and that the *fruit*, being of good taste, grows out of the *bark*. It may be that there are *plants* that pour out the *sap* so fast that they have no time either to divide into many *leaves* or to put forth *stalks* for the *fruit*. Among us, *trees* (generally) have small *leaves* by comparison. The *fig* has the largest; and next are the *vine*, *mulberry*, and *sycamore*; and the smallest are those of the *willow*, *birch*, and *thorn*. But there are *herbs* found with far larger *leaves* than any *tree*, such as the *burdock* <note>original: "Burre"</note>, *gourd*, *cucumber*, and *cabbage* <note>original: "Cole-wort"</note>. The cause is (similar to that of the *Indian fig* <note>Bacon likely refers here to the banana plant, which was often called the "Indian Fig" in early botanical texts.</note>) the hasty and plentiful putting forth of the *sap*.

<margin>612</margin>
There are three things in use for *sweetness*: *sugar*, *honey*, and *manna* <note>A sweet secretion from certain plants, like the manna ash tree.</note>. As for *sugar*, it was scarcely known and little used by the *ancients*. It is found in *canes*. Inquiry <note>original Latin: "Quare"</note>: whether it is found only up to the first *knuckle* or further up? And whether the very bark of the *cane* itself yields *sugar* or not? As for *honey*, the *bee* makes it or gathers it; but I have heard from one who was industrious in husbandry that the labor of the *bee* is concerned with the *wax*, and that he has known *honeycombs* to be empty of *honey* in the beginning of *May*, and within a fortnight—when the *sweet dews* fall—they are filled like a *cellar*. It is also reported by some of the *ancients* that there is a *tree* called *Occhus* in the valleys of *Hyrcania* <note>A region southeast of the Caspian Sea.</note> that distills *honey* in the mornings. It is not unlikely that the *sap* and "tears" <note>Exudations or resins.</note> of some *trees* may be sweet. It may also be that some sweet *juices*, fit for many uses, may be prepared <note>original: "concocted"</note> out of *fruits* to the thickness of *honey* or perhaps *sugar*. The most likely sources are *sun-dried raisins* <note>original: "Raisins of the Sunne"</note>, *figs*, and *currants* <note>original: "Corrans"</note>. The *methods* for this may be investigated.

<margin>613</margin>
The *ancients* report a *tree* by the *Persian Sea* <note>The Persian Gulf.</note>, upon the *shore sands*, which is nourished by *saltwater*; and when the *tide* ebbs, you shall see the *roots* appearing bare without *bark* (being, as it seems, corroded by the *salt*) and grasping the *sands* like a *crab*, yet it nevertheless bears *fruit*. It would be good to try growing some *hardy trees*, such as a *service-tree* or *fir-tree*, by planting them within the *sands*.

<margin>614</margin>
There are *plants* which they use for *garments*, including the following: *hemp*, *flax*, *cotton*, *nettles* (from which they make *nettle-cloth*), and *silk-cotton* <note>original Latin: "Sericum," meaning silk; here referring to "growing silk" or plant fibers resembling it.</note>. They also make *cables* from the *bark* of *lime trees*. It is usually the *stalk* that produces the *fibrous matter* <note>original: "Filaceous Matter"</note>, though sometimes it is the *down* that grows on top.

<margin>615</margin>
In some *countries*, they have a *plant* of a *rosy color* which shuts at *night*, opens in the *morning*, and opens wide at *noon*; the *inhabitants* of those *countries* say it is a *plant* that *sleeps*. There are *sleepers* enough, then; for almost all *flowers* do the like.

<margin>616</margin>
There are some *plants*, though rare, that have a *mossy* or *downy root*, and likewise some that have a number of *threads* like *beards*. One example is *mandrakes*, from which *witches* and *impostors* make an ugly *image*, giving it the form of a *face* at the *top* of the *root* and leaving those *strings* to form a broad *beard* down to the *foot*. Also, there is a *kind* of *nard* in *Crete* (being a *type* of *valerian* <note>original: "Phu"</note>) that has a hairy *root* like a *rough-footed dove's foot*.
