<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon's observations on the nature of plants, specifically discussing the classification of roots based on how sap moves within them, as well as the unique properties and cultivation methods of various trees and vines.</meta>

...foot. As you can see, there are *roots*, *bulbous roots*, *fibrous roots*, and *hirsute roots* <note>original: "Hirsute"; meaning hairy or shaggy</note>. In *bulbous roots*, I believe the sap moves most quickly toward the air and sun. In *fibrous roots*, the sap delights more in the earth and therefore grows downward. The *hirsute* root is a middle ground between both; besides growing upwards and downwards, it also grows outward in a circle.

<margin>617</margin>
There are some *tears* <note>In botany, 'tears' refer to drops of sap or resin that harden on the bark.</note> of *trees* which are combed from the *beards* of *goats*. When the *goats* bite and crop the trees, especially in the mornings when the dew is present, the *tear* comes out and hangs upon their *beards*. A certain kind of *ladanum* <note>Now known as labdanum, a sticky resin obtained from rockrose shrubs.</note> is of this sort.

<margin>618</margin>
The *irrigation* of the *plane tree* with *wine* is reported by the *ancients* to make it fruitful. This should also be tested with *roots*, for it has no great effect upon *seeds*.

<margin>619</margin>
The way to transport *foreign roots* over a long distance is to seal them closely in *earthen vessels*. However, if the *vessels* are not very large, you must make some holes in the bottom to give some refreshment <note>Likely referring to air circulation or drainage to prevent rot.</note> to the *roots*. Otherwise, it seems they will decay and suffocate.

<margin>620</margin>
Ancient *cinnamon* was the driest of all other *plants* while it grew. Those things known to nourish other *plants* made cinnamon more sterile; it prospered worst during *showers*. It also grew among *bushes* of other kinds, where *plants* usually do not thrive, and it did not like the sun. There might be one single *cause* for all those *effects*: namely, the meager nourishment that the *plant* required. Inquiry <note>original Latin: "Quære"</note> how far *cassia*, which is now the substitute for *cinnamon*, shares these traits.

<margin>621</margin>
It is reported by one of the *ancients* that when *cassia* is gathered, it is put into the *skins* of *beasts* that have been newly flayed. As the *skin* decays and breeds *worms*, the *worms* devour its *pith* and center <note>original: "marrow"</note>, making it hollow. However, they do not touch the *bark* because it is bitter to them.

<margin>622</margin>
In ancient times, there were *vines* with much larger *bodies* than any we know today; *cups* and even a *statue* <note>original: "Image"</note> of *Jupiter* were made from them. But it is likely they were *wild vines*. The *vines* used for *wine* are pruned so often, and so much digging and dressing is done, that their sap is spent on the *grapes*, and so the *stalk* <note>The main trunk or stem of the vine.</note> cannot increase much in *bulk*. The *wood* of *vines* is very durable and does not *rot*. Strange as it is, although no *tree* has *twigs* as brittle as the vine's while they are green, the dried *wood* is extremely *tough*. It was used by the *captains* of *armies* among the *Romans* for their *cudgels* <note>The 'vitis' was a vine-wood staff carried by Roman centurions as a mark of authority and used for discipline.</note>.

<margin>623</margin>
It is reported that in some places, *vines* are allowed to grow like *herbs*, spreading along the *ground*, and that the *grapes* of those *vines* are very large. It would be good to test whether *plants* usually supported by props will put forth larger *leaves* and larger *fruits* if they are laid along the *ground*, such as *hops*, *ivy*, *woodbine* <note>Honeysuckle</note>, etc.

<margin>624</margin>
If you wish to keep *quinces* or *apples*, etc., for a long time, drown them in *honey*. However, because *honey* might give them a taste that is over- <note>The text continues on the next page with "luscious" or "sweet."</note>

# Natural History:

...luscious, it would be good to experiment with **powdered sugar**; or in **syrup of wine**, boiled down until it is thick. Both of these should likewise be tested with **oranges**, **lemons**, and **pomegranates**; for the **powdered sugar** and **syrup of wine** can be used more than once.

<margin>625</margin>
The **preservation** of **fruit** should also be tested in **vessels** filled with fine **sand**, or with **powdered chalk**; or in **meal** and **flour**; or in the **dust of oak wood**; or in **moss**.

<margin>626</margin>
For such **fruits** as you intend for **long-term keeping**, you must gather them before they are fully **ripe**. Do this on a **fair** and **dry day**, towards **noon**, when the wind is not blowing from the **south**, and when the **moon** is below the **earth** and is **waning**. <note>In the 17th century, it was widely believed that the phases and position of the moon significantly influenced the sap and longevity of harvested plants.</note>

<margin>627</margin>
Take **grapes** and hang them in an **empty vessel** that is well **sealed**; place the **vessel** not in a **cellar**, but in some dry **place**. It is said they will last a long time. However, it is reported by some that they will keep better in a **vessel** half-filled with **wine**, provided the **grapes** do not touch the **wine**.

<margin>628</margin>
It is reported that **preserving** the **stalk** helps to preserve the **grape**, especially if the **stalk** is placed into the **pith** of an **elder** tree, as long as the **elder** does not touch the **fruit**.

<margin>629</margin>
It is reported by some of the **ancients** that **fruit** placed in **bottles**, and the **bottles** lowered into **wells** under **water**, will keep for a long time.

<margin>630</margin>
Of **herbs** and **plants**, some are good to eat **raw**, such as **lettuce**, **endive**, **purslane**, **tarragon**, **cresses**, **cucumbers**, **muskmelons**, **radishes**, and so on. Others are edible only after they have been **boiled** or have **passed through the fire**, such as **parsley**, **clary**, **sage**, **parsnips**, **turnips**, **asparagus**, and **artichokes** (though these are also eaten **raw** when young). But a number of **herbs** are not **edible** <note>original: "Esculent"</note> at all, such as **wormwood**, **grass**, **green corn**, **centaury**, **hyssop**, **lavender**, **balm**, etc. 

The **reasons** for this are that the **herbs** which are not **edible** lack the two **tastes** in which **nourishment** resides, which are **fat** and **sweet**. Instead, they have **bitter** and **over-strong tastes**, or a **juice** so **crude** <note>meaning raw, unprocessed, or chemically "unripe"</note> that it cannot be ripened to the point of providing **nourishment**. **Herbs** and **plants** that are **edible raw** possess **fatness** or **sweetness** (as do all **edible fruits**), such as **onions**, **lettuce**, etc. But it must be a type of **fatness** that is not **too heavy** and **burdening to the stomach** (for as for **sweet things**, they are essentially always **edible**). 

For example, **parsnips** and **leeks** have **fatness**, but it is too **heavy** and **dense** without **boiling**. The plant must also be somewhat **tender** in **substance**. We see that **wheat**, **barley**, and **artichokes** provide no good **nourishment** until they have **passed through the fire**; the **fire** ripens them and makes them soft and tender, and so they become **edible**. As for **radishes**, **tarragon**, and the like, they are for **condiments** and not for **nourishment**. Even some of those **herbs** which are not **edible** are nonetheless **drinkable** <note>original: "Poculent"</note>, such as **hops**, **broom**, etc. Investigate <note>original: "Quære"</note> what **herbs** are good for **drink** besides the two named above; for it may perhaps reduce the **cost** of **brewing** if they can make **beer** that requires less **malt** or make it last longer.

<margin>631</margin>
The **parts** of **plants** fit for the **nourishment** of **man** are **seeds**, **roots**, and **fruits**, but chiefly **seeds** and **roots**. As for **leaves**, they provide no **nourishment**—

nourishment <note>The text begins mid-word; the previous page ended with "nourish-".</note> at all, or very little. Neither do **flowers**, **blossoms**, or **stalks**. The reason is that **roots**, **seeds**, and **fruits** (inasmuch as all **plants** consist of an **oily** and **watery substance** mixed together) have more of the **oily substance**, while **leaves**, **flowers**, etc., have more of the **watery** substance. Secondly, they are more **ripened** <note>original: "concocted"; in early science, "concoction" referred to the process of ripening or maturing through natural heat.</note>. For the **root**, which remains always in the **earth**, is continuously **ripened** by the **earth**; and **fruits** and **grains** (as we see) take half a year or more to **ripen**, whereas **leaves** emerge and are **fully formed** in a **month**.

<margin>632</margin>
**Plants** (for the most part) have a stronger **taste** and **smell** in the **seed** than in the **leaf** or **root**. The cause is that in **plants** which do not have a **fierce and eager spirit** <note>original: "spirit"; referring here to the volatile oils or essential characteristics of the plant.</note>, their potency is increased by **ripening** and **maturation**, which is always greatest in the **seed**. But in **plants** that have a **fierce and eager spirit**, they are stronger while the **spirit** is enclosed in the **root**; the **spirits** only weaken and scatter when they come into contact with the **air** and **sun**, as we see in **onions**, **garlic**, **dragon-plant**, etc. In fact, there are **plants** that have very **hot** and **aromatic roots** but whose **seeds** are rather **tasteless**, such as **ginger**. The cause is (as touched upon before) that the **heat** of those **plants** is very **prone to evaporate** <note>original: "dissipable".</note>; while underground it is contained and held in, but when it meets the **air**, it exhales.

<margin>633</margin>
The **juices** of **fruits** are either **watery** or **oily**. I count among the **watery** ones all those **fruits** from which **drink** is pressed, such as the **grape**, the **apple**, the **pear**, the **cherry**, the **pomegranate**, etc. There are some others which, although not used for **drink**, appear to be of the same **nature**, such as **plums**, **service-berries**, **mulberries**, **raspberries**, **oranges**, **lemons**, etc. As for those **juices** that are so fleshy they cannot produce **drink** by **pressing**, perhaps they might make **drink** by **mixing with water**;

->And they imitate wine cups with mixed service-berries.<- <note>original Latin: "Poculaque admistis imitantur vitea Sorbis." This quote from Virgil's *Georgics* describes people in cold climates making a fermented drink from the fruit of the service tree.</note>

And it may be that **hips** and **briar berries** would do the same. Those that have **oily juice** are **olives**, **almonds**, **nuts** of all sorts, **pine nuts** <note>original: "pine-apples"; in the 17th century, this term referred to the seeds of pine cones.</note>, etc. Their **juices** are all **flammable**. You must also observe that some of the **watery juices**, after they have developed **spirit** <note>meaning they have fermented into alcohol</note>, will burn and ignite, such as **wine**. There is a third kind of **fruit** that is sweet without either **sharpness** or **oiliness**, such as the **fig** and the **date**.

<margin>634</margin>
It has been noted that most **trees**, especially those that bear **mast** <note>original: "mast"; the fruit of forest trees like acorns or beechnuts used for animal fodder.</note>, are fruitful only once every two years. The cause (no doubt) is the **depletion of sap**; for many **orchard trees**, when well **cultivated**, will bear fruit for several years together.

<margin>635</margin>
There is no **tree** which, besides its **natural fruit**, bears as many **abnormal fruits** <note>original: "bastard-fruits".</note> as the **oak** does. For besides the **acorn**, it bears **galls**, **oak-apples**, and certain **oak-nuts** which are **flammable**, as well as certain **oak-berries** that stick close to the **trunk** of the **tree** without a **stalk**. It also bears **mistletoe**, though rarely. The cause of all these may be the **density** and **solidity** of the wood and the **pith** of the **oak**, which forces different **juices** to find different **outlets** <note>original: "eruptions".</note>. <page-num>156</page-num>
# Naturall History

If you intend to create any **super-plants** <note>original: "Super-Plants"; refers to plants of exceptional size or vigor</note>, you must always allow the **sap** to rise plentifully but make its exit difficult.

<margin>636</margin> There are two **growths** <note>original: "Excrescences"</note> that grow upon **trees**, both of which are similar to **mushrooms**. One was called ***Boletus*** <note>original: "Boletus"; a term the Romans used for prized edible mushrooms like the Caesar's mushroom</note> by the Romans; it grows upon the **roots** of **oaks** and was one of the **delicacies** of their **table**. The other is **medicinal** and is called **agaric** (which we mentioned previously), and it grows upon the **tops** of **oaks**, though some claim it also grows at the **roots**. I believe that many tree **growths** occur primarily where the **tree** is dead or decaying, because the **natural sap** of the tree decomposes into an **abnormal substance** <note>original: "Preternaturall Substance"</note>.

<margin>637</margin> The majority of **trees** bear the **most** and **best** fruit on their **lower boughs**, such as **oaks**, **figs**, **walnuts**, **pears**, etc. However, some bear **best** on the **top boughs**, such as **crabapples**, etc. Those that bear best below are trees that are helped more than harmed by **shade**. Generally, all **fruits** bear best at the lowest point because the **sap** does not lose its vigor <note>original: "tireth not"</note> since it has a short distance to travel. Therefore, with **fruit** spread against **walls**, the lowest are the **greatest**, as was previously stated. Thus, it is the **shade** that hinders the **lower boughs**, except in trees that delight in **shade** or at least tolerate it well. For this reason, they are either strong **trees** like the **oak**, or they have large **leaves** like the **walnut** and **fig**, or they grow in a **pyramid** <note>original: "Pyramis"</note> shape like the **pear**. But if they require a great deal of **sun**, they bear best at the **top**, as is the case with **crabapples**, **apples**, **plums**, etc.

<margin>638</margin> There are some **trees** that bear best when they begin to grow **old**, such as **almonds**, **pears**, **vines**, and all **trees** that produce **mast** <term>mast: the fruit of forest trees like acorns or beech nuts, historically used as animal feed</term>. The reason is that all trees bearing mast have an **oily fruit**, and **young trees** have a more **watery juice** that is less **ripened** <note>original: "Concocted"; in this context, the natural process of maturing or thickening juice through heat</note>; the **almond** is also of this kind. The **pear** likewise, though not **oily**, requires a great deal of **sap** that is well **ripened**. We see it is a heavy and solid **fruit**, much more so than **apples**, **plums**, etc. As for the **vine**, it is noted that it bears more **grapes** when it is **young**, but **grapes** that make better **wine** when it is **old**, because the **juice** is better **matured**. We see that **wine** is **inflammable**, so it has a kind of **oiliness**. However, most **trees**, including **apples**, **plums**, etc., bear best when they are **young**.

<margin>639</margin> There are **plants** that contain a **milky sap** <note>original: "Milke"</note> when they are cut, such as **figs**, **old lettuce**, **sow-thistles**, **spurge**, etc. The **cause** may be the **beginning** of **decay** <note>original: "Inception of Putrefaction"</note>; for these **milky saps** all have a **sharpness** <note>original: "Acrimony"</note>, though one would expect them to be **soothing** <note>original: "Lenitiue"</note>. For if you write upon paper with the **milky sap** of a **fig**, the letters will be invisible until you hold the paper before a **fire**, and then they turn **brown**. This shows that it is a **sharp** or **corrosive juice**. **Lettuce** is thought to be **poisonous** when it is old enough to have **milky sap**. **Spurge** is a kind of **poison** in itself. As for **sow-thistles**, though **rabbits** <note>original: "Coneys"</note> eat them, **sheep** and **cattle** will not touch them. Additionally, their **milky sap**, if rubbed on **warts**, wears them away in a short time. This shows the **milky sap** of

<margin>640</margin>
**Mushrooms** <note>original: "Mushbromes"</note> are reported to grow as well upon the **trunks** <note>original: "Bodies"</note> of trees as upon their **roots** or upon the **earth**, and especially upon the **oak**. The cause is that **sturdy trees** are, regarding such **growths** <note>original: "Excreſcences"</note>, like the **earth**; and therefore they put forth **moss**, **mushrooms**, and the like.

<margin>641</margin>
Hardly any **plant** is found that yields a **red juice** in the **blade** or **ear**, except for the **tree** that bears **dragon’s blood** <note>original: "Sanguis Draconis"; a bright red resin obtained from different species of several distinct plant genera</note>, which grows (chiefly) on the **island of Socotra** <note>original: "Saquotra"</note>. That **dragon’s blood tree** grows in the shape of a **sugarloaf** <note>original: "Sugar-loafe"; a conical shape common for refined sugar in the past</note>. It is likely that the **sap** of that plant **thickens** <note>original: "concocteth"</note> within the body of the tree. For we see that **grapes** and **pomegranates** have **red juice** but are **green in the droplet** <note>original: "Teare"; referring to the sap or first drop of juice before it fully matures or reacts</note>. And this makes the **dragon’s blood tree** narrower towards the **top** because the **juice** does not rush upward; besides, it is very **astringent** <note>original: "Aſtringent"; causing the contraction of body tissues</note> and therefore moves slowly.

<margin>642</margin>
It is reported that **sweet moss**, besides that which grows upon **apple trees**, also grows (sometimes) upon **poplars**; and yet generally the **poplar** has a smooth **bark** and has little **moss**. The **moss** of the **larch tree** <note>original: "Larix Tree"</note> also burns **sweetly** and **sparkles** while burning. **Inquire** <note>original: "Quære"; Latin for "inquiry"</note> into the **mosses** of **fragrant trees**, such as **cedar**, **cypress**, **aloeswood** <note>original: "Lignum Aloës"</note>, etc.

<margin>643</margin>
The **death** that is most **painless** has been noted to be from **taking** a **potion of hemlock**, which inhumanity was the method of **execution** for **capital offenders** in **Athens**. The **poison of the asp** that **Cleopatra** used has some similarity to it. The cause is that the **agonies** of **death** are chiefly caused by the **struggle of the vital spirits**; and these vapors quench the **spirits** by **degrees**, similar to the **death** of an extremely old man. I believe it is less **painful** than **opium**, because **opium** has elements of **heat** mixed within it.

<margin>644</margin>
There are **fruits** that are **sweet** before they are **ripe**, such as **myrobalans** <note>original: "Mirabolanes"; a plum-like fruit used in tanning and medicine</note>. Likewise, **fennel seeds** are **sweet** before they ripen, and afterward they become spicy. And some never **ripen** to be **sweet**, such as **tamarinds**, **barberries**, **crabapples**, **sloes**, etc. The cause is that the former kind has much **refined heat** <note>original: "ſubtill Heat"</note>, which causes early **sweetness**; the latter has a **cold** and **acidic juice** that no **sunlight** can sweeten. But as for the **myrobalan**, it has parts of **contrary natures**, for it is **sweet** and yet **astringent**.

<margin>645</margin>
There are few **herbs** that have a **salty taste**; conversely, all **blood** of **living creatures** has a **saltiness**. The cause may be that **salt**, although it is the **foundation** <note>original: "Rudiment"</note> of **life**, yet in **plants**, the **original taste**

But in *Living Creatures*, all those *strong tastes* <note>original: "High Taſtes"</note> may happen to be (sometimes) in the *bodily fluids* <note>original: "Humours"</note>, but are seldom in the *flesh* or *substance*. This is because flesh is of a more *oily nature*, which is not very *susceptible* to those *tastes*; and the *saltiness* itself of *blood* is but a light and secret *saltiness*. Even among *plants*, some do participate in *saltiness*, such as *seaweed* <note>original: "Alga Marina"</note>, *samphire*, *scurvy-grass*, etc. And they report there is, in some of the *Indian Seas*, a *floating plant* which they call *Sargassum* <note>original: "Salgazus"</note>, spreading over the *sea* in such a way that one would think it were a *meadow*. It is certain that from the *ashes* of all *plants*, they extract a *salt* which they use in *medicines*.

<margin>646.</margin>
It is reported by one of the *Ancients* that there is an *herb* growing in the *water* called *Lincostis* <note>Possibly a reference to a species of water-lily or pondweed</note>, which is full of *prickles*. This *herb* puts forth another small *herb* out of the *leaf*, which is attributed to some *moisture* that is gathered between the *prickles*; this moisture, having *decomposed* <note>original: "Putrified"</note> by the *sun*, *sprouts* <note>original: "Germinateth"</note>. But I remember also that I have seen, as a great *rarity*, one *rose* grow out of another, like *honeysuckles*, which they call *top and top-gallants* <note>original: "Top and Top gallants"; a nautical term for sails stacked one above the other, used here to describe the tiered growth of the flowers.</note>.

<margin>647.</margin>
*Barley* (as appears in the *malting* process), being steeped in *water* for three days, and afterwards the *water* drained from it and the *barley* spread upon a dry floor, will sprout at least half an inch long. And if it is left alone and not turned, it will sprout much more until the heart of the grain is exhausted. *Wheat* will do the same. Try it also with *peas* and *beans*. This *experiment* is not like that of the *orpine* <note>original: "Orpin"; a succulent plant</note> and *houseleek* <note>original: "Semper-Viue"</note>; for in those cases, growth comes from the plant's old *store* of energy, as no *water* is added. But here, the plant is nourished by the *water*. This *experiment* should be pushed further; for it already appears, by what has been said, that *earth* is not necessary for the first sprouting of *plants*. We see that *rosebuds* set in *water* will *bloom* <note>original: "Blow"</note>. Therefore, try whether the *sprouts* of such *grains* may not be raised to a further *degree*, such as into an *herb* or *flower*, with *water* only, or perhaps some small *mixture* of *earth*. For if they will grow this way, it would seem from the previous *experiments*—both of the *malt* and of the *roses*—that they will grow far faster in *water* than in *earth*. This is because the *nourishment* is more easily drawn out of *water* than out of *earth*. It may also provide some insight that *drink* infused with *flesh*—such as that made with a *capon* <note>A castrated rooster, used to make a restorative broth</note>, etc.—will nourish faster and easier than *meat* and *drink* eaten together. Try the same *experiment* with *roots* as well as with *grains*; for *example*, take a *turnip* and steep it a while, then dry it, and see whether it will sprout.

*Malt* will swell during the *steeping* <note>original: "Drenching"</note>. It swells in such a manner that, after the sprouting and the drying upon the *kiln* <note>original: "Keele"</note>, there will be a gain of at least one *bushel* in every eight; and yet the *sprouts* are rubbed off, and there will be a *bushel* of *dust* produced besides the *malt*. I suppose this increase occurs not only because of the loose and open *layering* of the *parts*, but by some addition of *substance* drawn from the *water* in which it was steeped.

<margin>650</margin>
*Most seeds* during *growth* leave their *husk* or *rind* near the *root*; but the *onion* will carry it up, so that it sits like a *cap* upon the *top* of the *young onion*. The *cause* may be that the *skin* or *husk* is not easy to break; as we see by the *peeling* of *onions*, the *skin* is a very *tough substance* <note>original: "Holding Substance"</note>.

<margin>651</margin>
*Plants* that have *curled leaves* all abound with *moisture*. This moisture comes on so fast that they cannot spread themselves *flat* <note>original: "Plaine"</note>, but must instead gather together. The weakest kind of *curling* is *roughness*, as seen in *clary* <note>original: "Clary"; likely Clary Sage</note> and *burr* <note>original: "Burre"; likely Burdock</note>. The second is *curling* on the *sides*, as in *lettuce* and *young cabbage*. The third is *folding* into a *head*, as in full-grown *cabbage* and *head lettuce* <note>original: "Cabbage-Lettuce"</note>.

<margin>652</margin>
It is reported that *fir* and *pine*, especially if they are *old* and *decayed* <note>original: "Putrified"</note>, will sparkle like *sugar crystals* <note>original: "Hard Sugar"</note> when suddenly *broken*, even though they shine [in the dark] as some *rotten woods* do <note>A reference to "foxfire," or bioluminescent fungi on decaying wood</note>.

<margin>653</margin>
The *roots of trees* (some of them) push deep down into the *ground*, such as the *oak*, *pine*, *fir*, and others. Some spread more towards the *surface* of the *earth*, such as the *ash*, *cypress tree*, *olive*, and so on. The cause of this latter behavior may be that such *trees* as love the *sun* do not willingly descend far into the *earth*. Therefore, they are (commonly) *trees* that shoot upward significantly; in their *body*, their desire to reach for the *sun* makes them spread less. The same reason applies *underground*: to avoid retreating from the *sun*, they spread out more. 

We see this happen in some *trees* that have been planted too deep in the *ground*; out of a desire to *reach* for the *sun*, they abandon their first *root* and put out another closer to the *top* of the *earth*. We also see that the *olive* is full of *oily juice*, the *ash* makes the best *fire*, and the *cypress* is a *warm tree* <note>Referring to the "hot" or "cold" elemental qualities of plants in Renaissance science</note>. As for the *oak*, which is of the first sort, it loves the *earth* and therefore grows slowly. As for the *pine* and *fir* likewise, they have so much *heat* in themselves that they need less of the *sun's heat*. 

There are *herbs* also that have the same difference, such as the *herb* they call the *Devil's Bit* <note>original: "Morsus Diaboli"; likely Devil's-bit Scabious (*Succisa pratensis*)</note>, which puts its *root* down so low that you cannot pull it up without *breaking* it. This gave *rise* to the *name* and the *fable*: for it was said it was such a wholesome *root* that the *Devil*, when it was gathered, bit it out of *envy*. Some of the *ancients* also report that there was a *stately fir* (which they desired to move whole) that had a *root* eight *cubits* <note>A cubit is about 18 inches; thus, 12 feet deep</note> deep *underground*, and so the *root* came up broken.

It has been observed that a *branch* of a *tree*, having its *bark stripped* <note>original: "Vnbarked"</note> for some space at the *bottom* and then set into the *ground*, has grown—even from such *trees* that would not grow if the *branch* were set with the *bark* on. <header>Natural History:</header>

If a tree is stripped of its bark near the ground, it will die. The *cause* may be that the *unbarked part* <note>original: "Unbarkt Part"; the inner wood of the trunk</note> draws the *nourishment* best, but the *bark* is what allows that nourishment to continue flowing.

<margin>655</margin> *Grapes* will remain *fresh* and *moist* all *winter* long if you hang them, *cluster* by *cluster*, from the *ceiling* <note>original: "Roofe"</note> of a *warm room*. This is especially effective if, when you gather the *cluster*, you also take some of the *vine stem* <note>original: "Stocke"</note> with it.

<margin>656</margin> The *reed* or *cane* is a water-loving *plant* and grows only in *water*. It has these properties: it is *hollow*; it is *jointed* <note>original: "Knuckled"</note> at both the *stalk* and the *root*; and when *dry*, it is *harder* and more *fragile* than other wood. It does not put out *branches*, though many *stalks* come from a single *root*. Reeds differ greatly in *size* <note>original: "Greatnesse"</note>. The smallest are used for thatching *houses* and plugging the cracks in *ships*, working better than *glue* or *pitch*. The *medium-sized* ones <note>original: "Second Bignesse"</note> are used for *fishing rods* <note>original: "Angle-Rods"</note> and *walking sticks* <note>original: "Staves"</note>, and in *China* for beating *offenders* on the thighs. The different *kinds* of them are the *common reed*, the *cassia fistula* <note>original: "Cassia Fistula"; a tropical tree with medicinal pods, though Bacon groups it here by its cane-like shape</note>, and the *sugar-cane* <note>original: "Sugar-Reed"</note>. Of all *plants*, it bends the easiest and stands back up. It seems that among *plants* nourished by a *mixture* of *earth* and *water*, the reed draws most of its *nourishment* from *water*. This makes its *bark* the *smoothest* and its *body* the *hollowest* of all plants.

<margin>657</margin> The *sap* of *trees*, when they are tapped <note>original: "let Bloud"</note>, has different *qualities*. Some are more *watery* and *clear*, such as those of *vines*, *beeches*, and *pears*. Some are *thick*, like *apples*. Some are *gummy*, like *cherries*. Some are *frothy*, like *elms*. Some are *milky*, like *figs*. In *mulberries*, the *sap* seems to stay almost entirely near the *bark*; for if you cut slightly into the *bark* with a *stone*, the sap will come out, but if you pierce deeper with a *tool*, the wood will be dry. *Trees* that have the *moistest juices* in their *fruit* usually have the *moistest sap* in their *trunks* <note>original: "Body"</note>; for *vines* and *pears* are very *moist*, while *apples* are somewhat more *spongy*. The *milk* of the *fig* has the quality of *rennet* <note>an enzyme used to curdle milk</note> to make *cheese*, as do certain *sour herbs* used to make *cheese* during *Lent* <note>the period of fasting before Easter when meat was prohibited</note>.

<margin>658</margin> The *timber* and *wood* of some *trees* are *cleaner*, while others are more *knotty*. A good *test* <note>original: "Triall"</note> of this is to *speak* into one *end* of the wood while someone else lays an *ear* at the *other*. If the wood is *knotty*, the *voice* will not pass through well. Some woods have more varied and marbled *grain* <note>original: "Veines... chamlotted"</note>, such as *oak* (used for *paneling* <note>original: "wainscot"</note>) and *maple* (used for *wooden plates* <note>original: "Trenchers"</note>). Others are smoother, like *fir* and *walnut*. Some easily breed *worms* and *spiders*, while others do so with difficulty, as is said of *Irish trees*. Furthermore, there are many *differences* concerning their use. *Oak*, *cedar*, and *chestnut* are the best for *building*. Some are best for *plow timber*, such as *ash*. Some are best for *piers* <note>original: "Peeres"</note> that are sometimes wet and sometimes dry, like *elm*. Some are for *plank floors* <note>original: "Planchers"</note>, such as *pine* <note>original: "Deale"</note>. Some are for *tables*, *cupboards*, and *desks*, like *walnut*. Some are for *ship-timber*, such as *oaks* that grow in *moist ground*, because that makes the *timber tough* and less likely to crack when hit by *cannon fire* <note>original: "Ordnance"</note>; in this, *English* and *Irish timber* are thought to excel. Some are for the *masts* of *ships*, such as *fir* and *pine*, because of their

<margin>659</margin>
...length, straightness, and lightness: some for *fencing* <note>original: "Pale"</note>, such as *oak*; some for *fuel*, such as *ash*; and so on for the rest.

The *arrival* <note>original: "Comming"</note> of *trees* and *plants* in certain *regions*, and not in others, is sometimes *accidental* <note>original: "Casuall"</note>. Many have been transplanted and have thrived, such as *Damask roses*, which were unknown in *England* until about a hundred years ago and are now very common. However, the preference of *plants* for certain *soils* over others is purely *natural*. For instance, *fir* and *pine* love the *mountains*; *poplar*, *willow*, *sallow* <note>a species of willow</note>, and *alder* love *rivers* and *moist places*. *Ash* loves *coppices* <note>thickets of small trees</note> but is best as a lone *standard* <note>a full-sized, freestanding tree</note>. *Juniper* loves *chalky soil*, as do most *fruit trees*. *Samphire* <note>original: "Sampire"; a coastal succulent used in pickling</note> grows only upon *rocks*. *Reeds* and *osiers* <note>willow branches used for basketry</note> grow where they are washed by *water*. The *vine* loves the sides of *hills* facing the *southeast sun*, and so forth.

<margin>660</margin>
The *growth* <note>original: "Putting forth"</note> of certain *herbs* reveals the nature of the *ground* where they sprout. For example, *wild thyme* indicates good *pasture* <note>original: "Feeding Ground"</note> for *cattle*. *Betony* and *strawberries* indicate *grounds* suitable for *wood*. *Chamomile* <note>original: "Camomill"</note> shows *mellow* <note>rich, well-tilled</note> *grounds* fit for *wheat*. *Mustard seed* growing after the *plow* <note>original: "Plough"</note> also indicates a *strong ground* good for *wheat*. *Burnet* indicates a good *meadow*, and the like.

<margin>661</margin>
In various *countries*, other *plants* besides *mistletoe* are found growing out of *trees* and *plants*. In *Syria*, there is an *herb* called *cassytas* <note>original: "Cassytas"; likely dodder</note> that grows out of tall *trees* and winds itself around the same *tree* where it grows, and sometimes around *thorns*. There is a type of *polypody* <note>original: "Polypode"; a type of fern</note> that grows out of *trees*, though it does not wind around them. Likewise, an *herb* called *faunos* grows upon the *wild olive*, and an *herb* called *hippophaston* <note>original: "Hippophaston"</note> grows upon the *fuller's thorn* <note>the teasel plant</note>, which they say is good for *epilepsy* <note>original: "Falling-Sicknesse"</note>.

<margin>662</margin>
It has been observed by some of the *ancients* that although *cold* and *easterly winds* are thought to be great *enemies* to *fruit*, *south winds* are also found to do *harm*, especially during the *blossoming* time—and even more so if *showers* follow. It seems they draw out the *moisture* too quickly. *West winds* are the best. It has also been observed that *mild* <note>original: "Greene"</note> and *open winters* harm *trees*; so much so that if two or three such *winters* occur in a row, *almond trees* and some other *trees* will die. The *cause* is the same as mentioned before: the *vitality* <note>original: "Lust"</note> of the *earth* overspends itself, even though some other *ancients* have praised *warm winters*.

<margin>663</margin>
*Snow*, when it lies on the ground for a long time, leads to a *fruitful year*. First, it keeps in the *strength* of the *earth*. Second, it waters the *earth* better than *rain*, for in *snow*, the *earth* (as it were) sucks the *water* as if from a *breast* <note>original: "Teate"</note>. Third, the *moisture* of *snow* is the finest moisture, for it is the *froth* of the *cloudy waters*.

<margin>664</margin>
*Showers*, if they come shortly before the *ripening* of *fruits*, are beneficial to all *succulent* and *moist fruits*, such as *vines*, *olives*, and *pomegranates*. However, this is better for the *quantity* <note>original: "Plentie"</note> rather than the *quality* <note>original: "Goodnesse"</note>, for the best *wines* come from the *driest vintages*. *Small showers* are also good for *grain* <note>original: "Corne"</note>, provided that...

<page-num>162</page-num>
<header>Natural History:</header>

*Scorching heats* <note>original: "Parching Heats"</note> do not come upon them. Generally, *night showers* are better than *day showers*, because the *sun* does not follow so quickly after them. We see even in *watering by hand* that it is best, in *summer* time, to water in the *evening*.

<margin>665</margin>
The *varieties of soils* <note>original: "Differences of Earths"</note> and the *testing* of them are worthy of diligent inquiry. The *soil* that *softens* most easily with *showers* is recommended; and yet some *soil* of that kind will be very *dry* and *hard* before the *showers*. The *soil* that casts up a *large clod* from the *plow* is not as good as that which casts up a *smaller clod*. The *soil* that easily puts forth *moss*, and may be called *mouldy*, is not good. The *soil* that smells well upon *digging* or *plowing* is recommended, as it contains the *juices* of *vegetables* almost already prepared. It is thought by some that the *ends* of low *rainbows* fall more upon one kind of *soil* than upon another; this may well be, because that *soil* is the most *dewy* <note>original: "Roscide"; from the Latin 'roscidus'</note>, and therefore it is praised as a sign of good *soil*. 

The *poorness* of the *herbs* clearly shows the *poorness* of the *soil*, especially if they are darker in *color*. But if the *herbs* appear withered or *blighted* <note>original: "Blasted"</note> at the *top*, it shows the *soil* to be very *cold*; the *mossiness* of *trees* indicates the same. The *soil* where the *grass* is soon *scorched* by the *sun* and *parched* <note>original: "Toasted"</note> is commonly *artificial soil* <note>original: "Forced Earth"; soil moved or modified by humans</note> and *barren* in its own *nature*. The *tender*, *crumbly* <note>original: "Ches-some"; an archaic term for friable or loose soil</note>, and *mellow soil* is the best, being pure *mould* between the two *extremes* of *clay* and *sand*, especially if it is not *loamy* and *binding* <note>clumping together too tightly</note>. The *soil* that can hardly be *plowed* after *rain* is commonly *fruitful*, for it is *clinging* <note>original: "Cleauing"</note> and full of *juice*.

<margin>666</margin>
It is strange, as observed by some of the *ancients*, that *dust* helps the *fruitfulness* of *trees*—and of *vines* specifically—so much so that they throw *dust* upon them on purpose. It would seem that this *powdering*, when a *shower* comes, creates a kind of *fertilizer* <note>original: "Soyling"</note> for the *tree*, being *soil* and *water* finely applied. They also note that *countries* where the *fields* and *roads* are *dusty* bear the best *vines*.

<margin>667</margin>
It is recommended by the *ancients* as an excellent *help* to *trees* to lay the *stalks* and *leaves* of *lupines* <note>a type of flowering legume often used as green manure</note> around the *roots*, or to *plow* them into the *ground* where you will sow *grain*. The *burning* of the *cuttings of vines* and *spreading* them upon the *land* also does much *good*. It was generally accepted in ancient times that the *manuring* of *grounds* when the *west wind* blows and during the *waning of the moon* <note>original: "Decrease of the Moone"</note> greatly helps, the *soil* (as it seems) being then more thirsty and open to receive the *manure*.

<margin>668</margin>
The *grafting of vines upon vines* (as I understand it) is not currently in use. The *ancients* practiced it in three ways: the first was *insertion* <note>original: "Insition"</note>, which is the *ordinary manner of grafting*; the second was *boring* <note>original: "Terebration"</note> through the *middle* of the *stock* and *inserting* the *scions* <note>original: "Cions"</note> there; and the third was *paring* two *vines* that grow together down to the *pith* <note>original: "Marrow"</note> and *binding* them close.

Therefore, in **hills** or large **open fields** <note>original: "Champaigne Grounds"</note>, it seldom occurs, such as in our **Yorkshire Wolds** <note>original: "York's-woald"</note>. This cannot be remedied, except that in regions of small, enclosed plots, the **grounds** should be turned into larger **fields**—which I have known to do good on some **farms**. <margin>428</margin> Another **disease** is the **production of wild oats**, into which **grain** <note>original: "Corne"; in this period, "corn" referred to any cereal crop like wheat or barley, not maize</note> oftentimes (especially **barley**) degenerates. It happens chiefly from the **weakness of the grain** that is sown; for if it be either too **old** or **moldy**, it will bring forth **wild oats**. Another **disease** is the **exhaustion of the ground** <note>original: "Saciety of the Ground"</note>; for if you always sow one **plot** with the same **grain** (I do not mean the same individual seeds that grew upon that ground, but the same **kind of grain**, such as **wheat**, **barley**, etc.), it will prosper poorly. Therefore, besides **letting the ground rest**, you must vary the **seed**. <margin>572</margin> Another ill **occurrence** <note>original: "Accident"</note> comes from the **winds**, which do harm at two times: at the **flowering**, by **shaking off the blossoms**, and at the full **ripening**, by **shaking out the grain**. <margin>475</margin> Another ill **occurrence** is **drought** at the **stalking of the grain** <note>original: "Spindling of the Corne"</note>, which is rare with us but common in hotter **countries**. This is so much the case that the word **calamity** <note>original: "Calamitas"</note> was first derived from the word for **stalk** <note>original: "Calamus"</note>, referring to when the **grain** could not emerge from the **stalk**. Another ill **occurrence** is **excessive wetness at sowing time**, which causes much **scarcity** <note>original: "Dearth"</note> among us, because the **grain** never sprouts; and many times farmers are forced to resow **summer grain** where they had previously sown **winter grain**. <margin>514</margin> Another ill **occurrence** is **bitter frosts** that continue without **snow**, especially in the beginning of winter after the **seed** is newly sown. Another **disease** is **worms**, which sometimes breed in the **root** and occur during **hot sun** and **showers** immediately after **sowing**; and another **worm** breeds in the **ear** itself, especially when **hot sun** often breaks out from behind **clouds**. Another **disease** is **weeds**; and these are such as either **choke and overshadow the grain** and weigh it down, or starve the **grain** and rob it of **nourishment**. Another **disease** is **excessive luxuriance** <note>original: "Ouer-Rancknesse"</note> of the grain, which they usually remedy by **mowing** it after it has come up or by putting **sheep** into the field to graze. Another ill **occurrence** is the **flattening of grain** <note>original: "Laying of Corne"</note> by great rains near or during **harvest**. Another ill **occurrence** is if the **seed** happens to have touched **oil** or any **fatty substance**; for those **substances** have a natural **aversion to being nourished by water**.

It is also reported that if **grain** <note>original: "Corne"; in this period, "corn" refers to any cereal crop like wheat or barley</note> is **mowed** <note>likely referring to harvesting the crop while still slightly green</note>, it will make the **grain longer**, but emptier, and having more of the **husk**.

<margin>671</margin>
It has been noted that **seed** one year old is the **best**; seed two or three years old is **worse**; and that which is older is quite barren—though, no doubt, some **seeds** and **grains** last better than others. The **grain** which lies lowest during **fanning** <note>original: "Vanning," the process of winnowing or sifting grain to separate the heavy seeds from the light chaff</note> is the best. Furthermore, **grain** that retains a little **yellowness** when broken or bitten is better than that which is very **white**.

<margin>672</margin>
It has been observed that of all **roots of herbs**, the **root of sorrel** goes the furthest into the **earth**, so much so that it has been known to go three cubits <note>about 4.5 feet or 1.3 meters</note> deep. It is also the **root** that remains fit to be replanted the longest of any **root** that grows. It is a **cold** and **acidic herb** that (so it seems) loves the **earth** and is not much drawn by the **sun**.

<margin>673</margin>
It has been observed that some **herbs** grow best when watered with **salt water**, such as **radish, beet, rue**, and **pennyroyal**. This trial should be extended to other **herbs**, especially those that are strong, such as **tarragon, mustard seed, rocket**, and the like.

<margin>674</margin>
It is strange, though generally accepted, how some **poisonous beasts** are attracted to fragrant and wholesome **herbs**—for instance, that the **snake** loves **fennel**, that the **toad** will often be found under **sage**, and that **frogs** will stay in **cinquefoil**. It may be that it is the **shade** or other **cover** <note>original: "Couerture"</note> they like, rather than the **medicinal property** <note>original: "Vertue"</note> of the **herb**.

<margin>675</margin>
It would be a matter of great profit (except that I suspect it is too speculative to rely upon) if one could discern which **grain, herbs**, or **fruits** are likely to be in **plenty** or **scarcity** by certain **signs** and **prognostics** <note>omens or physical indicators used for forecasting</note> at the beginning of the year. As for those likely to be in **plenty**, they may be contracted for while still in the **ground**. This relates to the old story of **Thales** <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624 – c. 546 BC), a Greek philosopher</note>, who, to show how easy it was for a philosopher to be rich, foresaw a great **plenty of olives** and created a **monopoly** on them. For **scarcity**, men may profit by better preserving their old stores. A **long-lasting snow** is believed to create a **fruitful year for grain**; an **early winter** or a very **late winter** leads to a **barren year for grain**; and an **open and clear winter** results in a poor **year for fruit**. We have touched on some of these before, but other **prognostics** of a similar nature should be diligently investigated.

<margin>676</margin>
There seem to be **singularities** in some **plants** where they differ from all others. The **olive** has its **oily part** only on the **outside**, whereas all other **fruits** have it in the **nut** or **kernel**. The **fir** has (effectively) no **stone, nut**, or **kernel**, unless you count the little **grains** as kernels. Only the **pomegranate** and **pine cone** <note>original: "Pine-Apple"; in this period, this referred to the cone of a pine tree</note> have **seeds** <note>original: "Graines"</note> distinct in several **cells**. <header>Century. VII.</header>

No **flower** has that kind of spread that the **woodbine** <note>original: "Woodbine," usually referring to honeysuckle</note> has. This may be a large field of **contemplation**; for it shows that in the **framework of nature**, there is—in the producing of some **species**—a composition of matter which happens often and is much diversified. In others, such as happen rarely, it admits little variety. For it is the same way with **beasts**: **dogs** have a resemblance to **wolves** and **foxes**; **horses** to **asses**; **cattle** <note>original: "Kine"</note> to **buffaloes** <note>original: "Bufles"</note>; **hares** to **rabbits** <note>original: "Conies"</note>, and so on. And it is the same with **birds**: **kites** and **kestrels** have a resemblance to **hawks**; **common doves** to **ring-doves** and **turtles** <note>referring to turtle-doves</note>; **blackbirds** to **thrushes** and **song thrushes** <note>original: "Mauisses" (mavises)</note>; **crows** to **ravens**, **jackdaws** <note>original: "Dawes"</note>, and **choughs**, etc. But **elephants** and **swine** among **beasts**, and the **bird of paradise** and the **peacock** among **birds**, and some few others, have scarcely any other **species** that have an affinity with them.

We leave the description of **plants** and their **virtues** <note>medicinal properties or powers</note> to **herbals** and other similar books of **natural history**. In these, **men's** diligence has been great, even to the point of **curiosity** <note>original: "Curiosity"; in this context, it refers to excessive or fastidious detail</note>. Our **experiments** are only those that always ascend a degree toward deriving **causes** and extracting **axioms**. We are not ignorant of the fact that some **ancient and modern writers** have also labored at this, but their **causes** and **axioms** are so full of **imagination** and so infected with the old **received theories** that they are mere **corruptions** <note>original: "Inquinations" (from the Latin *inquinatio*)</note> of **experience** and do not **assimilate** <note>original: "Concoct"; meaning to refine or process into useful knowledge</note> it.

<margin>*Solitary Experiment regarding the Healing of Wounds.* 677</margin>
It has been observed by some of the **ancients** that **skins** (especially of **rams**) newly pulled off and applied to the **wounds** of **lashes** <note>original: "Stripes," referring to wounds from being whipped</note> keep them from swelling and **festering** <note>original: "Exulcerating"</note>; and likewise heal them and close them up; and that **egg whites** do the same. The **cause** is a temperate **binding** <note>original: "Conglutination"</note>; for both substances are clammy and viscous and they restrain the **flow of humors** <note>original: "Deflux of Humours"; refers to the old medical theory that bodily fluids flowed to an injured site</note> to the injuries without penning them in too much.

<margin>*Solitary Experiment regarding Fat diffused in Flesh.* 678</margin>
You may turn (almost) all **flesh** into a **fatty substance** if you take **flesh**, cut it into pieces, and put the pieces into a **glass** covered with parchment; then let the **glass** stand for six or seven hours in **boiling water**. It may be an **experiment of profit** for making **fat** or **grease** for many uses; but it must be made from **flesh** that is not **edible**, such as **horses**, **dogs**, **bears**, **foxes**, **badgers**, etc.

<margin>*Solitary Experiment regarding the Ripening of Drink before the Time.* 679</margin>
It is reported by one of the **ancients** that **new wine** put into **vessels** well-stopped, and the **vessels** let down into the **sea**, will very much accelerate the process of making them **ripe** and **drinkable** <note>original: "Potable"</note>. The same should be tried with **unfermented beer** <note>original: "Wort"</note>.

<header>Natural History:</header>

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning *hairiness and feathers.* 680</margin>
Animals <note>original: "Beasts"</note> are more **hairy** than **humans**; and **wild humans** <note>original: "Savage Men"</note> are more hairy than **civilized** ones. Furthermore, the **feathers** <note>original: "Plumage"</note> of **birds** exceed the **hairiness** of animals. The **cause** of smoothness in **humans** is not an abundance of **heat** and **moisture**, though those factors do indeed cause **hairiness**. Rather, hairiness requires not just heat and moisture, but **waste-related heat and moisture** <note>original: "Excrementitious Heat and Moisture"; in Bacon's time, "excrement" referred to any byproduct or superfluity the body could not turn into tissue, including hair, nails, and sweat</note>. (For whatever the body **assimilates** <note>turns into its own substance</note> does not go into the **hair**.) This **waste moisture** is most abundant in **animals** and in **humans** who are more **wild**. The reason for the **feathers** of **birds** is much the same; for **birds** assimilate less of their food and **excrete** <note>original: "excerne"</note> more than **animals** do. Their **waste** is always liquid, and their **flesh** is generally drier. Besides, they lack **organs for urine** <note>such as a bladder</note>, and so all the **waste moisture** goes into the **feathers**. Therefore, it is no wonder that **birds** are commonly better **meat** than **animals**, because their **flesh** assimilates nutrients more finely and separates waste more precisely. Furthermore, a **human's head** has **hair** at **birth**, which no other **part** of the **body** has. The **cause** may be a lack of **perspiration**; much of the material that forms **hair** in other **parts** of the **body** is released through **invisible perspiration** <note>original: "Insensible Perspiration"</note>. Additionally, because the **skull** is made of a more solid **substance**, it nourishes and assimilates less and excretes more—the same applies to the **chin**. We also see that **hair** does not grow on the **palms** of the **hands** or the **soles** of the **feet**, which are **parts** that **perspire** more easily. **Children** likewise are not **hairy** because their **skins** allow for more **perspiration**.

<margin>Solitary experiments concerning the *quickness of motion in birds.* 681</margin>
**Birds** move **faster** than **animals**: for the **flight** of many **birds** is **swifter** than the race of any **animal**. The **cause** is that the **spirits** <note>the "vital spirits" believed to be the subtle fluids driving movement and life</note> in **birds** are in greater proportion to the size of their **body** than they are in **animals**. As for the reason some give—that birds are partly **carried** by the air while **animals** walk—that is **irrelevant** <note>original: "Nothing"</note>. By that logic, swimming would be swifter than running; furthermore, that kind of carriage in the air is not achieved without the labor of the **wing**.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the different *clarity of the sea.* 682</margin>
The **sea** is **clearer** when the **north wind** blows than when the **south wind** blows. The **cause** is that **saltwater** has a slight **oiliness** on its **surface**, as is apparent on very hot days. Additionally, the **southern wind** thins <note>original: "relaxeth"</note> the **water** somewhat; just as no **boiling** water is as clear as **cold water**.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the different *heats of fire and boiling water.* 683</margin>
**Fire** burns wood, making it first **glowing** <note>original: "Luminous"</note>; then **black** and **brittle**; and lastly, **broken** and **turned to ash** <note>original: "Incinerate"</note>. **Scalding water** does none of these. The **cause** is that through **fire**, the **spirit** of the body is first **refined** and then **released** <note>original: "Emitted"</note>. This **refining** or thinning <note>original: "Attenuation"</note> causes the **light**, and the **release** causes first the **brittleness** and later the **breakdown** into **ashes**. No other **body** <note>substance</note> enters the wood during this process. But in **water**, the **spirit** of the body is not **refined** as much; furthermore, **part** of the **water** enters the wood, which increases the **spirit** <note>the internal moisture/essence</note> and, to a degree, extinguishes it. <margin>Solitary experiment concerning the qualification of heat by moisture. 684</margin>
The bottom of a **vessel** of **boiling water** (as has been observed) is not very much **heated**, so that men may put their hand under the vessel and remove it. The **cause** is that the **moisture** of **water**, just as it quenches **coals** where it enters, also allays <note>moderates or diminishes</note> **heat** where it touches. And therefore note well that **moisture**, although it does not pass through **bodies** without the **communication** <note>transfer</note> of some **substance** (as **heat** and **cold** do), yet it works manifest **effects**, not by the entrance of the **body** <note>the liquid itself</note>, but by **qualifying** <note>altering the properties of</note> the **heat** and **cold**, as we see in this **instance**. We see likewise that the **water** of **things distilled** in **water** (which they call **the bath** <note>original: "the Bath"; likely referring to a *bain-marie*, a water bath used for gentle heating</note>) does not differ much from the **water** of **things distilled** by **fire**. We see also that **pewter dishes** with **water** in them will not **melt** easily, but without it, they will. Nay, we see more: that **butter** or **oil**, which in themselves are **flammable**, yet by virtue of their **moisture** will do the same.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning yawning. 685</margin>
It has been noted by the **ancients** that it is dangerous to **pick** one's **ear** while he **yawns**. For in both **yawning** and **sighing**, the **spirit** is first strongly **drawn in** and then strongly **expelled**.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the hiccup. 686</margin>

For first, we see that the **hiccup** comes from a **fullness** of **food** <note>original: "Meat"; used here as a general term for food</note> (especially in **children**), which causes a **stretching** <note>original: "Extension"</note> of the **stomach**. We see also it is caused by **acidic foods** or **drinks**, which happens by the **pricking** <note>irritation</note> of the **stomach**. This **motion** is stopped either by **diversion** or by **detention** <note>holding</note> of the **spirits**. **Diversion** occurs as in **sneezing**; **detention** occurs as we see **holding the breath** helps somewhat to stop the **hiccup**. Putting a man into an **earnest study** <note>intense mental focus or concentration</note> does the same, as is commonly practiced. Also, **vinegar** applied to the **nostrils** or **gargled** <note>original: "Gargarized"</note> does it too, because it is **astringent** <note>causing the contraction of tissues</note> and inhibits the **motion** of the **spirits**.

**Fire**, such as that of a furnace, as soon as it cools even a little, congeals immediately. And (no doubt) this action is furthered by **copper ore** <note>original: "Chalcites"</note>, which has a **spirit** that will sprout and germinate, as we see in **chemical trials** <note>original: "Chymicall Trialls"</note>. Briefly, most **putrified things** bring forth **insects** <note>original: "Insecta"</note> of several names; but we will not take it upon ourselves now to list <note>original: "Enumerate"</note> them all.

<margin>697</margin>
**Insects** <note>original: "Insecta"</note> have been noted by the **ancient writers** to eat very little. But this has not been carefully observed; for **grasshoppers** eat up the **greenery** of whole countries; **silkworms** devour leaves quickly; and **ants** make great **provisions**. It is true that creatures that sleep and rest a lot eat little, such as **dormice**, **bats**, etc. They are all without **blood**; this may be because the juice of their bodies is almost all one thing—not distinct **blood**, **flesh**, **skin**, and **bone** as in **"perfect" creatures** <note>By "perfect creatures," Bacon refers to higher animals like mammals, which have complex, specialized organ systems.</note>. Their whole body parts <note>original: "Integrall Parts"</note> have extreme variety, but their basic tissues <note>original: "Similar Parts," a term from Aristotelian biology referring to uniform substances like bone or flesh.</note> have little. It is true that some of them have a **diaphragm** and an **intestine**; and they all have **skins**, which most insects shed <note>original: "cast"</note> often. Generally, they are not **long-lived**. Yet **bees** have been known to live seven years; and **snakes** are thought to live until they are old, particularly because they **shed their skins** <note>original: "Casting of their Spoile"</note>. **Eels**, which often breed from **putrefaction** <note>Spontaneous generation was a common belief for eels until the 19th century.</note>, will live and grow for a very long time. And those that change from **worms** to **flies** in the **summer**, and from **flies** to **worms** in the **winter**, have been kept in boxes for at least four years. Yet there are certain **flies** called **mayflies** <note>original: "Ephemera"</note> that live only a day. The cause is the **thinness** <note>original: "Exility"</note> of their **spirit**; or perhaps the **absence** of the **sun**; for if they were brought inside or kept enclosed, they might live longer. Many **insects** (such as **butterflies** and other **flies**) revive easily when they seem dead if they are brought to the **sun** or **fire**. The cause of this is the **spreading** <note>original: "Diffusion"</note> of the **vital spirit** and how easily it **expands** <note>original: "Dilating"</note> with a little **heat**. They continue to move for a good while after their **heads** are off or after they are cut in **pieces**. This is also because their **vital spirits** are more spread throughout all their **parts** and less confined to **organs** than in **"perfect" creatures**.

<margin>698</margin>
**Insects** have **voluntary motion** and, therefore, **imagination** <note>In the philosophy of the time, "imagination" referred to the faculty that allows a creature to form mental representations of goals or directions.</note>. While some **ancient writers** have said that their **motion** is **random** <note>original: "Indeterminate"</note> and their **imagination vague** <note>original: "Indefinite"</note>, this was carelessly observed. For **ants** go directly forward to their **hills**, and **bees** (wonderfully) know the way from a **flowery heath** two or three **miles** off back to their **hives**. It may be that **gnats** and **flies** have a more changeable and giddy **imagination**, as **small birds** also do. Some of the **ancient writers** said that they have only the **sense** of **touch** <note>original: "Feeling"</note>, which is clearly untrue. If they go directly to a **place**, they must have **sight**. Besides, they delight more in one **flower** or **herb** than in another, and therefore they must have **taste**. **Bees** are also summoned by the **sound** of clashing **brass** <note>A traditional beekeeping practice where clashing metal was thought to encourage a swarm to settle.</note>, and therefore they have **hearing**. This also shows that although their **spirit** is spread throughout the body, there is a central **seat** of their **senses** in their **head**.

*Other observations concerning insects, together with the listing* <note>original catchword: "enumeration"</note>

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning leaping. 699
</margin>
A man leaps better with **weights** in his **hands** than without. The **cause** is that the **weight** (if it is proportional) strengthens the **sinews** <note>original: "Sinewes"; here meaning tendons or muscles</note> by **contracting** them. Otherwise, where no **contraction** is needed, **weight** hinders. As we see in **horse races**, **men** are careful to ensure that there is not the slightest **weight** on one **horse** more than on the other. In **leaping** with **weights**, the **arms** are first cast backward and then forward with much greater force; for the **hands** go backward before they take their **rise** <note>original: "Raise"; the upward momentum or jump</note>. **One might ask** <note>original: "Quære"</note> if the contrary **motion** of the **spirits** <note>Bacon refers to "animal spirits," which were thought to be the fluid or energy that moved through the nerves to trigger muscle action.</note> immediately before the **motion** we intend causes the **spirits**, as it were, to break forth with more force—just as **breath** that is drawn and held in comes out more forcibly. Also, in **throwing** <note>original: "Casting"</note> anything, the **arms** are first cast backward to make a greater **swing**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the pleasures and displeasures of the senses, especially hearing. 700
</margin>
Of **musical tones** and **unequal sounds**, we have spoken before; but regarding the **pleasure** and **displeasure** of the **senses**, we have not yet spoken so fully. **Harsh sounds**, such as a **saw** being sharpened, the **grinding** of one **stone** against another, or a **squeaking** or **shrieking noise**, cause a **shivering** or a sense of **dread** <note>original: "Horrour"; in this context, it refers to the physical sensation of bristling or shuddering.</note> in the **body** and set the **teeth** on edge. The **cause** is that the **objects** of the **ear** affect the **spirits** most directly with **pleasure** and **offense**. We see that there is no **color** that affects the **eye** with much **displeasure**. There are **sights** that are **horrible** because they trigger the **memory** of **things** that are **hateful** or **fearful**, but those same **things**, when painted, affect us very little. 

As for **smells**, **tastes**, and **touches**, they are **things** that affect us by a **physical involvement** <note>original: "Participation"</note> or **impact** <note>original: "Impulsion"</note> of the **object** upon the **body**. Thus, it is **sound** alone that affects us most directly and **incorporeally** <note>that is, without a physical, material substance touching the body</note>. This is most obvious in **music**, and in the **concords** and **discords** of **music**. For all **sounds**, whether they are sharp or flat, have a **roundness** and **equality** if they are sweet; and if they are harsh, they are **unequal**. For a **discord** itself is nothing but a **harshness** of **various sounds meeting**. 

It is true that **inequality**, if it is not dwelt upon but is merely passing, actually increases **sweetness**—as in the **vibration** <note>original: "Purling"</note> of a **twisted string**, the **hoarseness** <note>original: "Raucitie"</note> of a **trumpet**, the **nightingale-pipe** of a **regal** <note>A regal is a small portable pipe organ with reeds.</note>, and in a **discord** immediately resolving into a **concord**. But if you dwell upon it, it is **offensive**. Therefore, there are these three **levels** of **pleasing** and **displeasing** in sounds: **sweet sounds**, **discords**, and **harsh sounds** (which we call by various names, such as **shrieking** or **grating**, like the ones we are discussing now). As for the **setting** of the **teeth** on **edge**, we see clearly what a **connection** there is between the **teeth** and the **organ** of **hearing** when someone takes the **end** of a **bow** between the **teeth** and **strikes** the **string**.

# (Century 7)

<margin>
Experiment solitary regarding leaping.
693.
</margin>

A man leaps better with weights in his hands than without them. The cause is that the weight (if it is proportionate) strengthens the muscles <note>original: "Sinews"; in this context, it refers to the tendons and muscles responsible for movement.</note> by contracting them. Otherwise, where no contraction is needed, weight is a hindrance. As we see in horse races, people are careful to ensure that there is not the slightest extra weight on one horse compared to the other. In leaping with weights, the arms are first cast backward and then forward with as much force as possible, so that the motion of the weight forces the body to follow it. Additionally, the swing of the arms helps to lift the body into the air. The reason is that it helps the "spirits" <note>original: "Spirits"; Bacon refers to "animal spirits," which 17th-century science believed were invisible fluids or energies that moved through the nerves to trigger muscle action.</note>, as it were, to break forth with more force. We see this in anything that is to be shot: it must first be drawn back and then let go. And in throwing anything, the arms make a larger swing if they are first cast backward.

---

<margin>
Experiment solitary regarding the pleasure and displeasure of sounds, and "teeth on edge."
694.
</margin>

We have spoken before of musical tones and "Phrygian" sounds <note>original: "Phrigian Sounds"; an ancient Greek musical mode associated with excitement, passion, or agitation.</note>, and about the feelings they stir in the heart of man. But as for the unpleasantness of the sound of iron scraping and other such sounds—which we call "setting the teeth on edge"—it must be something of the same kind as what we discussed before regarding the trembling or shivering of the spirits immediately before movement, as seen in cold or fear. It is a phenomenon of such a nature that it immediately affects the spirits. We see that color does not have this effect; for even if a color is harsh or horrible, it does not work as immediately upon the spirits as sounds do. The reason is that sounds are a communication of the spirits of the object <note>Bacon suggests that sound is a physical transmission of the internal "vibration" or energy of an object to the listener’s own internal spirits.</note>. 

Although some say that the heart is affected by the sight of a Basilisk <note>A mythical reptile said to be able to kill with a single glance.</note>, and we see that some smells can do it. As for smells, even if they are very loathsome, it is a question of whether they affect the spirits directly or if it is only a secondary reaction of the stomach. But it is sound that immediately and non-physically <note>original: "incorporeally"</note> affects the spirit. This is most obvious in music and sounds. In music, it is hard to give a reason for the discord of sounds, or why they are sharp or flat, or to explain the sweetness or sharpness of a sound, or intervals like a fourth, fifth, or octave—all of which depend upon the physical proportions of the air. 

As for discord, it occurs because the ear is offended; a discord in music means the spirit does not rest upon the sound but passes on, as it lacks harmony <note>original: "Symmetry"</note>. This is like the ringing of a continuous sound, such as in a bell, or the jarring of a harp string. In a "nightingale" passage of music <note>original: "Nighting-gale of a Musick"; likely referring to a complex trill or a specific musical ornament intended to mimic a bird.</note> or in a pipe, when the notes fall into a harmony <note>original: "Concord"</note>, do you think the spirits rest on the single sound? No, they rest upon the whole. Therefore, there are three degrees of musical sounds: simple sounds (some sweet, some harsh); concords; and thirds, which we call "low falling" <note>likely referring to a musical resolution or cadence</note>. Regarding the sensation of "teeth on edge," we clearly see the connection between the teeth and the organ of hearing by placing the end of a musical bow between the teeth and striking the string.

<keywords>leaping, physics of motion, animal spirits, acoustics, music theory, discord, concords, teeth on edge, bone conduction, Basilisk</keywords>

<margin>*Solitary experiment regarding veins of medicinal earth.* 701</margin>
<image-desc>A square decorative drop cap letter 'T' featuring an engraving of a man sitting at a table, possibly a scholar or scribe.</image-desc>
There are *minerals* and *fossils* in great variety, but there are few *veins of medicinal earth*. The chief ones are *Terra Lemnia* <note>original: "Terra Lemnia"; Lemnian earth, a medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos</note>, *Terra Sigillata communis* <note>original: "Terra Sigillata communis"; common "sealed earth," so called because it was sold in cakes stamped with an official seal to prevent forgery</note>, and *Bolus Arminus* <note>original: "Bolus Arminus"; Armenian bole, a red clay used as an astringent</note>. Of these, *Terra Lemnia* is the primary one. Their *virtues* <note>original: "Vertues"; medicinal properties or powers</note> are for *curing wounds*, *staunching blood*, *stopping flows* <note>original: "Fluxes"</note> and *mucus* <note>original: "Rheumes"</note>, and *arresting the spreading of poison, infection*, and *decay* <note>original: "Putrifaction" </note>. Compared to all other *simples* <note>original: "Simples"; individual medicinal herbs or ingredients</note>, they have the most perfect and purest quality of *drying*, with little or no mixture of any other quality. Yet it is true that *Armenian bole* is the *coldest* of them, and *Terra Lemnia* is the *hottest*. For this reason, the island of *Lemnos*, where it is dug, was consecrated to *Vulcan* <note>the Roman god of fire</note> in the *ancient mythical ages* <note>original: "Old Fabulous Ages"</note>.

It is all the more noteworthy because there are few *plant-like substances* that grow deep within the sea; for they are sometimes gathered fifteen fathoms deep. And when they are

<margin>
Solitary experiment regarding *sea-fish* put in *freshwater*. 703
</margin>
It seems that *fish* accustomed to *saltwater* nevertheless enjoy *freshwater* more. We see that *salmons* and *smelts* love to enter *rivers*, even against the current. At the harbor of *Constantinople*, there are great *quantities* of *fish* coming from the *Black Sea* <note>original: "Euxine Sea"</note>; when they reach the *freshwater*, they become intoxicated <note>original: "inebriate"</note> and turn onto their *bellies*, so that you can catch them by hand. I suspect there has not been enough *experimentation* made with putting *sea-fish* into *freshwater ponds* and *pools*. This would be of great *use* and *pleasure*, as you could then have fresh fish at a good distance from the *sea*. Furthermore, the *fish* might taste better and might begin to breed. It is also said that *Colchester oysters*, which are kept in pits where the *tide* comes and goes (but where *freshwater* also reaches them when the *sea* recedes), become fatter and larger by that means.

<margin>
Solitary experiment regarding *attraction* by *similarity* <note>original: "Similitude"</note> of substance. 704
</margin>
The *Turkish bow* provides a very powerful *shot*; it has been known for an *arrow* to pierce a *steel target* or a piece of *brass* two inches thick. Even stranger, an *arrow* tipped with *wood* has been known to pierce through a piece of *wood* eight inches thick. It is certain that we once used *short arrows* for *sea-fights* called *sprights* <note>original: "Sprights"; short, heavy wooden bolts fired from muskets</note>, which had no metal heads, only sharpened *wood*. These were discharged from *muskets* and would pierce the sides of *ships* where a *bullet* would not. 

This depends upon one of the greatest *secrets* in all *nature*: that *similarity of substance* will cause *attraction* when a body is completely free from the *motion of gravity*. If gravity were removed, *lead* would draw *lead*, *gold* would draw *gold*, and *iron* would draw *iron* without the help of a *lodestone* <note>original: "Load-stone"; a natural magnet</note>. But this same *motion of weight* or *gravity* (which is purely a *motion* of *matter* and has no connection to the *form* or *type* of substance) kills the other *motion*, unless gravity itself is overcome by a violent *motion*, as in these *examples* of *arrows*. In such cases, the *motion of attraction* by *similarity of substance* begins to show itself. We shall handle this point of nature fully in its proper place.

They dissolve these in *water* to make their *drink*, because they are forbidden *wine* by *law*. I am very surprised that no *Englishman*, *Dutchman*, or *German* has set up a brewery in *Constantinople*, considering they have such a *quantity* of *barley*. For as for the...

Among the general sort of **men**, **frugality** may be the **cause** of **drinking water**; for it is no small **saving** to pay nothing for one's **drink**. But the wealthier **sort** might well afford the **cost**.
