<margin>
Experiments in association <note>original: "in Consort"</note> regarding sweat. 706
</margin>
**In** bathing in **hot water**, **sweat** (nevertheless) does not come out on the **parts** under the water. The **cause** is: first, because **sweat** is a **kind** of liquefaction <note>original: "Colliquation"; the process of melting or turning into liquid</note>. And that **kind** of **liquefaction** is not produced by either an **overly dry heat** or an **overly moist heat**. For **over-moisture** somewhat extinguishes the **heat**—as we see that even **hot water** quenches **fire**—and **over-dry heat** shuts the **pores**. Therefore, **men** will sooner **sweat** when covered before the **sun** or **fire** than if they stood **naked**. And **earthen bottles** filled with **hot water** provoke a more refined <note>original: "daintily"</note> **sweat** in **bed** than **hot bricks** <note>original: "Brick-bats"</note>. Secondly, **hot water** causes **evaporation** from the **skin**, so it uses up the **matter** in those **parts** under the water before it can be released as **sweat**. Again, **sweat** comes more plentifully if the **heat** is increased by **degrees** than if it is greatest at first, or remains equal. The **cause** is that the **pores** are better opened by a **gentle heat** than by a more **violent** one; and by their opening, the **sweat** issues more abundantly. Therefore, **physicians** may do well when they provoke **sweat** in **bed** by using **bottles** containing a **decoction** of **sweat-inducing herbs** <note>original: "Sudorificke"</note> in **hot water**, to create two **degrees** of **heat** in the **bottles**: laying the **less heated** one in the **bed** first, and after half an hour, the **more heated** one.

<margin>
707
</margin>
**Sweat** is **salt** in **taste**. The **cause** is that the **part** of the **nourishment** which is **fresh** and **sweet** turns into **blood** and **flesh**; and the **sweat** is only that **part** which is **separated** and **excreted** <note>original: "Excerned"</note>. **Raw blood** also has some **saltiness**, more so than **flesh**, because the **absorption** <note>original: "Assimilation"</note> into **flesh** is not without a small and subtle **excretion** from the **blood**.

<margin>
708
</margin>
**Sweat** comes forth more from the **upper parts** of the **body** than the **lower**. The **reason** is because those **parts** are more replenished with **spirits** <note>original: "Spirits"; in Early Modern medicine, these were vital fluids or gases that powered the body's functions</note>; and the **spirits** are what put forth **sweat**. Besides, they are less **fleshy**, and **sweat** issues (chiefly) out of the **parts** that are less **fleshy** and more **dry**, such as the **forehead** and **breast**.

<margin>
709
</margin>
**Men sweat** more in **sleep** than when **waking**; and yet **sleep** stays other **flows** <note>original: "Fluxions"</note> rather than causing them, such as **mucus** <note>original: "Rheumes"</note>, **looseness** of the **body**, etc. The **cause** is that in **sleep**, the **heat** and **spirits** naturally move inwards and rest there. But when they are once collected within, the **heat** becomes more **violent** and **irritated**, and thereby expels **sweat**.

<margin>
710
</margin>
**Cold sweats** are (many times) **fatal** <note>original: "Mortall"</note> and near **death**; and they are always **bad** and **suspect**, as in **great fears**, **hypochondriacal conditions** <note>original: "Passions"</note>, etc. The **cause** is that **cold sweats** come from a **relaxation** or **failure** <note>original: "Forsaking"</note> of the **spirits**.

...spirits, through which the moisture of the **body**—which **heat** kept firm in the different **parts**—separates and flows out.

<margin>711</margin>
In those **diseases** where the body cannot be cleared through **sweat**, **sweating** is a bad sign and should be stopped instead; such as in **diseases** of the **lungs** and diarrhea <note>original: "Fluxes of the Belly"</note>. However, in those **diseases** that are expelled by **sweat**, it provides ease and relief, as in fevers <note>original: "Agues"</note>, plagues <note>original: "Pestilences"</note>, and so on. The cause is that **sweat** in the latter group is partly a "crisis" <note>original: "Criticall"; meaning a turning point in the disease where the body attempts to purge the infection</note> and sends out the **matter** that is harmful. But in the former group, it either comes from the struggle of the **spirits** (which shows they are **overwhelmed**) or from a "sympathetic reaction" <note>original: "Motion of Consent"</note>, where **nature**—unable to expel the **disease** from where it is specifically located—moves to a general **expulsion** across the entire **body**.

<margin>Solitary experiment regarding the glow-worm. 712</margin>
The nature of the **glow-worm** has not been well-observed until now. We see this much: that they breed mainly in the **hottest months** of **summer**, and that they do not breed in **open fields** <note>original: "Champaigne"</note>, but rather in **bushes** and **hedges**. From this, it may be understood that their **spirit** is very delicate and can only be refined by **summer heats**; and also, because of its **delicacy**, it evaporates easily. In **Italy** and hotter countries, there is a **fly** they call a *lucciola* <note>original: "Lucciola"; the Italian word for firefly</note> that shines just as the **glow-worm** does, and it may be that it is a **flying glow-worm**. However, that **fly** is found mostly on **fens** and **marshes**. Yet the two previous **observations** still hold: they are only seen in the heat of **summer**, and **sedge** or other greenery in the **fens** provides as much **shade** as **bushes** do. It may be that the **glow-worms** of colder countries do not develop enough to grow wings.

<margin>Experiments in association regarding the impressions which the emotions of the mind make upon the body. 713</margin>
**Emotions** <note>original: "Passions of the Minde"</note> create the following **effects** <note>original: "Impressions"</note> on the **body**. **Fear** causes **paleness**, **trembling**, **hair standing on end**, **starting** <note>a sudden involuntary jump or flinch</note>, and **screeching** <note>original: "Skritching"</note>. **Paleness** is caused because the **blood** runs inward to help the **heart**. **Trembling** is caused because the **spirits** flee inward, leaving the **outer parts** abandoned and unsupported. **Hair standing upright** is caused because the **pores** of the **skin** shut tight, forcing the **hair**—which usually lies at an angle—to **rise**. **Starting** is both a recognition of the **thing** feared (in which case it is a **shrinking motion**) and also an investigation at the start into what the **matter** is (in which case it is a **rising motion**). Therefore, when a **man** wants to listen suddenly to **anything**, he **starts**; for **starting** is an **alerting** <note>original: "Erection"</note> of the **spirits** to pay attention. **Screeching** is an **urge** <note>original: "Appetite"</note> to **expel** whatever has suddenly shocked the **spirits**. It should be noted that many **motions**, though they may be useless for expelling what hurts us, are nonetheless **attempts** by **nature** and cause **sympathetic reactions** <note>original: "Motions by Consent"</note>, such as **groaning** or **crying out** in **pain**.

<margin>714</margin>
**Grief** and **pain** cause **sighing**, **sobbing**, **groaning**, **screaming**, and **roaring**; **tears**, **facial distortions**, **grinding** of the **teeth**, and **sweating**. **Sighing** is caused by drawing in a larger **amount** of **breath** to refresh the **heart** that is struggling—much like taking a long **drink** when one is thirsty.

Sobbing is the same thing, only stronger. *Groaning*, *screaming*, and *roaring* are caused by an *appetite for expulsion* <note>original: "Appetite of Expulsion"; an internal biological drive to force something out</note>, as has been said. For when the *spirits* <note>original: "Spirits"; in 17th-century science, these were subtle fluids or life-forces that governed bodily functions and emotions</note> cannot expel the *thing* that hurts, in their struggle to do so by a *sympathetic reaction* <note>original: "Motion of Consent"</note>, they expel the *voice* instead. This occurs when the *spirits* yield and give up resisting; for if one constantly resists *pain*, he will not groan. *Tears* are caused by a *contraction* of the *spirits* of the *brain*. This *contraction* consequently squeezes <note>original: "astringeth"</note> the *moisture* of the *brain*, thereby sending *tears* into the *eyes*. This *contraction* or *compression* also causes the *wringing of the hands*; for *wringing* is a *gesture of expression*—literally a squeezing out—of *moisture*. The *distorting of the face* is caused by a *struggle* <note>original: "Contention"</note>, first to bear and resist, and then to expel. This makes the facial features knit together first, and afterwards open. *Grinding of the teeth* is likewise caused by a *gathering* and *pressing together* <note>original: "Serring"</note> of the *spirits* to resist, which makes the *teeth* also set hard against one another. *Sweating* is also a *compound motion* caused by the *labor* of the *spirits*, first to resist and then to expel.

<margin>715</margin>
*Joy* causes a *cheerfulness* and *vigor* in the *eyes*, as well as *singing*, *leaping*, *dancing*, and sometimes *tears*. All these are the *effects* of the *expansion* <note>original: "Dilatation"</note> and *coming forth of the spirits into the outward parts* of the body, which makes them more *lively* and *active*. We know it has been seen that *excessive, sudden joy* has caused *instant death*, occurring when the *spirits* spread so much that they could not retreat again. As for *tears*, they are the *effects* of the *compression* of the *moisture* of the *brain* upon the *expansion* of the *spirits*. For the *compression* of the *spirits* works to squeeze out the *moisture* of the *brain* by *sympathetic reaction*, as was said regarding *grief*. But in *joy*, it works differently: namely <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note>, by the *pushing forward* <note>original: "Propulsion"</note> of the *moisture* when the *spirits* expand and occupy more *room*.

<margin>716</margin>
*Anger* causes *paleness* in some and the *shifting* <note>original: "Going and Comming"</note> of *color* in *others*. It also causes *trembling* in some, as well as *swelling*, *foaming* at the *mouth*, *stamping*, and *clenching of the fist*. *Paleness* and the *shifting* of *color* are caused by the *burning* of the *spirits* around the *heart*; to refresh themselves, they call in more *spirits* from the *outer parts* of the body. If the *paleness* occurs alone, without the *color* returning, it is commonly joined with some *fear*. But in many people, there is no *paleness* at all, but on the contrary, *redness* in the *cheeks* and *gills* <note>original: "Gils"; likely referring to the neck or lower face</note>. This is caused by the *sending forth* of the *spirits* in a *desire* for *revenge*. *Trembling* in *anger* is likewise caused by a *calling in* of the *spirits* and commonly happens when *anger* is joined with *fear*. *Swelling* is caused both by an *expansion* of the *spirits* through *overheating* and by a *liquefaction* or *boiling* of the *humors* <note>original: "Humours"; the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament</note> because of it. *Foaming* at the *mouth* is from the same cause, being a literal *boiling over* <note>original: "Ebullition"</note>. *Stamping* and *clenching of the fist* are caused by an *imagining of the act of revenge*.

These *effects* arise from the same causes as *trembling* and *shuddering* <note>original: "Horrour"</note>: namely, from the *retreating* of the *spirits*, but to a lesser degree. Although the *blushing* will be seen across the whole *chest* if it is *bare*, yet that is only on its *way* to the *face*. <margin>719</margin> *Pity* sometimes causes *tears* and a *turning* or *cast* of the *eye* aside. *Tears* come from the same *cause* as they do in *grief*, for *pity* is simply *grief* on someone else's *behalf*. The *turn* of the *eye* is a *gesture* of *aversion*, or a *reluctance* to behold the *object* of *pity*.

<margin>720</margin> *Wonder* causes *astonishment*, or an *immovable posture* of the *body*, the *casting up* of the *eyes* to *heaven*, and the *lifting up* of the *hands*. *Astonishment* is caused by the *fixing* of the *mind* upon one *object* of *thought*, whereby it does not wander or move about as it usually does. In wonder, the *spirits* do not fly away as they do in *fear*, but only settle and are made less likely to move. As for the *casting up* of the *eyes* and the *lifting up* of the *hands*, it is a *kind* of *appeal* to the *Deity*, who is the *author*, by *power* and *providence*, of *strange wonders*.

<margin>721</margin> *Laughing* causes an *expansion* of the *mouth* and *lips*; a *continued expulsion* of the *breath* with a loud *noise*, which creates the *sound* <note>original: "Interiection"</note> of *laughing*; a *shaking* of the *chest* and *sides*; and the *watering* of the *eyes* if it is *violent* and *continued*. In this, it must first be understood that *laughing* is scarcely (properly speaking) an *emotion* <note>original: "Passion"</note>, but has its *source* in the *intellect*; for in *laughing*, there always precedes a *thought* <note>original: "Conceit"</note> of something *ridiculous*. Therefore, it is *unique* to *humans*. Secondly, the *cause* of *laughing* is only a *light touch* of the *spirits*, and not as deep an *impression* as in other *emotions*. Therefore (which has no *connection* with the *emotions* of the *mind*), it is triggered—and with great intensity—only by *tickling* certain *parts* of the *body*. We see that *men*, even in a *grieved state* of *mind*, still cannot sometimes *refrain* from *laughing*. Thirdly, it is always joined with some *degree* of *delight*. Therefore, *exhilaration* has some *connection* with *joy*, though it is a much *lighter motion*; "True joy is a serious thing" <note>original: "Res seuera est verum Gaudium." From Seneca the Younger, suggesting that deep joy is profound and steady, unlike the light amusement of laughter.</note>. Fourthly, the *object* of laughter is *deformity*, *absurdity*, *mischievous tricks* <note>original: "Shrewd Turnes"</note>, and the like. <header>Century VIII.</header>

General notes give some light. For the expansion <note>original: "Dilatation"</note> of the mouth and lips, the continued expulsion of the breath and voice, and the shaking of the chest and sides—they all proceed from the expansion of the spirits; especially when it is sudden. Likewise, the watering of the eyes (as has been formerly touched upon where we spoke of the tears of joy and grief) is an effect of the expansion of the spirits. As for suddenness, it is a great part of the matter: for we see that any clever trick <note>original: "Shrew'd Turne"</note> that happens to someone else, or any deformity, etc., moves us to laughter in the instant; which after a little time it does not. So we cannot laugh at anything after it is stale, but only while it is new. Even in tickling, if you tickle the sides and give warning, or use a hard or continuous touch, it does not move laughter as much.

<margin>722</margin>
Lust causes a brightness <note>original: "Flagrancie," referring to a glowing or flushing redness</note> in the eyes, and priapism <note>a prolonged physical arousal</note>. The cause of both is that in lust, the sight and the touch are the things desired; and therefore the spirits travel to those parts which are most affected. Note well in general (for great use may be made of this observation) that the spirits, in all passions <note>strong emotions</note>, always travel most to the parts that labor most or are most affected. As in the last example mentioned, they travel to the eyes and sexual <note>original: "Venereous"</note> parts; in fear and anger, to the heart; in shame, to the face; and in mild dislikes, to the head.

It has been observed by the ancients, and is still believed, that the sperm of drunk men is unfruitful. The cause is that it is over-moistened and lacks thickness <note>original: "Spissitude"</note>. And we have a humorous saying that those who go drunk to bed father daughters.

Drunk men are overcome with a plain defect or lack of voluntary motion. They reel; they tremble; they cannot stand, nor speak strongly. The cause is that the spirits of the wine overwhelm the animal spirits <note>the fine fluids believed to flow through the nerves to control movement and sensation</note> and occupy part of the place where they reside; and so they make them too weak to move. Therefore, drunk men are prone to falling asleep. Opiates and sedatives <note>original: "Stupefactiues"</note> (such as poppy, henbane, hemlock, etc.) induce a kind of drunkenness by the heaviness <note>original: "Grossenesse"</note> of their vapor, just as wine does by the quantity of its vapor. Besides, they rob the animal spirits of their substance <note>original: "Matter"</note> by which they are nourished; for the spirits of the wine prey upon it as much as they do, and so they make the spirits less supple and less able to move.

<margin>725</margin>
Drunk men imagine everything turns round; they imagine also that things come toward them; they see not well things far off; those things that they see near at hand they see out of their place; and sometimes they see things double. The cause of the imagination that things turn round is that the spirits themselves turn, being compressed by the vapor of the wine (for any liquid body upon compression turns, as we see in water). It is all the same to the sight whether the visual spirits move, or the object moves, or the medium <note>the air or space between the eye and the object</note> moves. And we see that long spinning around produces the same illusion.

<header>### Natural History</header>

The cause of the imagination that **things are coming toward them** is because the **visual spirits** <note>subtle fluids within the body believed to enable sight</note> themselves draw back; this makes the **object** seem to approach. Besides, when people see **things turning around** and **moving**, **fear** makes them think the objects are coming upon them. The **cause** for not being able to see **things far away** is the **weakness of the spirits**; for in every **migraine** <note>original: "Megrim"</note> or **vertigo**, there is a **darkening of vision** <note>original: "Obtenebration"</note> joined with an **appearance of spinning**; we see this also in lighter types of **fainting** <note>original: "Swounings"</note>. The cause of **seeing things out of their place** is the **refraction of the visual spirits**; for the **vapor** acts as an **uneven medium**, and it is like the **sight of things out of place in water**. The cause of **seeing things double** is the **swift and restless motion of the spirits** (being **oppressed**) moving back and forth. For (as was said before), the **motion of the visual spirits** and the **motion of the object** create the same **appearances**. Regarding the **swift motion of the object**, we see that if you flick <note>original: "fillip"</note> a **lute string**, it appears double or triple.

<margin>726</margin>
Men are sooner **drunk** with **small sips** <note>original: "Draughts"</note> than with **large ones**. Furthermore, **sugared wine** intoxicates <note>original: "inebriateth"</note> less than **pure wine**. The **cause** of the **former** is that the **wine** does not descend as fast to the **bottom** of the **stomach**, but stays longer in the **upper part** of the **stomach** and sends **vapors** faster to the **head**; therefore, it intoxicates sooner. For the same reason, **bread soaked in wine** <note>original: "Sops in Wine"</note> (**quantity for quantity**) intoxicates more than **wine** by itself. The **cause** of the **latter** is that the **sugar** does **thicken** <note>original: "inſpiſſate"</note> the **spirits** of the **wine** and makes them not so easy to turn into **vapor**. Nay, further, it is thought to be a **remedy** against **intoxication** if **sugared wine** is taken after **pure wine**. The same **effect** is produced by either **oil** or **milk** taken after much **drinking**.

The use of **wine** in **dry** and **wasted** <note>original: "Consumed"</note> **bodies** is harmful; in **moist** and **full bodies**, it is good. The **cause** is that the **spirits** of the **wine** prey upon the **"dew"** or **radical moisture** <note>the vital fluid thought to sustain life and heat in the body</note> (as they call it) of the **body**, and deceive the **animal spirits** <note>the subtle fluids responsible for sensation and movement</note>. But where there is **enough moisture**, or a **surplus** of it, **wine** helps to digest and **dry out** <note>original: "desiccate"</note> the **moisture**.

They breed chiefly in the **spring** because then there is both **dew** and **leaves**. They commonly breed when the **east winds** have blown frequently. <margin>Solitary experiment concerning **Spanish flies** <note>original: "Cantharides"</note>. 729</margin>
**Spanish flies** <note>original: "Cantharides"</note> are bred from a **worm** or **caterpillar**, but they are specific to certain **fruit trees**, such as the **fig tree**, the **pine tree**, and the **wild briar**. All of these bear **sweet fruit**, and fruit that has a kind of secret **sting** or **sharpness**. For the **fig** has a **milky sap** <note>original: "Milke"</note> in it that is both **sweet** and **corrosive**. The **pinecone** <note>original: "Pine-Apple"</note> has a **kernel** that is **strong** and **cleansing** <note>original: "Abstersive"</note>. The **fruit of the briar** <note>likely rosehips</note> is said to cause **sores** <note>original: "Scabbed"</note> in **children** or those who eat them. Therefore, it is no wonder that **Spanish flies** have such a **corrosive** and **blistering** <note>original: "Cauterizing"</note> **quality**, for no other **insect** is bred from such **potent material** <note>original: "Duller Matter"</note>. The **body** of the **Spanish fly** is brightly colored, and it may be that delicately colored **dragonflies** also have some **corrosive quality**.

<margin>Experiments in combination concerning **fatigue** <note>original: "Lassitude"</note>. 730</margin>
**Fatigue** is remedied by **bathing** or **anointing** the body with **oil** and **warm water**. The **cause** is that all **fatigue** is a kind of **tension** <note>original: "Contasion," likely meaning contraction or pressure</note> and **compression** of the **body parts**. **Bathing** and **anointing** provide **relaxation** or **softening** <note>original: "Emolition"</note>. A **mixture of oil and water** is better than either alone, because **water enters** the **pores** more easily, and **oil softens** better after it has entered. It is also found that the **smoking of tobacco** helps to relieve and discharge **fatigue**. The **reason** for this is partly because, by **cheering** or **comforting** the **internal spirits**, it opens the **parts** that were **compressed** or **bruised**. Chiefly, however, it refreshes the **spirits** through its **numbing effect** <note>original: "Opiate Vertue"</note>, and so discharges **weariness**, just as **sleep** does.

<margin>731</margin>
In **walking up a hill**, the **knees** will become most weary; in **walking down a hill**, the **thighs** will. The **cause** is that, when a person **walks up a hill** and **lifts their feet**, the **weight of the body** bears most upon the **knees**; but in **walking down a hill**, it bears upon the **thighs**.

Lying down, not *flat* <note>original: "Erect"</note> but in a *curved* <note>original: "Hollow"</note> position (as one might arrange a bed), or with the *legs gathered up*, is a more *wholesome* posture for the body. We see that for those with *weak stomachs*, raising the legs high—with the knees almost to the mouth—helps and provides comfort. We see also that *galley slaves*, despite their *misery* in other respects, are commonly fat and fleshy. The reason is that the *stomach* is supported somewhat while *sitting*, whereas it is suspended while *standing* or *walking*. Therefore, to *prolong life*, it is good to choose those *exercises* where the *limbs* move more than the *stomach* and *belly*, such as *rowing* or *sawing* while *seated*.

The *cause* is that the *vapors* <note>historical medical term for internal gases or humors thought to affect health</note> gathered during *sitting* are sent flying more up into the *head* by the *sudden motion*.

</margin>

The *cause* is that the *compression* of that *part* does not allow the *spirits* <note>historical term for the vital forces or signals thought to travel through the nerves</note> to have free *access*. Therefore, when we release the pressure, we feel a *stinging* or *pricking*, which is the *re-entry* of the *spirits*.

Solitary experiment concerning plague years.

</margin>

The same *prediction* <note>original: "Prognosticke"</note> holds true, as mentioned before, if you find *worms* in *oak galls* <note>original: "Oake-Apples"</note>. This is because the state of the *air* reveals itself more subtly in these *things* than it does to *human senses*.

<margin>Solitary Experiment concerning medicines that condense and relieve the spirits. 738</margin>
In *Turkey*, they have a *drink* called *coffee* <note>original: "Coffa"</note>, made from a *berry* of the same name. It is as *black* as *soot* and has a *strong scent*, but it is not *aromatic*. They take it beaten into a powder and mixed with *water*, drinking it as *hot* as they can endure. They sit and drink it in their *coffee-houses*, which are similar to our *taverns*. This *drink* comforts the *brain* and *heart*, and helps *digestion*. Certainly, this *coffee berry*; the *betel root* and *leaf*; the *tobacco leaf*; and the *tears of the poppy* (*opium*), which the *Turks* take in great quantities (supposing it expels all fear), all *condense* the *spirits* and make them *strong* and *lively* <note>original: "Aleger"; from the French *allègre*, meaning brisk or cheerful.</note>. 

However, it seems they are consumed in different ways. *Coffee* and *opium* are swallowed; *tobacco* is taken only as *smoke*; and *betel* is merely chewed <note>original: "champed"</note> in the *mouth* with a little *lime*. It is likely there are more such substances if they were properly identified and refined. *Investigate* <note>original: "Quære"</note> the effects of *henbane seed*; *mandrake*; *saffron* (both *root* and *flower*); *Indian leaf* <note>original: "Folium Indum"; likely Malabathrum, an aromatic leaf used in ancient medicine</note>; *ambergris*; *Assyrian amomum* <note>original: "Assyrian Amomum"; an ancient spice, possibly a type of cardamom</note>, if it can be obtained; and the *scarlet powder* which they call *kermes* <note>original: "Kermez"</note>; and generally all such things that intoxicate <note>original: "inebriate"</note> and induce *sleep*. Note that *tobacco* is not taken as a *root* or *seed*, which are always more potent than *leaves*.

<margin>Solitary Experiment concerning paintings of the body. 739</margin>
The *Turks* have a *black powder* made of a *mineral* called *kohl* <note>original: "Alcohole"; referring to the fine mineral powder used as eyeliner, not liquid alcohol</note>. With a fine, long *brush* <note>original: "Pencill"</note>, they apply it under their *eyelids*, which colors them *black*; this makes the *white* of the *eye* appear even *whiter*. With the same *powder*, they also color the *hairs* of their *eyelids* and their *eyebrows*, which they draw into *curved arches*. You will find that *Xenophon* <note>Greek historian, c. 430–354 BC</note> mentions that the *Medes* <note>An ancient Iranian people</note> used to paint their *eyes*. The *Turks* also use the same *tincture* to color the *hair* of their *heads* and *beards black*. Many among us who have grown *gray*, yet wish to appear *young*, find ways to make their *hair black* by combing it (so they say) with a *leaden comb* or something similar. 

As for the *Chinese*, who have a sallow complexion (being *olive-colored* <note>original: "Olive-ster"</note>), they paint their *cheeks scarlet*—especially their *king* and *nobles* <note>original: "Grandes"</note>. Generally, *barbarous people* who go *naked* do not only paint themselves, but they also prick and cut <note>original: "pounce and raze"</note> their *skin* so that the *painting* cannot be removed, creating permanent patterns. So do the *West Indians* <note>Indigenous peoples of the Americas</note>; and so did the *ancient Picts* and *Britons*. It seems that *men* would have the *colors* of *birds' feathers* if they knew how; or at least, they will have *vibrant skins* instead of *vibrant clothes*.

I am of the opinion that the *use* of it, as it was practiced by the *Romans*, was harmful to health because it made the *body soft* and prone to wasting away. For the *Turks*, it is more appropriate because of their *drink*ing...

<margin>
Solitary Experiment concerning the marbling <term>original: "Chamoletting"</term> of paper.
741
</margin>

The *Turks* have a clever art of *marbling* <term>original: "Chamoletting"; the process of creating a wavy, veined pattern like camlet fabric</term> *paper*, which is not in use with us. They take various *oil-based colors* and put them separately (in drops) upon *water*; they stir the *water* lightly and then wet their *paper* (it being of some thickness) with it; and the *paper* will be *waved* and *veined* like *camlet* or *marble*.

Solitary Experiment concerning cuttlefish ink.
742
</margin>

It is somewhat strange that the *blood* of all *birds*, *beasts*, and *fishes* should be of a *red color*, and only the *blood* of the *cuttlefish* should be as *black* as *ink*. One would think that the *cause* must be the *high cooking* <term>original: "concoction"; here referring to the internal heat or digestive processing of the blood</term> of that *blood*; for we see in ordinary *puddings* that *boiling* turns *blood* to *black*; and the *cuttlefish* is considered a delicate *meat* and is much in demand.

<margin>
Solitary Experiment concerning the increase of weight in earth.
743
</margin>

It is reported by credible sources that if you take *earth* from land adjoining the *River Nile* and preserve it in such a manner that it neither becomes wet nor is wasted, and weigh it daily, it will not alter in *weight* until the seventeenth of *June*, which is the day when the *river* begins to rise; and then it will grow more *heavy* <note>original: "ponderous"</note> until the *river* reaches its height. If this is true, it can only be caused by the *air*, which begins to *condense* and so turns within that small amount of *soil* into a degree of *moisture*, which produces *weight*. Similarly, it has been observed that *tobacco*, when cut and weighed and then dried by the fire, loses weight; and afterward, being laid in the open *air*, it recovers *weight* again. And it would seem that as soon as the *river* begins to increase, the whole *body* of the *air* thereabouts undergoes a change: for (which is more strange) it is credibly affirmed that upon that very day when the *river* first rises, great *plagues* in *Cairo* usually suddenly end <note>original: "breake vp"</note>.

<margin>
Experiments in concert concerning sleep.
744
</margin>

Those who are very *cold*, and especially in their *feet*, cannot get to *sleep*. The *cause* may be because *sleep* requires *free respiration*, which *cold* shuts in and hinders; for we see that in great *colds*, one can scarcely draw his *breath*. Another *cause* may be that *cold* calls the *spirits* <note>In 17th-century medicine, "spirits" were invisible fluids that circulated through the body to maintain life and sensation.</note> to help the body; and therefore they cannot so easily close and gather together in the *head*, which is always required for *sleep*. For the same *cause*, *pain* and *noise* hinder *sleep*; and *darkness* (on the contrary) furthers *sleep*.

# Century VIII.

<margin>745</margin>
Certain noises (which we mentioned in the 112th Experiment) help sleep; such as the blowing of the wind, the trickling of water, the humming of bees, soft singing, reading, and so on. The cause is that these sounds induce a gentle focus in the spirits <note>original: "Spirits"; referring to the "vital spirits," a historical concept of the fluid or energy that animated the body and mind</note>. Whatever engages the attention without requiring too much effort calms the natural and wandering movement of the spirits.

<margin>746</margin>
Sleep nourishes, or at least preserves, bodies for a long time without other nourishment. Animals that sleep in winter (as has been noted of wild bears) grow very fat during their sleep, even though they eat nothing. Bats have been found in ovens and other hollow, enclosed places, matted one upon another; therefore, it is likely that they sleep during the winter and eat nothing. We should ask <note>original: *Quære*</note> whether bees do not sleep all winter and save their honey? Butterflies and other flies do not only sleep but lie as if dead all winter; and yet, with a little heat from the sun or a fire, they revive again. A dormouse, both in winter and summer, will sleep for several days together and eat nothing.

### Experiments in a Series regarding Teeth and Hard Substances in the Bodies of Living Creatures.

<margin>747</margin>
To restore **teeth** in old age would be one of the great works of nature <note>original: *Magnalia Naturæ*; Latin for "great works of nature," referring to extraordinary or miraculous scientific achievements</note>. It is worth considering. However, the **nature** of the **teeth** deserves to be investigated as much as the other **parts** of **living creatures' bodies**.

There are **five parts** in the **bodies** of **living creatures** that are of a **hard substance**: the **skull**, the **teeth**, the **bones**, the **horns**, and the **nails**. The greatest **quantity** of continuous **hard substance** is found toward the **head**. For there is the **skull**, which is one entire **bone**; there are the **teeth**; there are the **jawbones** <note>original: "maxillary bones"</note>; there is the **hard bone** that is the **instrument** of **hearing**; and from there the **horns** grow. Thus, the **construction** of **living creatures' bodies** is like the **building** of a **timber-framed house**, where the **walls** and other **parts** have **columns** and **beams**, but the **roof**—in the better sort of **houses**—is all **tile**, or **lead**, or **stone**. As for **birds**, they have three other **hard substances** unique to them: the **bill**, which is made of a **material** similar to **teeth** (for no **birds** have **teeth**); the **shell** of their **eggs**; and their **quills**. As for their **spur**, it is merely a **nail**. However, no **living creatures** that have very hard shells (such as **oysters**, **cockles**, **mussels**, **scallops**, **crabs**, **lobsters**, **crayfish**, **shrimps**, and especially the **tortoise**) have **bones** inside them, but only little pieces of **gristle**.

<margin>749</margin>
**Bones**, after reaching full **growth**, stay the same size <note>original: "continue at a stay"</note>; and so does the **skull**. **Horns**, in some creatures, are cast and renewed. **Teeth** stay the same size, except for wearing down. As for **nails**, they grow continually. **Bills** and **beaks** will overgrow and are sometimes shed, as in **eagles** and **parrots**.

Most of the **hard substances** are found at the **extremities** of the **body**, such as the **skull**, **horns**, **teeth**, **nails**, and **beaks**. Only the **bones** are more **internal** and covered with **flesh**. As for the **internal organs**, they are all without **bones**, except that a **bone** is sometimes found in the **heart** of a **stag** <note>The *os cordis* is a real bony structure found in the hearts of some large mammals like deer</note>; and perhaps in some other **creature**.

<page-num>188</page-num>
# Natural History:

<margin>750</margin>
The skull has *brains* within it, acting as a kind of *marrow*. The *backbone* has one kind of *marrow*, which has an affinity with the *brain*; and other *bones* of the *body* have another. The *jawbones* do not have a separate *marrow*, but a small amount of *pulp* of *marrow* diffused throughout. *Teeth* likewise are thought to have a kind of *marrow* diffused within them, which causes *sensation* and *pain*; but it is likely *sinew* <note>original: "sinnew"; in this context, it refers to nerves, which were often called sinews</note> instead. This is because *marrow* has no *sensation*, no more than *blood* does. *Horn* is the same throughout, and so is the *fingernail*.

<margin>751</margin>
No other *hard substances* have *sensation* except the *teeth*. The *teeth* have *sensation* not only of *pain*, but also of *cold*. However, we will leave the investigation of other *hard substances* to their respective *places* and now inquire only regarding the *teeth*.

<margin>752</margin>
The *teeth* in *humans* are of three kinds: *sharp*, such as the *front teeth*; *broad*, such as the *back teeth* (which we call the *molar teeth* or *grinders*); and *pointed teeth*, or *canine teeth*, which are between both. There have been some *men* who had their *teeth* undivided, as if made of one whole *bone* with some small *marks* in the *place* of the *division*, as *Pyrrhus* <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus (c. 319–272 BC), a Greek king said to have a single bone in place of teeth</note> had. Some *creatures* have *overly long* or *out-growing teeth*, which we call *fangs* or *tusks*, such as *boars*, *pikes*, *salmon*, and *dogs* (though smaller). Some *living creatures* have *teeth set against teeth*, such as *humans* and *horses*; and some have *teeth*—especially their *main teeth*—notched into one another like *saws*, such as *lions* and *dogs*. Some *fish* have several *rows* of *teeth* in the *roofs* of their *mouths*, such as *pikes*, *salmon*, *trout*, and so on, and many more in *saltwater*. *Snakes* and other *serpents* have *venomous teeth*, which are sometimes mistaken for their *sting*.

<margin>753</margin>
No *beast* that has *horns* has *upper teeth*; and no *beast* that has *teeth* above lacks them below. Yet, if they are of the same kind, it does not follow that if the *hard matter* does not go into the *upper teeth*, it will go into the *horns*; nor does it happen conversely <note>original: *è converso*</note>. For *does* <note>female deer</note>, which have no *horns*, also have no *upper teeth*.

<margin>754</margin>
*Horses*, at three years old, put forth a *tooth* which people call the *colt's tooth*. At four years old, the *mark-tooth* appears, which has a *hole* as big as a *pea* inside it. That hole wears shorter and shorter every year until, at eight years old, the *tooth* is smooth and the *hole* is gone. Then they say *that the mark is out of the horse's mouth* <note>a phrase meaning the horse's age can no longer be determined by its teeth</note>.

<margin>755</margin>
The *teeth* of *humans* grow first when the *child* is about a year and a half old. Then they shed them, and new ones arrive around seven years old. However, several people have *wisdom teeth* <note>original: "back-ward teeth"</note> come forth at *twenty*, or even *thirty* or *forty*. One should inquire <note>original: *quære*</note> into the manner of their emergence. They tell a *story* of the old *Countess of Desmond*, who lived until she was 140 years old, saying that she *grew new teeth* <note>original: *dentire*</note> twice or thrice, shedding her old *teeth* and having others come in their *place*.

<margin>756</margin>
*Teeth* are greatly harmed by *sweets* <note>original: "sweet-meats"</note>, by *cosmetics containing mercury* <note>original: "painting with mercury"</note>, by *things that are too hot*, by *things that are too cold*, and by *fluids* <note>original: "rheumes"; referring to inflammation or discharge</note>. The *pain* of the *teeth* is one of the sharpest of *pains*.

And whether *children* might be given some wash or something to make their *teeth better* and *stronger*? Coral is currently used as a help for the *teeth* of children.

Experiments in coordination, concerning the generation and bearing of living creatures in the womb.

Some living creatures reproduce only at certain *seasons* of the *year*, such as *deer, sheep, wild rabbits* <note>original: "conneyes"</note>, etc., and most types of *birds* and *fishes*. Others reproduce at *any time* of the *year*, such as *humans* and all *domestic creatures*, like *horses, hogs, dogs, cats*, etc. The *cause* of *generation* at *all seasons* seems to be *fullness*, for *reproduction* <note>original: "generation"</note> comes from <term>redundance</term> <note>an overflow or excess of nutrients and vital spirits in the body</note>. This *fullness* arises from two *causes*: either from the *nature* of the *creature* (if it is *hot*, *moist*, and <term>sanguine</term> <note>the humor associated with blood, characterized by a warm and social temperament</note>), or from an *abundance of food*. Regarding the first cause, *humans, horses, dogs*, etc., which breed at all *seasons*, are full of *heat* and *moisture*. *Doves* are the fullest of *heat* and *moisture* among *birds*, and therefore they breed often; the *tame dove* breeds almost continually. But *deer* are a <term>melancholy, dry creature</term> <note>referring to the humor of "black bile," associated with a cold, dry, and fearful temperament</note>, as is shown by their *fearfulness* and the *hardness* of their *flesh*. *Sheep* are a *cold creature*, as shown by their *mildness* and the fact that they seldom *drink*. Most types of *birds* are of a dry substance compared to *beasts*. *Fishes* are cold. Regarding the second *cause*, *fullness of food*: *humans, cows* <note>original: "kine"</note>, *swine, dogs*, etc., eat their fill. We see that those *creatures* which reproduce seldom when *wild* will reproduce often when *tame*, which results from *warmth* and *fullness of food*. We find that the *rutting time* of *deer* is in *September*, because they need the entire *summer's feed* and *grass* to make them fit for *reproduction*. And if *rain* comes early, around the middle of *September*, they go to *rut* somewhat sooner; if there is *drought*, somewhat later. Similarly, *sheep*, due to their low *heat*, reproduce around the same time or somewhat before. But for the most part, *creatures* that reproduce at certain...

# Naturall History:

<margin>759</margin>
Certain animals <note>original: "Seafons"</note> generate in the *Spring*, such as *birds* and *fishes*; this is because the end of the *winter*, and the *heat* and *comfort* of the *spring*, prepares them. There is also another *reason* why some *creatures* breed at certain *seasons*: the *relationship* between their *gestation period* <note>original: "Time of Bearing"</note> and their *time of breeding* <note>original: "Time of Generation"</note>. No *creature* seeks to breed while the *female* is pregnant <note>original: "full"</note>, nor while she is busy *sitting on eggs* or *rearing* her *young*. Therefore, it is found by *experience* that if you take the *eggs* or *young ones* out of the *nests* of *birds*, they will begin to breed again, three or four times, one after another.

Among *living creatures*, some stay a longer time in the *womb* and some a shorter time. *Women* commonly go nine *months*; the *cow* and the *ewe* about six *months*; *does* <note>female deer</note> go about nine *months*; *mares* eleven *months*; *bitches* nine *weeks*; *elephants* are said to go two *years* (the *received tradition* of ten *years* is *mythical* <note>original: "Fabulous"</note>). For *birds*, there is a *double inquiry*: the *time* between *mating* <note>original: "Treading or Coupling"</note> and the *laying* of the *egg*, and again between the *egg being laid* and the *hatching* <note>original: "Disclosing" </note>. Among *birds*, there is less *diversity of time* than among other *creatures*, yet some exists: for the *hen* sits for only three *weeks*, while the *turkey-hen*, *goose*, and *duck* sit for a *month*. Inquire <note>original: "Quaere"</note> about others. 

The *cause* of the great *difference of times* among *living creatures* is either from the *nature of the species* or from the *constitution of the womb*. Regarding the former, those that take longer to reach *maturity* or full *growth* stay longer in the *womb*; this is chiefly seen in *humans*. Similarly, *elephants*, which stay long in the *womb*, take a long time to reach their full *growth*. But in most other *kinds*, the *constitution of the womb* (that is, its *hardness* or *dryness*) acts alongside the first *cause*. For the *colt* takes about four *years* to grow, as does the *fawn* and the *calf*. However, *puppies* <note>original: "Whelpes"</note>, which reach their *growth* (commonly) within nine months <note>original: "three Quarters of a yeare"</note>, stay only nine *weeks* in the *womb*. As for *birds*, just as there is less *diversity* among them in the time of their *birth*, so there is less *diversity* in their time of *growth*; most of them reach their full *growth* within a *year* <note>original: "Twelve-Moneth"</note>.

<margin>760</margin>
Some *creatures* bring forth many *young ones* at a *birth* <note>original: "Burthen"</note>, such as *bitches*, *hares*, and *rabbits* <note>original: "Conneyes"</note>, etc. Some (ordinarily) only *one*, such as *women*, *lionesses*, etc. This may be caused either by the *quantity of sperm* required to *produce one* of that *kind* (if less is required, it may allow for a greater *number*; if more, fewer), or by the *partitions* and *cells* of the *womb*, which may separate <note>original: "feuer"</note> the *sperm*.

<margin>Experiments in concert touching visible species. 761</margin>
There is no doubt that *light* viewed through *refraction* will appear larger, just as *colored things* do. For just as a *shilling* at the *bottom* of the *water* will appear larger, so will a *candle* in a *lantern* at the *bottom* of the *water*. I have heard of a *practice* where *glowworms* in *glass jars* were put in the *water* to make the *fish* come. But I am not yet informed whether when a *diver* *dives* <note>original: "Diner Dineth" (OCR error for Diver Diveth)</note>, having his *eyes* open and swimming upon his back,

<header>Century VIII.</header>

For it is manifest that when the *eye* stands in the *thinner medium* <note>original: "Finer Medium"; referring to air vs. water</note> and the *object* is in the *denser* <note>original: "Grosser"</note>, things appear larger. But conversely, when the *eye* is placed in the *denser medium* and the *object* in the *thinner*, I do not know how it works.

<margin>762</margin>
It would be well investigated <note>original: "boulted out"</note> whether great *refractions* may not be made upon *reflections*, as well as upon *direct beams*. For example, we see that if you take an empty basin and put an *Angel of Gold* <note>An English gold coin depicting the archangel Michael</note>, or whatever you like, into it, then go so far from the basin until you cannot see the *Angel* because it is not in a *straight line*; then fill the basin with *water*, and you shall see it out of its place because of the *refraction* <note>original: "Reflection," though the phenomenon described is refraction</note>. To proceed, therefore, put a *looking-glass* into a basin of *water*. I suppose you shall not see the *image* in a *straight line*, or at equal *angles*, but to the side. I do not know whether this *experiment* may be extended so that you might see the *image* and not the *glass*; which, for its *beauty* and *strangeness*, would be a fine proof. For then you would see the *image* like a *spirit* in the *air*. As for example, if there is a *cistern* or *pool* of *water*, you shall place opposite it a *picture* of the *devil*, or whatever you wish, so long as you do not see the *water*. Then put a *looking-glass* in the *water*. Now, if you can see the *devil's picture* from the side without seeing the *water*, it will look like a *devil* indeed. They have an old tale in *Oxford* that *Friar Bacon* <note>Roger Bacon, a 13th-century philosopher associated with early optics and legend</note> walked between two *steeples*, which was thought to be done by *glass* while he actually walked upon the *ground*.

<margin>
Experiments in combination, regarding *impulsion* and *percussion* <note>The force of a moving body and the impact it makes</note>.
763
</margin>
A heavy *body* put into *motion* is more easily pushed <note>original: "impelled"</note> than at first when it is *at rest*. The *cause* is partly because *motion* breaks the *sluggishness* <note>original: "Torpuour"</note> of *solid bodies*, which—beside their *motion* of *gravity*—have in them a *natural inclination* <note>original: "Appetite"</note> not to move at all. And it is partly because a *body* that rests gains, by the *resistance* of the *body* upon which it rests, a stronger *compression* of its *parts* than it has by *itself*, and therefore it needs more force to be put into *motion*. For if a *heavy body* is hanging <note>original: "Pensile"</note> and hangs only by a thread, the *impact* <note>original: "Percussion"</note> will create a *thrust* <note>original: "Impulsion"</note> almost as easily as if it were already in *motion*.

<margin>764</margin>
A body that is too great, or too small, will not be thrown as far as a *body* of a *middle size*. So it seems there must be a *proportion* <note>original: "Commensuration"</note> between the *body moved* and the *force* to make it move well. The *cause* is because for *impulsion*, both the *force* of the *body* that *moves* and the *resistance* of the *body* that is *moved* are required. If the *body* is too great, it yields too little; and if it is too small, it resists too little.

<margin>765</margin>
It is *common experience* that no weight will press or cut as strongly when simply laid upon a *body* as it will when falling or struck from above. It may be that the *air* has some part in aiding the *impact*, but the chief *cause*, I believe, is that the *parts* of the *body moved* have—by *impulsion* or by the continued *motion* of *gravity*—a *compression* in them downwards, just as they have when they are thrown or shot through the *air*

<margin>Solitary Experiment touching Tickling. 766</margin>
Tickling is most intense in the *soles* of the *feet*, under the *armpits* <note>original: "Arme-Holes"</note>, and on the *sides*. The *cause* is the *thinness* of the *skin* in those *parts*, combined with the *rarity* of being touched there. For all *tickling* is a light *motion* of the *spirits* <note>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" refers to the subtle fluids believed to flow through nerves to animate the body</note>, which the *thinness* of the *skin*, and the *suddenness* and *rarity* of *touch*, promote. For we see that a *feather* or a *rush* <note>A slender marsh plant</note> drawn along the *lip* or *cheek* tickles, whereas a *thing* more *blunt* <note>original: "Obtuse"</note> or a *touch* more *hard* does not. And as for *suddenness*, we see no *man* can tickle himself. We see also that the *palm* of the *hand*, though it has as *thin* a *skin* as the other *parts mentioned*, yet is not *ticklish* because it is accustomed to being *touched*. *Tickling* also causes *laughter*. The *cause* may be the *emission* of the *spirits*, and thus of the *breath*, by a *flight* from *titillation* <note>The physical sensation of being tickled</note>. For upon *tickling*, we see there is always a *starting* or *shrinking* away of the *part* to avoid it. And we see also that if you *tickle* the *nostrils* with a *feather* or *straw*, it induces *sneezing*, which is a *sudden emission* of the *spirits* that also expels *moisture*. And *tickling* is always *painful* <note>Meaning distressing or uncomfortable rather than strictly sharp pain</note> and not well endured.

<margin>Solitary Experiment touching the Scarcity of Rain in Egypt. 767</margin>
It is strange that despite the *river* *Nile* <note>original: "Nilus"</note> overflowing the *country* of *Egypt* as it does, there should nevertheless be little or no *rain* in that *country*. The *cause* must be either in the *nature* of the *water*, or in the *nature* of the *air*, or *both*. Regarding the *water*, it may be ascribed either to the *long course* <note>original: "Race"</note> of the *water*—for *swiftly running waters* do not evaporate <note>original: "vapour"</note> as much as *standing waters*—or else to the *concoction* <note>A term from early science referring to a process of refinement or "ripening" through heat or digestion</note> of the *water*. For *waters* that are well *concocted* do not evaporate as much as *raw waters*, no more than *waters* upon the *fire* evaporate as much after some time of *boiling* as they do at first. And it is true that the *water* of the *Nile* is sweeter than other *waters* in *taste*, and it is excellently *good* for the *stone* <note>Kidney or bladder stones</note> and *hypochondriac melancholy* <note>A condition thought to be caused by an imbalance of the spleen or organs beneath the ribs</note>, which shows it is *soothing* <note>original: "Lenefying"</note>. And it runs through a *country* with a *hot climate* that is flat, without *shade* from either *woods* or *hills*, whereby the *sun* must necessarily have great *power* to *concoct* it. As for the *air* (from which I conceive this *lack* of *showers* chiefly comes), the *cause* must be that the *air* is, of itself, *thin* and *thirsty*. As soon as it gets any *moisture* from the *water*, it absorbs <note>original: "imbibeth"</note> and dissipates it into the whole body of the *air*, and does not allow it to remain as *vapor* where it might produce *rain*.

And it is certain that in *Egypt*, they prepare and clarify the water of the *Nile* by putting it into great *jars* of *stone* and *stirring* it about with a few

# Century 8

<margin>Solitary Experiment touching plants without leaves. 769</margin>
There are scarcely any *plants* <note>original: "Vegetables"</note> to be found that have *branches* and no *leaves*, unless you count *coral* as one. But there is also in the *deserts* of *Saint Macarius* <note>original: "S. Macario"</note> in *Egypt* a *plant* that is *long*, *leafless*, *brown* in color, and *branched* like *coral*, except that it closes at the *top*. When this is placed in *water* inside a *house*, it spreads and unfolds strangely. The people in that area have a superstitious *belief* that during the *labor* of *women*, it helps with an *easy delivery* <note>original: "Deliuerance"; refers to childbirth</note>.

<margin>Solitary Experiment touching the materials of glass. 770</margin>
The *crystalline Venice glass* is reported to be a mixture, in equal *portions*, of *stones* brought from *Pavia* by the *River Ticino* <note>original: "Ticinus"</note> and the *ashes* of a weed called *kali* <note>alkali or glasswort</note> by the *Arabs*, which is gathered in a *desert* between *Alexandria* and *Rosetta*. It is first used by the *Egyptians* as *fuel*, and then they crush the *ashes* into *lumps* like *stone* and sell them to the *Venetians* for their *glassworks*.

<margin>Solitary Experiment touching the prevention of putrefaction and the long conservation of bodies. 771</margin>
It is strange and noteworthy how long *carcasses* have remained *uncorrupted* and in their former *dimensions*, as seen in the *mummies* of *Egypt*, some of which are believed to have lasted three thousand years. It is true they find ways to draw out the *brains* and remove the *entrails*, which are the *parts* most prone to rot. But that does not lessen the *wonder*, for we see what a *soft* and *corruptible substance* the *flesh* is compared to all other *parts* of the *body*. However, it seems that according to our *observation* and *axiom* in our hundredth *experiment*, *putrefaction* <note>original: "Putrefaction"; refers to decomposition or rotting</note>—which we think of as such a *natural end* for *bodies*—is actually just an *accident*. *Matter* does not hasten toward *corruption* as quickly as is thought. Therefore, *bodies* are preserved for a very long time in *shining amber*, in *mercury* <note>original: "Quick-Siluer"</note>, in *balms* (which we are discussing now), in *wax*, in *honey*, in *gums*, and (perhaps) in *repositories* <note>original: "Conseruatories"</note> of *snow*, and so on. It is worth repeating what we said in the aforementioned *experiment* concerning *annihilation*: namely, that if you provide protection against three *causes* of *putrefaction*, *bodies* will not rot. The first is that *air* must be excluded, for air undermines the *body* and works with the *spirit* <note>the internal vital fluids or gases that Bacon believed caused decay when they escaped</note> of the *body* to dissolve it. The second is that the *adjacent* and *surrounding* <note>original: "Ambient"</note> *body* <note>the substance touching the object</note> must not be of the *same material* <note>original: "Commateriall"</note>, but entirely *different in nature* <note>original: "Heterogeneall"</note> from the *body* that is to be preserved. For if *nothing* can be received by the *one*, *nothing* can leave the *other*. Such are *mercury* and *white amber* to *herbs*, *flies*, and similar *bodies*. The third is that the *body* to be preserved must not be so *large* <note>original: "Grosse"</note> that it might rot from within itself, even if no *part* of it escapes into the *surrounding substance*. Therefore, it must be *thin* and *small* rather than having great *bulk*. There is also a fourth *remedy*, which is:

# Natural History

If the *body* to be preserved is of great *bulk*, such as a *corpse*, then the *material* that encloses it must have the *power* <note>original: "Vertue"</note> to draw out and dry the *moisture* of the *inner body*. Otherwise, *putrefaction* <note>rotting</note> will occur inside, even if nothing leaks out. I remember *Livy* <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian</note> relates that two *lead coffins* were found in a *tomb* at one time. One contained the *body* of King *Numa* <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome</note> about four hundred years after his death. The other contained his *books* of *sacred rites* and *ceremonies*, and the *discipline* of the *high priests* <note>original: "Pontifes"</note>. In the *coffin* that held the *body*, nothing at all could be seen except for a few light *ashes* around the *sides*. But in the *coffin* that held the *books*, they were found as fresh as if they had been newly written; they were written on *parchment* and covered with three or four layers of *wax coatings* <note>original: "watch-Candles of wax"</note>. By this, it seems that the *Romans* in *Numa’s* time were not as skilled at *embalming* as the *Egyptians* were, which was the *reason* the *body* was utterly consumed. However, I find in *Plutarch* and others that when *Augustus Caesar* visited the *tomb* of *Alexander the Great* in *Alexandria*, he found the *body* still maintained its *shape*. Yet, despite all the *embalming* (which was undoubtedly of the best quality), the *body* was so *fragile* <note>original: "Tender"</note> that when *Caesar* touched its *nose*, he damaged it. This makes it very strange to me that *Egyptian mummies* are reported to be as *hard* as *asphalt* <note>original: "Stone-Pitch"</note>. I find only one difference which may indeed be very *important*: namely, that ancient *Egyptian mummies* were shrouded in many *folds* of *linen* smeared with *gums* in the manner of *waxed cloth* <note>original: "Seare-Cloth"</note>, which does not appear to have been done to the *body* of *Alexander*.

<margin>
Solitary Experiment regarding the *abundance* of *nitre* on certain *sea-shores*. 
772
</margin>

Near the *Castle* of *Catie* and by the *Wells* of *Assan* in the land of *Idumea* <note>a biblical region south of the Dead Sea</note>, for a great *part* of the *way*, you would think the *sea* was close at hand, even though it is a good distance away. This is nothing but the *shining* of the *nitre* <note>saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note> upon the *sea sands*; the *shores* there produce such an *abundance* of *nitre*.

<margin>
Solitary Experiment regarding *bodies* that are buoyed up by *water*.
773
</margin>

The *Dead Sea*, which *spits up* *bitumen* <note>asphalt or tar</note>, is of such *density* <note>original: "Crassitude"</note> that *living bodies* bound hand and foot and cast into it have been buoyed up and did not sink. This shows that all *sinking* into *water* is merely a result of the *body* being *heavier* than the *water* it is placed in. Thus, you could make *water* so strong and heavy with *mercury* <note>original: "Quick-Siluer"</note> (perhaps) or something similar that it might bear up *iron*. I see no *use* for this, however, except for *deception* <note>original: "Imposture"</note>. We also see that all *metals* except *gold* swim upon *mercury* for the same reason.

# Century VIII

...time so: For **iron**, as soon as it is out of the fire, dies out immediately. Certainly, it would be a thing of great use and profit if you could find a **fuel** that would burn hot and yet last a long time. I am not entirely skeptical that there may be such **candles** as are said to be made of **salamander's wool** <note>original: "Salamanders wooll," an archaic term for asbestos, which was once believed to be the wool of the mythical fire-dwelling salamander</note>. This is a kind of **mineral** which whitens in the burning and is not consumed. The **question** is this: **flame** must be made of something; and commonly it is made of some **solid body** <note>original: "Tangible Body"</note> which has **weight**. But it is perhaps not impossible that it could be made of **gas** or **vapor** <note>original: "Spirit or Vapour"</note> within a **body** (which **gas** or **vapor** has no **weight**), such as the matter of a **will-o'-the-wisp** <note>original: *Ignis Fatuus*, literally "foolish fire"</note>. But then you will say that such a **vapor** can also last only a short time. To that, it may be answered that with the help of **oil**, **wax**, and other **candle materials**, the **flame** may continue while the **wick** does not burn.

<margin>
Solitary economic experiment concerning cheap fuel.
775
</margin>

**Coal** <note>original: "Sea-Coale," meaning mineral coal mined from the earth and transported by sea, as opposed to charcoal made from wood</note> lasts longer than **charcoal**; and **charcoal** made from **roots**, being charred into large **pieces**, lasts longer than ordinary **charcoal**. **Turf**, **peat**, and **dried dung** <note>original: "Cow-Sheards"</note> are cheap **fuels** and last a long time. **Small coal** or **briar coal**, poured upon **charcoal**, makes it last longer. **Sedge** <note>a grass-like marsh plant</note> is a cheap **fuel** for brewing or baking; it is used primarily because it is good for nothing else. A trial should be made of some mixture of **coal** with **earth** or **chalk**. If that **mixture** is used secretly by **coal merchants** to increase the bulk of the **coal**, it is a deception; but if it is used intentionally and made known, it is a saving.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the gathering of wind for freshness.
776
</margin>

It is, at this day, in use in **Gaza** to embed **pottery shards** or **earthen vessels** in their **walls** to gather the **wind** from the top and pass it down through spouts into **rooms**. It is a device for **freshness** during great heats. It is said there are some **rooms** in **Italy** and **Spain** designed for **freshness** and for **gathering** the **winds** and **air** in the **heats of summer**. But those are merely **trappings** of the **winds**, enlarging them again and making them **reverberate** and go around in **circles**, rather than this device of **spouts** in the **wall**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the testing of air.
777
</margin>

Much diligence should be used in the choice of certain **objects** and **places** to serve, as it were, for the **tasting of air**, in order to discover the **wholesomeness** or **unwholesomeness** of the **seasons** as well as the **locations of dwellings**. It is certain that there are some **houses** where **preserves** <note>original: "Confitures"</note> and **pies** will grow **mold** more than in others. I am persuaded that a **piece of raw meat** or **fish** will rot sooner in some **atmospheres** than in others. These are noble **experiments** that can make this **discovery**; for they serve as a **natural way of predicting** <note>original: "Naturall Diuination"</note> the **seasons** better than **astronomers** can by their **charts** <note>original: "Figures"</note>. Furthermore, they teach **men** where to choose their **dwelling** for better **health**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning sand with the nature of glass.
779
</margin>
It is reported that in the valley near **Mount Carmel** in Judea, there is a sand which, above all others, has the most affinity with glass. It is so much so that other minerals placed in it turn into a glassy substance without the use of fire; and conversely, glass put into it turns back into the original sand. The thing is very strange, if it be true; it is most likely caused by some natural furnace or heat in the earth, and yet they do not speak of any eruption of flames. It would be good to test in glassworks whether the raw materials of glass, when mingled with glass that is already made and remelted, facilitate the making of glass with less heat.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the growth of coral.
780
</margin>
In the sea to the southwest of Sicily, much **coral** is found. It is an underwater plant <note>original: "Sub-Marine Plant"; at the time, coral was often classified as a plant rather than an animal</note>. It has no leaves; it branches only when it is underwater. It is soft and green in color, but when brought into the air, it becomes hard and a shining red, as we see. It is also said to have a white berry, but we do not find it brought over with the coral. Likely it is cast away as being worth nothing; inquire better into this for the discovery of the nature of the plant.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the gathering of manna.
781
</margin>
The **manna** <note>original: "Manna," a sweet, edible substance produced by certain plants and insects, highly valued in early modern medicine</note> of Calabria is the best and most plentiful. They gather it from the leaf of the mulberry tree, but not from such mulberry trees as grow in the valleys. Manna falls upon the leaves by night, just as other dews do. It would seem that before those dews reach the trees in the valleys, they dissipate and cannot hold out. It would also seem that the mulberry leaf itself has some coagulating power which thickens the dew, because it is not found upon other trees. We see by the silkworm, which feeds upon that leaf, what a dainty, smooth juice it has; and the leaves also (especially of the black mulberry) are somewhat bristly, which may help to preserve the dew. Certainly, it would not be amiss to observe a little better the dews that fall upon trees or herbs growing on mountains; for it may be that many dews fall that are spent before they reach the valleys. And I suppose that he who would gather the best **May dew** <note>original: "May-Dew," dew collected in the month of May, which was believed to have special medicinal and cosmetic properties</note> for medicine should gather it from the hills.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the correcting of wine.
782
</margin>
It is said they have a method to prepare their Greek wines to keep them from releasing fumes and causing intoxication <note>original: "Fuming, and Inebriating"</note> by adding some sulfur or **alum** <note>original: "Allome," a chemical compound used as an astringent</note>. One of these is oily and the other is astringent, and it is certain that those two natures best repress fumes. This experiment should be applied to other wine and strong beer by putting in some similar substances while they ferment <note>original: "worke"</note>, which may make them both release fewer fumes and cause less inflammation.

<summary>This page explores various natural phenomena, including the properties of "glass-making" sand in Judea, the transition of coral from a soft sea plant to a hard red mineral, the collection of manna from mountain mulberry trees, and the chemical treatment of wine to reduce intoxication.</summary>
<keywords>animal husbandry, glassmaking, Mount Carmel, coral, manna, Calabria, mulberry trees, May dew, wine preservation, sulfur, alum</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Century VIII of Francis Bacon’s natural history, transitioning from a discussion on the properties of coral to experiments regarding the chemistry of fire, the hardening of materials, medical observations on healing, and the effects of climate on health.</meta>

# Century VIII.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the materials of wildfire.
783
</margin>
It is believed by some (and not without reason) that the reason why **wildfires** <note>original: "Wilde-Fires"; early incendiary weapons, often called Greek Fire, that were difficult to extinguish</note>, of which the principal ingredient is **bitumen** <note>a naturally occurring petroleum substance like asphalt or tar</note>, do not extinguish with **water** is because the first **solidification** <note>original: "Concretion"</note> of bitumen is a mixture of a **fiery** and a **watery substance**. This is not the case with **sulfur**. This is evident because in the **place** near **Pozzuoli** <note>original: "Puteoli," a city in Italy</note> which they call the **Court of Vulcan** <note>original: "Court of Vulcan"; the Solfatara crater, known for its volcanic activity</note>, you shall hear beneath the **earth** a horrible thundering of **fire** and **water** conflicting together, and boiling water **spouts** also break forth there. Now, that **place** yields great **quantities** of **bitumen**, whereas **Etna**, **Vesuvius**, and similar volcanoes, which consist of **sulfur**, shoot forth **smoke**, **ashes**, and **pumice**, but no **water**. It is also reported that **bitumen mixed with lime** and put under **water** will create, as it were, an **artificial rock**, so hard does the **substance** become.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning plaster growing as hard as marble.
784
</margin>
There is a **cement** compounded of **flour**, **whites of eggs**, and **powdered stone** that becomes as hard as **marble**. The walls of the ***Piscina Mirabilis*** <note>original: "Piscinæ mirabilis," meaning "Miraculous Pool"; a large Roman cistern near Naples</note> near **Cumae** are said to have been **plastered** with this. And it is certain and has been tested that the **powder** of **loadstone** <note>magnetic iron ore</note> and **flint**, with the addition of **whites of eggs** and **gum dragon** <note>original: "Gum-Dragon"; gum tragacanth, a natural gum used as a binder</note> made into a **paste**, will in a few days harden to the hardness of a **stone**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the judgment of the cure in certain ulcers and hurts.
785
</margin>
It has been noted by the **ancients** that in **full or impure bodies** <note>bodies with an excess of "humors" or fluids</note>, **ulcers** or **injuries** in the **legs** are hard to cure, while those in the **head** are easier. The **cause** is that **ulcers** or **injuries** in the **legs** require **drying out** <note>original: "Desiccation"</note>, which is hindered by the **flowing down of humors** <note>original: "Defluxion of Humours"; the perceived movement of bodily fluids according to ancient medical theory</note> to the **lower parts**. Conversely, **injuries** and **ulcers** in the **head** do not require such drying; on the contrary, **dryness** makes them more likely to **heal** <note>original: "Consolidate"</note>. In modern observation, a similar difference has been found between **Frenchmen** and **Englishmen**, as the **constitution** of the former is more **dry** and the latter more **moist**. Therefore, an **injury** of the **head** is harder to cure in a **Frenchman**, and one of the **leg** in an **Englishman**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the healthfulness or unhealthfulness of the south wind.
786
</margin>
It has been noted by the **ancients** that **south winds**, when blowing often without **rain**, cause a **feverish disposition** in the **year**; but with **rain**, they do not. The **cause** is that **south winds** by themselves condition the **air** to be prone to causing **fevers**. But when **showers** are joined with them, they **cool** the air in part and check the **sultry heat** of the **south wind**. Therefore, this does not apply to the **sea coasts**, because the **vapor** of the **sea** refreshes the air even without **showers**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning wounds.
787
</margin>
It has been noted by the **ancients** that **wounds** made with **brass** <note>often used interchangeably with bronze in historical texts</note> heal more easily than **wounds** made with **iron**. The **cause** is that **brass** has a **healing power** <note>original: "Sanatiue Vertue"</note> in itself, and so helps somewhat at the very moment of the injury; but **iron** is **corrosive** and not **healing**. Therefore, it would be good if the **instruments** used by **surgeons** <note>original: "Chirurgians"</note> on wounds were made of **brass** rather than **iron**.

<keywords>bitumen, wildfire, Pozzuoli, Piscina Mirabilis, loadstone, gum dragon, humoral theory, ulcers, south wind, medical surgery, brass vs iron</keywords>
