<meta>This page continues Century VIII of Francis Bacon’s natural history, moving from construction materials to medical observations on frostbite, chemical experiments on weight and density, and early physics regarding the motion of projectiles and fluids.</meta>

# Natural History:

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning tissue death caused by cold.
788
</margin>

**In** **cold countries**, when men's **noses** and **ears** are **mortified** <note>original: "Mortified"; tissue death caused by severe frostbite</note>, and (as it were) **gangrened** with **cold**, if they come to a **fire**, they rot off immediately. The **cause** is that the few **spirits** <note>original: "Spirits"; in Bacon's theory, these were active, subtle substances that animated matter and maintained its health</note> that remain in those **parts** are suddenly drawn forth, and so **putrefaction** is made **complete**. But **snow** put upon them helps; for it preserves those **spirits** that remain until they can revive. Besides, **snow** has in it a **secret warmth**, as the **monk** proved from the **scripture**: *He gives snow like wool, and scatters frost like ashes* <note>original: "Qui dat Niuem sicut Lanam, Gelu sicut Cineres spargit"; Psalm 147:16</note>. By this, he inferred that **snow** warmed like **wool**, and **frost** irritated like **ashes** <note>original: "fret"; to wear away or corrode like lye or caustic ashes</note>. **Warm water** also does good, because little by little it opens the **pores** without any sudden **action** upon the **spirits**. This **experiment** may be transferred to the **cure of gangrenes**, whether **coming** of themselves or induced by the excessive **application** of **opiates** <note>referring to medicines used to numb pain, which Bacon believed could "cool" the tissue to the point of death</note>. In these cases, you must beware of **dry heat** and resort to **things** that are **refrigerant** <note>cooling</note> but possess an **inward warmth** and the **power** of **cherishing** <note>sustaining or nourishing life</note>.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning weight.
789
</margin>

**Weigh** **iron** and ***aqua fortis*** <note>original: "Aqua Fortis"; nitric acid</note> separately; then dissolve the **iron** in the ***aqua fortis***. Weigh the **dissolution**, and you shall find it to weigh as much as the **bodies** did separately, despite a good deal of **waste** through a thick **vapor** that is issued during the **reaction**. This shows that the opening <note>the chemical breakdown or dissolving</note> of a **body** increases its **weight**. This was tried once or twice, but I do not know whether there was any **error** in the **trial**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the floating of bodies.
790
</margin>

**Take** two **ounces** of ***aqua fortis*** and two **drams** of **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> (for that **load** the ***aqua fortis*** will bear). The **dissolution** will not float a **flint** as large as a **nutmeg**. Yet (no doubt) increasing the weight <note>density</note> of **water** will increase its **power** of **bearing**; as we see **brine**, when it is **salty** enough, will float an **egg**. And I remember well a **physician** who used to give certain **mineral baths** for the **gout**, etc. When the **body** was put into the **bath**, it could not sink as easily as in **ordinary water**. But it seems the **weight** of the **quicksilver**, though more than the **weight of a stone**, does not compensate for the **weight of a stone** being more than the **weight of the aqua fortis**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the flight of unequal bodies in the air.
791
</margin>

**Let** there be a **body** of **unequal weight** (such as one made of **wood** and **lead**, or **bone** and **lead**). If you throw it from you with the **light end** forward, it will turn, and the **weightier end** will recover its position to be **forward**, unless the **body** is **too long**. The **cause** is that the more **dense body** has a more **violent pressure** of its **parts** from the first **impulse**. This is the **cause** (though not found out before now, as has been often said) of all **violent motions**. When the **hind part** moves swifter (because it less endures the **pressure of parts**) than the **forward part** can make way for it, it must necessarily be that the **body** turns over; for once turned, it can more easily draw forward the **lighter part**. **Galileo** <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), the famous Italian physicist and astronomer</note> notes it well: that if an **open trough** containing **water** is driven faster than the **water** can...

<summary>This page explores medical treatments for frostbite using snow rather than heat, chemical experiments measuring the weight of dissolved metals, and physical observations on the buoyancy and flight of objects.</summary>
<keywords>frostbite, gangrene, chemistry, aqua fortis, nitric acid, quicksilver, mercury, density, buoyancy, physics, ballistics, Galileo Galilei</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the motion of fluids and the causes of tides before moving on to experiments regarding water as a medium for sound, the physical reactions of the body's "spirits" to offensive sensations, and the acoustics of echoes in specific architectural spaces.</meta>

He supposes—holding confidently to the *motion* of the *Earth*—this to be the cause of the ebbing and flowing of the *ocean*, because the *Earth* outruns the *water*. Although this *theory* is false, the first *experiment* is true. As for the *inequality* of the *pressure* of *parts*, it appears clearly in this: if you take a *body* of *stone* or *iron* and another of *wood* of the same *magnitude* and *shape* and throw them with equal *force*, you cannot possibly throw the *wood* as far as the *stone* or *iron*.

<margin>Experiment Solitary touching Water, that it may be the Medium of Sounds. 792</margin>
It is certain (as it has been previously mentioned in part) that *water* may be the *medium* of *sounds*. If you dash a *stone* against a *stone* in the *bottom* of the *water*, it makes a *sound*. So a long *pole* struck upon *gravel* in the *bottom* of the *water* makes a *sound*. Indeed, if you should think that the *sound* comes up through the *pole* and not through the *water*, you shall find that an *anchor*, let down by a *rope*, makes a *sound*; and yet the *rope* is no solid *body* through which the *sound* can ascend.

<margin>Experiment Solitary of the Flight of the Spirits upon Odious Objects. 793</margin>
All objects of the *senses* which are very *offensive* cause the *spirits* <note>original: "Spirits"; in Bacon's natural philosophy, these were active, invisible substances within the body that governed sensation and vital functions</note> to retire; and upon their *flight*, the *parts* of the body are (in some degree) left destitute. Thus, there is induced in them a *trembling* <note>original: "Trepidation"</note> and *horror*. For *sounds*, we see that the *grating* of a *saw*, or any very *harsh* *noise*, will set the *teeth* on edge and make the whole *body* *shiver*. For *tastes*, we see that in the taking of a *potion* or *pills*, the *head* and the *neck* shake. For *offensive* <note>original: "Odious"</note> *smells*, a similar *effect* follows, which is less perceived because there is a *remedy* at hand by *stopping* of the *nose*. But in *horses*, which can use no such *help*, we see the *smell* of a *carrion*—especially of a *dead horse*—makes them fly away and carry on almost as if they were *mad*. For *feeling*, if you come out of the *sun* suddenly into a *shade*, there follows a *chilliness* or *shivering* in all the *body*. And even in *sight*, which has (in *effect*) no *offensive* *object*, *coming* into *sudden darkness* induces an *unpleasant* <note>original: "Offensiue"</note> *shiver*.

<margin>Experiment Solitary touching the Re-percussion of Echoes. 794</margin>
There is, in the *city* of *Ticinum* <note>original: "Ticinum"; the Roman name for Pavia in Italy</note> in *Italy*, a *church* that has *windows* only from above. It is in *length* an *hundred feet*, in *breadth* *twenty feet*, and in *height* near *fifty*, having a *door* in the *middle*. It reports the *voice* twelve or thirteen times if you stand by the *close end* of the *door*. The *echo* fails and dies by little and little, as the *echo* at *Charenton-le-Pont* <note>original: "Pont-charenton"; a town near Paris famous in the 17th century for its multi-repeating echo</note> does. And the *echo* sounds as if it came from above the *door*. And if you stand at the *lower end*, or on either *side* of the *door*, the *echo* holds; but if you stand in the *door*, or in the *middle* just opposite the *door*, it does not. Note that all *echoes* sound better against *old walls* than *new*; because they are more *dry* and *hollow*.

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon's "Natural History," transitioning from experiments on the movement of fluids and the nature of sound to the psychological effects of imagination, methods of preservation, and the properties of metals.</meta>

# Natural History

<margin>
Experiment Solitary regarding the force of imagination, imitating that of the senses.
795
</margin>

Those **effects** which are produced by the **physical impact on the senses**, and by **actual events**, are also produced to some degree by the **imagination**. Therefore, if a man sees another eat **sour** or **acidic things** which set the **teeth** on edge, this **sight** affects the **imagination**. Consequently, the one who sees the **act** done by another feels his own **teeth** also set on edge. Similarly, if a man sees another turn around swiftly and for a long time, or if he looks upon **wheels** that turn, he himself becomes **dizzy** <note>original: "Turne-sicke"</note>. So, if a man is in a **high place** without **railings** or a good **handhold**, unless he is used to it, he is ready to fall; for by **imagining** a fall, he puts his **spirits** <note>In Bacon’s natural philosophy, "spirits" were invisible, active fluids that moved throughout the body to control sensation and movement.</note> into the very **action** of a **fall**. Likewise, upon **seeing** others **bleed**, or be **strangled**, or **tortured**, many people are ready to faint, as if they themselves **bled** or were in **physical distress**.

<margin>
Experiment Solitary regarding the preservation of bodies.
796
</margin>

Take a **stock flower** <note>original: "Stock-Gilly-Flower"; a fragrant garden flower of the genus Matthiola.</note> and tie it gently to a **stick**, and put them both into a **deep glass jar** full of **mercury** <note>original: "Quick-siluer"</note> so that the **flower** is covered. Then lay a small **weight** on **top** of the **glass** to keep the **stick** down. Look at them after four or five days, and you shall find the **flower** fresh and the **stalk** harder and less **flexible** than it was. If you compare it with another **flower** gathered at the same time, the difference will be even more obvious. This shows that **bodies** are preserved excellently in **mercury**; and they are not only preserved, but by the **coldness** of the **mercury**, they **harden** <note>original: "Indurate"</note>. While the **freshness** of the **flower** may be purely due to **preservation** (which is especially notable because the **mercury** presses against the **flower**), the **stiffness** of the **stalk** cannot occur without **hardening** caused, it seems, by the **cold** of the **mercury**.

<margin>
Experiment Solitary regarding the growth or multiplying of metals.
797
</margin>

It is reported by some of the **ancients** that in **Cyprus** there is a **kind** of **iron** that—if cut into **small pieces** and put into the **ground** and well **watered**—will increase into **larger pieces**. This is certain and has been known since **ancient times**: that **lead** will multiply and increase. This has been seen in **old stone statues** that have been kept in **cellars**; where the **feet** were bound with **lead bands**, it appeared (after a time) that the **lead** swelled, to the point that it hung upon the **stone** like warts.

<margin>
Experiment Solitary regarding the drowning of a base metal in a more precious one.
798
</margin>

I use the term **"drowning of metals"** when a **baser metal** is so incorporated with a more **rich** one that it can by no means be separated again. This is a kind of **transformation** <note>original: "Version"</note>, though a false one—as if **silver** should be inseparably incorporated with **gold**, or **copper** and **lead** with **silver**. The ancient **Electrum** <note>An alloy of gold and silver used in antiquity.</note> contained one-fifth **silver** to the **gold** and created a **compound metal** as fit for most uses as **gold**, and more radiant and better **characterized** in some other **properties**; but in that case, the metals were easily separated. To do this secretly, or to make the **compound** pass for the **pure rich metal**, is an **adulteration** or **counterfeiting**. But if it is done openly and without **disguise**, it may be a great **saving** of...

<meta>This page continues Bacon’s observations on the physical properties of matter, specifically focusing on the metallurgical behavior of gold, silver, and lead, and transitioning into a philosophical discussion on the "appetites" of different substances to absorb or combine with one another.</meta>

<header>Century VIII. Page 201</header>

...the **richer metal**. I remember hearing from a man skilled in **metals** that a fifteenth part of **silver**, when combined with **gold**, cannot be **recovered** by any **water of separation** <note>original: "water of separation"; refers to acids like nitric acid (aqua fortis) used by refiners to dissolve silver while leaving gold intact.</note>, unless you add a greater **quantity** of **silver** to draw the smaller amount toward it. He said this is the last resort in **separations**. However, that is a tedious method that almost no one would consider. This should be investigated further, perhaps by changing the **quantity** from a fifteenth to a twentieth, and also with some small **addition** that might further the **intrinsic incorporation** <note>The deep physical mixing of the two metals.</note>. Note that **silver** in **gold** can be detected by weight when compared with its **dimensions** <note>This is a test of density; gold is significantly denser than silver.</note>. But **lead** in **silver** (**lead** being the heavier **metal**) will not be detected if you add just enough more **silver** to compensate for the **extra weight** of the **lead**.

<margin>Solitary experiment regarding the fixation of bodies. 799</margin>
**Gold** is the only **substance** which has nothing **volatile** <note>A substance that easily evaporates or turns into vapor when heated.</note> in it, and yet melts without much difficulty. Its **melting** shows that it is not **lean** <note>original: "ieiune"; lacking in substance or "spirits."</note> or lacking in **spirit**. Therefore, its **fixation** <note>The state of being "fixed," or resistant to change and evaporation by fire.</note> is not caused by a **lack** of **spirit** to fly out, but by the **equal spreading** of the **tangible parts** and their **close gathering** <note>original: "coaceruation"; a huddling together or accumulation.</note>. Because of this, they have less **desire** and no means at all to escape. It would therefore be good to test whether **re-melted glass** loses any weight? For the **parts in glass** are evenly spread, but they are not as close together as in **gold**, as we see by the easy admission of **light**, **heat**, and **cold**, and by its low **weight**. There are other **fixed bodies** which have little or no **spirit**, so there is nothing to fly out; we see this in the **material** from which **cupels** <note>original: "Copples"; small, porous bowls used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals.</note> are made, which are put into **furnaces** and upon which **fire** has no effect. Thus, there are three **causes of fixation**: the **even spreading** of both the **spirits** and **tangible parts**; the **closeness** of the **tangible parts**; and the **leanness** or **extreme breakdown** <note>original: "comminution"; reducing to very small particles.</note> of the **spirits**. Of these **three**, the **first two** can be combined with a **liquefiable nature**, but the **last** cannot.

<margin>Solitary experiment regarding the restless nature of things in themselves, and their desire to change. 800</margin>
It is a profound **contemplation in nature** to consider the **emptiness** (as we may call it) or **dissatisfaction** of several **bodies**, and their **appetite** to take in **others**. **Air** takes in **lights**, **sounds**, **smells**, and **vapors**; and it is most obvious that it does this with a kind of **thirst**, as if not satisfied with its own previous **consistency**. Otherwise, it would never receive them so suddenly and easily. **Water** and all **liquids** quickly receive **dry** and more **earthly bodies** that are compatible with them. Conversely, **dry bodies** drink in **waters** and **liquids**. Thus (as it was well said by one of the **ancients** regarding **earthly** and **watery substances**), "One is a **glue** to another." **Parchment, skins, cloth, etc.** drink in **liquids**, even though they are **entire bodies** and not **broken down** <note>original: "comminuted"; pulverized into dust or sand.</note> like **sand** and **ashes**, nor are they visibly porous. **Metals** themselves readily receive **acids** <note>original: "Strong-Waters"; powerful acidic solutions like aqua fortis.</note>; and **acids** likewise readily pierce into **metals** and **stones**. And that **acid** which will affect **gold** will not affect **silver**, and **vice versa** <note>original: "è converso"; and the opposite.</note>.

It also introduces the concept of "natural appetite," explaining how different substances like air, water, and metals have a natural tendency to absorb or combine with other materials.</summary>

<page-num>202</page-num>
<header>Natural History:</header>

<margin>Experiment 799</margin>
Gold, which seems by its **weight** to be the **densest** <note>original: "Closest"; referring to the compactness of the atoms or "parts" of the metal.</note> and most **solid body**, greedily drinks in **mercury** <note>original: "Quick-siluer." Gold and mercury naturally bond to form an amalgam.</note>. And it seems that this **reception** of other **bodies** is not **violent**; for it is (many times) **mutual**, and occurs, as it were, by **consent**. Consider carefully the **cause** of this, and to what **principle** <note>original: "Axiome."</note> it may be referred. As for the clever assertion that **matter** is like a **common prostitute** <note>original: "Common Strumpet"; a metaphor suggesting that matter is passive and willing to take on any shape or "form."</note> who desires all **forms**, it is merely a **vague idea** <note>original: "wandring Notion."</note>. Only **flame** is not content to simply take in any other **body**; instead, it seeks either to overcome and turn another **body** into **itself**, as if by **victory**, or it **dies** and goes out.

## HISTORY.

### Ninth Century.

<margin>
Experiments in association <note>original: "in Consort."</note> regarding perception in inanimate bodies <note>original: "Bodies Insensible."</note>, tending toward natural divination or subtle trials.
</margin>

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'I' depicting a scholar or philosopher seated at a desk with open books and scientific instruments.</image-desc>

It is certain that all **bodies** whatsoever, though they have no **sense** <note>Meaning conscious awareness or feeling.</note>, yet they have **perception**. For when one **body** is applied to another, there is a kind of **election** <note>original: "Election"; a natural affinity or selective attraction.</note> to embrace that which is agreeable and to exclude or expel that which is unpleasant <note>original: "Ingrate."</note>. And whether the **body** is the **alterant** <note>The substance causing a change.</note> or the **altered** <note>The substance being changed.</note>, a **perception** always precedes the **operation** <note>The physical action or change taking place.</note>. For otherwise, all **bodies** would be exactly alike to one another. 

Sometimes this **perception** in some kinds of **bodies** is far more **subtle** than **sense**, so much so that the **sense** is but a dull thing in comparison. We see that a **weather-glass** <note>An early scientific instrument, similar to a thermometer, used to measure atmospheric changes.</note> will find the smallest difference in the **weather**, in **heat** or **cold**, even when men do not notice it. This **perception** also sometimes acts at a **distance**, as well as upon **touch**, such as when a **lodestone** <note>original: "Load-Stone"; a naturally magnetized mineral.</note> draws **iron**, or

<page-num>204</page-num>
<header>Natural History:</header>

Flame ignites *naphtha* <note>original: "Naphtha of Babylon"; a highly flammable petroleum-based liquid known in antiquity</note> from a great distance away. It is therefore a *subject* of a very *noble inquiry* to investigate these more *subtle perceptions*. For this is another *key* to unlocking *nature*, just as our *senses* are—and sometimes it is a *better* one. Furthermore, it is a *principal means* of *natural divination* <note>The ability to predict future natural events, such as weather or disease, by observing early, subtle physical signs</note>. This is because what appears early in these *perceptions* leads to much greater *effects* that come long after. It is also true that this inquiry serves to *discover* what is *hidden*, as well as to *foretell* what is *to come*. This is seen in many *subtle trials* <note>tests or experiments</note>. For example, if you wish to test whether *seeds* are old or new, your *senses* cannot inform you; but if you boil them in *water*, the *new seeds* will sprout sooner. Similarly, regarding *water*, your *taste* will not reveal the best source, but its *speedy consumption* <note>Meaning how quickly it evaporates or is absorbed</note>—and many other means we have previously established—will reveal it. Likewise, in all *physiognomy* <note>The practice of judging a person's character or mind from their physical features</note>, the features of the *body* will reveal those *natural inclinations* of the *mind* which *dissimulation* <note>deception or hiding one's true feelings</note> would conceal or *discipline* would suppress. 

Therefore, we shall now discuss only those two *perceptions* that relate to *natural divination* and *discovery*, leaving the discussion of *perception* in other *things* to be addressed elsewhere. Now, it is true that *divination* can be achieved by other means—for instance, if you know the *causes* or the *concomitants* <note>accompanying circumstances or signs</note>, you may judge the *effect* that will follow. The same may be said of *discovery*. However, we limit ourselves here primarily to the *divination* and *discovery* caused by an *early* or *subtle perception*.

The *aptness* or *propensity* of *air* or *water* to *corrupt* or *putrefy* (no doubt) can be found before it breaks out into manifest *effects* like *diseases*, *blastings* <note>blights or diseases affecting plants</note>, or the like. We will therefore set down some *prognostics* <note>signs or indicators used to predict the future</note> of *pestilential* <note>plague-ridden</note> and *unwholesome years*.

<margin>801</margin> The wind blowing frequently from the *South* without *rain*, and the presence of *worms* in the *oak-apple* <note>A type of gall or growth on oak trees caused by wasps</note>, have been mentioned before. Also, a *plenty* of *frogs*, *grasshoppers*, *flies*, and similar *creatures* bred from *putrefaction* <note>decay</note>, portends *pestilential years*.

<margin>802</margin> *Great* and *early heats* in the *spring* (specifically in *May*) without *winds* portend the same; and generally, so do *years* with *little wind* or *thunder*.

<header>Century IX.</header>

<margin>803</margin>
Great *droughts* in *summer*, lasting until toward the *end* of *August*, followed by some *gentle showers* and then some *dry weather* again, portend a *pestilential summer* <note>original: "Pestilent Summer"; a summer marked by outbreaks of the plague or other deadly diseases</note> the following year. By the *end* of *August*, all the *sweetness* of the *earth* that goes into *plants* and *trees* has been exhaled (and even more so if *August* is dry). Therefore, nothing can then breathe forth from the *earth* but a coarse *vapor*, which is likely to corrupt the *air*. That *vapor* is released and comes forth abundantly during the first *showers*, if they are *gentle*. Therefore, those who go outdoors soon after those *showers* are commonly taken with *sickness*. In *Africa*, no one will stir out of doors after the first *showers*. However, if the *showers* come vehemently, they wash and fill the *earth* rather than allowing it to breathe immediately. But if *dry weather* returns, it fixes and continues the *corruption* of the *air* begun by the first *showers*. This creates an ill *influence* even until the *next summer*, unless a very *frosty winter* clears it, which seldom follows such a *drought*.

<margin>804</margin>
The *lesser infections* of *smallpox*, *purple fevers* <note>original: "Purple Feuers"; likely referring to spotted fever or typhus, characterized by purple spots on the skin</note>, and *agues* <note>original: "Agues"; fevers involving shivering and chills, often associated with malaria</note> in the *preceding summer*, lingering throughout the *winter*, portend a great *pestilence* in the following *summer*. This is because *putrefaction* <note>the process of decay or rotting</note> does not reach its height all at once.

<margin>805</margin>
It would be wise to lay a *piece* of *raw meat* or *fish* in the *open air*. If it putrefies quickly, it is a *sign* that the *air* is disposed toward *putrefaction*. Because you cannot know whether the *putrefaction* is fast or slow unless you compare this *experiment* with a similar *experiment* in another *year*, it would be helpful to do the following: in the same *year* and at the same *time*, lay one *piece* of *meat* or *fish* in the *open air*, and another of the same *kind* and *size* *indoors*. I judge that if there is a general *disposition* in the *air* to rot, the *meat* or *fish* will rot sooner outdoors, where the *air* has more power, than in the *house*, where the air is less powerful and corrected in many ways. This *experiment* should be made around the *end* of *March*, for that *season* is most likely to reveal what the *winter* has done and what the following *summer* will do to the *air*. And because the *air* (no doubt) receives a great *tincture* <note>an infusion of qualities or characteristics</note> and *infusion* from the *earth*, it would be good to try *exposing* the *meat* or *fish* both on a *wooden stake* some height above the *earth* and on the *flat ground* itself.

<margin>806</margin>
Take *May-dew* and see whether it putrefies quickly or not. That may likewise disclose the *quality* of the *air* and whether the *vapor* of the *earth* is more or less *corrupted*.

<margin>807</margin>
A *dry March* and a *dry May* portend a *wholesome summer* if there is a *showery April* between them. Otherwise, it is a *sign* of a *pestilential year*.

<margin>808</margin>
Just as the *discovery* of the *disposition* of the *air* is good for *prognosticating* <note>predicting</note> healthy and *unhealthy years*, it is of much more use for the *choice* of *places* to live. At the least, it helps in choosing *lodges* and *retirement places* for *health*. (For *manor house provisions*, as well

<margin>809</margin> Regarding the *Choice of Places* or *Sites* for building, it is wise to test not only the *Air's tendency* to corrupt, but also the *Moisture* and *Dryness* of the *Air* and its *Temper* <note>original: "Temper"; the general condition or balance of qualities</note> in *Heat* or *Cold*, for that may affect *Health* in various ways. We see that there are some *Houses* where *Sweets* <note>original: "Sweet Meats"; sugary treats or preserved fruits</note> will soften and *Baked Goods* will mold more than in others. *Wood paneling* <note>original: "Wainscots"</note> will also sweat more, to the point of almost running with *Water*. All of these conditions, no doubt, are caused chiefly by the *Moisture* of the *Air* in those *Sites*. But because it is better to know this before a *Man* builds his *House* than to find it out afterward, perform the following *Experiments*.

<margin>810</margin> Lay *Wool*, a *Sponge*, or *Bread* in the *Place* you would like to test, comparing it with some other *Places*. See whether it does not become moist and make the *wool* or *Sponge*, etc., more *Heavy* <note>original: "Ponderous"</note> than the others. If it does, you may judge that *Place* to be *Situated* in a *Thick* <note>original: "Grosse"</note> and *Moist Air*.

<margin>811</margin> Because it is certain that in some *Places*—either by the *Nature of the Earth* or by the *Position of Woods* and *Hills*—the *Air* is more *Unstable* <note>original: "Vnequall"; meaning the temperature or quality fluctuates more</note> than in *Others*, and *Instability* of *Air* is always an *Enemy* to *Health*, it would be good to take two *weather-glasses* <note>original: "weather-Glaſſes"; early instruments like thermoscopes used to measure temperature changes before modern thermometers were standardized</note> that are identical in every way. Set them for the same *Hours* of *one day* in several *Places* where there is no *Shade* or *Enclosure*. Mark when you set them how high the *water* reaches, and compare them when you return to see how the *water* stands then. If you find them *Unequal*, you may be sure that the *Place* where the *water* is lowest is in the *warmer Air*, and the other is in the *Colder*. The greater the *Difference* in the *Rise* or *Fall* of the *water*, the greater the *Inequality* of the *Air's Temperature*.

<margin>812</margin> The *Predictions* of *Cold* and *Long Winters*, and *Hot* and *Dry Summers*, are also good to know—both for the *Discovery* of the *Causes* and for various *Provisions* <note>original: "Prouiſions"; preparations or supplies</note>. The sign of a *Plenty* of *Hawthorn berries* <note>original: "Hawes"</note>, *Rose hips* <note>original: "Heps"</note>, and *Brier-berries* has been spoken of before. If *Wood paneling* or *Stone* that usually *Sweats* is drier at the *Beginning of Winter*, or if the *Drops* from the *Eaves of Houses* fall more slowly than they usually do, it portends a *Hard* and *Frosty Winter*. The *Cause* is that it shows an *Inclination of the Air* toward *Dry Weather*, which in *Winter* is always joined with *Frost*.

<margin>813</margin> Generally, a *Moist* and *Cool Summer* portends a *Hard winter*. The *Cause* is that the *Vapors of the Earth* are not dispersed in the *Summer* by the *Sun*, and so they remain to affect the *winter*.

<margin>814</margin> A *Hot* and *Dry Summer* and *Autumn*—especially if the *Heat* and *Drought* extend far into *September*—portends a *Mild* <note>original: "Open"</note> *Beginning* of *winter*, with *Colds* to follow toward the latter *Part* of the *Winter* and the *Beginning of the Spring*. Until then, the previous *Heat* and *Drought* hold *Sway*, and the *Vapors* have not yet *Multiplied* sufficiently.

<margin>815</margin> A *Mild* <note>original: "Open"</note> and *warm Winter* portends a *Hot* and *Dry Summer*, for the *Vapors* disperse into the *Winter Showers*; whereas *Cold* and *Frost* keepeth

<margin>816</margin> Birds that usually migrate between *Countries* at certain *Seasons*, if they arrive earlier, reveal the *Weather's temperature* according to the *Country* from which they came. For instance, *winter birds* (namely *Woodcocks*, *Fieldfares* <note>original: "Feldefares"; a member of the thrush family that migrates to Britain in winter</note>, etc.), if they arrive earlier from the *Northern Countries*, indicate *Cold Winters* for us. <margin>817</margin> The *Prognostics* <note>Signs or indicators used to predict the future</note> that are more *Immediate* regarding the *weather* to follow soon after are more *Certain* than those predicting the *Seasons*. The *Resounding* of the *Sea* upon the *Shore*, and the *Murmur* of *Winds* in the *woods* without any apparent *Wind*, indicate that wind is coming. This is because such *Winds*, breathing chiefly out of the *Earth*, are not perceived at first unless they are trapped by *Water* or *wood*. Therefore, a *Murmur* coming out of *Caves* likewise portends the same.

<margin>818</margin> The *Upper Regions* of the *Air* perceive the *Collection* of the *Matter* of *Tempests* and *winds* before the *Air* here below. Therefore, the *Obscuring* of the *Smaller Stars* is a *Sign* of *Tempests* following. You shall find a *Number* of *Instances* of this kind in our *Inquiry into the Winds* <note>original: "Inquisition De Ventis"; one of Bacon's scientific treatises</note>.

<margin>819</margin> *Great Mountains* have a *Perception* of the *Disposition* of the *Air* toward *Tempests* sooner than the *Valleys* or *Plains* below. Therefore, they say in *Wales*, when certain *Hills* have their *Night-Caps* <note>A folkloric term for clouds or mist covering a mountain peak</note> on, they mean *Mischief* <note>In this context, "mischief" refers to severe or damaging weather</note>. The *Cause* is that *Tempests*, which are for the most part bred above in the *Middle Region* (as they call it) <note>In early meteorology, the "Middle Region" was the layer of the atmosphere where clouds, rain, and storms were thought to form</note>, are first perceived to gather in the *Places* nearest to it.

<margin>820</margin> The *Air* and *Fire* have *Subtle Perceptions* of a *Wind Rising* before *Men* notice it. We see that the *Trembling* of a *Candle* will reveal a *wind* that we do not otherwise feel; and the *Wavy Burning* <note>original: "Flexuous Burning"</note> of *Flames* shows that the *Air* is beginning to be unsettled; so too do *Coals* of *Fire* by casting off their *Ashes* more than they usually do. The *Cause* is that no *wind*, at first—until it has struck and driven the *Air*—is apparent to the *Senses*. But *Flame* is easier to move than *Air*. As for the *Ashes*, it is no marvel that *Wind* unperceived shakes them off; for we usually test which way the *wind* blows by casting up *Grass*, *Chaff*, or such light *Things* into the *Air*.

<margin>821</margin> When *wind* emerges from under the *Sea*, it causes some *Resounding* of the *water* (which we mentioned before), and also causes some *Light Motions* of *Bubbles* and *White Circles* of *Froth*. The *Cause* is that the *wind* cannot be perceived by the *Senses* until there is a *Bursting forth* <note>original: "Eruption"</note> of a *great Quantity* from under the *water*, and so it forms into a single *Body*; whereas when it first *Rises*, it comes in little *Portions*.

<header>Natural History:</header>

...wind, shows a *wind* is near; as when *feathers*, or the *down* of *thistles*, fly back and forth in the *air*.

Regarding *prognostics* of *weather* from *living creatures*, it should be noted that *creatures* that *live* in the *open air* (under the open sky <note>original: "Sub Diô"</note>) must necessarily receive a *faster impression* from the *air* than *men* who live mostly *indoors*. This is especially true for *birds*, who live in the *air* most freely and clearly, and are most likely to tell *tales* with their *voice* about what they find, and likewise express the same through the *motion* of their *flight*.

<margin>823</margin>
*Waterfowl* (such as *sea gulls*, *moorhens*, etc.), when they flock and fly together from the *sea* toward the *shores*—and conversely, *land birds* (such as *crows*, *swallows*, etc.), when they fly from the *land* to the *waters* and beat the *waters* with their *wings*—foreshow *rain* and *wind*. The *cause* is the *pleasure* that both *kinds* take in the *moisture* and *density* of the *air*. They desire to be in *motion* and *on the wing*, wherever they might otherwise be going. For it is no *marvel* that *waterfowl* enjoy that *air* most which is most like *water*, and many *land birds* also delight in *bathing* and *moist air*. For the same *reason*, many *birds* preen <note>original: "proine"</note> their *feathers*, *geese* cackle, and *crows* seem to call for *rain*. All of this is merely the *comfort* they seem to receive from the *softening* <note>original: "relenting"; referring to the air becoming more humid and less dry or harsh</note> of the *air*.

<margin>824</margin>
The *heron*, when she soars high (so that she is sometimes seen to pass over a *cloud*), indicates *winds*. But *kites* flying aloft indicate *fair* and *dry weather*. The *cause* may be that they both mount highest into the *air* of that *temperature* in which they delight. The *heron*, being a *waterfowl*, takes pleasure in the *air* that is *condensed*; besides, being *heavy-winged*, she needs the *help* of the *thicker air* <note>original: "grosser air"</note>. But the *kite* is not attracted so much to the *thickness* of the *air* as to its *cold* and *freshness*. Since she is a *bird of prey* and therefore *hot* <note>In the science of the time, birds of prey were thought to have "hot" physical temperaments</note>, she delights in the *fresh air*. She often flies against the *wind*, just as *trout* and *salmon* swim against the *stream*. It is also true that all *birds* find *ease* in the depth of the *air*, just as *swimmers* do in *deep water*; therefore, when they are aloft, they can uphold themselves with their *wings spread*, scarcely moving them.

<margin>825</margin>
*Fish*, when they play near the *top* of the *water*, commonly foretell *rain*. The *cause* is that a *fish*, hating *dryness*, will not approach the *air* until it grows *moist*; and when it is *dry*, it will flee from it and swim *lower*.

<margin>826</margin>
*Beasts* generally take *comfort* in a *moist air*, and it makes them eat their *food* <note>original: "meat"</note> better. Therefore, *sheep* will get up *early* <note>original: "betimes"</note> in the *morning* to feed in anticipation of *rain*; and *cattle*, *deer*, and *rabbits* <note>original: "conneyes"</note> will feed heavily before *rain*. A *heifer* will put up its *nose* and sniff the *air* before *rain*.

<margin>827</margin>
The *Trifoil* <note>original: "Trifoile"; clover</note>, as a sign of *rain*, swells in the *stalk* and stands more upright; for when it is *wet*, *stalks* stand erect and *leaves* bow down.

There is a small *red flower* in the *stubble fields* which country people call the *Wincopipe* <note>likely the Scarlet Pimpernel, often called the "Poor Man's Weatherglass" because it closes its petals before rain</note>. If it opens in the *morning*, you can be sure of a fair *day* to follow.

<margin>828</margin>
Even in *men*, *aches*, *injuries*, and *corns* become more painful either toward *rain* or toward *frost*. For the rain makes the *humors* <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—once thought to determine health and temperament</note> more abundant, and the frost makes them sharper. Thus, we see that both extremes can bring on the *gout*.

<margin>829</margin>
*Worms*, *vermin*, and other such creatures also foreshadow *rain*. For *earthworms* will come out of the ground, *moles* will cast up more dirt, and *fleas* bite more when *rain* is coming.

<margin>830</margin>
*Solid bodies* likewise foreshadow *rain*. Examples include *stones* and *wainscot* <note>wooden wall paneling</note> when they "sweat" <note>collect condensation</note>; and *boxes* and *wooden pegs* when they contract and *bind* <note>original: "winde hard"; tighten due to moisture</note>. However, the former is caused by an outward *cause*, because the *stone* or *wainscot* turns and reflects the *air* back against itself; but the latter is an *inward swelling* of the *body of the wood* itself.

<margin>
Solitary experiment regarding the nature of appetite in the stomach.
831
</margin>
Appetite is stimulated chiefly by things that are *cold* and *dry*. The *cause* is that *cold* is a kind of *natural deficiency* <note>original: "Indigence of Nature"</note> and calls for a new supply, as does *dryness*. Therefore, all *sour things* (such as *vinegar*, *lemon juice*, *oil of vitriol* <note>sulfuric acid, which was historically used in highly diluted forms as a digestive aid</note>, etc.) provoke *appetite*. And the disease which they call *canine appetite* <note>original: "Appetitus Caninus"; an old term for bulimia or ravenous hunger</note> consists of the *matter* of an *acidic* and *glassy phlegm* in the *mouth* of the *stomach*. *Appetite* is also stimulated by *sour things* because they cause a *contraction* in the *nerves* located at the *mouth* of the *stomach*, which is a major *cause* of *appetite*. As for the *reason* why *onions*, *salt*, and *pepper* in baked meats stimulate *appetite*, it is by the *irritation* <note>original: "Vellication"; a localized twitching or stimulation of the nerves</note> of those *nerves*; for motion sharpens the senses. As for *wormwood*, *olives*, *capers*, and others of that kind which have some *bitterness*, they stimulate *appetite* by *cleansing* <note>original: "Abstersion"; the act of wiping or scouring clean</note>. Thus, there are four principal *causes of appetite*: the *cooling* of the *stomach* joined with some *dryness*; *contraction*; *irritation*; and *cleansing*. Besides these, there is *hunger*, which is an *emptiness*. Yet *excessive fasting* often causes the *appetite* to cease because the *lack of food* makes the *stomach* draw *humors*—specifically light and *choleric* <note>referring to yellow bile, thought to be hot and dry</note> humors—which quench *appetite* the most.

It may also be that the water itself has some *sweetness*, for the *rainbow* consists of a *cluster* <note>original: "Glomeration"</note> of *small drops* which cannot possibly fall except from the *air* that is very *low*. ...it therefore may hold the very *sweetness* of the *herbs* and *flowers*, like a *distilled water*. For *rain* and other *dew* that fall from high above cannot preserve the *smell*, as it is scattered when drawn up into the air. We also do not know whether *water* itself might have some degree of *sweetness*. It is true that we do not detect this sweetness in any *pool*, *river*, or *fountain*; however, good *earth*, newly turned over, has a *freshness* and a pleasant *scent*. Water might also possess this, provided it is not too *uniform* <note>original: "Equall"; the idea that the senses only respond to change or contrast, not to a perfectly uniform stimulus</note> (for *uniform objects* never stimulate the *senses*). It is certain that *bay salt*, which is essentially a type of *solidified* water, will sometimes smell like *violets*.

<margin>
Solitary experiment regarding sweet smells.
833
</margin>
For *sweet smells*, *heat* is required to *mature* <term>concoct: to refine, ripen, or process a substance using heat</term> the *matter*, along with some *moisture* to *spread* their *scent*. Regarding *heat*, we see that *woods* and *spices* are more *fragrant* <note>original: "Odorate"</note> in *hot countries* than in *cold* ones. Regarding *moisture*, we see that things that are too dry lose their *sweetness*, and growing *flowers* smell better in the *morning* or *evening* than at *noon*. Some *sweet smells* are destroyed by proximity to *fire*, such as *violets*, *wallflowers*, *gillyflowers*, and *pinks*—generally all *flowers* that have *cool* and *delicate spirits* <note>volatile or subtle essences</note>. Some smells persist both on and off the *fire*, such as *rosewater*, etc. Some hardly emerge, or at least not as pleasantly, except by means of *fire*, such as *juniper*, *sweet gums*, and so on, and any *smells* that are enclosed in a *dense body* <term>fast body: a solid, non-porous material that traps scents</term>. But generally, those *smells* are the most pleasing where the degree of *heat* is *low*, or where the *strength* of the *smell* is softened; for these scents entice the *senses* rather than overwhelming them. Therefore, the *smell* of *violets* and *roses* surpasses the *sweetness* of *spices* and *gums*; and the strongest types of *smells* are best when carried on a light breeze from a distance.

---

<margin>
Solitary experiment regarding the physical substance of smells.
834
</margin>
It is certain that no *smell* is released without the *emission* of some *physical substance* <note>original: "Corporeall substance"</note>; this is not the case with *light*, *colors*, or *sounds*. For we see plainly that *smell* does not travel nearly as far as those other phenomena do. It is true that some *orange groves* and *rosemary heaths* will smell far out into the *sea*, perhaps twenty miles; but what is that compared to a *cannon blast* <note>original: "Peale of Ordnance"</note>, which carries just as far despite originating from a small area? In contrast, those *woods* and *heaths* cover vast spaces. Besides, we see that *smells* adhere to *hard objects*, as in the *perfuming* of *gloves*, etc., which shows they are *physical*. They also last a long time, whereas *sounds* and *light* do not.

A *cat* also buries its waste. This is especially true for *animals* that feed upon *meat*. *Dogs* are almost the only *animals* that delight in *foul odors*, which shows there is something in their *sense* of *smell* that differs from other *animals*. Those from the *second digestion* are less offensive, such as *urine*; and those from the *third* are even less so, for *sweat* is not as bad as the other two, especially in some *persons* who are full of *heat*. Likewise, most *putrefactions* <note>original: "Putrifactions"; the process of rotting or decay</note> have an *odious smell*, for they smell either *fetid* or *moldy*. The *cause* may be that *putrefaction* produces a *consistency* that is most contrary to the *consistency* of the *body* while it is *healthy*. For it is a mere dissolution of that *form*.

Besides, there is another *reason* which is profound: it is that the *objects* that please any of the *senses* all have some *equality* and (as it were) *order* in their *composition*. But where those are lacking, the *object* is always *unpleasant* <note>original: "Ingrate"</note>. So a *mixture* of many *disagreeing colors* is always unpleasant to the *eye*; a *mixture* of *discordant sounds* is unpleasant to the *ear*; a *mixture*, or *hotch-potch* of many *tastes*, is unpleasant to the *taste*; and the *harshness* and *ruggedness* of *bodies* is unpleasant to the *touch*. Now it is certain that all *putrefaction*, being a *dissolution* of the original *form*, is a mere *confusion* and *unformed mixture* of the *parts*. 

Nevertheless, it is strange—and seems to *contradict* the former *observation*—that some *putrefactions* and *excrements* do yield *excellent odors*, such as *civet* and *musk*, and as some think, *ambergris* <note>original: "Amber-Greece"</note>. For various people believe (though improbably) that it comes from the *sperm* of *fish*. And the *moss* we spoke of from *apple trees* is little better than an *excretion*. The reason may be that some good *spirits* <term>volatile essences or vital energies</term> pass into the *excrements* and remain in the *putrefactions*, especially where they proceed from *creatures* that are very *hot*. But it may also be joined with a further *cause*, which is more subtle: it is that the *senses* do not like to be "over-pleased," but rather to have a *mixture* of something that is in itself *unpleasant*. 

Certainly, we see how *discords* in *music*, when resolved into *concords*, create the *sweetest strains*. And we see again what strange *tastes* delight the *taste*, such as *red herrings*, *caviar* <note>original: "Caveary"</note>, *parmesan* <note>original: "Parmizan"</note>, etc. And it may be that the same principle holds in *smells*. For those kinds of *smells* that we have mentioned are all strong, and they *pull* and *stimulate* <term>vellicate: to twitch, nip, or stimulate the nerves</term> the *sense*. And we find also that *places* where men *urinate* commonly have some *smell* of *violets*; and *urine*, if one has eaten *nutmeg*, has that smell too.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning the causes of putrefaction. 836.</margin>
All *putrefaction* <note>original: "putrifaction"; the process of rotting or decay</note> arises chiefly from the *inward spirits* <note>original: "spirits"; in early modern science, these were active, subtle substances within matter that caused change and movement</note> of the *body*, and partly also from the *surrounding environment* <note>original: "ambient body"</note>, whether it be *air*, *liquid*, or whatever else. This last influence happens by two *means*: either by the *entry* of the *substance* of the *surrounding environment* into the *rotting body*, or by the *excitation* and *stimulation* of the *rotting body* and its *parts* by the *surrounding environment*. As for the *received opinion* that *putrefaction* is caused either by *cold* or by *foreign* and *unnatural heat*, it is mere *nonsense* <note>original: "nugation"</note>. For *cold* in *inanimate things* is the greatest *enemy* there is to *putrefaction*, even though it extinguishes *vivification* <note>original: "vivification"; the process of coming to life</note>, which always consists of *thinned spirits* that the *cold* congeals and hardens. And as for *foreign heat* <note>original: "peregrine heat"</note>, this much is true: if the *proportion* of the *external heat* <note>original: "adventive heat"</note> is much greater than the *natural heat* and *spirits* of the *body*, it leads to *dissolution* or *notable alteration*. But this is brought about by the *release*, *suppression*, or *suffocation* of the *native spirits*, and also by the *disorder* and *disarrangement* of the *tangible parts* and other *natural passages*, and not by a *conflict of heats*.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning imperfectly mixed bodies. 837.</margin>
In *transformations* or *major alterations* of *bodies*, there is a *medium* <note>original: "medium"; a middle state</note> between the *body* as it is at first and the *resulting body*. This *medium* is *an imperfectly mixed body* <note>original: "Corpus imperfectè Mistum"</note> and is *transitory* rather than durable. Examples include *mists*, *smoke*, *vapors*, *chyle* <note>original: "chylus"; a milky fluid produced in the stomach during digestion</note> in the *stomach*, and *living creatures* in their first *animation*. The *middle action* which produces such *imperfect bodies* is appropriately called (by some of the *ancients*) *pollution* <note>original: "inquination"</note> or *undigested state* <note>original: "inconcoction"</note>, which is a *kind of putrefaction*; for the *parts* are in *confusion* until they settle one way or another.

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning concoction and rawness. 838.</margin>
The word *concoction* <note>original: "concoction"; the process of ripening, maturing, or digesting through heat</note>, or *digestion*, is primarily adapted from the terminology of *living creatures* and their *organs*, and from there extended to *liquids*, *fruits*, and so on. Therefore, people speak of *digested meat*, *matured urine* and *excrements*, and the *four digestions* (in the *stomach*, in the *liver*, in the *arteries and nerves*, and in the *various parts of the body*) are likewise called *concoctions*. They are all considered to be the *works of heat*. All of these *notions* are merely ignorant *snatches* of a few *things* that are most obvious to *men's observations*. The most consistent *notion* of *concoction* is that it should signify the *degrees of alteration* of one *body* into another, from *rawness* <note>original: "crudity"</note> to perfect *concoction*, which is the *final result* <note>original: "ultimity"</note> of that *action* or *process*. While the *body* to be *converted* and *altered* is too strong for the *active cause* <note>original: "efficient"</note> that should *convert* or *alter* it (whereby it resists and holds fast in some degree to its first...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of natural processes, specifically transitioning from the causes of putrefaction to the mechanics of "concoction"—the process by which matter is matured, refined, or transformed by heat and other internal forces.</meta>

# Century IX.

Until a substance achieves its proper form or consistency, it is (during that entire time) **crude** and **unrefined** <note>original: "Inconcoct"; a state where matter has not yet been transformed by heat or natural processes.</note>; and the process is to be called **crudity** and **lack of refinement**. It is true that **concoction** <term>Concoction: In early modern science, this referred to the "ripening" or "digestion" of matter, usually through the application of heat, to make it more refined or useful.</term> is, in great part, the work of **heat**. However, it is not the work of heat alone. All things that further the conversion or alteration—such as **rest**, or the **mixture with a substance already processed**, and so on—are also means toward concoction. 

There are two stages of concoction. The first is **assimilation**, or **absolute conversion** and **subaction** <note>original: "Subaction"; the process of bringing a substance under control or reducing it to a new form.</note>. The second is **maturation**. 

The former is most obvious in the bodies of **living creatures**, in which there is an absolute conversion and assimilation of nourishment into the body. It is likewise seen in the bodies of **plants**, and again in **metals**, where there is a full transmutation. 

The other stage, **maturation**, is seen in **liquids** and **fruits**. In these, a complete conversion is neither desired nor intended; rather, the goal is only an alteration into the form most sought for human use, such as in the **clarifying of drinks**, the **ripening of fruits**, and so on. 

But note that there are two kinds of absolute conversions. One occurs when a body is converted into another body that already existed, such as when nourishment is turned into flesh. This is what we call **assimilation**. The other occurs when the conversion results in a body that is entirely new and did not exist before, such as if silver were turned to gold, or iron to copper. For the sake of distinction, this type of conversion is better called **transmutation**.

---

<margin>Solitary experiment concerning alterations which may be called **greater alterations** <note>original: "Alteratio Maior"</note>. **839**</margin>

There are also various other **great alterations of matter** and bodies besides those that lead toward concoction and maturation. Whatever alters a body so significantly that it cannot return to what it was before may be called a **greater alteration** <note>original: "Alteratio Maior"</note>. This occurs when meat is boiled, roasted, or fried; when bread and meat are baked; when cheese is made of curds, butter of cream, charcoal of wood, or bricks of clay; and in many other instances. 

To apply philosophical notions to common terms—or to say that where the notions cannot be easily reconciled, there is a lack of a specific term or naming system (as the ancients did)—is merely an **excuse for ignorance** <note>original: "Shifts of Ignorance"</note>. Knowledge will always be a wandering and **unorganized thing** if it is only a mixture of a few ideas that are easily available, and not drawn from a sufficient number of instances that have been well compared.

---

The **consistencies of bodies** are very diverse: **dense** and **rare**; **tangible** and **gas-like** <note>original: "Pneumaticall"</note>; **volatile** and **fixed**; **determinate** (having a fixed shape) and **not determinate**; **hard** and **soft**; **sticky** <note>original: "Cleaving"</note> and **not sticky**; **congealable** and **not congealable**; **liquefiable** and **not liquefiable**; **fragile** and **tough**; **flexible** and **inflexible**; **tractile** (able to be drawn out in length) and **intractile**; **porous** and **solid**; **equal and smooth** and **unequal**; **veined** <note>original: "Venous"</note> and **fibrous**...

To refer all these things to **heat**, and **cold**, and **moisture**, and **drought**, is a brief and useless theory <note>original: "Compendious and Inutile Speculation"</note>. But regarding these, see primarily our *Alphabet of Nature* <note>original: "Abecedarium Naturae"</note>; and otherwise scattered <note>original: "Sparsim"</note> throughout this, our *Forest of Materials* <note>original: "Sylva Sylvarum"</note>. <margin>
Experiment 
Solitary touching Bodies Liquefiable, and 
not Liquefiable. 
840
</margin>
Whether a body is **meltable** <note>original: "Liquefiable"</note> or **not meltable** proceeds from these causes: **liquefaction** is always caused by the **trapping** <note>original: "Detention"</note> of the **spirits** <term>Spirits: In Bacon’s natural philosophy, "spirits" are the active, subtle, and often vaporous substances trapped within the "tangible" or solid parts of matter.</term>, which move within the body and open it up. Therefore, those bodies that are more **swollen with spirit**, or that have their spirits more **tightly imprisoned**, or again that hold them **better satisfied and content**, are meltable. For these three conditions of bodies stop the **release** <note>original: "Emission"</note> of the spirits. 

An example of the first two properties is found in **metals**, and of the last in **grease**, **pitch**, **sulfur**, **butter**, **wax**, etc. The condition of not melting proceeds from the **easy release** of the spirits, which causes the **solid** <note>original: "Grosser"</note> **parts** to contract. Therefore, bodies **lacking in spirits** <note>original: "jeune of Spirits"</note>, or those which part with their spirits more willingly, are not meltable, such as **wood**, **clay**, **sandstone** <note>original: "Free-Stone"</note>, etc. 

But yet, even many of those bodies that will not melt, or will hardly melt, will nevertheless **soften**, such as **iron** in the forge, and a stick soaked in hot ashes, which thereby becomes more flexible. Moreover, there are some bodies which melt or dissolve by **fire**, such as **metals**, **wax**, etc., and other bodies which dissolve in **water**, such as **salt**, **sugar**, etc. The cause of the former proceeds from the **expansion** <note>original: "Dilatation"</note> of the spirits by heat. The cause of the latter proceeds from the **opening** of the **tangible parts**, which desire to receive the liquid. Again, there are some bodies that dissolve with both, such as **gum**, etc. And those are such bodies as, on the one hand, have a good supply of spirit and, on the other hand, have tangible parts **lacking in moisture**. For the former helps the expansion of the spirits by the fire, and the latter stimulates the parts to receive the liquid.

<margin>
Experiment 
Solitary touching Bodies 
Fragile, and 
Tough. 
841
</margin>
Of bodies, some are **fragile**, and some are **tough** and **not fragile**. And in breaking, some fragile bodies break only where the force is applied; some shatter and fly into many pieces. The cause of **fragility** is an **inability to be stretched** <note>original: "Impotency to be Extended"</note>. Therefore, **stone** is more fragile than **metal**, and so **pottery clay** <note>original: "Fictile Earth"</note> is more fragile than **raw earth**, and **dry wood** more than **green wood**. 

And the cause of this unfitness for stretching is the **small quantity of spirits** (for it is the spirit that promotes the stretching or expansion of bodies), and it is always accompanied by **porosity** and **dryness** in the tangible parts. On the contrary, **tough bodies** have more spirit, fewer pores, and moister tangible parts. Therefore, we see that **parchment** or **leather** will stretch; **paper** will not. **Woolen cloth** will stretch on a frame <note>original: "tenter"</note>, but **linen** scarcely at all.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the internal properties of matter, moving from the causes of melting to the distinction between "pneumatic" (spirit-based) and "tangible" (physical) substances, and how these affect hardness and fluidity.</meta>

Century IX.

All solid **bodies** consist of **parts** of two different **natures**: **pneumatic** <term>Pneumatic: In Bacon's time, this referred to things composed of air, gas, or "spirits" rather than solid matter.</term> and **tangible**. It is well to be noted that the **pneumatic substance** is, in some **bodies**, the **native spirit** of the **body**; and in others, it is plain **air** that has entered in, as in **bodies dried out** <note>original: "Desiccate"</note> by **heat** or **age**. In those dried bodies, when the **native spirit** goes out, and the **moisture** with it, the **air** over time gets into the **pores**. Those **bodies** are always more **fragile**, for the **native spirit** is more **yielding** and **flexible** <note>original: "Extensive"</note>—especially in following the movement of the physical parts—than **air** is. The **native spirits** also admit great **diversity**, being **hot**, **cold**, **active**, **dull**, etc. From these spirits proceed most of the **virtues** <term>Virtues: The inherent powers, medicinal properties, or natural qualities of a substance.</term> and **qualities** (as we call them) of **bodies**. But the **intermixed air** is without **virtues** and makes things **tasteless** <note>original: "Insipide"</note> and without any **vitality** <note>original: "Extimulation"</note>.

The **solidifying** <note>original: "Concretion"</note> of **bodies** is commonly reversed by its **opposite**. For example, **ice**, which is congealed by **cold**, is dissolved by **heat**. **Salts** and **sugar**, which are **boiled down** <note>original: "Excocted"</note> by **heat**, are dissolved by **cold** and **moisture**. The **cause** is that these **operations** are **returns** to their former **nature** rather than total **alterations**, so that the **opposite** state cures them. As for **oil**, it does neither easily congeal with **cold** nor thicken with **heat**. The **cause** of both **effects**, though they are produced by **opposite factors** <note>original: "Contrary Efficients"</note>, seems to be the **same**: because the **spirit** of the **oil** does not easily evaporate by other **means**. The **cold** keeps the spirit in, and the **heat** (unless it is **intense** <note>original: "Vehement"</note>) does not draw it out. As for **cold**, though it takes hold of the **tangible parts**, regarding the **spirits**, it makes them **swell** rather than **congeal**. For example, when **ice** is frozen in a **cup**, the **ice** will **swell** instead of **contracting**, and sometimes it will even **split** <note>original: "Ritt"</note> the container.

Of **bodies**, we see that some are **hard** and some are **soft**. The **hardness** is caused chiefly by the **scarcity** <note>original: "lessenes"</note> of the **spirits** and their **imbalance** <note>original: "Imparity"</note> with the **tangible parts**. If both of these conditions are present to a high degree, it makes the body not only **hard** but **fragile** and less **enduring** of **pressure**, such as **steel**, **stone**, **glass**, **dry wood**, etc. **Softness** comes, conversely, from a greater **quantity of spirits** (which always helps to **induce yielding** <note>original: "Teelding and Cession"</note>) and by the more **equal spreading** of the **tangible parts**, which are thereby more **fluid** <note>original: "sliding"</note> and **compliant**. This is seen in **gold**, **lead**, **wax**, etc. But note that **soft bodies** (as we use the word) are of two **kinds**. The one kind easily gives way to another **body** but does not change its total **bulk** by **rising** in other **places**. Therefore, we see that **wax**, if you put any **thing** into it, does not rise in **bulk** but only **gives way**. You should not think that in **stamping** <note>original: "Printing"</note> **wax**, the **wax** rises at all; rather, only the **depressed part** gives way and the rest remains as it was. The other kind changes its **bulk** as it **yields**, such as **water** or other **liquids**. If you put a **stone** or any **thing** into them, they indeed give way easily, but then they rise all over. This is a **false yielding** <note>original: "False Cession"</note>, for the change is in **location** <note>original: "Place"</note> and not in the **body** itself.

# Natural History:

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning **ductile** and **tensile** bodies. 
845
</margin>

All **ductile** <term>Ductile: Materials that can be hammered thin or drawn into wire without breaking.</term> and **tensile** <term>Tensile: Materials capable of being stretched or drawn out.</term> **bodies** (such as **metals** that can be drawn into **wires**, or **wool** and **tow** <note>original: "Tow" — the coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp.</note> that can be drawn into **yarn** or **thread**) have a strong **urge to remain connected** <note>original: "Appetite of not Discontinuing"</note>. This quality makes them follow the force that pulls them outward, yet in such a way that they do not **break apart** <note>original: "discontinue"</note> or leave their own **body**. **Viscous bodies** (likewise), such as **pitch**, **wax**, **bird-lime** <note>original: "Bird-Lime" — a sticky substance spread on branches to catch birds.</note>, and **toasted cheese**, will stretch out and form "ropes" or strings. However, the difference between **fibrous bodies** and **viscous bodies** is plain. All **wool**, **tow**, **cotton**, and **silk** (especially raw **silk**) have—besides their desire for **continuity**—a **greediness for moisture** due to the **thinness** of their **threads**. Through **moisture**, they join and incorporate with other **threads**, especially if there is a little **wreathing**, as is seen in the **twisting** of **thread** and the practice of **spinning** <note>original: "Twirling about of Spindles"</note>. We also see that **gold** and **silver thread** cannot be made without **twisting**.

---

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning other reactions of matter and characteristics of bodies. 
846
</margin>

The differences between being **impressible** and **not impressible**, **formable** <note>original: "Figurable"</note> and **not formable**, **moldable** and **not moldable**, or **splittable** <note>original: "Scissile"</note> and **not splittable**, along with many other **properties of matter**, are **commonplace ideas** <note>original: "Plebeian Notions"</note> applied to the **tools** and **uses** that men ordinarily practice. However, these are all merely the **effects** of some of the following **causes**, which we will **list** without **applying** them individually, as that would be too long.

1.  The first is the **yielding** <note>original: "Cession"</note> or not yielding of **bodies** into a **smaller space**, while maintaining their **outer size** and not escaping.
2.  The second is the **stronger** or **weaker urge** in **bodies** to maintain **continuity** and to avoid **breaking apart**.
3.  The third is the **disposition** of **bodies** to **contract** or **not contract**, and again, to **extend** or **not extend**.
4.  The fourth is the **small** or **large amount** of the **gaseous content** <note>original: "Pneumaticall"</note> in **bodies**.
5.  The fifth is the **nature** of the **gaseous content**, whether it is the **native spirit** of the **body** or **common air**.
6.  The sixth is the **nature** of the **native spirits** in the **body**, whether they are **active** and **eager**, or **dull** and **gentle**.
7.  The seventh is the **release** or **trapping** <note>original: "Emission or Detention"</note> of the **spirits** in **bodies**.
8.  The eighth is the **expansion** <note>original: "Dilatation"</note> or **contraction** of the **spirits** in **bodies** while they are trapped.
9.  The ninth is the **arrangement** <note>original: "Collocation"</note> of the **spirits** in **bodies**: whether the **arrangement** is **equal** or **unequal**, and again, whether the **spirits** are **clumped together** <note>original: "Coacervate"</note> or **spread out** <note>original: "Diffused"</note>.
10. The tenth is the **density** or **thinness** of the **physical parts** <note>original: "Tangible Parts"</note>.
11. The eleventh is the **uniformity** or **variation** of the **physical parts**.
12. The twelfth is the **ripeness** <note>original: "Digestion"</note> or **rawness** <note>original: "Crudity"</note> of the **physical parts**.
13. The thirteenth is the **nature** of the **matter**, whether **sulfurous** or **mercurial** <term>Sulfurous and Mercurial: In early modern science, these were considered the two primary principles of matter; sulfur represented flammability and oiliness, while mercury represented volatility and fluidity.</term>, **watery** or **oily**, **dry** and **earthy**, or **moist** and **liquid**. These **sulfurous** and **mercurial** natures seem to be the **fundamental** and **principal** natures.
14. The fourteenth is the **placement** of the **physical parts**, whether **lengthwise** or **crosswise** (as seen in the **warp** and the **woof** of **fabrics**), and whether they are **more inward** or **more outward**, etc.
15. The fifteenth is the **porosity** (presence of pores) or **lack of pores** between the **physical parts**, and the **large** or **small size** of the **pores**.
16. The sixteenth is the **arrangement** and **position** of the **pores**.

There may be more **causes**, but these occur to me for the present.

<header>Century IX.</header>

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning **hardening** by **affinity**.
847
</margin>
Take **Lead** and melt it. In the middle of it, when it begins to **congeal** <note>original: "congeale" — to solidify from a liquid state.</note>, make a little dent or hole and put **mercury** <term>Quick-silver: The archaic name for the element mercury.</term> wrapped in a piece of **linen** into that hole. The **mercury** will **solidify** <note>original: "fix"</note>, run no more, and endure the strike of a hammer. This is a notable **example** of **hardening** <note>original: "Induration"</note> caused by the **affinity** <note>original: "Consent"</note> of one **body** with another and an **impulse** to **imitate** the state of the surrounding material; for to ascribe it only to the **vapors** of the **lead** is less probable. One might **ask** <note>original: "Quære"</note> whether this **solidifying** can reach such a degree that it can be shaped like other **metals**? For if so, you may make useful items from it, provided they do not come near the **fire**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning **honey** and **sugar**.
848
</margin>
**Sugar** has replaced the use of **honey**, to the point that we have lost those **observations** and **preparations** of **honey** which the **ancients** had when it was more valuable. First, it seems that in old times there was **tree-honey** as well as **bee-honey**, which was the **sap** or **fluid** <note>original: "Teare or Bloud"</note> issuing from the **tree**. One of the **ancients** relates that in **Trebizond** <note>A city on the Black Sea coast of modern-day Turkey.</note> there was **honey** issuing from **box-trees** which made **men mad**. Again, in ancient times, there was a kind of **honey** which—either by its own nature or by art—would grow as hard as **sugar** and was not as cloying as ours. They also had a **wine** made of **honey**, which they prepared like this: they crushed the **honey** into a great **quantity** of **water** and then strained the **liquid**. Afterward, they boiled it in a **copper** vessel until it was reduced by half, then poured it into **earthen vessels** for a short time, and finally **stored** <note>original: "tunned"</note> it in **wooden vessels** and kept it for many years. Today in **Russia** and those **northern countries**, they still have **plain mead**, which (when well-made and seasoned) is a good, wholesome, and very clear **drink**. In **Wales**, they also use a **compound drink** of **mead** mixed with **herbs** and **spices**. Meanwhile, as a compensation for what we have lost in **honey**, there has been brought into use a **sugar-mead** (as we may call it), though it contains no **mixture** of **honey** at all. It is brewed and kept until aged <note>original: "stale"</note> just as they use **mead**. Certainly, while it would not be as **cleansing** <term>Abstersive: Having a cleansing or purging quality.</term>, **opening**, and **laxative** <term>Solutive: Having the power to dissolve or loosen the bowels.</term> a **drink** as **mead**, it will be more agreeable to the **stomach** and more **soothing** <term>Lenitive: Having the quality of softening or mitigating pain or irritation.</term>, making it fit for use in **acute diseases** <note>original: "Sharpe Diseases"</note>. We see that the use of **sugar** in **beer** and **ale** has good **effects** in such **cases**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the finer sort of **base metals**.
849
</margin>
It is reported by the **ancients** that there was a kind of **steel** in some places which would polish almost as white and bright as **silver**, and that there was in **India** a kind of **brass** which (when polished) could scarcely be distinguished from **gold**. This was found in the **natural ore**. However, I doubt whether men have sufficiently refined those **metals** which we consider **base**. For instance, have **iron**, **brass**, and **tin** been refined to their highest potential? Usually, when they reach a fineness that serves ordinary uses, men attempt no further refinement.

Solitary experiment concerning the altering of the color of hair and feathers.
851
</margin>

Living creatures generally change their **hair** with **age**, turning **gray** and **white**. This is seen in **men** (though some earlier, some later); in **horses** that are dappled and turn **white**; in old **squirrels** that turn **grizzled**; and many others. Some **birds** do the same: **cygnets** <note>Young swans.</note> turn from **gray** to **white**; **hawks** turn more **white** from **brown**. There are also some **birds** that change color upon **molting**; for example, **robin redbreasts** gradually grow **red** again after their **molting**, as do **goldfinches** on their **heads**. The cause is that **moisture** primarily colors **hair** and **feathers**, while **dryness** turns them **gray** and **white**. As **hair** ages, it grows **drier**, and so do **feathers**. Regarding **feathers**, after **molting**, they are **young feathers** and are therefore the same as the **feathers** of **young birds**. Similarly, the **beard** is younger than the **hair** of the **head** and usually grows **gray** <note>original: "wax Hoare"</note> later. Based on this **principle** <note>original: "Ground"</note>, one may devise the **means** of **altering** the **color** of **birds** and the **delaying** of **gray hair**. For more on this, see the fifth **experiment**.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the differences between male and female living creatures.
852
</margin>

The **difference** between **male** and **female** in some **creatures** is not to be discerned except by their **reproductive organs** <note>original: "Parts of Generation"</note>, such as in **horses** and **mares**, **dogs** and **bitches**, male and female **doves**, and others. But some differ in **size** <term>Magnitude: Physical size or bulk.</term>, and in various ways: in most, the **male** is the larger, as in **men**, **pheasants**, **peacocks**, **turkeys**, and the like; yet in a few, such as **hawks**, the **female** is larger. Some differ in **hair** and **feathers**, regarding their **quantity**, **curliness** <term>Crispation: The quality of being curled or frizzled.</term>, and **colors**. For example, **male lions** are **hairy** <term>Hersute: An archaic spelling of hirsute, meaning hairy.</term> and have great **manes**, while the **females** are smooth like **cats**. **Bulls** have **curlier** hair on their **foreheads** than **cows**. The **peacock**, the **male pheasant**, and the **male goldfinch** have glorious and fine **colors**, while the **hens** do not. Generally, the **males** among **birds** have the fairest **feathers**. Some differ in various **features**: **bucks** have **horns**, while **does** have none; **rams** have more twisted **horns** than **ewes**; **roosters** <note>original: "Cocks"</note> have large **combs** and **spurs**, while **hens** have little or none; **boars** have large **tusks** <note>original: "Fangs"</note>, while **sows** have much smaller ones; the **turkey cock** has large and swelling **wattles** <note>original: "Gills"</note>, while the **hen** has smaller ones; **men** generally have deeper and stronger **voices** than **women**. Some differ in **ability** <note>original: "Facultie"</note>; for instance, the **males** among **singing birds** are the best **singers**. The **primary cause** of all these differences (no doubt) is that **males** have a greater **intensity of heat** than **females**. This is clearly shown by the fact that all young **male creatures** resemble **females**, as do **eunuchs** and **castrated** <note>original: "Gelt"</note> **creatures** of all kinds, which are more like **females**. Now, **heat** generally causes **greatness of growth** where there is enough **moisture** to work upon. However, if there is found in any **creature** (which is rarely seen) an excessive **heat** in proportion to the **moisture**, the **female** is the larger, as in **hawks** and **sparrows**. If the **heat** is balanced with the **moisture**, then there is no difference to be seen between **male** and **female**. <term>Heat and Moisture: In early modern science, the balance of "innate heat" and "radical moisture" was believed to determine growth, aging, and sex.</term>
