male: as in the **examples** of **horses** and **dogs**. We also see that the **horns** of **oxen** and **cows** are, for the most part, larger than those of **bulls**; this is caused by an abundance of **moisture**, which is lacking in the **horns** of the **bull**. Furthermore, **heat** causes **hairiness** <term>pilosity</term> and **curling** <term>crispation</term>, as seen in the **beards** of **men**. Heat also expels finer **moisture**, which a **lack** of **heat** cannot **expel**; this is the **cause** of the **beauty** and **variety** of **feathers**. Again, **heat** produces many **growths** <term>excrescences</term> and much **solid matter** which a **lack** of **heat** cannot produce. This is the **cause** of **horns** and their **great size**, as well as the **large size** of the **combs** and **spurs** of **roosters**, the **wattles** <note>original: "Gills"</note> of **turkeys**, and the **tusks** <note>original: "Fangs"</note> of **boars**. **Heat** also dilates the **pipes** and **organs**, which causes the **deepness** of the **voice**. Finally, **heat** refines the **spirits** <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to the vital internal energies believed to animate living things.</note>, and that is why the **male songbird** **surpasses** the **female** in singing.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the relative size of living creatures. 853
</margin>

There are fish larger than any land animals; for instance, the **whale** is far larger than the **elephant**. Also, **land animals** <note>original: "Beasts"</note> are generally larger than **birds**. Regarding **fish**, the cause may be that because they do not live in the **air**, their **moisture** is not drawn out and evaporated <note>original: "Soaked"</note> by the **air** and **sunlight**. Also, they are almost always at rest and are supported by the water, whereas **movement** and **labor** consume energy and moisture. As for the **greater size** of **land animals** compared to **birds**, it is because **animals** stay for a longer time in the **womb** than **birds**, where they are **nourished** and **grow**. In **birds**, after the **egg** is laid, there is no further **growth** or **nourishment** from the **female**, for **sitting** <note>Incubating the egg.</note> brings it to life <note>original: "Viuifie"</note> but does not **nourish** it.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning the removal of seeds from fruits. 854
</margin>

We have previously touched upon the **means** of **producing fruits** without **cores** or **stones** <note>This process is called "exossation" in the marginal note, meaning "de-boning."</note>. To this we add that the **cause** must be an **abundance** of **moisture**, for the **core** and **stone** are made of a **dry sap**. We see that it is possible to make a **tree** produce only **blossoms** without **fruit**, as with **cherries** with **double flowers**; it should be even easier to produce **fruit** without **stones** or **cores**. It is reported that a **scion** <note>original: "Cions"; a young shoot or twig of a plant used for grafting.</note> of an **apple**, grafted onto a **cabbage** <term>colewort</term> stalk, produces a large **apple** without a **core**. It is not unlikely that if the **inner pith** of a **tree** were removed so that the **juice** flowed only through the **bark**, it would achieve this effect. It has been observed that in **pollarded trees** <note>original: "Pollards"; trees with the top branches cut back to encourage new growth.</note>, if **water** gets into the **top** and they become **hollow**, they produce more. We also add that it is stated as a certainty by some that if the **scion** is grafted with the **small end** pointing downward, it will result in **fruit** with little or no **cores** or **stones**.

However, **English tobacco** has a poor reputation, as it is too **bland** <note>original: "Dull"</note> and **earthy**. Even **Virginian tobacco**, though grown in a **hotter climate**, can get no reputation for the same **reason**. So, a trial...

An experiment to make *Tobacco* more *aromatic* <note>original: "Aromaticall"</note>, and better *processed* <note>original: "Concocted" - here meaning ripened or chemically transformed by heat</note> here in *England*, would be a thing of great profit. Some have attempted to do it by soaking <note>original: "Drenching"</note> the *English Tobacco* in a *decoction* or *infusion* of *Indian Tobacco*. But those are merely tricks <note>original: "Sophistications"</note> and trifles <note>original: "Toyes"</note>; for nothing that is once perfect and has finished its growth <note>original: "run his Race"</note> can receive much improvement. You must always return to the beginning of things for *improvement* <note>original: "Melioration"</note>. The way to achieve the *ripening* <note>original: "Maturation"</note> of *Tobacco* must, as in other *plants*, come from *heat*—either from the *earth* or from the *sun*. We see some guidance <note>original: "Leading"</note> for this in *musk-melons*, which are sown upon a *hotbed*, fertilized <note>original: "Dunged"</note> below, on a bank turned toward the *southern sun* to provide *heat* by *reflection*; laid upon *tiles*, which increases the *heat*; and covered with straw to keep them from the *cold*. They also transplant <note>original: "remoue"</note> them, which adds some *vigor* <note>original: "Life"</note>; and by these aids, they become as good in *England* as in *Italy* or *Provence*. These and similar means may be tried with *Tobacco*. Inquire also into the *steeping* of the *roots* in some such *liquid* that may give them the vigor to grow strong.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning different types of heat producing the same effects. 856
</margin>
The heat of the *sun* for the *ripening* <note>original: "Maturation"</note> of *fruits*, and even the *heat* for the *animation* <note>original: "Viuification"</note> of *living creatures*, are both represented and provided by the *heat* of *fire*. Likewise, the *heats* of the *sun* and of *life* are represented by one another. *Trees* planted against the *backs* of *chimneys* ripen *fruit* sooner. *Vines* that have been pulled in through the window of a *kitchen* have produced *grapes* ripe at least a month before others. *Heated rooms* <note>original: "Stoues"</note> at the *back* of *walls* allow *oranges* to grow here with us. *Eggs*, as is reported by some, have been hatched in the warmth of an *oven*. It is reported by the *ancients* that the *ostrich* <note>original: "Estrich"</note> lays her *eggs* under *sand*, where the *heat* of the *sun* hatches <note>original: "discloseth"</note> them.

<margin>
Solitary experiment concerning swelling and expansion in boiling. 857
</margin>
Barley does not swell much during *boiling*; *wheat* swells more; *rice* extremely, so much so that a *quarter-pint* (unboiled) will grow to a *pint* boiled. The *cause* (no doubt) is because the more close and compact the *body* is, the more it will expand. Now *barley* is the most hollow; *wheat* is more solid than that; and *rice* is the most solid of all. It may be also that some *bodies* have a kind of *viscosity* <term>lentour</term> and a more *dispersible nature* <term>depertible nature</term> than others. As we see clearly in *coloration*; for a small quantity of *saffron* will *tint* more than a very great *quantity* of *brazilwood* <note>original: "Brefill" - a red wood used to produce dye</note> or *wine*.

Regarding *time* and *keeping*: it is because the *spirits* within the *body* always feed upon the *tangible parts* and thin <note>original: "attenuate"</note> them. Regarding various *maturations* <note>ripening or processing by heat</note>: it is by some *degree* of *heat*. All *sourness* consists of some *coarseness* <note>original: "Grosnesse"</note> of the *body*, and all *incorporation* makes the *mixture* of the *body* more *equal* in all its *parts*, which always results in a *milder taste*.

<margin>Solitary Experiment touching edible and non-edible flesh. 859</margin>
Of meats <note>original: "Fleshes"</note>, some are edible; some are not, unless it be during a *famine*. For those that are not edible, the reason is that they commonly have too much *bitterness* of *taste*. Therefore, those *creatures* which are *fierce* and *choleric* <note>hot-tempered or aggressive, according to the ancient theory of the four humors</note> are not edible, such as *lions*, *wolves*, *squirrels*, *dogs*, *foxes*, *horses*, etc. As for *cattle* <note>original: "Kine"</note>, *sheep*, *goats*, *deer*, *swine*, *rabbits* <note>original: "Conneyes"</note>, *hares*, etc., we see they are *mild* and *fearful*. Yet it is true that *horses*, which are *beasts* of *courage*, have been and are eaten by some *nations*. For example, the *Scythians* <note>ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia</note> were called *Hippophagi* <note>original: "Hippophagi" — Greek for "horse-eaters"</note>, and the *Chinese* <note>original: "Chineses"</note> eat *horseflesh* to this day; some *gluttons* have even been known to eat baked *colt's flesh*. Among *birds*, those that are *carnivorous* and *birds* of *prey* are commonly not *good meat*. But the reason is the *choleric nature* of those *birds* rather than their *feeding* upon *flesh*. For *peewits* <note>original: "Puits"</note>, *gulls*, *shoveler ducks* <note>original: "Shouelers"</note>, and *ducks* do feed upon *flesh* <note>here meaning fish or small aquatic animals</note>, and yet are *good meat*. And we see that those *birds* of *prey*, or those that feed upon *flesh*, are good *meat* when they are very young, such as *hawks*, *rooks* taken from the *nest*, *owls*, etc. Human *flesh* is not eaten. There are three reasons: first, because *men*, out of *humanity*, abhor it. Second, because no *living creature* that *dies* of *natural causes* <note>original: "it selfe"</note> is good to eat; therefore, *cannibals* themselves eat no *human flesh* from those who *die* of *natural causes*, but only from those who are *slain*. The third reason is that there must generally be some *disparity* between the *nourishment* and the *body being nourished*; they must not be *too similar* <note>original: "Ouer-neere"</note> or alike. Yet we see that in cases of great *weakness* and *wasting diseases* <note>original: "Consumptions"</note>, *men* have been sustained with *woman's milk*. And *Ficino* <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an Italian philosopher who wrote on health and longevity</note> foolishly <note>original: "fondly"</note> (as I believe) advises, for the *prolongation of life*, that a *vein* be opened in the *arm* of some healthy *young man* and the *blood* be sucked out. It is said that *witches* greedily eat *human flesh*. If this is true, besides a *devilish appetite* in them, it likely occurs because *human flesh* may send up high and *pleasing vapors* which can stir the *imagination*; and a *witch's happiness* <note>original: "Felicity"</note> lies chiefly in *imagination*, as has been said before.

<margin>Solitary Experiment touching the salamander. 860</margin>
There is an ancient, accepted *tradition* of the *salamander*: that it lives in *fire* and also has the power to extinguish *fire*. If this is true, it must have two things for this *operation*. *One* is a very *tough skin* <note>original: "Close Skin"</note>, through which *flame*—which is not as hot in the *middle*—cannot enter. For we see that if the *palm* of the *hand* is coated thickly with *egg white*, and then *strong spirits* <note>original: "Aquavitæ" — Latin for "water of life," referring to high-proof alcohol</note> are poured upon it and *set on fire* <note>original: "Enflamed"</note>, one can endure the *flame* for a good while. The other is some *extreme cold* and *quenching*...

### Experiment Solitary touching the Contrary Operations of Time, upon Fruits and Liquors. 861

Time does change *fruit* (such as *apples*, *pears*, *pomegranates*, etc.) from more *sour* to more *sweet*. But, on the contrary, it changes *liquors* (even those made from the *juice of fruit*) from more *sweet* to more *sour*, such as *wort* <note>unfermented beer</note>, *must* <note>unfermented grape juice</note>, *new verjuice* <note>the acidic juice of unripened fruit</note>, etc. The *cause* is the *gathering* of the *spirits* <note>in Bacon's theory, "spirits" are the active, thin fluids within matter that drive change</note> together. In both *kinds*, the *spirits* are thinned <note>original: "attenuated"</note> by *time*. However, in the *fruit kind*, the spirit is more *diffused* and more *mastered* by the *coarser parts*, which the *spirits* merely *process* <note>original: "disgest"</note>. But in *drinks*, the *spirits* dominate, and finding less *opposition* from the solid *parts*, they become *stronger* themselves. This also causes more *strength* in the *liquor*, such that if the *spirits* are of the *hotter sort*, the *liquor* becomes likely to *burn*. But in *time*, it also causes more *sourness* when the *higher spirits* have *evaporated*.

### Experiment Solitary touching Blows and Bruises. 862

It has been observed by the *Ancients* that *plates* of *metal*, and especially of *brass*, applied immediately <note>original: "presently"</note> to a *blow*, will keep it from *swelling*. The *cause* is *repulsion* <note>original: "repercussion"</note> without *moistening* <note>original: "humectation"</note> or the *entrance* of any *body*. For the *plate* has only a *potential cold* <note>original: "virtuall cold"</note> which does not penetrate into the *hurt*, whereas all *plasters* and *ointments* do enter. Surely, the *cause* that *blows* and *bruises* induce *swellings* is because the *spirit*, resorting to *aid* the *part* that *suffers* <note>original: "laboureth"</note>, also draws the *humors* <note>bodily fluids</note> with them. For we see that it is not the *repelling* and the *return* of the *humor* in the *part struck* that causes it; for *gout* and *toothaches* cause *swelling* where there is no *impact* <note>original: "percussion"</note> at all.

### Experiment Solitary touching the Orris Root. 863

The *nature* of the *Orris root* is almost *unique* <note>original: "singular"</note>; for there are few *fragrant roots*. And in those that are, to any degree, *sweet*, it is only the same *sweetness* found in the *wood* or *leaf*. But the *Orris* is not *sweet* in the *leaf*, nor is the *flower* nearly as *sweet* as the *root*. The *root* seems to have a *tender, dainty heat*, which vanishes when it comes above *ground* to the *sun* and the *air*. For it is a great *softener* <note>original: "mollifier"</note> and has a *smell* like a *violet*.

### Experiment Solitary touching the Composition of Liquors. 864

It has been observed by the *Ancients* that a large *vessel* full of liquid, drawn into *bottles* and then put back into the *vessel*, will not fill the *vessel* as full as it was before, but that it may take in more *liquor*. This holds true more in *wine* than in *water*. The *cause* may be *trivial*—namely, the *loss* of the *liquor* because some may stick to the *sides* of the *bottles*. But there may be a more *subtle* *cause*: that the *liquor* in the *vessel* is not as *compressed* as in the *bottle*. This is because in the *vessel*, the *liquor* meets with *liquor* chiefly, but in the *bottles*, a *small quantity* of *liquor* meets <note>catchword: meeteth</note>

<margin>Experiment Solitary, touching the working of Water upon Air Contiguous. 865</margin>
Water, being in contact with *air*, cools it but does not moisten it unless it turns into *vapor*. The *cause* is that *heat* and *cold* have a *virtual transition* <note>meaning they can transfer their properties through a barrier</note> without a *transfer* of *substance*, but *moisture* does not. For any *moistening* <term>original: "madefaction"</term> to occur, there must be an *absorption* <term>original: "imbibition"</term>. But where bodies are of such different *lightness* <note>original: "levity"</note> and *weight* <note>original: "gravity"</note> that they do not mix, no *absorption* can follow. Therefore, *oil* likewise sits on top of the *water* without mixing; and a *drop* of *water* running swiftly over a *straw* or *smooth body* does not wet it.

<margin>Experiment Solitary touching the Nature of Air. 866</margin>
Starlight nights—and even bright *moonlight nights*—are colder than *cloudy nights*. The *cause* is the *dryness* and *fineness* of the *air*, which thereby becomes more *piercing* and *sharp*. Therefore, *great continents* are colder than *islands*. As for the *moon*, though it naturally inclines the *air* toward *moisture*, when it shines brightly, it indicates that the *air* is dry. Also, *trapped air* <note>original: "close air"</note> is warmer than *open air*. This is perhaps because the true *cause* of *cold* is an *exhalation* <term>original: "expiration"</term> from the globe of the *Earth*, which is stronger in open *places*. Furthermore, *air* itself, if it is not altered by that *exhalation*, is not without some *secret degree* of *heat*—just as it is not without some *secret degree* of *light*. Otherwise, *cats* and *owls* could not see in the *night*; but *air* has a little *light* proportionate to the *visual spirits* <note>In Bacon’s theory, "spirits" are active, invisible fluids within the body that enable sensation and movement</note> of those *creatures*.

<margin>Experiments in Concert touching the Eyes, and Sight. 867</margin>
The eyes move in the same way; for when one eye moves toward the *nose*, the other moves away from the *nose*. The *cause* is a *motion of agreement* <note>original: "motion of consent"</note>, which is strong in the *spirits* and *spiritual parts* of the body. Yet *practice* will induce the *contrary*, for some can *squint* whenever they wish. The *common tradition* is that if *children* are placed on a table with a candle behind them, both *eyes* will move *outward* in an effort to see the light, thus causing *squinting*.

We see more accurately <note>original: "exquisitely"</note> with one *eye shut* than with *both open*. The *cause* is that the *visual spirits* unite themselves more and so become stronger. For you may see by looking in a *mirror* <note>original: "glasse"</note> that when you shut one *eye*, the *pupil* of the other *eye* that is *open* *dilates*.

If the *sight* does not meet at one *angle*, the *eyes* *see things double*. The *cause* is that seeing two things and seeing one thing twice produce the same *effect*. Therefore, a small *pellet* held between two *fingers* that are crossed seems *double*.

**Men** see better when their **eyes** are facing the **sun** or a **candle** if they put their **hand** a little in front of their **eye**. The **cause** is that the **visual spirits** are disturbed by a sudden change and put out of order; until they are recovered, they do not perform their function well. For when they are much **dilated** by **light**, they cannot contract suddenly; and when they are much **contracted** by **darkness**, they cannot **dilate** suddenly. An excess of both these states (that is, of the **dilation** and **contraction** of the **visual spirits**), if prolonged, destroys the **eye**. For just as looking at the **sun** or a **fire** for a long time hurts the **eye** through **dilation**, so **intricate painting** <note>original: "Curious Painting"</note> in **small books** and the **reading** of **small letters** hurt the **eye** by **contraction**.

For no **man**, in that **passion**, looks out strongly, but rather **downward**; and that **repulsion** from the **eyes** **diverts** the **spirits** and **heat** more toward the **ears** and the **parts** near them.

But the **cause** (chiefly) is that there are no **active objects** to offend the **eye**. <margin>Individual experiment concerning the color of the sea or other water. 874</margin>
**Water** of the **sea**, or otherwise, looks **blacker** when it is moved and whiter when it is still. The **cause** is that by means of the **motion**, the **beams** of light do not pass **straight** and therefore must be darkened; whereas, when it is still, the **beams** do pass **straight**. Besides, **splendor** has a **degree** of **whiteness**, especially if there is a little **reflection** <note>original: "Repercussion"</note>. For a **looking glass** with **steel** behind it looks whiter than **simple glass**. This **experiment** deserves to be taken further, by trying to determine by what means **motion** may hinder **sight**.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning shellfish. 875</margin>
**Shellfish** have been compared and categorized with **insects** by some of the **ancients**, but I see no reason why they should be. For they have **male** and **female**, as other **fish** do; neither are they bred from **decay** <note>original: "Putrifaction"</note>, especially those that **move**. Nevertheless, it is certain that **oysters**, **cockles**, and **mussels** <note>original: "Muscles"</note>, which do not **move**, have no distinct **sex**. **Inquiry** <note>original: "Quære"; Latin for "inquire"</note>: in what time and how are they bred? It seems that the **shells** of **oysters** are bred where none were before. It has also been tested that the great **horse mussel** with the fine shell, which breeds in **ponds**, has appeared within thirty years. But then—which is strange—it has been tested that they do not only **gape** and **shut** as **oysters** do, but **move** from one place to another.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning the right side and the left. 876</margin>
The **senses** are equally strong on both the **right side** and the **left**, but the **limbs** on the **right side** are stronger. The **cause** may be that the **brain**, which is the **instrument** of **sense**, is the same on both **sides**; but **motion** and the **ability** to move are somewhat helped by the **liver**, which lies on the **right side**. It may also be because the **senses** are put into **exercise** equally on both **sides** from the time of our **birth**, but the **limbs** are used most on the **right side**, whereby **habit** <note>original: "Custome"</note> helps. For we see that some people are **left-handed**, and these are those who have used the **left hand** the most.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning friction. 877</margin>
**Friction** <note>In Bacon's time, this referred to therapeutic massage or "currying."</note> makes the **body parts** more **fleshy** and **full**, as we see both in **men** and in the **grooming** <note>original: "Currying"</note> of **horses**, etc. The **cause** is that it draws a greater **quantity** of **spirits** and **blood** to those **parts**. Additionally, it draws **nourishment** <note>original: "Aliment"</note> more forcibly from within, and it relaxes the **pores**, making a better **passage** for the **spirits**, **blood**, and **nourishment**. Lastly, it dissipates and digests any **useless** <note>original: "Inutile"</note> or **waste**...

<margin>Individual experiment concerning globes appearing flat at a distance. 878</margin>
...waste <note>original: "crementitious"; referring to superfluous or leftover moisture in the body that has not yet been assimilated into tissue</note> moisture, which lies in the flesh: all of which help assimilation. Rubbing <note>original: "Frictions"; therapeutic massage</note> also fills and fattens <note>original: "Impinguate"</note> the body more than exercise. The cause is that during rubbing, the internal parts are at rest, which during exercise are often shaken <note>original: "beaten"</note> too much. For the same reason (as we have noted before), galley slaves are fat and fleshy because they move their limbs more and their internal organs less.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning shadows. 879</margin>
All globes far away appear flat. The cause is that distance, being a secondary object of sight, is only discerned by more or less light; when this difference cannot be seen, everything seems uniform. This is generally true for objects not clearly discerned. For example, letters, if they are so far away that they cannot be read, appear only as dark spots <note>original: "Duskish Paper"</note>; and all engravings and carvings <note>original: "Embossings"</note> appear flat from a distance.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning the rolling and breaking of the seas. 880</margin>
The outermost edges of shadows always seem to tremble. The cause is that the tiny dust motes we see in the sunlight are always moving, even when there is no wind. Therefore, as they move across the boundary where light meets shadow—moving from light to shadow and from shadow to light—they make the shadow appear to move, because the medium <note>the air through which the light passes</note> itself is moving.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning the sweetening of salt water. 881</margin>
Shallow and narrow seas break more than deep and large ones. The cause is that, while the force <note>original: "Impulsion"</note> is the same in both, where there is a greater quantity of water and enough space, the water rolls and moves more slowly and with a gentler <note>original: "Sloper"</note> rise and fall. But where there is less water and less space, and the wave dashes more against the bottom, it moves more swiftly and more steeply; for in the breaking of waves, there is always a steep drop <note>original: "Precipice"</note>.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning the return of saltiness in pits upon the seashore. 882</margin>
It was observed by the ancients that salt water, once boiled or boiled and cooled again, is more drinkable <note>original: "Potable"</note> than when it is raw. And yet, the taste of salt does not rise during distillation by fire, for distilled water will be fresh. The cause may be that the salty part of the water partly rises into a kind of scum on the top and partly settles as a sediment at the bottom; thus, it is a separation rather than an evaporation. Salt is too coarse <note>original: "grosse"</note> to rise into a vapor. Bitter tastes behave the same way; for simple distilled waters of wormwood and similar plants are not bitter.

It has been noted before that pits on the seashore turn into fresh water by the filtering <note>original: "Percolation"</note> of the salt through the sand. But it is further noted by some of the ancients that in some parts of Africa <note>original: "Affricke"</note>, after a time, the water in such pits will become brackish again. The cause is that, after a time, the very sand through which the salt water passes becomes salty, and so the strainer itself is tainted with salt.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning attraction by similarity of substance. 883</margin>
It has been observed by the *ancients* that *saltwater* will dissolve *salt* put into it in less time than *freshwater* will. The cause may be that the *salt* already in the *previous water* <note>original: "Precedent Water"</note> draws the new *salt* to it because of their *similarity of substance*, causing it to diffuse through the *liquid* more quickly. This is a noble experiment, if true, for it shows methods for *faster* and *easier infusions*. It is also a good example of *attraction* by *similarity of substance*. Try it with *sugar* put into *water* that has already been *sweetened*, compared to other *unsweetened water*.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning attraction. 884</margin>
Put *sugar* into *wine*, with part of it above and part under the *wine*. You will find—though it may seem strange—that the *sugar* above the *wine* will soften and dissolve sooner than the part submerged in the *wine*. The cause is that the *wine* enters the *part of the sugar* under the liquid by simple *infusion* or *spreading*; however, the *part* above the *wine* is also drawn up by *suction*. All *spongy bodies* expel *air* and draw in *liquid* if they are touching <note>original: "Contiguous"</note>, as we also see in *sponges* when only part of them is placed in *water*. It is worth investigating to see how one might create more *precise infusions* with the help of *attraction*.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning heat under the earth. 885</margin>
Water in wells is warmer in *winter* than in *summer*, and the same is true for *air* in *caves*. The cause is that in the *nearer parts* <note>original: "Hither Parts"</note> under the *earth*, there is a degree of *some heat* (as seen in *sulfurous veins*, etc.). This heat, when shut in closely (as in *winter*), is *greater*; but if it can evaporate <note>original: "Perspire"</note> (as it does in *summer*), it is *lesser*.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning flying in the air. 886</margin>
It is reported that among the *Leucadians* <note>original: "Leucacians"; inhabitants of Leucas, modern Lefkada, known for the ritual "Leucadian Leap"</note> in *ancient times*, based on a *superstition*, they used to throw a *man* from a *high cliff* into the *sea*. They would tie many large *birds* to him with *strings* at some distance and fix various *feathers* to his *body*, spread out to break the *fall*. Certainly, many *birds* with strong wings (such as *kites* and the like) would support a significant *weight* as they fly; and the *spreading of feathers*, thin and close over a great *breadth*, will likewise support a great *weight*, provided they are laid evenly without *tilting* to the *sides*. The further *extension* of this *experiment* for *flying* should be considered.

<margin>Individual experiment concerning the dye of scarlet. 887</margin>
There is in some places (namely in *Cephalonia*) a little *shrub* which they call *holy oak* or *dwarf oak*. On its *leaves*, there grows a *swelling* <note>original: "Tumour"</note> like a *blister*. They gather these and rub out a certain *red dust* that turns into *worms* after a while. They kill these worms with *wine* (so it is reported) when they begin to *come to life* <note>original: "Quicken"</note>. With this *dust*, they dye *scarlet* <note>This refers to kermes, a red dye derived from the dried bodies of the female scale insect *Kermes vermilio* found on the kermes oak</note>.

<margin>
Individual experiment concerning the rise of water by means of flame.
889
</margin>
It is a common *experiment*, but the *cause* is misunderstood. Take a pot (*or better a glass, because in it you may see the motion*), and set a lighted *candle* in the *bottom* of a *basin* of *water*. Then, turn the *mouth* of the *pot* or *glass* over the *candle*, and it will make the *water* rise. People ascribe this to the *drawing of heat*, which is not true. For it plainly appears to be nothing but a *motion of connection* <term>original: "Motion of Nexe"; from the Latin 'nexus', referring to the force that holds matter together to prevent a vacuum</term>, which they call *lest a vacuum be created* <note>original: "Ne detur vacuum"</note>. It proceeds like this: the *flame* of the *candle*, as soon as it is covered, is suffocated by the *trapped air* and diminishes little by little. During this time, there is some small *ascent of water*, but not much; for as the *flame* occupies less and less *room* as it diminishes, the *water* follows to fill the space. But at the *instant* the *candle goes out*, there is a sudden *rise* of a great deal of *water*, because the *body of the flame* no longer fills any space, and so the *air* and the *water* follow after it. It produces the same *effect* if, instead of *water*, you put *flour* or *sand* into the *basin*. This shows that it is not the *flame* drawing the *liquid* as *nourishment*, as is supposed, for all *bodies* react the same way to it, as it is always a *motion of connection*. Indeed, I have seen the *glass*, while held by the hand, lift up the *basin* and everything; the *motion of connection* gripped the *bottom* of the *basin* so tightly. That *experiment*, where the *basin* was lifted up, was performed with *oil* and not with *water*. Nevertheless, it is true that at the very first *setting* of the *mouth* of the *glass* upon the *bottom* of the *basin*, it draws up the *water* a little and then stays still until the *candle goes out*, as was said. This may show some *attraction* at first, but we will speak more of this when we handle *attractions caused by heat*.

<margin>
Experiments in association concerning the influences of the Moon.
</margin>

### Regarding the power of the celestial bodies and what more secret influences they have—besides the two obvious influences of heat and light—we shall speak when we handle experiments concerning the celestial bodies. In the meantime, we will give some directions for more certain trials of the power and influences of the Moon, which is our nearest neighbor.

The influences of the Moon (most frequently observed) are four: *the drawing forth of heat, the inducing of putrefaction, the increase of moisture, and the exciting of the motions of spirits.*

# Century IX.

<margin>890</margin>
For the *drawing out of heat*, we have previously directed to take *warm water* and set part of it against the *moonbeams*, and part of it with a *screen* in between, to see whether that which stands exposed to the *beams* will not *cool* sooner. But because this is only a small *interruption* (though in the *sun* we see a small *shade* does much), it would be good to try it when the *moon* shines and when the *moon* does not shine at all; and with *warm water* in a *glass bottle* as well as in a *dish*; and with *cinders*; and with *red-hot iron*; and so on.

<margin>891</margin>
For the *inducing of putrefaction* <term>original: "Putrifaction"; the process of decaying or rotting</term>, it would be good to try it with *flesh* or *fish* exposed to the *moonbeams*; and again exposed to the *air* when the *moon* does not shine for the same amount of time, to see which will corrupt sooner. And try it also with *capon* <note>A castrated rooster, often used for food</note> or some other *fowl* laid out to see whether it will mortify <note>original: "mortifie"; in this context, the process of meat becoming tender through the first stages of decomposition</note> and become tender sooner? Try it also with dead *flies* or dead *worms* having a little water cast upon them to see which will *putrefy* sooner. Try it also with an *apple* or *orange* having *holes* made in their *tops* to see which will *rot* or *mold* sooner? Try it also with *Holland cheese* having *wine* put into it to see whether it will breed *mites* sooner or larger?

<margin>892</margin>
For the *increase of moisture*, the commonly held opinion is that *seeds* will grow soonest, and *hair*, *nails*, *hedges*, and *herbs*—when *cut*—will grow back soonest if they are *planted* or *cut* during the *waxing* of the *moon*. It is also believed that *brains* in *rabbits, woodcocks, calves*, etc., are fullest during the *full moon*; and likewise the *marrow* in the *bones*; and also *oysters* and *cockles*, which of all the rest are the easiest to test if you have them in *pits* <note>Oyster beds or storage areas</note>.

<margin>893</margin>
Take some seeds or roots (such as *onions*, etc.) and plant some of them immediately after the *new moon* <note>original: "Change"</note>, and others of the same kind immediately after the *full moon*. Let them be as similar as can be; the *earth* also should be the same as nearly as possible, and therefore it is best to use *pots*. Let the *pots* also stand where no *rain* or *sun* may reach them, lest the *difference* in the *weather* confuse the *experiment*. Then see in what *time* the seeds *planted* during the *waxing* of the *moon* reach a certain height, and how they differ from those that are *planted* during the *waning* <note>original: "Decrease"</note> of the *moon*.

<margin>894</margin>
It is likely that the *brain of man* grows *moister* and *fuller* upon the *full moon*; and therefore it would be good for those who have *moist brains* and are great *drinkers* to inhale the *smoke* <note>original: "Fume"; a medicinal practice of inhaling scented vapors</note> of *agarwood* <note>original: "Lignum Aloes"</note>, *rosemary*, *frankincense*, etc., around the *full moon*. It is likely also that the *humors* <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which early modern medicine believed governed health</note> in *men's bodies* increase and decrease as the *moon* does; and therefore it would be good to purge <note>To induce bowel movements or vomiting for health reasons</note> a day or two after the *full moon*, for then the *humors* will not replenish themselves so quickly.

<margin>895</margin>
As for the *exciting of the motion of the spirits* <note>In Bacon's physiology, "spirits" are fine, invisible substances that circulate through the body to facilitate life and movement</note>, you must note that the *growth* of *hedges, herbs, hair*, etc., is caused by the *moon* stimulating the *spirits* as much as by increasing the *moisture*. But for *spirits* in particular, the great example is in *lunacies* <note>Insanity, which was traditionally thought to be influenced by the phases of the moon (Latin: "Luna")</note>.

<margin>896</margin>
There may be other *secret effects* of the *influence* of the *moon* which have not yet been brought into observation. It may be that if it so happens...

<margin>897</margin>

Solitary touching *Vinegar*. 
898
</margin>
The *turning* of *Wine* into *Vinegar* is a kind of *putrefaction* <term>original: "Putrifaction"; here meaning fermentation or decomposition</term>. In the *making* of *vinegar*, people usually place *vessels* of *wine* facing the *midday sun*, which draws out the more *oily spirits* and leaves the *liquid* more *sour* and *harsh*. We also see that *mulled wine* <note>original: "Burnt-Wine"; wine that has been heated or distilled</note> is harsher and more *astringent* than *unheated wine*. It is said that *Cider* ripens during *voyages* across the *Equator* <note>original: "under the Line"</note>, whereas *wine* or *beer* turns sour. It would be useful to place a *cask* <note>original: "Rundlet"</note> of *verjuice* <note>A highly acidic juice made from pressing unripe grapes or other sour fruit</note> in the *sun* during *summer*, just as they do with *vinegar*, to see whether it will ripen and sweeten.

<margin>
Experiment 
Solitary touching Creatures 
that *Sleep* all 
*Winter*. 
899
</margin>
There are various *creatures* that *sleep* all *winter*, such as the *Bear*, the *Hedgehog*, the *Bat*, the *Bee*, and others. These all grow *fat* while they *sleep* and do not *excrete waste* <note>original: "egest"</note>. The *cause* of their *fattening* during their *sleeping* time may be the *lack* of *assimilation* <term>The process of absorbing nutrients into the body's tissues</term>. Whatever does not *assimilate* into *flesh* turns into either *sweat* or *fat*. These *creatures* have been observed not to *move* at all for part of their *sleeping time*; for the rest of the time, they *move* but do not *change location*. They also find *warm* and *enclosed places* to *sleep* in. When the *Dutch* <note>original: "Flemmings"; likely referring to Willem Barentsz's 1596 expedition</note> spent the winter in *Novaya Zemlya* <note>original: "Nova Zembla"; an archipelago in the Arctic Ocean</note>, the *bears* went to *sleep* around the middle of *November*. Only then did the *foxes* begin to come out, which they did not dare do before. It is noted by some of the *ancient writers* that the *female bear* gives birth and stays with her *young* during that time of *rest*, and that a *bear* *pregnant* with *young* has seldom been seen.

<margin>
Experiment 
Solitary touching the Generating of 
Creatures by Copulation, and by 
*Putrifaction*. 
900
</margin>
Some *living creatures* are produced by *mating* <note>original: "Copulation"</note> between *male* and *female*. Others are produced by *putrefaction* <note>original: "Putrifaction"; this refers to the outdated theory of spontaneous generation, where life was thought to arise from decaying matter</note>. Of those that arise from *putrefaction*, many nonetheless *mate* with each other afterward. Regarding the *cause* of both types of *generation*: First, it is most certain that the *cause* of all *vivification* <term>The development of life or the act of becoming living</term> is a *gentle* and *proportional heat* working upon a *glue-like* and *yielding substance*. The *heat* brings forth *spirit* <note>In early science, "spirits" were vital forces or volatile substances believed to animate matter</note> within that *substance*. Because the *substance* is *glue-like*, it produces two *effects*: first, the *spirit* is *trapped* and cannot *break out*; second, because the *matter* is *soft* and yielding, it is driven forward by the *motion* of the *spirits*, eventually *swelling* into a *shape* with *limbs* <note>original: "Members"</note>.

<header>Century 9.</header>

---

Therefore all *sperm*, all *menstrual substance*, and all *matter* from which *creatures* are produced through *putrefaction* <term>original: "Putrifaction"; here referring to the belief in spontaneous generation from decaying matter</term>, always possess a certain *density* <note>original: "Closenesse"</note>, *viscosity* <term>original: "Lentour"; a thickness or sluggishness of fluid</term>, and *stickiness* <term>original: "Sequosity"; the quality of being gummy or following in a stream</term>. It appears, therefore, that *generation* by *sperm* alone, and generation by *putrefaction*, have two *different causes*. 

The first cause is that *creatures* which have a *definite* and *exact shape* (such as those produced through *sexual reproduction* <note>original: "Copulation"</note>) cannot be produced by a weak and *accidental heat*, nor from *matter* that has not been *precisely prepared* according to its *species*. 

The second cause is that more *time* is required for the *maturation* of *complex creatures* <note>original: "Perfect Creatures"</note>. If the *time* required for *bringing to life* <note>original: "Vivification"</note> is of any significant length, the *vital spirit* will *evaporate* <note>original: "Exhale"</note> before the *creature* is *mature*—unless it is *enclosed* in a *place* where it may have *continuous heat*, access to some *nourishment* to maintain it, and a *tightness* that may keep it from *evaporating*. Such *places* are the *wombs* and *birth canals* <note>original: "Matrices"</note> of *females*. 

Therefore, all *creatures* made from *putrefaction* have a more *uncertain shape* and are made in a *shorter time*. They do not need such a *perfect enclosure*, though some *density* is commonly required. As for the *pagan opinion* <note>original: "Heathen Opinion"</note> which suggested that during great *upheavals of the world*, *complex creatures* were first *begotten* from the *thickening of matter* <note>original: "Concretion"</note>—just as *frogs*, *worms*, *flies*, and similar things are now—we know it to be a foolish idea. But if any such *thing* were to be admitted, *reasoning* according to our *senses*, it could not happen unless you first admit a *state of chaos* and a *mixing* of *heaven* and *earth*.

# NATURAL HISTORY.

## Tenth Century.

<margin>
Experiments in association <note>original: "in consort"</note>, concerning the transmission and influence of **intangible powers** <note>original: "immateriate virtues"</note> and the force of **imagination**.
</margin>

The philosophy of **Pythagoras** (which was full of superstition) first planted a monstrous <note>In this context, "monstrous" means extraordinary, vast, or deviating from the natural order.</note> imagination, which was afterwards watered and nourished by the school of **Plato** and others. This idea was that the world was **one entire, perfect, living creature**. So much so that **Apollonius of Tyana**, a Pythagorean prophet, affirmed that the ebbing and flowing of the sea was the respiration of the world, drawing in water as breath and putting it forth again. They went further and inferred that if the world were a **living creature**, it had a soul and spirit, which they also maintained, calling it *spirit of the world* <note>original Latin: "spiritus mundi"</note>. By this, they did not mean God (for they did acknowledge a deity besides), but only...

<page-num>234</page-num>
<header>Natural History:</header>

...only the **Soul**, or **Essential Form** of the **Universe**. Once this foundation was laid, they could build upon it whatever they wished. For in a **living creature**, no matter how large (as, for **example**, in a great **whale**), the **senses** and **sensations** <note>original: "affects"</note> of any one **part** of the **body** instantly **travel** <note>original: "make a transcursion"</note> throughout the whole **body**. By this, they insinuated that no **distance of place**, nor **lack** <note>original: "want"</note> or **unsuitability** <note>original: "indisposition"</note> of **matter**, could hinder **magical operations**. They suggested that, for **example**, we might here in **Europe** have **knowledge** <note>original: "sense"</note> and **feeling** of what was being done in **China**. And likewise, we might produce any **effect** **without** or **against matter**. This was not to be **helped** by the **cooperation of angels** or **spirits**, but only by the **unity** and **harmony of nature**. There were some also who did not stop there but went further, holding that if the **spirit of man** (whom they call the **microcosm**) gives a proper touch to the **spirit of the world** through strong **imaginations** and **beliefs**, it might command **nature**. For **Paracelsus** and some obscure <note>original: "darksome"</note> **authors of magic** ascribe the **power of miracle-working faith** to an **exalted imagination**. Men have been (in part) entertained by these vast and **bottomless follies**.

But we, who hold firmly to the **works of God** and to our **senses** (which are **God’s lamp**—**the spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord** <note>original Latin: "Lucerna Dei spiraculum hominis"; a reference to Proverbs 20:27</note>), will inquire with all **sobriety** and **strictness** whether there can be found in the **footsteps of nature** any such **transmission** and **influence** of **intangible powers** <note>original: "immateriate virtues"</note>. We will also examine what the **force of imagination** is, whether it acts upon the **body of the person imagining** <note>original: "body imaginant"</note> or upon **another body**. In this, it will be like the **labor of Hercules** in **cleaning the Augean stables** <note>One of the Twelve Labors of Hercules, involving the cleaning of enormous, filthy stables in a single day—a metaphor for a monumental task of purification.</note>: we must separate anything that is clean and purely **natural** from **superstitious** and **magical arts** and **observations**, so that it may be neither **despised** <note>original: "contemned"</note> nor **condemned**. And although we shall have occasion to speak of this in more than one place, we will now make an **introduction** to it.

Having previously discussed the "spirit of the world," Bacon now focuses on why certain people are more susceptible to mental impressions and why many "magical" successes are actually the result of psychological self-confidence rather than external spells.</meta>

<page-num>235</page-num>
<header>Century X.</header>

Infection is often received by a **Passive Body**, but is repulsed and worked out by its **Strength** and good **Condition** <note>original: "disposition"</note> before it develops into a **Disease**. Similarly, in **Impressions** passed from **Mind** to **Mind**, or from **Spirit** to **Spirit**, the **Impression** takes hold, but it is encountered and overcome by the **Mind** and **Spirit** that is **Passive** <note>In this context, "passive" refers to the person receiving the influence rather than the one exerting it.</note> before it produces any obvious **Effect**. Therefore, these influences work most effectively upon **Weak Minds** and **Spirits**, such as those of **women**, **Sick Persons**, **Superstitious** and **Fearful Persons**, **Children**, and **Young Creatures**.

> <note>original: "Nescio quis teneros Oculus mihi fascinat Agnos"; translation: "I do not know what eye is bewitching my tender lambs." This quote is from Virgil’s *Eclogues*, referring to the ancient belief in the "evil eye."</note>

The **Poet** does not speak of **Sheep**, but of **Lambs**. As for why these **Powers** are **weak** when directed at **Kings** and **Magistrates**, it can be attributed (besides the main reason, which is the **Protection** of **God** over those who hold His office) to the **weakness** of the **Imagination** of the person performing the magic. For it is difficult for a **witch** or a **Sorcerer** to truly **Believe** that they can hurt such high-ranking **Persons**.

<margin>902</margin>
**Men** should be warned, on the other hand, not to easily give in or grant credit to these **Operations** just because they **Succeed many times**. The **Cause** of this **Success** is often truly due to the **Force** of **Emotion** <note>original: "affection"</note> and **Imagination** upon the **Acting Body** <note>original: "Body Agent"; the person performing the action.</note>. Then, by **Secondary Means**, it may work upon a **Different Body**. For example, if a man carries a **Planetary Seal** <note>An astrological talisman engraved with symbols of a planet, believed to grant specific powers.</note>, or a **Ring**, or some **Part of a Beast**, believing strongly that it will help him obtain his **Love**, or keep him from the danger of being hurt in a **Fight**, or help him prevail in a **legal case**, it may make him more **Active** and **Industrious**. Furthermore, it may make him more **Confident** and **Persistent** than he would otherwise be. Now, who does not know the great **Effects** that can come from **Industry** and **Perseverance** (especially in **Public Affairs**)? For we see that **Audacity** almost binds and conquers the **Weaker Sort** of **Minds**. Because the **State** of **Human Actions** is so unpredictable, trying things often and never giving up produces **Wonders**. Therefore, it would be a complete **Fallacy** and a mistake to credit the **Force** of **Imagination** upon another **Body** for what is actually just the **Force** of **Imagination** upon **One's Own Body**. For there is no doubt that **Imagination** and **Vehement Emotion** work greatly upon the **Body** of the person imagining, as we shall show in the proper place.

<margin>903</margin>
**Men** are also to be warned that just as they should not mistake the **Causes** of these **Operations**, they should even less mistake the **Fact** or **Effect**, and rashly assume something has been done which has not. Therefore, as various wise **Judges** have advised and cautioned, **Men** must not too readily believe the **Confessions** of **witches**, nor the **Evidence** against them. For the **witches** themselves are **Imaginative** and often believe they do things that they actually do not. Furthermore, **People** are **Gullible** <note>original: "credulous"</note> in that regard and ready to blame **Accidents** and **Natural Operations** on **Witchcraft**. It is worth observing that in both **Ancient** and **Recent times** (such as with the **Thessalian witches** <note>Witches from the Thessaly region of Greece, famous in antiquity for their supposed ability to draw down the moon.</note> and the meetings of **Witches** recorded in so many recent **Confessions**), the great **wonders** they describe—such as being **Carried** through the **Air** or **Transforming** themselves into...

<header>Natural History:</header>

<margin>902</margin>
...other bodies, and so forth, are still reported to be achieved, not by **incantations** or **ceremonies**, but by **ointments** and **anointing** themselves all over. This may rightly move a **man** to think that these **fables** are the **effects** of **imagination**. For it is certain that **ointments** (if they are applied quite thickly) do everything by **stopping the pores**, trapping the **vapors**, and sending them intensely to the **head**. As for the particular ingredients of those **magical ointments**, it is likely they are **opiates** and **sleep-inducing** <note>original: "soporiferous"</note>. For we know that **anointing** the **forehead**, **neck**, **feet**, **backbone**, and so on, is used for procuring **deep sleeps**. And if any **man** says that this **effect** would be better achieved by inward **potions**, the **answer** may be made that the **medicines** used in the **ointments** are so strong that if they were used internally, they would kill those who use them; therefore, they work powerfully, though applied externally.

<margin>903</margin>
We will divide the several kinds of **operations** involving the **transmission of spirits** and **imagination**, which will provide significant clarity to the **experiments** that follow. All **operations** by **transmission of spirits** and **imagination** have this in common: they work at a **distance** and not by **touch**. These are distinguished as follows:

<margin>904</margin>
The first is the **transmission** or **emission** of the **thinner** and more **airy parts of bodies**, as in **odors** and infections; and this is, out of all the rest, the most **physical** <note>original: "corporeal"</note>. But you must remember, at the same time, that there are a number of those **emissions**, both wholesome and **unwholesome**, that give off no **smell** at all. For the **plague**, many times when it is contracted, gives off no **scent** at all; and there are many **good** and **healthful airs** that are proven so by **habitation** <note>meaning: by the long-term health of people living there</note> and other **proofs**, which do not differ in **smell** from other **airs**. Under this head, you may place all **absorptions of air** <note>original: "imbibitions of aire"</note> where the **substance** is **material** and **odor-like**, some of which are nevertheless strange and very suddenly diffused—such as the **alteration** which the **air** receives in **Egypt** almost immediately upon the **rising** of the **River Nile** <note>original: "Nilus"</note>, which we have discussed previously.

<margin>905</margin>
The second is the **transmission** or **emission** of those **things** that we call **spiritual species**, such as **visuals** and **sounds**. We have handled one of these, and we shall handle the other in its proper place. These move swiftly and over great distances, but they require a **medium** <note>the substance through which a force or signal travels, like air or water</note> that is well-disposed, and their **transmission** is easily stopped.

<margin>906</margin>
The third is the **emissions** which cause **attraction** of **certain bodies** at a **distance**. Although the **magnet** <note>original: "loadstone"</note> is commonly placed in the **first** rank of these, we think it best to exclude it and refer it to another **heading**. However, the **drawing** of **amber** and **jet**, and other **electric bodies** <note>Early modern scientists used "electric" to describe materials like amber that attract light objects when rubbed.</note>; and the **attraction** of the **spirit** of **mercury** <note>original: "quick-silver"</note> to **gold** at a distance; and the **attraction** of **heat** at a distance; and that of **fire** to **naphtha**; and that of some **herbs** to water, even at a distance; and various others—these we shall handle, but not under this present **title**. Instead, they will be under the **title** of **attraction in general**.

The fourth is the **Emission of Spirits**, and **Non-material** <note>original: "Immateriate"</note> **Powers** and **Properties**, in those things which work by the **Universal Configuration** and **Sympathy of the world**. This does not happen through "Forms" or "Celestial Influences" (as is incorrectly taught and accepted), but by the **Primitive Nature of Matter** and the **Seeds of Things** <note>The "seeds of things" (Latin: *semina rerum*) refers to the fundamental particles or blueprints of matter.</note>. Of this kind is (as we currently believe) the **working** of the **Loadstone** <note>original: "Load-Stone," a naturally magnetized piece of mineral.</note>, which works by **harmony** <note>original: "Consent"</note> with the **Globe of the Earth**. Of this kind is the **Motion of Gravity**, which works by the **harmony** of **Dense Bodies** with the **Globe of the Earth**. Of this kind is the **tendency of some bodies to rotate**, particularly from **East to West**. We believe the **Main Ebb and Flow of the Sea** is also of this kind, occurring by the **harmony** of the **Universe** as part of the **Daily** <note>original: "Diurnall"</note> **Motion**. These **Non-material Properties** have a characteristic that differs from others: the **variety of the medium** (the material through which they pass) does not hinder them. They pass through all **mediums**, yet only at **fixed distances**. We shall speak of these as they occur under various headings.

<margin>908</margin>
The fifth is the **Emissions of Spirits**, and this is the principal subject we intend to handle here: namely, the **Operation of the Spirits of the Human Mind** upon other **spirits**. This is of a double nature: the **Operations of the Passions** <note>original: "Affections"</note>, if they are intense, and the **Operation of the Imagination**, if it is strong. These two are so coupled that we shall handle them together; for when an **envious** or **loving look** <note>original: "Amorous Aspect"</note> infects the **spirits** of **another**, both **passion** and **imagination** are joined together.

<margin>909</margin>
The sixth is the **Influences of the Heavenly Bodies**, besides those two obvious ones of **Heat** and **Light**. But we will handle these when we discuss **Celestial Bodies** and **Motions**.

<margin>910</margin>
The seventh is the **Operations of Sympathy**, which the writers of **Natural Magic** have turned into an **art** or **set of rules**. Their theory is this: if you desire to instill <note>original: "Super-induce"</note> any **virtue** or **trait** into a **person**, you should take the **living creature** in which that **virtue** is most prominent and in **perfection**. From that creature, you must take the **parts** where that **virtue** is mainly **located**. Furthermore, you must take those **parts** at the **time** and during the **act** when that **virtue** is most in **exercise**. Then, you must apply it to the **part of the human** where that **virtue** primarily **resides**. For example, if you would instill **courage** and **bravery**, take a **lion** or a **rooster**. Take the **heart**, **tooth**, or **paw of the lion**, or the **heart** or **spur of the rooster**. Take those **parts** immediately after the **lion** or the **rooster** has been in **fight**, and let them be worn over a **man's heart** or on his **wrist**. We shall speak of these and similar **sympathies** under this present **heading**.

<margin>911</margin>
The eighth and last is an **Emission of Non-material Virtues** that we are somewhat hesitant to propose because it is so extraordinary <note>original: "prodigious"</note>. However, it is so constantly asserted by many, and we have set it down as a law for ourselves to examine things to the bottom—neither accepting things on credit nor rejecting them due to improbability until a proper examination has passed. This is the **Sympathy of Individuals**. For as

Just as there is a *Sympathy of Species*, so (perhaps) there is a *Sympathy of Individuals*. That is, in *things*, or the *parts of things*, that have once been *connected* or *whole*, there should remain a *transmission of power* <note>original: "Vertue"</note> from the *one* to the *other*—such as between the *weapon* and the *wound*. Because of this, the *operation of the Weapon Salve* <note>original: "Unguentum Teli," a famous "sympathetic" remedy where ointment was applied to the weapon that caused a wound, rather than the wound itself, in the belief it would heal the person from a distance.</note> is widely publicized; and the same is said of a *piece of lard* or a *stick of elder*, etc., suggesting that if *part* of it is consumed or rotted, it will affect the other *separated part*. Now we will pursue the *instances* themselves.

The plague is often contracted without any *obvious sensation* <note>original: "Manifest Sense"</note>, as has been said. And people report that where it is found, it has a *scent* like the *smell of a mellow apple*; and (as some say) of *May-flowers*. It is also accepted that the *smells of flowers* that are *mellow* and *luscious* are bad during the *plague*, such as *white lilies, cowslips*, and *hyacinths*.

<margin>913</margin>
The *plague* is not easily contracted by those who are continually around the sick, such as *nurses* <note>original: "Keepers of the Sicke"</note> and *physicians*. Nor is it easily caught by those who take *antidotes*, whether *internally* (such as *Mithridate* <note>A complex herbal paste used as a universal antidote.</note>, juniper berries, and the leaves and seeds of rue) or *externally* (such as *angelica* <note>An aromatic herb believed to protect against contagion.</note>, *zedoary* <note>A root similar to ginger, used medicinally.</note>, and the like held in the mouth; or perfumes of tar, galbanum, and the like). Nor is it easily caught by *elderly people* or those of a *dry and cold temperament* <note>original: "Complexion," referring to the Four Humors.</note>. On the other hand, the *plague* takes hold most quickly of those who come out of *fresh air*, those who are *fasting*, and *children*. It is likewise noted to spread among *relatives* <note>original: "goe in a Bloud"</note> more than to strangers.

<margin>914</margin>
The most *deadly infection*, next to the *plague*, is the *smell of the jail*, occurring when *prisoners* have been kept for a *long* time in *close* and *filthy* conditions. We have had experience of this twice or thrice in our own time, when both the *judges* who presided over the jail trials and many of those who attended the *proceedings* or were present *became sick from it and died* <note>This likely refers to the "Black Assize" of 1577, where a typhus outbreak killed judges and jurors.</note>. Therefore, it would be good wisdom in such cases to *air out the jail* before the prisoners are brought out.

<margin>915</margin>
Without question, if such *foul smells* are created by *art* (by human hands), they consist chiefly of *putrefied human flesh or sweat*. For it is not those *stinks* that the nostrils immediately abhor and reject that are the most *deadly*, but rather those *airs* that have some *similarity to the human body*; these sneak in <note>original: "insinuate themselves"</note> and betray the *spirits* <note>In Bacon’s science, "spirits" are the vital, subtle fluids that govern life and health within the body.</note>. There may be great danger in using such *compositions* in large *gatherings of people indoors*, such as in *churches, at trials, at plays and ceremonies*, and the like. For the *poisoning of air* is no less dangerous than the *poisoning of water*, which has been used by the *Turks* in wars and was used by *Manuel I Komnenos* <note>original: "Emanuel Commenus," a Byzantine Emperor (r. 1143–1180) rumored to have poisoned the supplies of the Crusaders.</note> against the *Christians* when they passed through his *country* to the *Holy Land*. These *poisonings of air* are more dangerous in *crowds* because the sheer amount of *breath from people* helps the *reception* of the *infection*. Therefore, where any such thing is feared, it would be wise if those *public places* were perfumed before the *assemblies* meet.

# Natural History

There is a belief, which seems legendary <note>original: "Fabulous"</note>, that menstruous women walking through a field or garden benefit the grain <note>original: "Corne"</note> and herbs by killing the worms.

<margin>924</margin>
The tradition is no less ancient that the **basilisk** <note>a mythical reptile said to be the king of serpents</note> kills by its **gaze** <note>original: "Aspect"</note>; and that the **wolf**, if he sees a **man** first, strikes the **man** hoarse by his **gaze**.

<margin>925</margin>
Suitable **perfumes** dry and strengthen the brain, and stop colds and mucus drainage <note>original: "Rheumes and Defluxions"</note>. We find this in the **smoke** of dried **rosemary**, **aloeswood** <note>original: "Lignum Aloes"</note>, and **sweet flag** <note>original: "Calamus"</note>, taken through the mouth and nostrils. No doubt there are other perfumes that moisten and refresh, and are fit to be used in **burning fevers** <note>original: "Agues"</note>, **wasting diseases** <note>original: "Consumptions"</note>, and excessive **insomnia** <note>original: "Wakefulnesse"</note>; such as **rose water**, **vinegar**, **lemon peels**, **violets**, and the **leaves** of **vines** sprinkled with a little **rose water**, etc.

<margin>926</margin>
In cases of **sudden fainting** and **swooning**, it is common to put a **handkerchief** with **rose water** or a **little vinegar** to the **nose**. This gathers together the **spirits** again, which are on the point of dissipating <note>original: "resolue"</note> and falling away.

<margin>927</margin>
**Tobacco** soothes the **spirits** and relieves weariness. It achieves this partly by **opening** the passages, but chiefly by its **opiate quality** <note>original: "Vertue"</note>, which condenses the **spirits**. It would be good, therefore, to try **taking** the **smoke** <note>original: "Fumes"</note> of other **things** by **pipes** (as is done with **tobacco**), as much to dry and comfort the body as for other **purposes**. I wish trials were made using a **pipe** for the **drying smoke** of **rosemary** and **aloeswood** mentioned before, and likewise for **nutmeg** and **Indian leaf** <note>original: "Folium Indum"; likely the leaf of the Malabathrum tree, related to cinnamon</note>, etc.

<margin>928</margin>
The **following** of the **plow** has been approved for refreshing the **spirits** and **stimulating appetite**. However, doing this during the **plowing** for **wheat** or **rye** is not as good, because the **earth** has already spent her **sweet fragrance** <note>original: "Breath"</note> on the **vegetables** produced in **summer**. It is better, therefore, to do it when you sow **barley**. But because plowing is tied to **seasons**, it is best to take in the **air** of the **earth** when it is newly turned up by **digging** with the **spade**, or by **standing** by one who **digs**. **Noblewomen** <note>original: "Gentlewomen"</note> may do themselves much good by kneeling upon a **cushion** and **weeding**. These **things** you may practice in the best **seasons**, which is always the **early spring**, before the **earth** puts forth its **plants**; and in the **sweetest earth** you can choose. It should also be done when the **dew** is a little off the **ground**, lest the **vapor** be too **moist**. I knew a great **man** who lived a **long** life, who had a **clean clod** of **earth** brought to him every **morning** as he sat in his **bed**, and he would hold his **head** over it for a good long while. I **recommend** also, sometimes, while **digging** **new earth**, to pour in some **Malmsey** <note>a sweet, fortified wine</note> or **Greek wine**, so that the **vapor** of the **earth** and **wine** together may comfort the **spirits** even more—provided always that it is not mistaken for a **heathen sacrifice** or a **ritual offering** <note>original: "Libation"</note> to the **earth**.

<margin>929</margin>

<margin>941</margin>
There are beliefs <note>original: "Conceits"</note> that some **men** who have an **unpleasant** and **melancholic disposition** <note>original: "Ill, and Melancholy Nature"</note> tend to make the **company** they join **sad** and **ill-disposed**. Furthermore, some **men** are considered **lucky** to be around and **employed**, while others are **unlucky**. <margin>942</margin>
It has been observed that **old men** who have loved **young company** and have been **frequently associating** <note>original: "Conuersant"</note> with them have enjoyed **long lives**. Their **spirits** (it seems) were **refreshed** by such **company**. Such were the **ancient Sophists** and **rhetoricians** <note>teachers of philosophy and public speaking</note> who always had **young listeners** and **disciples**, such as **Gorgias**, **Protagoras**, **Isocrates**, etc., who lived until they were a hundred years **old**. Many of the **grammarians** and **schoolmasters**, such as **Orbilius** <note>a famous Roman teacher mentioned by Horace</note>, did the same.

<margin>943</margin>
**Audacity** and **confidence** produce such great **effects** in **public business** <note>original: "Ciuill Businesse"</note> that a **man** might reasonably wonder if—beyond simple **daring**, **earnestness**, **persistence**, and **insistence**—there might be some **secret binding** and **humbing** <note>original: "Stooping"</note> of other **men's spirits** toward such **persons**.

<margin>944</margin>

These are two: **love** and **envy**, which is called the **evil eye** <note>original: "Oculus Malus"</note>. As for **love**, some **Platonists** <note>followers of Plato’s philosophy</note> go so far as to claim that the **spirit** of the **lover** passes into the **spirits** of the **person loved**. This causes a desire to **return** into the **body** from which it was **emitted**, leading to 그 **desire** for **touch** and **union** found in **lovers**. It is also observed that the **looks** that inspire **love** are not **stares**, but **sudden glances** and **flashes** <note>original: "Dartings"</note> of the **eye**. As for **envy**, it emits a **malignant and poisonous spirit** that takes hold of **another's spirit**. It is most **forceful** when the **glance** of the **eye** is **sideways** <note>original: "Oblique"</note>. It has also been noted that it is most **dangerous** when an **envious eye** is cast upon **people** in moments of **glory**, **triumph**, and **joy**. The **reason** for this is that at such times, the **spirits** come out most into the **outer parts** of the body and so meet the **impact** <note>original: "Percussion"</note> of the **envious eye** more **directly** <note>original: "at Hand"</note>. Therefore, it has been noted that after great **triumphs**, **men** have felt **unwell** for several **days** following. We see the belief in **fascination** <note>the power to influence or harm through a look</note> is ancient for both **effects**: for **inspiring love** and for **sickness** caused by **envy**. **Fascination** is always channeled through the **eye**. Yet, if there is any such **infection** from **spirit** to **spirit**, there is no doubt that it works through **physical presence** and not by the **eye** alone, though it is most powerful through the **eye**.

And when one **man** is **embarrassed** <note>original: "out of Countenance"</note> in a **group**, others also **blush** on his behalf.

# Natural History:

Now we will speak of the **force of imagination** upon other **bodies**, and of the **means** to **exalt** and **strengthen** it. **Imagination**, in this context, I understand to be the **representation** of an **individual thought**. **Imagination** is of three **kinds**: the **first**, joined with **belief** of **that which is to come**; the **second**, joined with **memory** of **that which is past**; and the **third** is of **things present**, or as if they were **present**. For I include in this **imaginations** that are **feigned** <note>original: "Fained"</note> and created at **pleasure**, such as if one should **imagine** a certain **man** to be in the **vestments** of a **Pope**, or to have **wings**. I select, for this time, that which is accompanied by **faith** or **belief** in **that which is to come**. The **investigation** <note>original: "Inquisition"</note> of this **subject** by our method (which is by **induction** <note>the process of drawing general conclusions from specific observations</note>) is wonderfully difficult; for the **things** that are reported are full of **fables**, and **new experiments** can hardly be conducted except with **extreme caution**, for the **reason** which we will declare hereafter.

The **power of imagination** is of three **kinds**. The **first** is its power upon the **body** of the **imaginant** <term>the person who is imagining</term>, including also the **child** in the **mother's womb**. The **second** is the **power** of it upon **inanimate bodies** <note>original: "Dead Bodies"</note>, such as **plants, wood, stone, metal, etc.** The **third** is the **power** of it upon the **spirits** of **men** and **living creatures**; and with this last kind alone we will deal.

The **problem**, therefore, is whether a **man constantly** and **strongly believing** that such a **thing** shall happen (as that a certain **person** will **love him**, or that a certain **person** will **grant him his request**, or that a certain **person** shall **recover** from a **sickness**, or the like) helps at all toward the **effecting** of the **thing** itself. And here again, we must carefully distinguish; for it is not meant (as has been partly said before) that it should help by **making** a **man more brave** <note>original: "Stout"</note> or more **industrious** (in which kind a **constant belief** does much), but merely by a **secret operation**, or **binding**, or **changing** the **spirit** of **another**. And in this, it is difficult (as we began to say) to conduct any **new experiment**; for I cannot **command myself** to **believe** whatever I wish, and so no **trial** can be made. Indeed, it is even worse; for whatever a **man imagines** doubtingly or with **fear** must necessarily do harm, if **imagination** has any **power** at all.

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon’s discussion on the "force of imagination." He argues that imagination is more effective when directed through another person, as an individual's own doubts or fears often hinder the process.</meta>

For a **man** imagines what he fears more often than the opposite. The remedy, therefore, is for a **man** to work through **another person** in whom he can create **belief**, rather than working by **himself**, until he has found by **experience** that **imagination** does prevail. For then **experience** creates **belief** within **himself**, provided that the **belief** that such a **thing** shall happen is joined with a **belief** that his **imagination** can bring it about.

<margin>946</margin>
For example, I once told a **man** who was curious and vain enough in these **matters** <note>original: "Things"</note> that I saw a **kind** of **juggler** <term>juggler: a magician or performer of sleight-of-hand</term> who had a **deck** <note>original: "Paire"</note> of **cards** and would tell a **man** what **card** he was thinking of. This supposedly learned man told me that I was mistaken. For (said he) it was not the **knowledge** of the man’s thought (for **that is reserved for God alone**), but it was the **enforcing** of a **thought** upon him, and binding his **imagination** by a stronger one, so that he could think of no other **card**. 

And thereupon he asked me a **question** or two, which I thought he did craftily, already knowing what the **feats** of the **juggler** usually were. "**Sir**," (said he), "do you remember whether he named the card the man thought of **himself**, or if he told **another** to name it?" I answered (as was true) that he told **another** to name it. To which he said, "**So I thought.** For" (said he) "**the juggler himself could not have projected so strong an imagination; but by telling the other person the card (who believed that the juggler was a strange man and could do strange things), that other man caught a strong imagination.**" 

I listened to him, thinking that, despite his vanity, he spoke quite cleverly. Then he asked me another **question**: "Do you remember," he said, "**whether he told the man to think of the card first, and afterwards whispered in the other man's ear what he should say? Or did he whisper first in the ear of the man who was to name the card, telling him that the subject would think of a certain card, and only after that told the subject to think of a card?**" 

I told him the truth: "**That he first whispered in the ear of the man who was to name the card.**" Upon this, the learned **man** was greatly delighted and pleased with himself, saying, "**Look, you can see that my opinion is correct. For if the man had thought of it first, his thought would have been fixed; but because the other person imagined it first, they bound his thought.**" 

Although this explanation made some sense to me <note>original: "did somewhat sinke with mee"</note>, I acted more dismissive than I actually felt and said, "**It was a conspiracy between the juggler and the two servants.**" (In truth, I had no reason to think so, for they were both my **father's servants**, and the juggler had never performed in the house before). 

The **juggler** also had a **garter** held up and claimed to know that a certain **person** would point to a specific **place** on the **garter**—predicting it would be so many **inches** from the **longer end** and so many from the **shorter end**. And he always did it by **first telling the imaginer** <note>the person intended to influence the subject</note> and afterwards **telling the actor** <note>the subject being influenced</note> **to think**.
