# Naturall History:

Because it does effectively reveal the **Nature** of the **Question**, I return to what I said: that **Experiments** of **Imagination** must be practiced by **Others**, and not by a **Man’s Self**. For there are Three **Means** to fortify **Belief**: the First is **Experience**; the Second is **Reason**; and the Third is **Authority**. And of these, the one that is far more **Potent** is **Authority**; for **Belief** based upon **Reason** or **Experience** will **Stagger** <note>original: "Stagger" — here meaning to hesitate or waver in conviction</note>.

<margin>947</margin>
As for **Authority**, it is of two **Kinds**: **Belief** in an **Art**, and **Belief** in a **Man**. Regarding things of **Belief** in an **Art**, a **Man** may exercise them by **Himself**; but for **Belief** in a **Man**, it must be through **Another**. Therefore, if a **Man** believes in **Astrology** and finds a **Figure Prosperous** <term>Figure Prosperous: a favorable astrological chart or horoscope</term>, or believes in **Natural Magic**—that a **Ring** with such a **Stone**, or such a **Piece** of a **Living Creature** carried with him will do good—it may help his **Imagination**. But the **Belief** in a **Man** is far more **Active**. 

However, all **Authority** must be outside of a **Man's Self**, directed (as was said) either upon an **Art** or upon a **Man**. And where **Authority** is passed from one **Man** to another, the second person must be **Ignorant**, and not **Learned** or **Full of Thoughts**. Such are (for the most part) all **Witches** and **Superstitious Persons**, whose **Beliefs**, tied to their **Teachers** and **Traditions**, are not at all controlled either by **Reason** or **Experience**. For the same **Reason**, in **Magic**, they mostly use **Boys** and **Young People**, whose **Spirits** most easily take on **Belief** and **Imagination**.

Now, to fortify **Imagination**, there are three **Ways**: the **Authority** from which the **Belief** is derived; **Means** to **Quicken** and **Corroborate** <note>original: "Corroborate" — to strengthen or reinforce</note> the **Imagination**; and **Means** to **Repeat** and **Refresh** it.

<margin>948</margin>
Regarding **Authority**, we have already spoken. As for the Second—namely, the **Means** to **Quicken** and **Corroborate** the **Imagination**—we see what has been used in **Magic** (if there is anything in those **Practises** that is purely **Natural**): such as **Vestments**; **Characters** <term>Characters: symbolic marks, inscriptions, or magical sigils</term>; **Words**; **Seals**; some **Parts of Plants** or **Living Creatures**; **Stones**; **Choice of the Hour**, **Gestures**, and **Motions**; also **Incenses** and **Odors**; **Choice of Society**, which increases **Imagination**; and **Diets** and **Preparations** for some time beforehand. 

As for **Words**, there have always been used either **Barbarous words** of no **Sense**, lest they should disturb the **Imagination**, or **words** of **Similitude** <note>original: "Similitude" — words that use analogies or likenesses to the desired outcome</note> that may support and feed the **Imagination**. This was always the case in **Heathen Charms** as well as in **Charms** of later **Times**. **Scripture words** are also used, because the **Belief** that **Religious Texts** and **words** have **Power** may strengthen the **Imagination**. And for the same **Reason**, **Hebrew Words** (which among us is counted the **Holy Tongue**, and the **Words** considered more **Mystical**) are often used.

...and the like, which should melt bit by bit; or some other *things buried in muck* <note>original: "Mucke" — manure or compost used for its steady heat</note>, which should putrefy bit by bit, or the like. For as often as the *imaginant* <term>imaginant: the person performing the act of imagination</term> thinks of those *things*, so often does he represent the *effect* he desires to his *imagination*.

<margin>950</margin>
If there is any power in *imagination*, it is less credible that it should be such an *incorporeal* and *immaterial* *power* <note>original: "Vertue" — used here in the sense of a latent power or efficacy</note> as to work at great *distances*, or through all *mediums*, or upon all *bodies*. Instead, the *distance* must be appropriate, the *medium* not adverse, and the *body* suitable and proportionate. Therefore, if there is any operation upon *bodies* in their absence by nature, it is likely to be conveyed from *person* to *person*, just as *fame* <note>original: "Fame" — here meaning a rumor or report spreading through a crowd</note> is. For instance, if a *witch* should hurt someone far away through *imagination*, it cannot happen naturally except by working upon the *spirit* of someone who comes to the *witch*; and from that *person* upon the *imagination* of *another*; and so upon *another*, until it reaches one who has access to the *intended party*; and so by *him* to the *intended party himself*. And although people say that it is enough to take a *point* <note>original: "Point" — a lace or cord used to fasten clothing, often used in folk magic</note>, or a *piece* of a *garment*, or the *name* of the *party*, or the like, there is less credit to be given to those *things*, unless it is through the *working of evil spirits*.

The *experiments* that might certainly demonstrate the power of *imagination* upon other *bodies* are few or none. For the *experiments* of *witchcraft* are not clear proof, because they may be caused by a *tacit* <note>original: "Tacite" — silent or hidden</note> *operation of malignant spirits*. We shall therefore be forced in this *inquiry* to resort to *new experiments*, wherein we can only give *directions* for *trials*, rather than any *positive experiments*. And if anyone thinks that we should have waited until we had made *experiments* on some of them ourselves (*as we commonly do in other sections*), the truth is that these *effects* of *imagination* upon other *bodies* have so little credit with us that we shall try them at our leisure. But in the meantime, we will lead the way for others.

<margin>951</margin>
When you work through the *imagination* of *another*, it is necessary that he through whom you work has a *prior opinion* of you—that you can do *strange things*, or that you are a *man of art* <term>man of art: an expert or practitioner of a specialized skill, often referring to a physician, scientist, or even an occultist</term>, as they call it. For otherwise, a simple *affirmation* to *another* that this or that shall happen can only make a weak *impression* on his *imagination*.

<margin>952</margin>
Because you cannot fully discern the *strength* of *imagination* in one *man* more than another, it would be good to use the *imagination* of more than *one*, so that you may happen upon a *strong one*. This is like a *physician* telling *three* or *four* of his *patient's servants* that their *master* shall surely recover.

<margin>953</margin>
The *imagination* of *one* person whom you use (such is the variety of men's minds) cannot always be equally *constant* and *strong*. And if the...

<header>Natural History:</header>

If success does not follow speedily, the imagination will faint and lose *strength*. To remedy this, you must suggest to the person whose *imagination* you use several *stages* of *means* by which to *operate*; <margin>951</margin> such as prescribing to him that every three days, if he does not find the success apparent, he should use another *root*, or *part* of a *beast*, or *ring*, etc., <margin>952</margin> as being of more *force*; and if that fails, another; and if that, another, until seven times. <margin>953</margin> Also, you must prescribe a good *long time* for the *effect* you promise; for example, if you should tell a *servant* of a *sick man* that his *master* shall recover, but it will be fourteen days before he finds it apparently so, etc. All this is to entertain the *imagination* so that it wavers less.

<margin>954</margin>
It is certain that *potions*, or *things* taken into the *body*; *incenses* and *perfumes* taken through the *nostrils*; and *ointments* on some *parts*; do (naturally) work upon the *imagination* of *him* who takes them. And therefore it must necessarily greatly *cooperate* with the *imagination* of the person you use if you prescribe to him—before he uses the *receipt* <note>original: "Receit" — a recipe or medicinal prescription</note> for the *work* which he desires—that he takes such a *pill*, or a *spoonful* of *liquor*; or burns such an *incense*; or *anoints* his *temples*, or the *soles* of his *feet*, with such an *ointment* or *oil*. And you must choose, for the *composition* of such a *pill*, *perfume*, or *ointment*, such *ingredients* as make the *spirits* <term>spirits: the "animal spirits," thought to be a subtle fluid in the body that governed sensation and movement</term> a little more *gross* <note>original: "Groſſe" — dense or heavy</note> or *muddy*, whereby the *imagination* will fix better.

<margin>955</margin>
The *body passive* and to be worked upon (I do not mean the *imaginant*), is better worked upon (as has been partly touched upon) at some *times* than at others. For instance, if you should prescribe to a *servant* attending a *sick person* (whom you have persuaded that his *master* shall recover) to use such a *root* or such a *root* when his *master* is fast asleep. For *imagination* is likely to work better upon *sleeping men* than *men awake*, as we shall show when we handle the subject of *dreams*.

<margin>956</margin>
We find in the *Art of Memory* <note>The "Art of Memory" was a classical method of mental discipline using "loci" (places) and "images" to store information</note> that *visible images* work better than other *concepts*. As if you would remember the word *philosophy*, you shall more surely do it by *imagining* that such a *man* <margin>**best places**</margin> (for *men* are **best places**) is reading from *Aristotle's Physics* <note>original: "Ariſtotles Phyſickes" — Aristotle's influential work on natural philosophy</note>, than if you should *imagine* him saying, "I'll go study philosophy." And therefore, this observation should be translated to the *subject* we now speak of; for the more *lustrous* the *imagination* is, the better it fills and fixes. And therefore I conceive that you shall, in that *experiment* (of which we spoke before) of *binding of thoughts*, fail less if you tell *one* person that such a *person* shall name one of *twenty men*, rather than if it were *one of twenty cards*. The *experiment* of *binding of thoughts* <term>binding of thoughts: a supposed effect where one person's mind constrains or directs the thoughts of another</term> should be diversified and tried to the *full*; and you are to note whether it hits for the most part, though not always.

<margin>957</margin>
It is good to consider upon what *things* *imagination* has most *force*. And the *rule* (as I conceive it) is that it has most *force* upon *things* that have the *lightest* and *easiest motions*. And therefore, above all, it works upon the *spirits of men*; and in them, upon such *affections* <note>original: "Affections" — emotions or mental states</note> as move *lightest*, such as the *procuring of love* or the *binding of lust*, which is...

<meta>This page continues Francis Bacon’s investigation into the "force of imagination." He is exploring how the mental state of an individual might physically influence other people, plants, and even inanimate objects through subtle natural motions.</meta>

<header>Century X.</header>

ever with *Imagination*: upon *men* in a state of *fear*, or *men* in *irresolution*, and the like. Everything of this kind should be thoroughly investigated. *Trials* should likewise be made upon *plants*, and that diligently. For example, you might tell a *man* that a certain *tree* will die this year, and instruct him to go to it at specific times to see how it *thrives*. As for *inanimate things*, it is true that the *motions* of *shuffling cards* or *casting dice* are very *light motions*. There is a common *folly* among *gamesters* <note>original: "Gamesters" — gamblers</note> who imagine that some who stand by them bring them ill luck. Trials should also be made of holding a *ring* by a *thread* in a *glass*, telling the person holding it beforehand that it shall strike against the *side* of the *glass* a certain number of times and no more. Or try holding a *key* between two *men's fingers* without using a *charm*, and telling those holding it that at a specific *name*, it shall fall off their *fingers*. These two examples involve extremely *light motions*. And however little *opinion* I have of these things, yet I conceive this much to be true: that *strong imagination* has more force upon *living things* (or things that have been *living*) than upon things merely *inanimate*; it also has more force upon *light* and *subtle motions* than upon *vehement* or *heavy* motions.

<margin>958</margin>
It is a common *observation* that if the *body* of *someone murdered* is brought before the *murderer*, the *wounds* will bleed afresh. Some affirm that the *dead body*, upon the *presence* of the *murderer*, has opened its *eyes*; and that there have been similar *motions* when the *murdered party* was *strangled* or *drowned*, just as when they were *killed* by *wounds*. It may be that this involves a *miracle* by *God's* just judgment, who usually brings *murders* to light. But if it is *natural*, it must be attributed to *imagination*.

<margin>959</margin>
The *tying of the point* <note>original: "Tying of the Point" — a folk-magic practice of tying a knot in a lace or string during a wedding ceremony to magically cause impotence in the groom</note> on the day of *marriage* to make *men* impotent toward their *wives* (which, as we have previously mentioned, is very frequent in *Zante* and *Gascony*)—if it is *natural*, it must be attributed to the *imagination* of *him* who *ties the point*. I believe it has less connection to *witchcraft* because it is not only peculiar persons (such as *witches*) who can do it, but *anyone*.

<margin>

There are many *things* that work upon the *spirits* of *man* by *secret sympathy* and *antipathy*. The *virtues* of *precious stones*, when worn, have been anciently and generally accepted, and they are carefully assigned to produce various *effects*. This much is true: that *stones* contain fine *spirits*, as shown by their *splendor* <note>original: "Splendor" — their brilliance or way they reflect light</note>. Therefore, they may work by *consent* <note>original: "Consent" — a natural harmony or resonance</note> upon the *spirits* of *men* to comfort and cheer them. Those that are best for that *effect* are the *diamond*, the *emerald*, the *oriental hyacinth* <note>original: "Iacinth Orientall" — likely a blue or reddish-orange gemstone like a sapphire or zircon</note>, and the *gold-stone* (which is the *yellow topaz*). As for their specific magical *properties*, no credit is to be given to them. But it is manifest that *light*, above all things, excels in *comforting* the *spirits* of *men*; and it is very probable that *varied light* produces the same *effect* with even more *novelty*. <meta>This page concludes the previous discussion on the force of imagination and shifts into practical applications of "natural magic" or sensory comforts. Bacon explores how visual stimuli and wearable objects (bracelets and rings) can affect the "spirits"—the subtle fluids believed to govern health and mood in the body.</meta>

<page-num>250</page-num>
<header>Natural History:</header>

...or tinted **screens** made of glass colored green, blue, pink <note>original: "Carnation"</note>, crimson, purple, and so on; and to use them with **candles** at night. It is also good to have round glasses, not only of glass colored throughout, but with colors laid between crystals, with **handles** to hold in one's hand. **Prisms** are also comfortable things. There is a style of **Paris-work** <note>ornate decorative mirrors or glasswork from Paris</note> consisting of looking-glasses bordered with broad frames of small crystal and large counterfeit **precious stones** of all colors, which are most glorious and pleasant to behold, especially at night. **Pictures made of Indian feathers** <note>likely referring to intricate feather-work from the Americas or Southeast Asia</note> are likewise comfortable and pleasant to behold. Similarly, fair and clear **pools** greatly comfort the eyes and **spirits** <note>In Bacon’s time, "spirits" were thought to be subtle, air-like fluids in the body that controlled sensation and movement</note>, especially when the **sun** is not **glaring** but **overcast**, or when the moon shines.

<margin>961</margin>
There are various sorts of **bracelets** fit to **comfort the spirits**, and they serve three **intentions**: **cooling** <note>original: "Refrigerant"</note>, **strengthening** <note>original: "Corroborant"</note>, and **opening** <note>original: "Aperient"—meaning to clear blockages in the body's channels</note>. For **cooling**, I recommend them to be made of **pearl** or **coral**, as is commonly used. It has been noted that **coral**, if the **person** wearing it is unwell, will turn pale; I believe this is true because a **feverish heat** <note>original: "Distemper of Heat"</note> will otherwise cause **coral** to lose its color. I also recommend **beads** or little **plates of lapis lazuli**, and **beads of nitre** <note>saltpeter</note>, either alone or mixed with some **cordial** <note>heart-strengthening</note> preparation.

<margin>962</margin>
For **strengthening** and **comforting**, use substances that have an **astringent quality** <note>contracting or binding</note> without being **noticeably cold**. I recommend **amber beads**, which are very **astringent** yet **oily** <note>original: "Vnctuous"</note> rather than **cold**. They are thought to **fatten** <note>original: "Impinguate"</note> those who wear such **beads**. I also recommend **beads of hart's-horn** <note>deer antler</note> and **ivory**, which are of a similar nature; also **orange beads**, and **beads of aloeswood** <note>original: "Lignum Aloes"</note> that have been first soaked <note>original: "Macerated"</note> in **rose water** and then dried.

<margin>963</margin>
For **opening** the pores or channels, I recommend **beads** or **pieces** of the **roots of blessed thistle** <note>original: "Carduus Benedictus"</note>; also the **roots of the male peony**, **orris**, **sweet flag** <note>original: "Calamus Aromaticus"</note>, and **rue**.

<margin>964</margin>
The **cramp**, without doubt, comes from the **contraction of tendons** <note>original: "Sinnewes"</note>. This is obvious because it is caused by either **cold** or **dryness**, such as after **wasting diseases** <note>original: "Consumptions"</note> or **long fevers** <note>original: "Agues"</note>; for both **cold** and **dryness** cause things to **contract** and **shrivel** <note>original: "Corrugate"</note>. We see also that **rubbing** <note>original: "Chafing"</note> a little above the **place** in pain eases the **cramp**, which is achieved by the **widening** of the **contracted tendons** through **heat**. There are two things currently in use for preventing the **cramp**: one is **rings of sea-horse teeth** <note>original: "SeaHorse-Teeth"—likely walrus or hippopotamus tusks, which were often called sea-horse teeth at the time</note> worn upon the **fingers**; the other is **bands of green periwinkle** (the herb) tied about the **calf** of the **leg** or the **thigh**, where the **cramp** usually occurs. I find this quite strange because neither of these has any **relaxing power** <note>original: "Vertue"</note>, but rather the **contrary**. I judge, therefore, that they **work** upon the **spirits** within the **nerves** to make them struggle less, rather than acting upon the **physical substance** of the **nerves** themselves.

<margin>965</margin>
I would like **trials** to be made of two other **kinds of bracelets** for **comforting the heart** and **spirits**. One would be made of **viper lozenges** <note>original: "Trochisch of Vipers"—tablets made of dried viper flesh, then a common medicine</note> formed into little **beads**. Since these do great **good internally** (especially for **plague-related fevers** <note>original: "Pestilent Agues"</note>), it is likely they will be **effective externally**, where they can be applied in greater **quantity**. **Lozenges** should likewise be made...

<page-num>251</page-num>
<header>Century 10.</header>

...made of **snakes**; whose **dried flesh** is thought to have a very **opening** <note>original: "Opening"—referring to clearing blockages in the body's channels or pores</note> and **cordial** <note>original: "Cordiall"—invigorating or heart-strengthening</note> **virtue**. The other is made of **beads** crafted from the **scarlet powder** called **kermes** <note>a red dye derived from scale insects, used in medicine</note>, which is the principal **ingredient** in their **cordial confection** called **Alkermes**. These **beads** should be made with **ambergris** <note>a waxy substance from sperm whales used in perfumes and medicine</note> and some **pomander** <note>a ball of aromatic substances carried to ward off disease</note>.

<margin>966</margin>
It has been long accepted and confirmed by various **trials** that the **root** of the **male peony**, dried and tied to the **neck**, helps with **epilepsy** <note>original: "Falling-Sickneſſe"</note> and also the **incubus**, which we call the **nightmare** <note>original: "the Mare"</note>. The **cause** of both these **diseases** (especially **epilepsy** originating in the **stomach**) is the **thickness** <note>original: "Groſſeneſſe"</note> of the **vapors** that rise and enter into the **cells** of the **brain**. Therefore, the remedy works through **extreme** and **subtle thinning** <note>original: "Attenuation"</note>, a quality that this **herb** <note>original: "Simple"—a medicinal herb or a medicine made from a single plant</note> possesses. I judge similar qualities to be in **castoreum** <note>a secretion from beavers</note>, **musk**, **rue-seed**, **chasteberry seed** <note>original: "Agnus Caſtus Seed"</note>, and so on.

<margin>967</margin>
There is a **stone** called the **bloodstone** <note>likely heliotrope, a green stone with red spots</note> which, when worn, is thought to be good for those who **bleed from the nose**. This is (no doubt) achieved by the **constriction** <note>original: "Aſtriction"</note> and **cooling** of the **spirits**. **Question**: Is the **stone** taken out of a **toad's head** <note>a mythical jewel called a toadstone, believed to be found inside the head of an old toad</note> not of similar **virtue**? For the **toad** loves **shade** and **coolness**.

<margin>968</margin>
**Insight** <note>original: "Light"</note> may be gained from the **experiment** of the **horse-tooth ring** and the **garland** of **periwinkle**—specifically, how those things that soothe the **conflict** <note>original: "Strife"</note> of the **spirits** help cure diseases in a way that seems contrary to the intended **goal**. For in **curing** a **cramp**, the **goal** is to relax the **sinews**, but the best **help** is the **contraction** of the **spirits** so that they struggle less. Similarly, to ensure easy **childbirth** <note>original: "Trauailes of women"</note>, the **goal** is to bring the **child** down, but the best **help** is to prevent the **descent** from happening too **fast**; they say the **toadstone** also helps with this. So too in **deadly fevers** <note>original: "Pestilent Feuers"</note>, the **goal** is to expel the **infection** through **sweat** and **evaporation**, but the best **means** to do it is with **saltpeter** <note>original: "Nitre"</note>, **diascordium** <note>an herbal opiate preparation used to treat the plague and fevers</note>, and other **cool things** that momentarily stop the **expulsion** until **nature** can do it more calmly. For as someone nicely put it: "**In quenching the flame of a deadly fever, Nature is like people coming to put out a house fire; they are so frantic that they get in each other's way** <note>original: "one of them letteth another"—where 'let' means to hinder or obstruct</note>." Surely, it is an excellent **principle** <note>original: "Axiome"</note> with many **uses** that whatever calms <note>original: "appeareth"—likely a printer's error for "appeaseth" or "quiets"</note> the **conflict** of the **spirits** actually furthers their **action**.

<margin>969</margin>
Writers of **natural magic** recommend **wearing** the **shed skin** <note>original: "Spoile"</note> of a **snake** for **preserving health**. I suspect this is merely a **superstition** <note>original: "Conceit"</note> based on the idea that the **snake** renews her **youth** by **casting her skin**. They might as well use the **beak** of an **eagle** or a piece of a **deer's horn** <note>original: "Harts-Horne"</note>, because those also **renew**.

<margin>970</margin>
It has been accepted since **ancient times** (for **Pericles** the **Athenian** used it), and it is still in use today, to wear little **pouches** <note>original: "Bladders"</note> of **mercury** <note>original: "Quick-Siluer"</note> or **tablets** of **arsenic** as **preventatives** against the **plague**. This is done not because they provide any **comfort** to the **spirits**, as they believe, but because, being **poisons** themselves, they draw the **venom** to them and away from the **spirits**.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of "Natural Magic" and the medicinal properties of animal parts, moving from wearable roots to the sympathetic effects of consuming or wearing parts of wolves, apes, and hedgehogs. It also discusses how a mother's diet affects the development of her unborn child.</meta>

<page-num>252</page-num>
<header>Natural History:</header>

<margin>972</margin> It is said that the **intestines** <note>original: "Guts"</note> or **skin** of a **wolf** applied to the **belly** can cure **colic** <note>original: "Cholicke"</note>. It is true that the **wolf** is a **beast** of great **voracity** <note>original: "Edacity"</note> and **digestion**; and so it may be that his **parts** comfort the **bowels**.

<margin>973</margin> We see **scarecrows** <note>original: "Scare-Crowes"</note> are set up to keep **birds** from **corn** and **fruit**. It is reported by some that the **head** of a **wolf**, whole, dried, and hung up in a **dovecote** <note>original: "Dove-House"</note>, will scare away **vermin**, such as **weasels**, **polecats**, and the like. It may be that the **head** of a **dog** would do just as much; for those **vermin** among us know **dogs** better than **wolves**.

<margin>974</margin> The **brains** of some **creatures** (taken in **wine** when their **heads** are roasted) are said to strengthen the **memory**, such as the **brains** of **hares**, the **brains** of **hens**, the **brains** of **deer**, etc. And it seems this quality is common to the **brains** of those **creatures** that are **fearful**.

<margin>975</margin> The **ointment** that **witches** use is reported to be made of the **fat** of **children** dug out of their **graves**, and the **juices** of **wild celery** <note>original: "Smallage"</note>, **wolfsbane**, and **cinquefoil**, mixed with the **flour** <note>original: "Meale"</note> of **fine wheat**. But I suppose that the **sleep-inducing** <note>original: "Soporiferous"</note> **medicines** are most likely to produce the effect; these include **henbane**, **hemlock**, **mandrake**, **nightshade** <note>original: "Moone-Shade"</note>, **tobacco**, **opium**, **saffron**, **poplar leaves**, etc.

<margin>976</margin> It is reported by some that the **dispositions** <note>original: "Affections"</note> of **beasts**, when they are at their **strongest**, add some **power** <note>original: "Vertue"</note> to **inanimate things**. For example, the skin of a **sheep** devoured by a **wolf** is said to cause **itching**; or a **stone** bitten by a **dog** in **anger**, if thrown at him and later drunk in **powdered form**, provokes **anger** <note>original: "Choler"</note>.

<margin>977</margin> It has been observed that the **diet** of **pregnant women** <note>original: "Women with Childe"</note> has a great effect upon the **infant**. For instance, if the **mother** eats many **quinces** and **coriander seeds** (the **nature** of both being to suppress and hold back the **vapors** that rise to the **brain**), it will make the **child clever** <note>original: "Ingenious"</note>. On the contrary, if the **mother** eats many **onions**, **beans**, or such **gassy** <note>original: "Vapourous"</note> **foods**, or drinks **wine** or **strong drink** immoderately, or **fasts** often, or is given to much **ruminating** <note>original: "Musing"</note> (all of which send or draw **vapors** to the **head**), it risks the **child** becoming **insane** <note>original: "Lunaticke"</note> or having an **imperfect memory**. I make the same judgment regarding **tobacco** when taken often by the **mother**.

<margin>978</margin> The writers of **Natural Magic** report that the **heart** of an **ape**, worn near the **heart**, comforts the **heart** and increases **boldness** <note>original: "Audacity"</note>. It is true that the **ape** is a **merry** and **bold beast**. Likewise, the same **heart** of an **ape**, applied to the **neck** or **head**, helps the **wit** and is good for **epilepsy** <note>original: "Falling-Sicknesse"</note>. The **ape** is also a **clever** <note>original: "Witty"</note> **beast** and has a **dry brain**, which may be a **cause** for the **thinning** <note>original: "Attenuation"</note> of **vapors** in the **head**. Yet it is also said to cause **dreams**. It may be that the **heart** of a **man** would do even more, but it is too contrary to **people's minds** to use it—except in the case of the **relics** of **saints**.

<margin>979</margin> The **flesh** of a **hedgehog**, prepared and eaten, is said to be a great **drying agent** <note>original: "Drier"</note>. For **plants** as well that are full of **spines**...

<margin>981</margin>
**Mummy** <note>In the early modern period, "mummy" referred to a medicinal substance made from prepared or powdered human remains</note> has great force in **stanching** of **blood**; which, as it may be attributed to the **mixture** of **balms** <note>original: "Balmes"</note> that are sticky, so it may also partake of a **hidden property** <note>original: "Secret Propriety"</note>, in that the **blood** draws **man's flesh**. And it is proven that the **moss** which grows upon the **skull** of an unburied **dead man** will stanch **blood** powerfully. So do the **dregs** or **powder** of **blood**, separated from the **liquid** <note>original: "Water"</note> and **dried**.

<margin>982</margin>
It has been practiced to create white **swallows** by **anointing** the **eggs** with **oil**. This **effect** may be produced by the **blocking** of the **pores** of the **shell**, making the **fluid** <note>original: "Iuyce"</note> that produces the **feathers** afterward more **impoverished** <note>original: "Penurious"</note>. And it may be that **anointing** the **eggs** will be as **effective** as **anointing** the **body**; regarding which, **see** <note>original: "Vide"</note> **Experiment 93**.

It is reported that **egg white** or **blood**, mixed with **saltwater**, gathers the **saltiness** and makes the **water** sweeter. This may be by **adhesion**, as in the **6th Experiment of Clarification**. It may also be that **blood** and **egg white** (which are the **matter of a living creature**) have some **sympathy** with **salt**. For all **life** has a **sympathy** with **salt**. We see that salt, applied to a **cut finger**, heals it; so it seems **salt** draws **blood** as well as **blood** draws **salt**.

<margin>983</margin>
It has been anciently received that the **sea-hare** <note>a type of marine mollusk, or sea slug</note> has an **antipathy** toward the **lungs** (if it comes near the **body**) and erodes them. The **cause** is conceived to be a **quality** it has of **heating** the **breath** and **spirits**, just as **Spanish flies** <note>original: "Cantharides"</note> have upon the **watery parts** of the **body**, such as **urine** and **dropsical fluid** <note>original: "Hydropicall water"; fluid caused by swelling or edema</note>. And it is a good **rule** that whatever has an **operation** upon certain **kinds of matter**, that, in a **man's body**, works most upon those **parts** where that **kind of matter** abounds.

<margin>984</margin>
Generally, that which is **dead**, **corrupted**, or **excreted** <note>original: "Excerned"</note> has **antipathy** toward the same **thing** when it is **alive** and when it is **healthy** <note>original: "Sound"</note>; and with those **parts** which do **excrete** <note>original: "Excerne"</note>. For example, a **human carcass** is most **infectious** and **repulsive** to a **man**; the **carrion** of a **horse** to a **horse**, etc. **Pus** <note>original: "Purulent Matter"</note> from **wounds**, **ulcers**, **carbuncles**, **pox**, **scabs**, and **leprosy** is harmful to **healthy flesh**; and the **excrement** of every **species** is harmful to the **creature** that **excretes** them. But **excrements** are less **harmful** than **corruptions**.

<margin>985</margin>
It is a **common experience** that **dogs** recognize the **dog-killer** when, in times of **infection** <note>referring to outbreaks of the plague, when stray dogs were often culled by city officials</note>, some **lowly person** is sent out to kill **dogs**. Even though they have never seen him before, they will all come out, bark, and attack him.

<margin>

**Persons** of near **blood**; such as **parents**, **children**, **brothers**, **sisters**, **nurse-children**, **husbands**, **wives**, etc. There are many reports in **history** that upon the **death** of **persons** of such **nearness**, **men** have had an inward **feeling** of it. I myself remember that being in **Paris**, and my **father** dying in **London**, two or three days before my **father's** death, I had a **dream**, which I told to diverse **English gentlemen**: *That my father's house in the country was plastered all over with black mortar*. There is an **opinion** abroad (whether **idle** <note>meaning trivial or baseless</note> or not, I cannot say) that loving and kind **husbands** have a **sense** of their **wives' pregnancy** <note>original: "Breeding Childe"</note> by some **accident** <note>here meaning a physical symptom or occurrence</note> in their own **body**.

Next to those that are **near in blood**, there may be a similar **passage** and **instincts of nature** between great **friends** and **enemies**. And sometimes the **revealing** is to **another person**, and not to the **party himself**. I remember **Philippe de Commines** <note>original: "Philippus Comineus," a 15th-century French historian and diplomat</note> (a **grave writer**) reports that the **Archbishop of Vienne** (a **reverend prelate**) said one day after **Mass** to **King Louis XI** of **France**: "*Sir, your mortal enemy is dead*." This was at the time **Duke Charles of Burgundy** was **slain** at the **Battle of Grandson** <note>original: "Granson"; Charles the Bold was defeated at Grandson, though he actually died later at the Battle of Nancy</note> against the **Swiss** <note>original: "Switzers"</note>. Some trial should also be made whether **pact** or **agreement** does anything; for example, if two **friends** should agree that on a certain **day** in every week, while being in far **distant places**, they should **pray** for **one another**, or should put on a **ring** or **tablet** <note>a small ornament or locket</note> for one another's **sake**. If one of them should break their **vow** and **promise**, would the other have any **feeling** of it in their **absence**?

If there is any **force** in the **imaginations** and **affections** of **individual persons** <note>original: "Singular Persons"</note>, it is probable the **force** is much more in the **joint imaginations** and **affections** of **multitudes**. If a **victory** should be won or lost in **remote parts**, is there not some **sense** of it in the **people** whom it concerns, because of the great **joy** or **grief** that many **men** are possessed with at once? **Pius V** <note>original: "Pius Quintus"</note>, at the very time when that **memorable victory** was won by the **Christians** against the **Turks** at the **naval battle of Lepanto**, being then hearing **cases** in **consistory** <note>a formal meeting of the Pope and his cardinals</note>, broke off suddenly and said to those about him: "*It is now time we should give thanks to God for the great victory he has granted us against the Turks*." It is true that the **victory** had a **sympathy** with his **spirit**, for it was merely his **work** to conclude that **league** <note>The Holy League, an alliance of Catholic maritime states organized by the Pope to break Ottoman control of the eastern Mediterranean</note>. But what shall we say then to a **number** of **examples** among the **Greeks** and **Romans**, where the **people**, being in **theaters** at **plays**, had **news** of **victories** and **overthrows** some few days before any **messenger** could arrive?

It is true that what holds in these **things** is the general **root of superstition**: namely, that **men observe** when **things hit** and not when they **miss**, and commit to **memory** the one, and forget and pass over the other. But touching **divination** and the **misgiving of minds**, we shall

I shall speak more on this when we handle, in general, the *nature of minds, souls, and spirits.*

<margin>989</margin>
We have previously given some *rules of imagination* and how to *fortify* it. We have also set down a few *instances* and *directions* regarding the force of *imagination* upon *beasts, birds, etc.*, upon *plants*, and upon *inanimate bodies*. In these, you must always observe that your *trials* should be conducted upon *subtle* and *light motions*, and not the opposite. For you will sooner, by *imagination*, bind a *bird* from *singing* than from *eating* or *flying*. I leave it to every man to choose experiments which he himself thinks most *suitable* <note>original: "commodious"</note>, giving now but a few examples of each of the *three kinds*.

<margin>990</margin>
Use some *imaginant* <note>a person attempting to project their imagination onto a subject</note> (observing the rules formerly prescribed) to *bind* a *bird* from *singing*, and do the same to a *dog* from *barking*. Try also the *imagination* of someone—whom you shall provide with things to fortify their focus—in *cockfights*, to make one *cock* more *hardy* <note>bold or courageous</note> and the other more *cowardly*. It should also be tried in the *flying* of *hawks*, or in the *coursing* of a *deer* or *hare* with *greyhounds*, or in *horse races*, and similar *comparative motions*. For you may sooner, by *imagination*, quicken or slow a *motion* than start or stop it; just as it is easier to make a *dog* go slower than to make him stand still so that he cannot run.

<margin>991</margin>
In *plants* also, you may try the *force of imagination* upon the *lighter* sort of *motions*, such as the *sudden fading* or *lively growing up* of *herbs*, or upon their *bending* one way or another, or upon their *closing* and *opening*, and so on.

<margin>992</margin>
For *inanimate things*, you may try the *force of imagination* upon *stopping* the *fermentation* <note>original: "working"</note> of *beer* when the *yeast* <note>original: "barme"</note> is put in, or upon the *forming* of *butter* or *cheese* after the *churning* or the *rennet* has been added.

<margin>993</margin>
It is an *ancient tradition*, cited everywhere as an example of *secret properties* and *influences* <note>original: "influxes"</note>, that the **Electric Ray** <note>original: *Torpedo Marina*</note>, if it is touched with a long *stick*, numbs the *hand* of the person touching it. It is one degree of working at a *distance* to work through the *continuity* of a *suitable medium*. For instance, *sound* will be conveyed to the *ear* by striking a *bow-string* if the *horn* of the *bow* is held to the *ear*.

<margin>994</margin>
The writers of *Natural Magic* <note>a branch of philosophy seeking to understand the hidden laws of nature rather than the supernatural</note> attribute much to the *powers* <note>original: "vertues"</note> that come from the *parts* of *living creatures*, provided they are taken from them while the *creatures* remain alive. The idea is as if the *creature*, still living, infused some *immaterial power* and *vigor* into the *severed part*. This much may be true: any *part* taken from a *living creature* that has been newly *slain* may be of greater force than if it were taken from a similar *creature* that died of *natural causes*, because it is fuller of *spirit* <note>referring to "vital spirits," the subtle fluids then believed to animate the body</note>.

<margin>995</margin>
*Trials* should be made of similar *parts* of *individuals* in *plants* and *living creatures*. For example, cut off a *branch* <note>original: "stocke"</note> of a *tree* and lay the piece you cut off to *rot* <note>original: "putrifie"</note>, to see whether it will *decay* the *rest* of the *tree*. Or, if you should cut off part of the *tail* or *leg* of a *dog*...

<margin>996</margin>
It is commonly accepted that it helps to *sustain love* if one wears a *ring* or a *bracelet* made from the *hair* of the *beloved person*. But that may be due to the *stimulation* of the *imagination*; perhaps a *glove* or some other similar *token* <note>original: "favour"</note> might do just as well.

<margin>997</margin>
The *sympathy* between *individuals* <note>the mysterious connection between things that were once joined or in contact</note> who have been *whole* or have *touched* is the most *incredible* of all. Yet, according to our faithful way of *examining nature*, we will make some small mention of it. The *removal of warts* by *rubbing* them with something that is afterwards left to *waste away* and *rot* <note>original: "consume"</note> is a *common experiment*. I believe it all the more because of my own *experience*. Since childhood, I had a wart on one of my fingers. Later, when I was about sixteen years old and in *Paris*, a great number of *warts* (at least a hundred) grew on both my *hands* within a *month's time*. The *wife* of the English Ambassador—who was a woman far from *superstitious*—told me one day that she would help me get rid of my *warts*. She then took a *piece of lard* with the *skin* still on and rubbed the *warts* all over with the *fat side*, including that *wart* I had had since childhood. Then she nailed the *piece of lard*, with the *fat side* facing the *sun*, upon a *post* of her *chamber window* which faced the *south*. The *result* <note>original: "success"</note> was that within five weeks, all the *warts* went completely away—even that wart I had endured for so long alongside the others <note>original: "for company"</note>. I did not marvel much at the others, because they appeared in a *short time* and might go away in a *short time* as well. But the *disappearance* of the one that had stayed so long still sticks with me. They say the same is done by *rubbing warts* with a *green elder stick* and then *burying* the *stick* to *rot* in *manure* <note>original: "muck"</note>. This should be tested with *corns*, *wens* <note>benign cysts or tumors</note>, and other such *growths* <note>original: "excrescences"</note>. I would also have it tested with some *parts* of *living creatures* that are nearest to the *nature of growths*, such as the *combs* or *spurs* of *roosters* <note>original: "cocks"</note>, the *horns* of *beasts*, etc. I would have it tried both ways: first, by *rubbing* those *parts* with *lard* or *elder* as before; and second, by *cutting off* <note>original: "putting off"</note> a *piece* of those *parts* and leaving it to *rot*, to see whether it will *produce* any *effect* toward the *wasting away* of the *part* that was once *joined* with it.

<margin>998</margin>
It is constantly *accepted* and *affirmed* <note>original: "received and avouched"</note> that *anointing* the *weapon* that caused a *wound* will heal the *wound* itself. In this *experiment*, based on the *reports* of *trustworthy men* (though I myself am not yet fully inclined to believe it), you should note the following *points*. First, the *ointment* used for this is made of *various ingredients*, of which the *strangest* and *hardest* to find are the *moss* found upon the *skull* of a dead *man* who was left *unburied*, and the *fat* of a *boar* and a *bear* killed during the *act of mating* <note>original: "generation"</note>. I could easily suspect these last two were prescribed as a *loophole* <note>original: "starting hole"</note>; so that if the *experiment* did not work, it could be claimed that the *beasts* were not killed at the proper *time*;

# Century 10.

For as for the *moss*, it is certain there is a great quantity of it in *Ireland* found upon slain bodies laid in heaps, unburied <note>The author refers to *Usnea*, a type of lichen that grows on human skulls, which was a prized ingredient in "sympathetic" medicine</note>. The other *ingredients* are *bloodstone* in powder and some other *substances* which seem to have a *power* to *stanch bleeding*, just as the *moss* does. And the description of the entire *ointment* can be found in the *Chemical Dispensary* of *Crollius* <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609) was a German alchemist and physician who promoted the use of "signatures" and chemical medicines</note>. Secondly, the same *kind* of *ointment*, if applied to the *injury* itself, does not work; it only works when applied to the *weapon*. Thirdly (which I find promising), they do not require the *preparing* of the *ointment* under any specific *astrological constellation*. This is commonly the excuse used for *magical medicines* when they fail—that they were not made under a favorable *alignment of the heavens*. Fourthly, it may be applied to the *weapon* even if the *injured party* is a great *distance* away. Fifthly, it seems the *imagination* of the person to be cured is not necessary for it to work; for it may be done without the *wounded person's* knowledge. This much has been tested: for the sake of experiment, the *ointment* has been wiped off the *weapon* without the *injured person* knowing, and immediately the *injured person* felt an intense *outbreak of pain* <note>original: "Rage of Paine"</note> until the *weapon* was anointed again. Sixthly, it is claimed that if you cannot get the *weapon*, you may put an *instrument* of *iron* or *wood* resembling the *weapon* into the *wound* so that it bleeds; anointing that *instrument* will then serve the same purpose. I suspect this might be a *trick* to keep this strange *method* of *cure* in demand and use, because many times you cannot retrieve the actual *weapon*. Seventhly, the *wound* must first be washed clean with white *wine* or the *person's* own *urine* <note>original: "Water"</note>; it is then bound up tightly in *fine linen*, and the *dressing* is not changed until it is healed. Eighthly, the *sword* itself must be *wrapped* up *closely* wherever the *ointment* is applied so that it is not exposed to the *air* <note>original: "wind"</note>. Ninthly, if you wipe the *ointment* off the *sword* and save it, it will *serve* again, and its *power* will *increase* rather than *diminish*. Tenthly, it will *cure* in a much *shorter time* than *ointments* for *wounds* commonly do. Lastly, it will *cure* a *beast* as well as a *man*, which I like best of all because it makes the *matter* subject to an *easy trial* <note>The author values animal testing as it removes the "placebo effect" of human imagination</note>.

# To the Reader.

This *fable* my *Lord* <note>Referring to Francis Bacon, Lord Verulam.</note> devised with the intention that he might present in it a *model* or *description* of a *college* established for the *interpreting* of *nature* and the production of *great* and *marvelous works* for the *benefit* of *mankind*. This institution is described under the name of *Salomon’s House* <note>original: "Salomons House"</note>, or the *College* of the *Six Days' Works* <note>A reference to the biblical creation; the college aims to study everything created by God in the first six days.</note>. His *Lordship* proceeded far enough to finish that part of the work. Certainly, the model is more *vast* and ambitious than can possibly be imitated in every detail; nevertheless, most things described within it are within *human power* to achieve. 

His *Lordship* also intended, within this present *fable*, to have composed a *framework* of *laws*, or a description of the best *state* or *model* for a *commonwealth*. But foreseeing that it would be a long *work*, his desire to collect *natural history* <note>original: "Naturall Historie"; Bacon's project to document all natural phenomena as the foundation for his scientific method.</note> diverted him, as he preferred that project by far.

We took supplies <note>original: "Victuals"; food and provisions necessary for a journey.</note> with us for twelve months and had favorable winds from the east, though they were soft and weak, for five months' time and more. 

But then the wind shifted and stayed in the west for many days, so that we could make little or no progress, and we sometimes intended to turn back. But then again, there arose strong and great winds from the south, with a point toward the east, which carried us up (despite all we could do) toward the north. By this time our food supplies failed us, even though we had rationed them carefully. 

Finding ourselves in the midst of the greatest wilderness of waters in the world without food, we gave ourselves up for lost and prepared for death. Yet we lifted up our hearts and voices to God above, who shows his wonders in the deep. We beseeched Him in His mercy that, as in the beginning He uncovered the *face of the deep* and brought forth *dry land*, He would now reveal land to us so that we might not perish.

### New Atlantis

...appearance of land all that night. In the dawning of the next day, we could plainly see that it was land, flat to our sight and full of woods <term>boscage</term> <note>original: "Boscage"; a cluster of trees or thicket.</note>, which made it look even darker. After an hour and a half of sailing, we entered into a good harbor <note>original: "Hauen"</note>, which was the port of a beautiful city. It was not very large, but it was well built and provided a pleasant view from the sea. 

Since every minute felt like an hour until we were on land, we came close to the shore and prepared to land. Immediately, however, we saw several people with batons <note>original: "Bastons"; clubs or staffs used as a sign of authority.</note> in their hands who seemed to be forbidding us from landing. Yet they did this without any shouting or ferocity, only warning us away with the signs they made. 

Feeling quite discouraged by this, we consulted among ourselves about what we should do. During this time, a small boat with about eight people in it came out to us. One of them held a staff of office <term>tipstaff</term> <note>original: "Tipstaffe"; a staff with a metal tip, used by an officer to show authority.</note> made of a yellow cane, tipped at both ends with blue. He came aboard our ship without showing any distrust at all. When he saw one of our number step forward ahead of the rest, he pulled out a small scroll of parchment. It was somewhat yellower than our parchment and shiny like the pages of a notebook, but otherwise soft and flexible. He delivered it to our leader. 

On this scroll, these words were written in Ancient Hebrew, Ancient Greek, good scholarly Latin <note>original: "Latine of the Schoole"; the formal, academic Latin used in universities.</note>, and Spanish: 

*"Do not land, none of you, and prepare to be gone from this coast within sixteen days, unless you are given more time. In the meantime, if you need fresh water, food <note>original: "Victuall"</note>, or help for your sick, or if your ship needs repair, write down your needs, and you shall receive what mercy requires."* 

This scroll was signed with a stamp depicting cherubs' wings—not spread out, but hanging downward—and next to them, a cross. Once this was delivered, the officer returned to his boat, leaving only a servant with us to receive our answer. 

We consulted among ourselves and were quite perplexed. Being denied landing and being told to leave so quickly troubled us greatly. On the other hand, finding that the people were multilingual and so full of kindness <note>original: "Humanity"</note> comforted us significantly. And a...

Above all, the sign of the **Cross** on that instrument was a great cause of rejoicing for us, and was, as it were, a certain omen <note>original: "Presage"</note> of good fortune. Our answer was given in the Spanish tongue: that as for our ship, it was well, for we had encountered calms and contrary winds rather than any tempests. That king also desired to combine humanity and policy <term>policy: political wisdom or statecraft</term>. He thought it was against humanity to detain foreigners here against their will, yet against policy for them to return and reveal their knowledge of this state. The haunting of those dissolute places, or visiting *courtesans* <note>prostitutes</note>, is no more punished in married men than in bachelors. And the depraved custom of constant change, and the delight in *meretricious embraces* <note>prostitution; original: "Meretricious Embracements"</note> (where sin is turned into an art), makes *Marriage* a dull thing and a kind of imposition or tax. 

They hear you defend these things as being done to avoid greater evils, such as *adultery* <note>original: "Adououtries"</note>, the deflowering of virgins, unnatural lust, and the like. But they say this is a preposterous wisdom, and they call it *Lot’s offer* <note>In Genesis 19:8, Lot offered his daughters to a mob to protect his guests</note>, who, to save his guests from abuse, offered his own daughters. 

Furthermore, they say that little is gained by this, for the same vices and appetites still remain and abound. *Unlawful lust* is like a furnace: if you stop the flames altogether, it will be quenched, but if you give it any vent, it will rage. As for *homosexuality* <note>original: "Masculine Loue"</note>, they have no trace of it; and yet there are no friendships in the world as faithful and inviolable as theirs. And to speak generally (as I said before), I have not read of any such *chastity* in any people as is found in them. Their common saying is: "Whoever is unchaste cannot reverence himself." And they say...

They have ordained that none should intermarry or contract a marriage until a month has passed from their first meeting <note>original: "Inter-view"</note>. Marriage without the consent of parents they do not make void <note>legally cancel</note>, but they penalize the inheritance <note>original: "mulct it in the Inheritors"</note>. For the children of such marriages are not permitted to inherit more than a third of their parents' inheritance. 

I have read in a book by one of your men about a fictional commonwealth <note>a reference to Thomas More’s *Utopia* (1516)</note> where the married couple are permitted, before they contract, to see one another naked. This they dislike; for they think it a scorn to give a refusal after such intimate knowledge. But because of many hidden defects in men's and women's bodies, they have a more civil way: for near every town, they have a couple of pools (which they call *Adam* and *Eve's* pools), where it is permitted for one of the friends of the man, and another of the friends of the woman, to see them separately bathe naked."

And as we were thus in conversation, there came someone who seemed to be a messenger, wearing a rich cloak <term>original: "Huke"; a hooded cloak or mantle</term>, who spoke with the *Jew*. At this, he turned to me and said, "You will pardon me, for I am commanded away in haste." 

The next morning he came to me again, looking joyful, and said, "Word has come to the Governor of the city that one of the Fathers of Solomon's House will be here a week from today <note>original: "this day Seuen-night"</note>. We have seen none of them these twelve years. His coming is in great state <note>with formal ceremony</note>, but the cause of his coming is secret. I will provide you and your fellows with a good standing <note>a place to watch the procession</note>..."

Behind his chariot went all the officers and principals of the city guilds. The street was wonderfully well-maintained, so that no army ever had its men stand in better battle formation than the people stood. When the spectacle was over, the Jew <note>Referring to Joabin, the narrator's Jewish guide</note> said to me, "*I shall not be able to attend to you as I would like, because of certain duties the city has laid upon me for the entertainment of this great person.*" 

Three days later, the Jew came to me again and said, "*You are fortunate men; for the Father of* Salomon’s House *has taken notice of your being here, and commanded me to tell you that he will admit all your company to his presence and have a private meeting with one of you, whom you shall choose. We arrived at our appointed day and hour, and I was chosen by my fellows for the private audience. We found him in a beautiful room, richly hung with tapestries and carpeted underfoot, without any steps <note>original: "degrees"</note> leading up to his seat of honor <note>original: "the State"; referring to the throne and its canopy</note>. He was alone, except that he had two pages of honor, one on either side, finely dressed in white. His undergarments were like those we saw him wear in the chariot, but instead of his gown, he wore a mantle with a cape made of the same fine black cloth, fastened about him. When we entered, as we had been instructed, we bowed low at our first entrance. When we came near his chair, he stood up, holding out his bare hand in a posture of blessing, and every one of us stooped down and kissed the hem of his tippet <note>a scarf-like garment worn over the shoulders</note>. That being done, the rest of my companions departed, and I remained.

and called him away from us. So that was all that occurred in that conference.

The next day, the same Governor came to us again, immediately after dinner, and excused himself, saying that the day before he was called away from us somewhat abruptly; but now he would make amends and spend time with us, if we found his company and conversation agreeable. We answered that we found it so agreeable and pleasing that we forgot both past dangers and future fears during the time we heard him speak, and that we thought an hour spent with him was worth years of our former lives. He bowed himself a little to us, and after we were seated again, he said, "Well, the questions are on your part." 

One of our number said after a little pause that there was a matter we were no less desirous to know than fearful to ask, lest we might presume too far. But encouraged by his rare kindness <note>original: "humanity"</note> toward us—we who could scarcely think of ourselves as strangers, being his devoted and professed servants—we would take the boldness <note>original: "hardiness"</note> to propose it. Humbly beseeching him, if he thought it unfit to be answered, that he would pardon the request even if he rejected it. 

We said we well observed those words of his, which he spoke earlier: that this happy island where we now stood was known to few, and yet knew most of the nations of the world. We found this to be true, considering they had the languages of Europe and knew much of our state and business; and yet we in Europe (notwithstanding all the remote discoveries and voyages <note>original: "navigations"</note> of this last age) never heard the least inkling or glimpse of this island. This we found wonderfully strange, because all nations have mutual knowledge <note>original: "enterknowledge"</note> of one another, either by travel into foreign parts or by strangers who come to them. And though the traveler into a foreign country commonly knows more by sight than he who stays at home can know by the report of the traveler, yet both ways suffice to create a mutual knowledge, to some degree, on both sides. 

But regarding this island, we never heard tell of any ship of theirs that had been seen to arrive upon any shore of Europe—no, nor of either the East or West Indies—nor yet of any ship of any other part of the world that had returned from here.
